title: Football stars both flag and tackle: Vote for the Journal Star athlete of the week for Aug. 26-31
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Athletes from Richwoods, Pekin, Dunlap and more are among the nominees for the first Journal Star athlete of the week for 2024-25.
content:
After plenty of solid fall sports performers over the last week, here are the Journal Star high school athlete of the week nominees for Aug. 26-31.
Head to pjstar.com/sports to vote. The poll closes at noon Friday. Information about the nominees is below.
If you have a nominee for the honor, email us at sports@pjstar.com or tag us on Twitter @pjstarsports.
Aidin Hindert, East Peoria football
Hindert scored two touchdowns and came up with a key defensive play as East Peoria beat Springfield Southeast, 28-26. The 5-foot-10, 170-pound receiver and safety caught a pair of touchdown passes from quarterback Dalton Oakman. Hindert's fourth-down interception stopped any attempt at a Southeast comeback.
Bo Windish, Elmwood/Brimfield football
Windish accounted for 324 all-purpose yards as the Trojans beat Knoxville, 41-28. The senior running back score touchdowns, while running for 184 yards on 19 carries. He added three catches for 54 yards and a score. Plus, Windish combined for 86 yards on kickoff and return yards.
Danayshia Webster, Richwoods girls flag football
Webster helped make Peoria-area history last week. In Thursday's season-opener against Danville, Webster scored the first-ever girls flag football touchdown. Webster took an interception back for a touchdown, but the Knights lost 12-6.
Mia Lamberti, Limestone volleyball
The sophomore turned in a great Saturday as the Rockets went 4-1 at the Macomb Tournament. Lamberti posted two double-doubles: 12 kills and 14 assists against Athens JV, and 10 kills and 11 assists versus Pleasant Plains. She also added nine kills and 13 assists against Orion and 13 kills and eight assists in a loss to the hosts. Her second match of the day came with nine kills and 14 assists against West Prairie.
Elle Blunier, Eureka volleyball
Blunier helped the Hornets start the season with two victories. The setter went for 15 assists to beat East Peoria in straight sets on Thursday. She opened her senior campaign by going for 17 assists and three aces in a two-set win over Roanoke-Benson last Tuesday.
Eric Pincock, Illini Bluffs boys cross country
The junior won the Farmington XC Invitational individual title last Wednesday. The Tigers also won the team crown, scoring 20 points to runner-up Princeville (50 points). Pincock covered the 3-mile course in 16:41.90, taking first. IB saw its first four runners — Fischer Dickinson (16:46.3, second), Peter Stoltz (17:17.4, third) and Levi Thomas (18:01.3, fourth) — sweep the first four places.
Emily King, Knoxville girls cross country
King won the girls race at the Farmington XC Invitational this past Wednesday. The junior ran the 3-mile route in 20:28.9 at Farmington High School. She edged out teammate and runner-up finisher Alyssa Higgins (20:29) by 1.9 seconds.
Nolan Eccles, Dunlap boys golf
The sophomore shared medalist honors in Wednesday's Mid-Illini Conference triangular meet won by the Eagles. Eccles shot a 2-under 33 at Metamora Fields, tying with Owen Gruden of Pekin. Dunlap (146) outdistanced itself from runner-up Pekin (151) and the third-place host Redbirds (155).
Maris McKee, Macomb girls golf
McKee turned in a career-low round in Wednesday's four-team meet at Gold Hills Country Club in Colchester. The senior finished tied for sixth, shooting an 11-over 46 on the par-35 front 9. The Bombers (212) took third behind second-place finisher Quincy (195) and winner Quincy Notre Dame (160).
Kayden Hudson, Peoria Notre Dame boys soccer
The two-time reigning Journal Star boys soccer player of the year collected eight goals in the first three matches of 2024. He scored four goals in the Irish's season-opening victory over Quincy Notre Dame, 7-1 last Wednesday. Hudson then added a combined four goals in beating Chatham Glenwood, 4-0 on Thursday as well as beating Morton, 6-0 in Saturday's nonconference match.
Sophia Thomas, Olympia girls swimming and diving
Thomas won one event and placed second in three others during Monday's dual meet with Mahomet-Seymour. The senior teamed with Lola Finfrock, Nora Collins and Abbie Hoeft in the 200-yard medley relay to claim a 2:06.00 victory, winning by a half of a second. Thomas was then the runner-up finisher in the 100-yard freestyle (1:02.90) and 100-yard backstroke (1:13.30). She also teamed with those same medley relay members to take a runner-up finish in the 200-yard freestyle relay (1:56.60).
Annabelle Hiel, Washington girls tennis
The senior won a pair of matches in Thursday's Mid-Illini Conference victory over Pekin. Hiel won her No. 1 singles match, then joined doubles partner Anica Roozenboom for a No. 1 doubles win. Washington swept all six single matches and the three doubles matches for a 9-0 win.

title: 'This is it': Pekin football's father-son duo in final season together as head coach, player
author: Dave Eminian
description: Pekin football head coach Doug Nutter and his son, senior linebacker Hudson Nutter, have their final prep season together underway.
content:
PEKIN — The head coach has been at the helm for 16 seasons, his senior linebacker on the sideline with him for more than a decade.
Doug Nutter and his son, Hudson, play out the finale to their prep football journey together this season as the Pekin High School father-son duo goes through the 2024 campaign.
"This is it, our last year together," said Doug, the longtime Dragons head coach. "Hudson moves on after this season. It's going to be a sad day for us when it's all over.
"But we'll have so many memories to look back on."
One of those was how Hudson, a 5-foot-10, 180-pound outside linebacker, helped his father and teammates to a 28-14 win Friday over Rolling Meadows on opening night at Memorial Stadium.
How it all started
Hudson has been around the Pekin Dragons since he was 6 years old, serving as a ball boy at the games for his father's team.
"I wanted to be like the players," Hudson said. "I had so much fun doing that, and they were awesome to be around. I really looked up to them and that whole time was just a great experience for me. I fell in love with Dragons football before I ever played it.
"Walking out on the field now as a player on game night, it's a special feeling every time. I'm going to really miss it."
He might even miss film sessions at home and those rides that are different for any coach's kid after the team loses.
"My dad doesn't treat me any differently than any players on the team," Hudson said. "He expects the same from me that he asks from everyone else. I have to work hard and get the job done."
Nutter said he wants to continue playing after high school, and he has an offer from Loras College (Iowa). He's also visited Monmouth College and Aurora University programs.
His NFL dream? "To tackle Christian McCaffrey," he said, laughing. "If I did that, I'd have some great bragging rights."
From JFL to IHSA Friday night lights
Doug is 78-66 and in his 16th season at Pekin's helm, with eight trips to the playoffs included. His Dragons went 11-1 in the 2022-23 season, a school record for most wins in a single-season in program history.
He's helped guide and build a lot of good football players at Pekin, and one at home.
All the stories in one place: Peoria's ultimate guide to 2024 high school football
"Sometimes my wife reminds me we don't always need to talk about football at home," Doug said, laughing. "But it's been great seeing Hudson play at the high school level. It's easier for me to watch him at this level because he's with me.
"When he was young and playing flag football and later JFL, I didn't get to see him play a lot because I was coaching. He's always been advanced as a player, played up against older kids, and that's helped him compete. And he was our ball boy, so he's been part of this high school program ever since. He is a great leader and captain, and I can't ask him for anything else."
Getting the last word
Hudson knows and respects the Pekin football tradition and its history. And he knows his family football history as well, which led to a big play and a teasing shot last season. His father played at Limestone and now leads Pekin as its coach.
"Hudson got a pick-6 at Limestone last year, where I played," Doug said, grinning. "He ran down the sideline right past me.
"Afterward he came up to me and said, 'I did something at Limestone you never did — score a touchdown.'
"Loved it."

title: Rising costs lead to end of complimentary bread at longtime Peoria restaurant
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: Customers will still receive a third of the restaurant's bread alongside some menu items.
content:
For regular customers at Avanti's, receiving complimentary bread may seem like a typical part of the dining experience at the longtime Peoria establishment. It appears the practice, however, has come to an end.
Signs posted at the restaurant state: 'Due to the increased cost of food and labor wages we no longer can offer complimentary bread in the dining room.'
Instead, the restaurant announced customers will receive a third of the regular portion with a pat of butter when they order:
Kids meal with pasta
Pasta meals
Entrees
Entrée salads
Customers can also order bread, according to the sign.
In a Peoria, IL Community Facebook post, commentors had differing opinions on the change. Some questioned why the restaurant would not raise menu prices to accommodate rising costs, while others expressed support for the business.
The Journal Star reached out to Avanti's corporate phone for comment, but calls have not yet been returned.
Avanti's operates two locations in Peoria, plus restaurants in East Peoria and Pekin.

title: What are ‘forever chemicals'? What to know about PFAS, private wells and your tap water
author: Houston Harwood
description: Wondering what PFAS are and what "forever chemical" pollution means for private wells? Here's what to know about testing, filtration and regulation.
content:
More than 40 million Americans get their drinking water not from the public supply but from private sources, and nearly all of them rely on groundwater that could contain a hidden threat: a class of harmful pollutants often referred to as 'forever chemicals' because of their indestructible nature.
You won't taste, smell or notice any change to the color of your water if per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, are present. To date, there are no nationwide requirements to test private well water for PFAS, which comprise a class of thousands of compounds that have seen widespread use in industrial processes and consumer products, such as Teflon pans, since the 1950s.
Even in minuscule quantities − a few parts per trillion − long-term exposure to PFAS can increase cholesterol levels, damage the immune system, cause cancers and disrupt thyroid function, among other ailments, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
As the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency implements new, nation-spanning regulatory action on PFAS, the USA Today Network's Midwest community papers are exploring the impact these changes and years of pollution have had on Midwestern states, cities and towns.
For this article, the USA Today Network took a look at what private well users need to know about PFAS pollution, testing and water treatment.
While the federal government works to rein in PFAS pollution across the nation's public drinking water supply with first-of-their-kind standards and billions in funding, experts have also warned private well owners to reduce their risk of exposure to the toxins.
And that risk of exposure for private well users is about the same, statistically speaking, as their public supply counterparts, according to a 2023 study published by the U.S. Geological Survey.
One in five tap water samples collected from private wells by USGS researchers between 2016 and 2021, the most recent collections cited in the USGS Tap Water Survey, tested positive for at least one PFAS compound – including in Midwestern states such as Ohio, Michigan, Illinois and Iowa.
Overall, the study found similar rates of PFAS contamination in tap water samples traced to both public and private supplies. However, well users don't benefit from the mandated PFAS testing that many large public water systems currently employ.
Sources of PFAS pollution vary, experts say, and can be difficult to track and trace.
'With drinking water, going back to that kind of historical legacy of use, these types of chemicals were and still are to some extent widely used in firefighting foams,' said Jonathan Meiman of the Wisconsin Division of Public Health. 'And when those foams are applied outside, they can end up seeping into groundwater and affecting wells.'
What to know about PFAS regulations and private wells
In June, the EPA announced for the first time that it would limit contamination from six of the most toxic PFAS compounds in public drinking water by requiring water utilities to test for their presence and then take action to remove the toxins if contamination is detected above extremely low levels.
The EPA standard for PFAS in drinking water is now 4 parts per trillion, down from 70 ppt. The concentrations are so small that chemists testing water for PFAS often have to remove their makeup because beauty products can contain enough PFAS to throw off a test's accuracy.
'Exposure to PFAS has been linked to deadly cancers, impacts to the liver and heart, and immune and developmental damage to infants and children,' the EPA wrote in an April announcement detailing new policies. 'This final rule will reduce PFAS exposure for approximately 100 million people, prevent thousands of deaths, and reduce tens of thousands of serious illnesses.'
But the standards, which come under the purview of the Safe Drinking Water Act, do not apply to private wells. It's a problem the agency hopes to address through grants and collaboration with states and local governments.
For now, testing and treating well water for PFAS is largely up to individual well owners.
What to know about testing for 'forever chemicals'
Regulations governing water quality testing in private wells vary from state to state. The Indiana State Department of Health recommends bacteria and nitrate testing every five years and urges well owners to test for fluoride, arsenic, lead and copper after conducting major well maintenance.
But what about PFAS? According to the EPA, well owners should conduct regular testing 'for information on the overall quality of the water and whether it contains PFAS.'
'Contact your state environmental or health agency for detailed advice or to obtain a list of state-certified laboratories using EPA-developed testing methods in drinking water,' agency guidance states. 'The National Environmental Laboratory Accreditation Management System website may also be helpful in finding a laboratory to test for PFAS.'
The EPA has approved four methods to analyze 29 specific PFAS compounds in drinking water. According to a review of EPA-approved PFAS tests, they typically cost several hundred dollars. That's because the tests are technically complex and aim to detect PFAS at extremely low concentrations.
Microbac Laboratories, a Pennsylvania-based environmental, food and life sciences testing company, is one of many firms offering PFAS testing services to Midwestern customers, from public water utilities to private consumers. Anthony Canter, who directs Microbac's Marietta, Ohio, facility, said the market for PFAS testing has grown in recent years alongside bolstered state and federal regulations.
"You see this all the time, the testing just increases with regulation," Canter said.
The Microbac laboratory Canter directs sits just up the Ohio River from Parkersburg, West Virginia, a town of less than 30,000 residents that has often been described as an epicenter of the movement to clean up PFAS pollution. Parkersburg was the focus of the feature film "Dark Waters" and the Netflix documentary "The Devil We Know," both of which review the community's struggle with rampant PFAS pollution traced to local manufacturing of the compounds.
Canter, who grew up in the area, said Microbac and other testing companies provide consumers with detailed information about what tests to purchase, how to collect samples and how to send those samples in for testing.
Precautions must be taken to avoid PFAS contamination from the likes of beauty products, certain clothing items and other household wares, all of which can contain PFAS, when collecting a sample. Canter said Microbac provides customers with a "clean" bottle of water that the company knows is free of PFAS alongside an empty sample bottle.
While performing the test, the customer opens the clean bottle and pours that water into the empty bottle. Then they collect their sample. The switch helps Microbac technicians ensure the sample is not contaminated.
"That's one thing we do for accuracy, and that's all part of the instructions," Canter said.
PFAS tests that claim to offer results within minutes or at home should be avoided, according to Canter and Professor Mark D. Krahling, an analytical chemist at the University of Southern Indiana who, alongside students, has tested Ohio River water for PFAS compounds.
"It's just a different world from when you're trying to figure out the pH of your swimming pool," Krahling said. "When you're trying to look for things that are present at such a smaller concentration, it's just much, much more challenging."
In February 2023 the federal government announced a $2 billion effort to combat 'emerging contaminants' − such as PFAS − in disadvantaged communities, and the EPA says that program offers grants 'to help owners of private wells address PFAS contamination,' which includes testing and removal.
What to know about at-home filters
Even relatively cheap filters can remove PFAS from tap water, studies show, but their effectiveness can vary. At-home filtration solutions can cost as little as $20, but as feature sets and capabilities grow, so does the cost. According to the EPA, there are three primary filter types used to remove PFAS from drinking water:
Activated Carbon Treatment: This class includes the popular, handheld Brita water filters.
Reverse Osmosis: High-pressure membranes remove PFAS from water while allowing minerals to pass through.
Ion Exchange: Uses positively charged resins to remove negatively charged pollutants, such as PFAS.
Manufacturers offer filters of all three types in a range of sizes, from handheld pitchers to whole-house filtration systems, according to NSF International, a product testing, certification and inspection organization. Point-of-use systems treat the water where you use it, such as a filter pitcher. Whole-house or point-of-entry systems treat the water as it enters a home or building.
The Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit organization that has extensively monitored PFAS pollution, issued filter recommendations to consumers last year after testing 10 commonly used at-home, point-of-use water filters for 25 individual PFAS compounds, including two of the most common and potentially harmful: perfluorooctanoic acid, or PFOA, and perfluorooctane sulfonate, or PFOS.
Sydney Evans, a senior analyst at Environmental Working Group, said the organization tested the filters based on three criteria: 'How well do they actually filter out PFAS? What's the life of the filter? And how much is it going to cost you over the course of a year?'
What the EWG found is that filters' effectiveness at reducing PFAS in tap water varied. Here's how some of the most popular filters stacked up in EWG's tests.
Travel Berkey: 100% removal of PFAS; eight-year filter life. Listed Price: $362
Zero Water: 100% removal of PFAS; short filter life. Listed Price: $24.99
Clearly Filtered: 100% removal of PFAS; large container size for handheld filter. Listed Price: $90
Epic Water Filter: 98% removal of PFAS; easy filter replacement. Listed Price: $55.20
A popular Brita filter and an Amazon Basics filter pitcher tested by EWG reduced PFAS contamination by 22% and 54%, respectively.
According to EPA researcher Thomas Speth, activated carbon filters − like those found in popular point-of-use and whole-home systems − can be '100 percent effective' at removing PFAS from drinking water assuming the filter has not expired and that the water in question has already undergone some form of treatment to remove large particles and other contaminants.
But filtering PFAS at the point of use or even with a whole-home filtration system amounts to a 'Band-Aid' for the broader PFAS problem, Evans said. The long-term goal is to remove the pollution at the source, but experts say it could take years of expanded testing to adequately trace sources of PFAS pollution nationwide, especially among private wells.
Complicating the issue of PFAS cleanup, water filters do not destroy the PFAS they remove, and that has led to questions about how best to manage an ever-growing supply of discarded pollutants as public water systems and private citizens alike step up PFAS testing and filtration.
The pollution became a problem in the first place because the compounds do not break down naturally in the environment.
'PFAS are essentially being concentrated,' the Indiana Department of Environmental Management explained, with regard to filters. 'And the waste stream will have to be properly disposed of as a hazardous waste.'

title: Top performers from Week 2 in Peoria high school football: Rivalry heroes and shutout wins
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Players from Peoria High, Dunlap and more had some of the best IHSA performances from Week 2 of Illinois high school football in the Peoria area.
content:
Each week, the Journal Star will take a look at the top-performing teams and players from weekend games across the Peoria area.
Players from Peoria High, Notre Dame, Metamora and Dunlap lead our list for Week 2.
Breon Green to TQ Webb, Peoria High
The quarterback found his top target four times for 125 yards and two touchdowns in a 46-40 rivalry victory over Peoria Notre Dame. Green ended 12-for-20 overall with 290 yards and three TDs.
Detaurion Pollard, Peoria High
The Lions running back was huge in helping run out the clock on a 46-40 rivalry victory over Notre Dame. He ran 29 times for 127 yards and four TDs.
Lawson Alwan, Notre Dame
The Irish back was key in helping PND erase a 20-point second-half deficit before Peoria High won 46-40. Alwan finished with 153 yards and three TDs on 13 carries. Backfield mate Jack Hanley had 63 yards and two TDs on 15 rushes.
Jackson Oldham, Dunlap
The Eagles running back ran for a pair of touchdowns in the first half to help the top-ranked team in the Journal Star area to a 41-31 road win over Rock Island. Joe Weeks added a rushing TD of his own, plus 101 yards on the ground. Mack Sutter pulled in six catches for 121 yards as QB John Bargen threw for 181 yards including a 60-yard TD pass to Dawson Marmion.
Avery Grebner, Metamora
The defensive back came up big again this week with a key interception late in a 22-14 home win over LaSalle-Peru. Grebner snagged the key INT just moments after Metamora has gone ahead 15-14 on a 1-yard TD run. After the pick, Evan Keil went 76 yards for a score and set the final score. Keil finished with 150 yards on 16 carries for the Redbirds (2-0), who travel to face rival Washington (0-2) next week.
Colin Johnson, Canton
The Little Giants running back had 77 yards and a touchdown on nine carries, but Canton lost to Coal City, 56-6. Canton opens Mid-Illini Conference play next week at Morton.
Max Eccles, Deer Creek-Mackinaw
The Chiefs running back had 187 combined yards and two touchdowns to help them to a 36-0 road victory against Trenton Wesclin on Friday night. He ran 14 times for 151 yards and caught 3 balls for 36 yards. Dee-Mack moved to 2-0 on the season and next hosts Eureka (2-0) in a big game in Week 3.
Eddie Lorton, Fieldcrest
The running back is on our list again this week with another strong showing despite a 42-14 loss to Moweaqua Central A&M. He carried the ball 29 times for 195 rushing yards and a touchdown for the Knights (0-2).
Jeremy Yoss, El Paso-Gridley
The receiver scored both touchdowns for the Titans (0-2) in a 28-14 loss to Casey Westfield. His night included an 88-yard kick return for a touchdown, as well as a 26-yard TD reception from quarterback Owen Bergquist.
Ben Lapp, Eureka
The running back rushed for 97 yards and two TDs and added another score on a kickoff return to lead the Hornets to a 39-23 victory against St. Bede. Receiver Tory Kupferschnmid added 81 yards and a score for the Hornets (2-0), who meet unbeaten Deer Creek-Mackinaw (2-0) in a key Week 3 game.
Matthew Glenn, Elmwood/Brimfield

The wideout, who had scored a pair of 59-yard touchdowns as the Princes escaped with a 28-27 win over Havana. Linebacker Eli Christianson sacked Ducks QB Kaden Olson in the endzone for a safety with 47 seconds to play, sealing the victory for Princeville.

title: Pill bugs and intense sewage smell: The best and worst food inspections in Tazewell County
author: Mike Kramer
description: Three East Peoria restaurants were among the businesses with the most violations for food inspections in Tazewell County in August.
content:
The Tazewell County Health Department conducts monthly food inspections for a wide range of establishments in the area. Inspections look for issues that could contribute to the spread of foodborne illness, and general cleanliness and maintenance of the establishment.
The Journal Star examined the routine inspections that took place in August for restaurants, mobile establishments, and bars in Tazewell County. Nearly 80 routine inspections were conducted for these categories.
Terminology used by the Health Department
Foodborne Illness Risk Factors: Risk factors are practices and procedures identified as the most prevalent contributing factors to foodborne illness.
Public Health Interventions: These are control measures meant to prevent foodborne illness or injury.
Good Retail Practices: Good Retail Practices are preventive measures to control the addition of pathogens, chemicals, and physical objects into food.
Demerits: The Health Department's demerits system is based on the number of violations found during a regular food establishment inspection. A total demerit score of zero indicates no critical violations were noted at the time of the inspection. The Health Department noted that a score of zero demerits does not mean perfect conditions exist. Scores and demerits only represent the state of the facility at the time of inspection. Seventeen Tazewell County establishments had no demerits, and six had five or more demerits.
The establishments listed below received either no demerits or had five or more demerits.

Eight demerits: The Health Department marked Tequila's as 'out of compliance' because there was no Certified Food Protection Manager on site. An employee was observed scooping ice with a plastic cup rather than the provided scoop, and five large containers of queso were discarded due to improper cooling methods.

Six demerits: The Health Department reported finding several types of flies in several areas of the restaurant and dead pill bugs in the broom closet, an 'intense sewage smell' in the men's restroom due to the ventilation system not functioning, and a back door that did not fit tightly. The inspector also observed improper cold-holding temperatures and an employee turning off a faucet with bare hands after washing them.

Five demerits: The inspection revealed a soiled fan cover on the ceiling of a cooler, and dish machines in the bar and kitchen that were not sanitizing properly. The Health Department also cited the restaurant for a repeat violation for cooking steaks to order without including a link to a consumer food advisory on the menu.

Five demerits: Violations included a hand sink without a supply of paper towels, an accumulation of grease and debris on the legs and wheels of cook line equipment and the dish machine, and litter in several areas.

title: James Earl Jones, acclaimed 'Field of Dreams' actor and voice of Darth Vader, dies at 93
author: Brian Truitt
description: James Earl Jones, who played the voice of Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" films, died Monday. He was 93.
content:
James Earl Jones, whose acting career was every bit as rich and resonant as the iconic bass voice that gave sinister malevolence to Darth Vader in the "Star Wars" films, died Monday. He was 93.
Jones' representative Barry McPherson confirmed the actor's death in a statement to USA TODAY. A cause of death was not disclosed.
"He passed this morning surrounded by his loved ones," McPherson said. "He was a great man."
Jones was an acclaimed star of stage and screen, winning Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards, though later his unmistakable voice became as famous as his usually smiling face. He invited generations of TV viewers with the signature "This is CNN" line for the cable news channel, had parental gravitas as the brave Mufasa in Disney's classic 1994 animated "The Lion King" and its 2019 remake, but was most famous for his signature lines ("I am your father") as Vader.
"I've done a King Lear, too! Do the kids know that? No, they have the Darth Vader poster to sign. But it's OK," Jones said in a 2010 Broadway.com interview. "When you appear before an audience, you learn to accept whatever they give you. Hopefully they give you their ears, as Antony said."
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
A native of Arkabutla, Miss., Jones was raised by his grandparents in Michigan and overcame a stutter in early childhood. After studying drama at the University of Michigan, he moved to New York in 1957 to follow in the footsteps of his father, Robert Earl – who left before Jones was born – as an actor.
That same year, he made his Broadway debut as Cinna The Senator in "Infidel Caesar," beginning a storied theater career that included Tony-winning turns in "The Great White Hope" (1969) and "Fences" (1987) as well as high-profile roles in "Cat on a Hot Tin Roof," "Driving Miss Daisy" and "You Can't Take It With You."
On the big screen, Jones first appeared in 1964's classic Cold War satire "Dr. Strangelove," earned a best-actor Oscar nomination for the 1970 film adaptation of "Great White Hope," and over the course of five decades also starred in "Conan the Barbarian" (1982), "Coming to America" (1988), "Field of Dreams" (1989) and "The Sandlot" (1993).
"Field of Dreams," like the 1987 John Sayles coal-miner drama "Matewan," was "one of the very few movies I've done that I really cherish," Jones told USA TODAY in 2014 for the baseball-themed drama's 25th anniversary.
"Movies that have very simple themes, simple stories to tell, but very powerful (and) compact," he continued. "Why they're important to me is because in that simplicity, magic can happen if you just let it happen and don't force it."
But Jones, who received an honorary Oscar at the 2011 Governors Awards and a special Tony for lifetime achievement in 2017, wasn't even seen on screen for arguably his most trademark role.
Beginning in George Lucas' original 1977 blockbuster "Star Wars," Jones voiced the intergalactic villain Darth Vader, who almost instantly became one of Hollywood's quintessential antagonists and still endures. (The fearsome menace was named the No. 3 film villain of all time by the American Film Institute, behind only Hannibal Lecter and Norman Bates.)
"I'm simply special effects," Jones said in a 2009 interview with the AFI about his role as Vader. He added that Lucas wanted a "darker voice" than that of David Prowse, the towering British actor under Vader's mask and body armor. "So he hires a guy born in Mississippi and raised in Michigan who stutters, and that's the voice and that's me. I lucked out. From all these so-called handicaps, I lucked out to get a job that paid me $7,000. I thought that was good money and I got to be a voice on a movie. It was great fun to be part of that."
Jones reprised his role as Mufasa in director Jon Favreau's 2019 remake of "The Lion King," which featured photorealistic animals. Favreau recalled that when working with Jones, "he asked me if I had any direction for him, and I didn't know what to say. It was like, 'Just do what you do. You are him.'"
"It would be like him asking me how to play Darth Vader. You've created this character and decades have gone and we've all grown with it."

title: Presidential debate fact check: Keeping an eye on claims from Trump, Harris
author: Joedy McCreary
description: Follow along with the USA TODAY Fact-Check Team as we keep tabs on the claims made by Donald Trump and Kamala Harris during their first debate.
content:
Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Donald Trump take the stage tonight in Philadelphia for their first presidential debate of the Nov. 5 election season.
Follow this space as the USA TODAY Fact-Check Team investigates claims from the nominees and adds context on the top issues for voters this year.
We'll be watching for statements that exaggerate, mislead, misrepresent or otherwise stray from reality. Our team uses primary documents, trustworthy nonpartisan sources, data and other research tools to assess the accuracy of claims. And you won't have to take our word for it, since we'll always link our sources as we go.
Catch up on our convention, debate fact-checks
We fact-checked key speakers throughout the Republican and Democratic conventions. Catch up here on what was false, what was true and what was in between from Kamala Harris, Donald Trump, JD Vance, Tim Walz and a host of others.
-Eric Litke
Debate background: Immigration a key issue even as encounters at southern border drop
Immigration has been one of the top issues for voters during the presidential campaign season. Under President Joe Biden, illegal border crossings reached record highs, averaging more than 2 million per year from 2021 to 2023, according to Customs and Border Protection. But more recently, illegal crossings – or 'encounters' – at the southern border fell to the lowest total in nearly four years only months after Biden announced broad restrictions on asylum.
Vice President Kamala Harris was never put in charge of the southern border or made "border czar," contrary to some posts on social media, but that hasn't stopped former president Donald Trump and other Republicans from attacking her immigration policy. In 2021, Biden announced Harris would lead his administration's diplomatic efforts with Mexico and the Central American countries of Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador to slow migration to the southern border. At the time, Harris said the administration 'must address the root causes that cause people to make the trek, as the president described, to come here.'
Trump, meanwhile, has promised the largest deportation effort in U.S. history if he is elected again. He also said he would reinstate strict immigration policies from his first term, limit asylum access at the U.S. southern border and eliminate automatic citizenship for people born in the U.S. to immigrant parents.
In February, Republican lawmakers blocked an immigration bill that would have revamped the country's immigration and border policies. Biden and Harris have blamed the bill's failure on opposition from Trump. Harris has vowed to bring back the bill and sign it into law if elected.
- Chris Mueller

title: How the Peoria Rivermen hockey defense just got bigger and better ahead of title defense
author: Dave Eminian
description: The Peoria Rivermen brought back three key players Monday among five players signing on for an SPHL title defense.
content:
PEORIA — The Peoria Rivermen brought back three key members from their SPHL championship team among five players signed Monday.
Defensemen Renat Dadadzhanov and Chase Spencer, and big winger Mike Gelatt all signed for a return to Peoria.
Rivermen coach Jean-Guy Trudel also added two newcomers in 6-foot-5 winger Jake Vaughan and winger John Kaljian, the latter whom was part of Adrian College's national championship team in 2022.
"A lot of our guys have earned looks from ECHL teams in their camps this fall," Trudel said. "So we have to see whether they all make it back to us. But we're excited about who we have and how strong this team can be, and we're going to keep adding to it."
The Russian on defense
Dadadzhanov is a 6-foot-3, 215-pound defenseman from Moscow, Russia.
The 25-year-old sat out of hockey for two years while pursuing a boxing career, then returned to the game in his pro debut with the Rivermen last season. He played 35 games with two goals, two assists and a plus-7 rating and was a big part of Peoria's championship run.
"If he gets back down here from ECHL Maine's camp, he'll be a huge addition," Trudel said. "He had an injury last season, and when he came back into the lineup it changed our whole defensive corps mentality. He's old-school, but he's a good enough skater to play the game fast."
Dadadzhanov played 110 games over three seasons in elite the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League, then spent a fourth year, in 2020-21, at Laurentian University in Canada's university system.
The chase is on
Chase Spencer is a 6-foot-2, 195-pound defenseman.
The 25-year-old played 23 games in his rookie season with the Rivermen last year, notching two goals with 10 assists. He added another three assists in seven playoff games.
"He came from a great program at Adrian College," Trudel said. "He's a very important part of our puzzle on defense and we expect him to have a big year. He's going to ECHL Tulsa camp."
Spencer played four years for Toronto in the Ontario Junior Hockey League, then three more at NCAA Division-III Adrian College. He turned pro last season overseas with Backen in Sweden, played 13 games there, then joined the Rivermen for their championship run.
Spencer was a part of two conference championship teams and one national championship team (2022) at Adrian. He was an NCHA All-Conference and All-Tournament team selection in 2023.
A proven scorer with size on the edge
Mike Gelatt is a 6-foot-2, 210-pound winger who looks like a next-level player.
The 27-year-old turned pro with the Rivermen from the college ranks (Skidmore College, Wisconsin-River Falls) two seasons ago, appearing in eight games. He turned in his first full pro season last year and helped Peoria to an SPHL championship with 11 goals, 16 assists, four game-winning goals and a plus-13 rating in 34 games.
He added another two goals and four assists in seven playoff games.
Gelatt is a postseason force with nine points in 12 games over two playoff springs. He has been signed to ECHL expansion Bloomington's camp.
"Gelatt has become part of our leadership group," Trudel said. "A true pro and a big reason we won a championship last year. He plays the game the right way day in, day out."
A prospect from Adrian College
John Kaljian is a 6-foot-1, 215-pound winger who played four seasons at NCAA D-III Adrian College, where he was part of its 2022 national championship team. He captained them in his final year last season, wrapping up a 102-game career with 23 goals and 33 assists.
A big man prospect on the wing
Jake Vaughan is a 6-foot-5, 215-pound winger from Colorado Springs, Colo.
The 24-year-old has been invited to ECHL South Carolina camp, and will come to Peoria if he doesn't make the higher team.
Vaughan played four years of junior hockey in the NAHL with Bismark, Odessa and Chippewa. Then two years each at Connecticut College and Saint Mary's University, both NCAA D-III programs.
He began his pro career last spring with a five-game stint at Port Huron in the low-A FPHL.
"He will be a project for us," Trudel said. "He has great size and he wants to get better, move forward in his career. If Jake buys into everything we do in Peoria every day, he'll have no choice but to become an important part of the Rivermen."

title: 'Larger than life': Creve Coeur honors late beloved founder of cruise-in fundraiser
author: Mike Kramer
description: Dan Jones, 62, of Creve Coeur died Aug. 30. He co-founded the Sweet Kids Cruise-In and served as a volunteer firefighter for many years.
content:
Friends and family say Dan Jones of Creve Coeur had a personality that was 'larger than life."
'He was definitely a person who loved to help and serve others,' said Mickey, Jones' wife. 'He loved God, his family, and his friends. He was a family man through and through.'
Jones, 62, died on Aug. 30. He was the former owner of the Tri-County Sports Shop in Creve Coeur, where he was known as a go-to vendor for local schools, studios and sports teams. When the shop closed 11 years ago, Jones worked at Costco in East Peoria as a gas station supervisor. He also worked as a volunteer firefighter and founded a still-active fundraising event called the Sweet Kids Cruise-In & Car Show, which benefits the Pediatric Diabetes Resource Center.
Jones' love for his community manifested in his willingness to socialize with customers and give back. His community clearly loved him back, because Mickey estimated that between 700 and 800 people attended his visitation earlier this month at Preston-Hanley Funeral Home.
'It showed how special a man he was,' Mickey said. 'To see so many people he impacted came to pay their respects and honor him was overwhelming.'
Jones' lifelong friend Tom Schatsiek of Creve Coeur attended elementary school with him. Even though they went on to attend different high schools, Schatsiek asserted that it was no deterrent to their friendship. They also went on to both serve as volunteer firefighters in Creve Coeur. 'When we got to be teenagers, we'd cruise Main Street (in Peoria) in his Camaro,' he said. 'That was probably every Friday and Saturday night.'
Mickey said Jones also was a fixture at all his childrens' sporting events, dance recitals, school plays and band concerts.
'I only remember him missing one event, and that was when his grandmother was in the (Intensive Care Unit),' she said. 'Other than that, we went to every one of our kids' events, and they did a multitude of things. ... We went to Florida twice for cheerleading competitions, and we went to Texas twice for soccer games when our son was in college.'
Jones was diagnosed with Type I diabetes at age 14; his daughter Emily Thigpen was diagnosed as a teenager. Both had a love of classic cars and combined that passion with a desire to help children newly diagnosed with diabetes into the Sweet Kids Cruise In. Since its inception in 2011, the Cruise In has raised over $100,000.
'We thought it would be a one-year thing,' Thigpen said. 'But we raised five or six thousand dollars and we had so much fun doing it that when people asked if we were going to make it annual event, it seemed like a no-brainer.'
'The Cruise In was always a great fellowship event,' said Jones' sister, Diane Hemp. 'Sometimes there would be more than 100 cars there, and people would talk and text. There would be silent auctions for baskets and a 50/50 raffle.'
In the spare time, Jones enjoyed hunting, cooking, his assortment of smokers and vacations at Lake of the Ozarks. He also loved rock music from the 1970s and 1980s — particularly Ted Nugent, AC/DC, Aerosmith and Lynyrd Skynyrd.
'There was always music on,' Thigpen said. 'There was a stereo system inside. There was a stereo system in the garage. There was a stereo system in the shop where he worked. Wherever he was, a stereo was always on, and it was always loud.'
Thigpen's favorite memories of her father include impromptu after-school dance parties and traditional family vacations that often included a party of friends.
'It will be difficult to return to Lake of the Ozarks without him, because he was part of every single memory,' she said. 'Whether it was skiing, teaching people how to ski, riding the Jet Ski, or fishing off the dock; he was there, just like he was there for us pretty much every day of our lives.'
In addition to Mickey, he is survived by his parents, Jerry and Pat Jones of Creve Coeur; his brother, Tom; his sister Hemp of Metamora; daughters Maria Bollinger of East Peoria, Danielle Keen of Tremont, and Thigpen of Creve Coeur; son Rob Jones of Groveland; 12 grandchildren; and a veritable army of friends.
Mickey said she had many fond memories of her life with Jones, but her single favorite was their wedding day, which occurred just eight months after they met. Their 25th wedding anniversary celebration with family and friends likely ranks a close second, she added.
'Our family and friends sent us on a belated honeymoon/anniversary trip to Hawaii,' said Mickey. 'That was probably the most peaceful, relaxing vacation we ever had. The fact that our family and friends had planned it for us made it even more special.'

title: A ‘heart the size of Texas': Family grieves young woman who was fatally shot in Peoria
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Mary Halcomb is remembered as a caring, kind person who was studying to become a nurse.
content:
It was 1:30 a.m. on Sept. 7 and Ashley Halcomb had awoken to hear the sound of a knock at the door. It's not the most convenient time for someone to be asking to come into her house and she felt a sense that something, anything, was awry.
"From the time I opened my eyes to the noise, I had a feeling that something wasn't right," Halcomb, who lives in Mapleton, said. "Both my husband and I knew something was wrong."
Indeed, something terrible had happened to their oldest daughter, 20-year-old Mary Halcomb, and a detective from the Peoria Police Department – along with Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood – had arrived at their home in the dark of night to give them the news no parents ever want to hear.
Mary had been killed earlier that night at a home in the 1400 block of South Griswold Street in Peoria. Upon hearing the news, Ashley went into a state of shock, not quite believing the facts that she had heard from the authorities.
"I went into sheer shock and numbness," Ashley said. "I didn't want to believe any of it was true."
Unfortunately for Ashley, her husband, Luke, her two other children Chloe and Braxton and the rest of her family, it was true. The circumstances surrounding her death were considered"brutal (and) violent" by a Peoria County judge and have the family wondering about the right way to move forward following a tremendous shock.
How it happened
According to the Peoria County State's Attorney's Office, detectives from the Peoria Police Department found Mary's body on the steps of stairs inside the home, with a gunshot wound in her neck. Located in her hands was a firearm with a bloody fingerprint.
Officers began searching the home, when they came across a bedroom soaked in blood. A sticky note was placed to the wall, with a promise that Mary wouldn't break the heart of her boyfriend, 18-year-old Nathaniel Archuleta. If she broke the promise, Archuleta would have no choice but to "euthanize" her.
Archuleta was at the scene that night and spoke with detectives. However, Assistant State's Attorney Terry Muench said that he frequently changed his story, at first telling detectives that the gun used to kill Mary accidentally went off when he was trying to clean it, but changed tack when it was discovered that he had nothing to clean the firearm available to him in the house.
He did tell detectives that he was upset Mary was talking to another man that evening and denied putting the gun in her hands. However, officers found a loaded clip inside his car, and an autopsy from Harwood's office indicated that when the gun was fired, it was 2 to 3 feet from Mary's neck.
Because of the inconsistencies in his story, Muench argued in court that Archuleta had been trying to cover up his alleged actions to frame it as a suicide.
Circuit Judge Mark Gilles ruled last week that Archuleta would have to be held at the Peoria County Jail before his trial on first-degree murder charges. Arraignment is set for Oct. 10 at 1 p.m.
'A heart as big as Texas'
Mary was born when Ashley was 20 years old, and her mother says that the two grew up together, in some ways. By the time she became an adult, the two thought of each other as close friends.
"We did everything together," Ashley said. "She told me everything – sometimes a little bit too much – but I knew she trusted me."
Ashley said that Mary had a "contagious" laugh and was someone who had a "heart the size of Texas."
"She'd do anything for anyone," Ashley said.
Jayne Halcomb, Mary's paternal grandmother, said that she was a "kind, giving" person who cared for people – appropriate considering she was studying to become a nurse at Midwest Technical Institute.
"At first, she wanted to become a doctor," Jayne said. "After she grew up, I think she realized that being a nurse would be best. She worked two to three jobs and was a nurse's aid at several nursing homes and hospitals."
Jayne also mentioned Mary's passion for softball, where she played catcher for several traveling teams. The family would frequently travel with her to watch her play, with Jayne noting that she was a solid teammate to those she shared the diamond with.
"She was a good, team player," Jayne said. "She was always looking out for the other person. She wasn't self-centered."
Trying to explain the unexplainable
Ashley says she didn't know much about Archuleta, the man that Mary was with on the night of her death. She knew that Mary frequented the house in South Peoria, but not much else.
"I knew that she would go to his house and (she) was friends with him," Ashley said. "(But) that's all I know."
Now, she has to figure out a way forward without her eldest daughter and must explain this to her younger children. Chloe is in high school and, according to Ashley, is struggling to comprehend what happened two weeks ago.
"They were best friends," Ashley said. "She is taking it pretty rough, grieving the best way she can, but trying to keep her mind busy through sports and school."
As for Braxton, the youngest of Ashley's three children, he didn't quite understand what happened to his big sister until he saw her body at the visitation held in Bartonville on Sept. 14.
"It's hard to explain with him," Ashley said. "He's only 10, so up until her services, I don't think he fully comprehended the forever-ness of it. But when he saw his sister at the funeral home over the weekend, it really hit him and he's grieving even harder."
Ashley described Mary as a best friend to her younger siblings, which matches the description of her obituary, which noted how she was always ready to lend a hand at home.
"I miss seeing the interactions between her and her siblings," Ashley said.
Even though two weeks have passed, Ashley remains stunned as to what she has witnessed, with her eldest child and best friend gone in a flash for no obvious reason.
"It feels like a really bad dream," Ashley said.

title: What is the toughest position to play in high school football? We asked Peoria-area players
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: QB? Corner? Line? We asked Peoria-area high school football players the toughest position to play in the sport.
content:
Football is a tough sport, with 22 players each playing a role in their team's success.
But which one is the toughest to play?
That's what we asked players around the Peoria area in the fourth of a multi-part series in which the Journal Star talks with high school football coaches and players about numerous topics relating to the world of preps pigskin. So far, we've asked coaches about program mottos and asked players who should get the ball in crunch time.
As we head into Week 4, here is what some of the large- and small-school football players had to say about the toughest position to play. Look for players' pregame routines coming in the next few weeks.
Being QB1
"I would say QB, because he is the leader on the field. He also must always remember routes, run scheme and read defensive backs." — Jackson Hakes, Fieldcrest
"QB. You control the offense if something doesn't work, it's on you for the most part. You have to remember everybody else's position along with yours." — Ben Lapp, Eureka
"QB, because they have to know all the plays and have a good arm and have to be very smart and athletic." — Carter Lambin, Farmington
"QB, because it requires lots of focus and the whole team relies on him to make decisions." — Cameron Nickel, Metamora
"QB, because you have to know everyone else's position." — Jake Williams, Princeville
"Quarterback. You have to know what everyone else is doing as well as read the defense. QB is the most tough to play." — Chuck Hathaway, Deer Creek-Mackinaw
"QB, because everything you do depends on everyone else doing their job right." — Mikah Hall, Illinois Valley Central
"QB. Got to know what every player on the field is doing and running a team in general." — Blaine Williams, Tremont
"QB, because you have to know every play, defensive schemes." — Carter Prina, Washington
Playing in the secondary
"I feel like it's (defensive back) because you need to mirror some of the best athletes on the field the whole way and one little mess up could be the deciding point from a catch or incompletion." — Aidin Hindert, East Peoria
"Corner. (You're) guarding the best athletes." — Sean Glover, Richwoods
"Corner, because you are often isolated alone which is tough to handle." — Lawson Alwan, Peoria Notre Dame
"Cornerback, because you are left on an island." — Avery Grebner, Metamora
"Cornerback. I feel running backward and guarding someone is harder than anything." — Cameron Clark, Richwoods
"Defensive back. You have to guard and do many other things." — Spencer Russell, Peoria High
"Cornerback takes great patience." — Aubre Yaun Bailey, Manual
"Defense back. Crazy good wide receivers/running backs in the Mid-Illini (Conference)." — Colin Johnson, Canton
Journal Star power rankings: Peoria-area high school football Top 20 for Week 4
On the line
"Lineman. They have a lot of pressure on them to do their job and if they don't then the play is ruined." — Hudson Nutter, Pekin
"Left tackle. You play against the best athletes on the other team." — Colton Barlow, Dunlap
"Offensive line. They all have to block for the play to work." — Max Eccles, Deer Creek-Mackinaw
"O-line/d-line. If you don't have a line, you don't succeed, and every play is a war." — Tyler Humphrey, Washington
"I'm going to be biased here and say offense and defensive line. I think that it is the hardest position because you have to go full contact every play with the person in front of you all game long. Also, when doing this the linemen don't get near the credit they should get." — Ty Dykes, Tremont
"O-line, because they get no credit." — Seandon Buffington, Morton
"O-line, because you've got to read a lot of things." — Eddie Lorton, Fieldcrest
"Center. You are in charge of communication to the rest of o-line, what the defense is doing and let the backfield know which way you are going to step as well as starting the play with the snap. If you mess it up, you can screw up the entire play." — Hunter Lamberson, Pekin
"Tackle and guard. You need to be fast and strong." — Erik Vazquez, Elmwood/Brimfield

title: 'Let's do this': Female kicker from Pekin makes football history for Monmouth College
author: Dave Eminian
description: Pekin grad Mylee Hansen kicked a PAT for Monmouth College to become first female to score point in program history.
content:
Mylee Hansen kicked a football between the uprights and into history Saturday when she scored for Monmouth College in an NCAA game.
The Pekin High School grad and Monmouth freshman kicker booted an extra point against Lawrence University, her first collegiate football point in a 52-6 victory in front of 2,501 at April Zorn Stadium and Woll Memorial Field.
The 5-foot-5, 140-pound kicker is the first female in Monmouth football program history to score a point.
"This was such an exciting moment," Hansen said. "It's a very new experience. They kind of mentioned something about it, happening, hinted at it. The coaches were calling 'Mylee, Mylee,' and I realized I was going in there. I'm always nervous before a kick. But nerves make me kick better. The whole moment was such a great experience."
Hansen had a busy day, playing for the Scots' women's soccer team Saturday morning against Illinois Wesleyan before her milestone afternoon. With 6:06 left in the fourth quarter, Monmouth running back Nate Wrublik added the final points of the game on a 13-yard scoring run.
Cody Zelc had kicked extra points for the Scots during the game. But the team sent in Hansen after this final TD to attempt her historic point-after kick, and she delivered.
"I wasn't even stretched," Hansen said, laughing. "I thought, 'Oh gosh, let's do this.' I ran out there, and my holder (East Peoria High School grad Gabriel Zeigler-Harris) said, 'No problem, you got this.' "
Piles of points and perfection: What we learned about Peoria-area football in Week 4
And she did, while her mother, Amy, and her father, Dan, and twin brother, Cooper, looked on.
"If you'd told me when I was younger that I'd kick a college point some day, I'd probably tell you I would not believe it," Hansen said, laughing. "It was a crazy experience. I wouldn't change it for anything."
Hansen was the first female kicker in Pekin's program history. She hit the game-winning extra point against Normal Community in the 2022 Class 7A second-round comeback playoff victory. Video of a tackle she made on a Washington kick returner also made headlines last season.
Hansen played soccer in high school as well, a center-back who earned first-team all-Mid-Illini Conference honors. She helped lead the Dragons to a Class 3A regional title match appearance this past spring.
Are there any female kickers in college football?
Women have an expanding presence on college football rosters. Here is a look at a list of women to score in college football:
1997: Liz Heaston played two games as a placekicker for then-NAIA Willamette University, becoming the first woman to play and score in a college game.
2001: Ashley Martin, kicking for Jacksonville State, became the first woman to score in an NCAA Division I-AA game.
2003: Katie Hnida kicked a pair of extra points for NCAA Division I-A New Mexico in 2003.
2003: Tonya Butler kicked a field goal for West Alabama.
2015: April Goss kicked an extra point for Kent State.
2020: Sarah Fuller kicked a pair of extra points for Vanderbilt.
2023: Leilani Armenta joined the Jackson State roster and kicked some extra points.
2024: Mylee Hansen kicked an extra point for NCAA Division III Monmouth College.

title: Chicago White Sox social media team delightfully managing baseball team's historic futility
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The Chicago White Sox social media team is having fun with its baseball team's historically bad season.
content:
The Chicago White Sox are having a rough 2024, but the MLB squad's social media team is making the best of it.
The White Sox have lost five consecutive games and 120 overall — tied with the 1962 New York Mets for the most losses in the single season since 1900.
After most games, MLB teams post graphics or the final score of their games on social media as a way to spread the news. Lately, the @whitesox account at X.com is using humor to soften the pain of historic humility.
And while not much is working for the Sox on the field, the social media gambit is working. The team's last four X.com posts have been liked a combined nearly 540,000 times — multiples beyond its usual engagement for final score posts.
The recent shenanigans started after the White Sox took a modest three-game win streak into their game Tuesday, Sept. 17, against the Los Angeles Angels. The Sox lost that one, 5-0, and the social media team posted this tongue-in-cheek line: "Narrator: the White Sox did not win 4 in a row," along with an emoji of an expressionless face.
That post garnered 3.5K likes, but nothing like what was to come. On Sept. 18, the White Sox lost to the Angels again, this time 4-3. The team then posted "FINAL: the other team scored more runs than us," a post that went viral. One week later, that post has nearly 150K likes.
The Sox did not stop losing — and their social media team kept rolling out banger posts. On Sept. 20, after yet another Sox loss (this time, a 3-2 setback to the San Diego Padres), the Sox posted "FINAL: the number of runs we scored was not greater than the number of runs they scored."
And like a never-ending fever dream, the Sox lost again, 6-2, to the Padres. The social media team dropped another: "FINAL: can be found on the MLB app."
On Sept. 22, the Sox again lost to the Padres, 4-2, as Chicago matched the modern era record for losses in a single season with 120. The social media team then got meta, addressing its recent string of self-reverential posts with a meme of a car screeching to avoid posting the final score and instead posting "literally anything else."

title: Art, food and autumn fun: Six popular outdoor festivals in the Peoria area for fall 2024
author: Josh Jenke
description: German food, fine art and Halloween activities are among the highlights for central Illinois fall festivals.
content:
Fall has arrived in central Illinois and there are plenty of upcoming activities to enjoy. Mark your calendar for the following events, which range from art festivals to culture, food and more.
1. Peoria Art Guild Fine Art Fair
The 62nd annual Peoria Art Guild Fine Art Fair will be Sept. 28-29 on the Peoria riverfront. As one of the oldest art organizations in the country, the art fair is nationally recognized and showcases national, regional and local artists. The art fair features original works of art will include jewelry, painting, ceramics, photography, digital art and more. This is the Peoria Art Guild's major fundraising event of the year. All proceeds benefit the Art Guild's community outreach and programming. For more information, visit https://www.peoriaartguild.org/fine-art-fair-event-info.
2. Spoon River Valley Scenic Drive
The Spoon River Valley Scenic Drive Fall Festival will take place Oct. 5-6 and Oct. 12-13 across several communities in Fulton County. There will be several sights to see, activities to enjoy and food to sample in Farmington, Canton, Lewistown, Ipava, Astoria and multiple other towns and locations. Each town will also have a large variety of vendors with unique crafts and other times available for purchase. For more information and a full map of Spoon River Drive locations, visit www.spoonriverdrive.org.
3. Peoria Zoo Fall Festival
The Peoria Zoo will present a day full of family-friendly fun and activities from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. each Saturday in October. Enjoy live entertainment, photo ops, special concessions and unique vendors, all while witnessing animal enrichment activities. Additional experiences like pumpkin and gourd decorating, creating your own harvest trail mix, and engaging games and crafts will also be available. The festival is included with regular zoo admission, but additional charges my apply for some activities.
4. Schlachtfest and German-American Heritage Day
The Peoria German-American Central Society will present their annual Schlachtfest from noon to 8 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 6, at Hickory Grove Park, 12403 Hickory Grove Road, Dunlap. The event will be combined with a celebration of German-American Day as a kick-off to German-American Heritage Month, and will feature German music by the Ratskellar Brummer's, Lindenhof Echoes and Al's Pals, complete German dinners with sides, a shooting tent and Nagelspielen, playground equipment for the kids, and a campfire at the end of the evening with complimentary marshmallows. A German Car Cruis'n will run from noon until 5 p.m. For more information, visit www.peoriagermans.net.
5. Peoria Food and Wine Festival
The 2024 Peoria Food and Wine Festival will be held on Oct. 10 in The Green Space of the Pabst Building, 4541 N. Prospect Road, Peoria Heights. VIP admission will begin at 5 p.m., with general admission at 6:30 p.m. The event will feature unique food and drink options from several central Illinois restaurants. VIP tickets are $250 each and general admission tickets are $125. Proceeds from the event will benefit Trillium Place Young Minds Center. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit www.peoriafoodandwinefestival.com.
6. Wheels O' Time Museum Fall Festival
The Wheels O' Time Museum will hold its Fall Festival from noon to 4 p.m. Oct. 13 at 1710 W. Woodside Drive, Dunlap. The museum will be decorated in its best fall and Halloween decor and attendees can enjoy blacksmithing demonstrations, folk music, modern and classic fire equipment, ambulance tours, beekeeping paraphernalia and honey tasting, classic cars, vintage garden tractors, trains and more. Light lunch and snack items will be available for purchase. Admission is $12 for adults, $5 for children and free for museum members.

title: Growing pet food boutique finds a new and larger home in Pekin
author: Mike Kramer
description: The organic pet food business Bear's Bites has moved to a Derby Street storefront in Pekin and will host a grand opening event Oct. 12.
content:
Bear's Bites owner and founder Samm Hutchison is moving her operation from East Peoria to Pekin largely because the new premises will allow her space to expand her national pet food operation.
'I had production in a spot in East Peoria, and I outgrew it,' she said. 'I had only about 1,000 square feet there. My husband and my best friend, who move all my equipment, told me if I moved, I had to own the building. So, I bought a building.'
The new Bear's Bites premises at 282 Derby Street, Pekin affords Hutchison an estimated 7,500 square feet of space. She plans to produce single-ingredient pet treats and organic pet food in the rear of the building and devote the front section to Bear's Bites Boutique and Education Center.
'We will carry no synthetic vitamins or minerals,' Hutchison said. 'It will all be good food and natural remedies. On the education side, I plan on teaching nutrition classes and first-aid classes. I have people coming to talk about CBD, essential oils, and what to do between grooming. There's a lot of education that I think pet parents will benefit from.'
Bear's Bites Boutique Education Center will host a grand opening of the Pekin location Oct. 12 from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. There will be refreshments and live music from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. The grand opening will also include a Tri-County Adoption event, with 13 rescued pets available for adoption.
"The City of Pekin and the Pekin community have been phenomenal,' Hutchison said. 'The customers we've had for six years in the (greater Peoria) area are really excited, because they won't have to order online. They can just walk into our store and get their Bear's Bites.'
Hutchison estimates 250 stores nationwide carry Bear's Bites products. The business also operates a non-profit called The Bear's Bites Foundation, which is a 2024 finalist for a Peoria's Community Choice Award. Award winners will be announced in November. Shop for Bear's Bites food and treats at bearsbites.net.
