title: Helene reaches hurricane status ahead of landfall in Florida: Live updates
author: Jorge L. Ortiz
description: The highest landfall probability is somewhere along the eastern part of the Florida Panhandle late Thursday evening, forecasters said.
content:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. − Helene reached hurricane status Wednesday and was forecast to grow more powerful and dangerous before making landfall late Thursday on Florida's Gulf Coast as a devastating, Category 3 hurricane.
The National Hurricane Center said Helene would rapidly strengthen over the eastern Gulf of Mexico before making landfall while driving winds of 120-125 mph − and warned that "upward adjustments to the forecast intensity" could be required as the storm closes in.
The highest landfall probability was somewhere along the eastern part of the Florida Panhandle − possibly the Big Bend area, the curve of Florida's peninsula around the Gulf of Mexico − late Thursday, AccuWeather forecasters said. Near where Helene makes landfall, general rainfall of 8-12 inches is expected, with 2 feet of rain possible in isolated areas.
More than 42 million people in Florida, Georgia and Alabama were under hurricane and tropical storm warnings, the National Weather Service said.
Helene could also become Tallahassee's worst wind event in recorded history as 100 mph winds blast the Florida capital. Ryan Truchelut, founder of WeatherTiger and a hurricane forecaster for the USA TODAY NETWORK-Florida, said Helene is a storm without precedent.
"Helene stands toe-to-toe with any of the threats that Florida has faced over the past 10 years or indeed really over hurricane history," Truchelut said.
A month ago, Jody Griffis rode out Hurricane Debby in his Cedar Island home along the Big Bend coast. But as he secured his stilt home with shutters and siding Wednesday, he told USA TODAY he will heed the local evacuation order issued ahead of Helene.
'My gut is telling me to get out,' he said.
Developments:
∎ Tampa International Airport said it will suspend operations at 2 a.m. Thursday because of the hurricane. The airport plans to reopen "when safe to do so." The smaller, nearby St. Pete-Clearwater Airport will be closed Thursday and is scheduled to reopen Friday, according to its website. Orlando International Airport said on X that it remains open but some flights could be delayed or cancelled for weather-related reasons.
∎ While U.S. flights weren't seeing a major impact early Wednesday, 12% of flights to Cancun, Mexico, had been canceled and another 16% delayed as of 1:30 p.m. ET, according to online flight tracker FlightAware. Elsewhere, airlines have issued travel waivers, allowing customers to rebook flights along the hurricane's path without penalties, though cities, dates and terms vary widely. Details here.
∎ The Tampa Zoo said it will close its door to the public Thursday and take measures to protect the animals from the approaching hurricane.
∎ The University of Florida cancelled classes for Thursday, joining Florida State and Florida A&M universities, whose closures will last through the weekend.
∎ Helene is the fifth hurricane of the 2024 Atlantic season, about the average number for the date, according to Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach. A typical season sees a total of seven hurricanes.
Big Bend resident: 'I don't know if my house can take it'
Griffis, 57, said he planned to leave with his wife for his brother's house Thursday morning, likely after a long night of fortifying his own home.
'Everything that I have of value will go with me,' he said, describing family heirlooms and photo albums. 'If this thing gets up to 135-140 miles an hour, I don't know if my house can take it.'
Steve Brown, 72, who lives just a few yards from the gulf in Cedar Island, spent the last 24 hours moving outdoor furniture into his home, which sits on stilts 21 feet above sea level.
Under a countywide evacuation, he plans to leave with his wife, Cindy, and their cat, Max, to a friend's home in the nearby city of Perry. 'People around here are busy,' said the retired school teacher. 'It's not a frenzy. Everybody's been through this before, so they have a plan and they're just executing it.'
What is rapid intensification and will it occur in Helene?
Rapid intensification is when a hurricane's winds accelerate by 35 mph or more within 24 hours. Computer models indicate a high chance Helene will experience rapid intensification over the next 24 hours, Robbie Berg, a specialist at the hurricane center, wrote in a Wednesday morning forecast.
Helene will be moving through an environment very conducive to intensification, with low wind shear and much warmer than normal sea surface temperatures. While the official forecast predicts sustained winds up to 125 mph on Thursday, Berg said those winds could be stronger if Helene "rapidly intensifies more than forecast."
Residents in southwest Florida brace for Helene
In Sarasota, Florida, hundreds of miles from where forecasters predict Hurricane Helene will come ashore, residents prepared for the storm Wednesday. Rick Munroe, owner of Sun Garden Cafe, brought in patio furniture and stacked sandbags in front of the doors. A long stretch of Florida's coast, including western Sarasota, could be exposed to storm surge of up to 7 feet, according to forecasters.
"If you don't take them serious,' he said, speaking about hurricanes, 'then you're foolish or you just moved here.'
Paul Samuel, a local general contractor, said many of his clients are similarly concerned about the hurricane. One homeowner had him move much of the furniture on the bottom floor of their home to the second floor. Samuel plans to wrap up several projects by the end of the day, including one that requires the installation of seven windows and doors before the winds and water pick up.
"It'll be airtight by tonight," Samuel said.
Helene could briefly reach Category 4 status
Helene was centered about 85 miles east-northeast of Cozumel, Mexico, early Wednesday, the hurricane center said. The storm was driving sustained winds of 80 mp, and was moving north-northwest at 10 mph. AccuWeather forecasters were predicting Helene could briefly reach Category 4 strength while still in the Gulf, which would mean maximum sustained winds ranging between 130 and 156 mph.
Tornadoes were possible late Wednesday on the western Florida Peninsula and southern Alabama, the hurricane center said. The risk of tornadoes expands Thursday across Florida and into parts of Georgia and South Carolina.
Florida counties order evacuations ahead of Helene
At least 22 Florida counties have some form of evacuation order in effect.
Three counties in the Big Bend coast, where storm surge could reach heights of 15 feet, issued mandatory evacuation orders for all residents and visitors in its jurisdiction. Officials in Wakulla, Franklin and Taylor counties – home to about 69,000 people – warned residents of the danger posed by the storm and urged them to take it seriously.
'Hurricane Helene is predicted to be a catastrophic and life threatening storm system,' the Taylor County Sheriff's Office said on Facebook. 'This system will be unlike anything we have experienced to date. A curfew is effective from sunset to sunrise. Repeat, this is a MANDATORY EVACUATION ORDER for everyone.'
Leon County, home to Tallahassee, ordered the evacuation of residents from mobile and manufactured homes because of the threat of high winds. "Seek shelter no later than 8 a.m. Thursday," an emergency alert from the county read.
Seventeen other counties stretching across the western coast of the state, from the panhandle to just south of Sarasota, have announced mandatory or voluntary evacuations, according to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Across the state, officials announced closures of government offices and facilities as well as public schools and several major universities.
Helene forecast is a 'nightmare scenario' for parts of North Florida, weather service says
Rick Minor, a county commissioner in Leon County, which encompasses Tallahassee, urged residents to take the approaching storm seriously.
In an email to constituents on Tuesday night, Minor said he was briefed by Leon County Emergency Management officials, who said that if the current track holds, Leon County will suffer a direct hit.
"On Thursday we'll face about six hours of sustained winds of 74-110 mph, leading to thousands of downed trees, more than a hundred blocked roads, hundreds of damaged structures, and many, many days of extended power outages," he said. "But we mustn't panic — fortunately, we all have enough time to carefully plan and prepare."
According to the National Weather Service in Tallahassee, Helene could render some areas "uninhabitable for weeks or months."
Widespread power and communications outages also are expected for prolonged periods.
For those living in Wakulla, Franklin and Taylor counties, National Weather Service forecasters offered a grim wakeup call hours after emergency managers ordered all county residents to evacuate: "This forecast, if realized, is a nightmare surge scenario for Apalachee Bay. Please, please, please take any evacuation orders seriously."
Will Helene hit Mexico and its beaches?
A hurricane warning was in effect for Cabo Catoche to Tulum, Mexico, including Cozumel. Additionally, there was a tropical storm warning in effect for Rio Lagartos to Cabo Catoche, the U.S. hurricane center said. On the forecast track, the center of Helene was expected to move across the eastern Gulf of Mexico later Wednesday and Thursday, according to the hurricane center. Helene is expected to produce total rain accumulations of 4-8 inches over western Cuba, the Cayman Islands and the northeast Yucatan Peninsula, with isolated totals around 12 inches, bringing a "risk of considerable flooding," according to the hurricane center.
What is storm surge and what makes the Gulf vulnerable during Helene?
Along with powerful wind speeds and high rainfall amounts, another deadly hazard is a major concern for the western coast of Florida: storm surge.
In the open ocean, hurricane winds push water toward the center of the storm and instead of piling up, the water spirals downward and flows outward.
As the water is pushed downward, some is pushed out to sea and some is pushed toward the coast. As the storm approaches land and shallow water, the ocean floor blocks the outflowing water, causing the ocean to surge onto land.
Forecasters predict the Helene will wallop the Big Bend coast of Florida with a surge of water as high as 15 feet, while other coastal areas, such as Tampa Bay, could see 8 feet of water. The storm is expected to rapidly intensify into a major hurricane as it churns over the warm waters of the Gulf.
Among the factors making coastal communities along the Gulf of Mexico more vulnerable to piling water is its continental shelves that extend well over 100 miles from the shore. On the Atlantic coast, narrower shelves with steep slopes produce a lower surge.
DeSantis urges Florida residents to prepare for Helene
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Floridians should prepare for a potential major hurricane after he expanded his state of emergency declaration to 61 counties.
"Right now you do have time, so take advantage of that time," DeSantis said. "Review your plan and make sure you're executing your hurricane preparedness plan."
"Don't get wedded to these cones. You could be out of the cone and still have major impacts."
Helene, expected to intensify rapidly, prompts hurricane warning for Florida Gulf Coast
Helene disrupts Gulf oil production
U.S. oil producers scrambled Monday to evacuate staff from Gulf of Mexico oil production platforms as the second hurricane in two weeks was predicted to tear through offshore oil-producing fields.
Oil companies BP, Chevron, and Shell have begun evacuating offshore staff, and several have paused some production. Just two weeks ago, Hurricane Francine roared across the Gulf of Mexico, peaking as a Category 2 with 100-mph winds as it made landfall in Louisiana.
Helene would be Florida's 9th major hurricane hit since 2000
The storm is forecast to become a major hurricane, a Category 3, before approaching the Florida Gulf Coast on Thursday, the National Hurricane Center said.
According to Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach, eight major hurricanes have made landfall in Florida since 2000: Charley and Jeanne in 2004; Dennis and Wilma in 2005; Irma in 2017; Michael in 2018; Ian in 2022; Idalia in 2023.

title: Early voting for the Nov. 5 election is about to begin. Here's what you need to know
author: Erich Murphy
description: Early voting is about to kick off in Illinois. Here's what you need to know if you're thinking about casting a ballot before Nov. 5.
content:
Early voting kicks off in Illinois on Sept. 26.
Here's what you need to know if you plan to vote in the General Election or cast a ballot during the state's early voting period.
Do I have to be registered to vote?
Yes. Anyone wishing to vote in the Nov. 5 election must register. Two forms of identification are required. One must be a government-issued ID.
How do I register to vote?
In Illinois, there are several options. You can register online. You can register in person at your local election office. You can register at the state's driver's license facilities or with a deputy registrar. There is also a mail-in form that can be found on the Illinois Board of Elections website.
Who is eligible to vote?
Voting is available to U.S. citizens over the age of 18. You may not vote in Illinois if you claim the right to vote elsewhere. Incarcerated individuals may not vote.
Is there a residential requirement?
Yes. You must live where you wish to vote for at least 30 days before the election. If you moved shortly before the election, you may be able to vote your old polling place, or you may be able to transfer your registration under grace period registration and voting.
What if I changed my name?
Anyone who has changed their name since they last registered to vote must re-register.
How can I check if I'm registered to vote?
You can check whether you are registered to vote through a portal on the Illinois State Board of Elections Website.
Is there a deadline to register?
Last day for regular registration or transfer of registration using local election authority offices is Oct. 8. Last day for voters to register to using the state's website is Oct. 20.
What is grace period registration?
If you missed the deadline to register to vote locally or online, you can still vote using grace period registration. The grace period runs from the end of regular registration through Election Day. Grace period registration takes place in person at local election offices, as well as at some early voting sites and at certain polling places on Election Day. Those taking advantage of grace period registration are required to vote the same day they register.
When is election day?
Election day is Nov. 5. Polls will be open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Can I vote early?
Anyone registered to vote can take advantage of early voting. Early voting kicks off Sept. 26 and ends Nov. 4. Early voting takes place at local election office. Local offices may designate satellite locations as well as additional dates and times.
Can I vote by mail?
Anyone who is registered to vote can request a ballot to vote by mail. Requests can be submitted through the state's election board website. Mailed requests must be received by Oct. 31. In-person requests must be made by Nov. 4.
If you mail your ballot, it must be postmarked by Election Day and received within two weeks after the election.

title: Pekin church getting a new $4 million parish center. Here's what is included in the project
author: Mike Kramer
description: A project to build a new parish center for St. Joseph's Catholic Church in Pekin bears a $4 million price tag. Parishioners donated $3.7 million.
content:
Construction of a $4 million new parish center at St. Joseph's Catholic Church in Pekin kicked off Friday with a ceremonial ground-breaking.
'This is a glorious day that has been long in coming,' said St. Joseph pastor Father Michael Andrejik. 'It's been anxiously awaited by so many in this parish.'
Andrejik said $3.7 million of the project's cost was funded through donations from parishioners.
Tremont-based CAD Construction Inc. is the general contractor for the project, which will include a building to be used as a gathering space for parish events and business offices, according to St. Joseph's Building Committee chair Bill Fleming. They will replace the former parish center that was built about 70 years ago as a convent.
'It was converted for use as our parish offices and parish gathering place about 40 years ago,' Fleming said. 'Unfortunately, it is no longer functional for our needs; is not energy efficient; and can't be cost-effectively maintained, remodeled, or updated.'

title: Top Illinois high school football games in Peoria area in Week 5 — and our predictions
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: It's Week 5 of Illinois high school football. See our picks for games this week.
content:
It's Week 5 of the Illinois high school football season, and predictions for the IHSA games around Peoria area are in. All games are Friday unless noted.
Last week, the picks in this space went 15-0 (1.000) and are 58-11 (.841) on the season. This year's team records are in parentheses.
Peoria High (4-0, 3-0) at Normal West (2-2, 2-2), 7 p.m.
Peoria High 56, Normal West 31: The Lions are coming off an 86-point effort last week, putting up 780 total yards (448 rushing, 332 passing). TQ Webb caught four balls for 134 yards and three touchdowns, while Kendall Netters rushed for 164 yards and two TDs on 13 carries in one half of action. Last week, Normal West gave up 48 points to Bloomington, but got two TD passes from QB Payne Mefford. Last season, Peoria High won 62-41.
Peoria Notre Dame (2-2, 2-2) at Champaign Centennial (3-1, 3-1), 7 p.m.
Peoria Notre Dame 34, Centennial 28: The Irish rushed for 391 yards paced by Jack Hanley's 227 yards and three TDs against rival Richwoods last week. PND is averaging 59.5 points a game and giving up 14.5 over its last two wins. Centennial QB Kellen Davis-Foltz is a threat on the ground, rushing for 125 yards and 3 TDs off 13 carries last week. Also, watch for Chargers RB Zi'yir Aker, who rushed for 247 yards and 2 TDs. Last season, Centennial won 40-20.
Champaign Central (1-3, 1-2) at Richwoods (1-3, 1-3), 7 p.m.
Richwoods 20, Champaign Central 18: The Knights look to bounce back following a loss to rival PND last week. Richwoods QB Bryce Hopkins threw for 187 yards highlighted by a 70-yard TD pass to Ayce Hawks. Hawks caught five balls for 150 yards against the Irish. After scoring 42 points in its first three weeks, Central ended its seven-game losing streak last week by scoring 59 points against Urbana. Last season, Richwoods won 18-15.
Normal Community (3-1, 3-0) at Manual (0-4, 0-3), 7 p.m.
Normal Community 48, Manual 16: The Rams look to bounce back from last week's lopsided loss to Peoria High. Manual QB Amare Breedlove helped put the Rams on the board with a first-quarter TD. Normal Community saw its 17-game regular season win streak end in Week 4 to Kankakee. Two TD catches by Calen Taylor from Kyle Beaty provided the Ironmen with their two scores. Last season, Normal Community won 42-0.
Limestone (0-4, 0-2) at Washington (2-2, 2-0), 7:30 p.m.
Washington 34, Limestone 21: The Panthers got a late score from A.J. Jones — a 25-yard TD pass from Tyler Humphrey — to seal the victory last week against Pekin. Washington RB Hunter Reed rushed for 164 yards and a TD for the Panthers, who got two field goals from Devin Miller. Limestone was shutout last week against Dunlap after scoring 28 points in Week 3. Last season, Washington 49-0.
Canton (0-4, 0-2) at Metamora (3-1, 1-1), 7:30 p.m.
Metamora 41, Canton 27: The Redbirds had great balance against Morton last week, getting 121 rushing yards by Evan Keil (2 TDs) and 264 passing yards from Stephen Petri (4 total TDs). Canton was a yard short of making an incredible comeback against East Peoria last week. The Little Giants 70-yard hook and lateral play was stopped short. Braxton Rock (two TDs) and Drake Haffner (TD) each had receiving scores for Canton. Last season, Metamora won 53-7.
East Peoria (4-0, 2-0) at Dunlap (3-1, 1-1), 7:30 p.m.
Dunlap 35, East Peoria 28: East Peoria needed a late-game comeback to beat Canton last week. EP QB Dalton Oakman, who threw for 356 yards and 5 TDs, started the game-winning drive with 1:20 left and went 70 yards with no timeouts, finding Aidin Hindert for a 26-yard score with 16 seconds to play. Dunlap had a shutout last week, using a big game from Joey Weeks, who had an interception, forced fumble, fumble recovery and rushing TD. Last season, Dunlap won 47-6.
Pekin (2-2, 1-1) at Morton (1-3, 1-1), 7:30 p.m.
Pekin 15, Morton 14: Pekin is coming off a tough loss to Washington last week. The Dragons scored nine points, getting 112 rushing yards by RB Ty Jackson, 147 passing yards from QB Brogan Benassi and an all-around standout game from WR Dylan Anderson (TD, interception, fumble recovery). The Potters, who got rushing multiple TDs from Isaac Davis and Vian Siems, scored 37 points in a loss for the second time this season. Last season, Morton won 42-14.
Illinois Valley Central (0-4, 0-4) at Fairbury Prairie Central (2-2, 2-2), 7 p.m.
IVC 28, Prairie Central 27: The Grey Ghosts need to win out to become playoff eligible for the first time since a 2019 Class 4A second-round appearance. IVC is averaging 15.6 points a game, while giving up 45.5 points. Prairie Central allowed 3 yards of offense in last week's shutout win over Rantoul. Last season, Prairie Central won 55-20.
Farmington (4-0, 3-0) at Elmwood/Brimfield (4-0, 3-0), 7 p.m.
Farmington 35, Elmwood/Brimfield 34: The Route 78 rivalry is in its 14th regular season meeting since 2010. The Farmers have won the last eight including the seven in the regular season. Elmwood has an impressive rushing attack, averaging 464.8 yards a game. Farmington's defense gives up 13 points a game. Last season, Farmington won 30-26.
Eureka (4-0, 2-0) at Clinton (4-0, 2-0), 7 p.m.
Eureka 49, Clinton 22: The Hornets defense has been impressive, shutting out their last two opponents and having gone the last 108 minutes of game time without allowing a point. Eureka QB Austin Gerber threw for 149 yards and rushed for two TDs last week. Clinton has allowed 29 points this season. Last season, Eureka won 47-28.
Tremont (0-4, 0-2) at Colfax Ridgeview/Lexington (1-3, 0-2), 7 p.m.
Colfax Ridgeview/Lexington 34, Tremont 14: The Turks continue to make strides this season, scoring 12 points last week after scoring 14 in the prior two weeks. Ridgeview has two single-digit losses including a 7-0 defeat to Gibson City-Melvin-Sibley in Week 1. Last season, Ridgeview won 51-0.
Shelbyville (3-1, 1-1) at Dee-Mack (2-2, 0-2), 7 p.m.
Deer Creek-Mackinaw 33, Shelbyville 30: The Chiefs got solid play in last week's loss, using WR Max Eccles (120 receiving, TD) and RB Zack Day (48 yards, TD) to score 14 points. Shelbyville has scored at least 42 points in its three victories, while managing 13 points in a Week 3 loss to Downs Tri-Valley. These teams didn't play last season.
Warrensburg-Latham (3-1, 3-1) at Fieldcrest (1-3, 0-3), 7 p.m.
Warrensburg-Latham 24, Fieldcrest 14: Fieldcrest got in the win column last week, getting a big week from Eddie Lorton, who rushed for three TDs and returned a punt for a score. Warrensburg-Latham's lone loss was a three-point defeat to Gibson City-Melvin-Sibley in Week 2. These teams didn't play last season.
Princeville (4-0, 3-0) at United (0-4, 0-3), 7 p.m.
Princeville 42, United 20: Princeville QB Jake Williams has stepped up big this season, throwing for 172 yards and 4 TDs in last week's win. He hooked up with WRs Jett Benningfield (35 yards, 2 TDs) and Brady Day (59 yards, 2 TDs) four times each. United suffered a six-point loss to ROWVA/Williamsfield in Week 3. Last season, Princeville won 36-20.
8-player: Galva (0-4) at Peoria Heights (0-4), 7 p.m.
Peoria Heights 42, Galva 38: The Patriots are looking for their first win of the season, having scored 14 points against last season's state runner-up AlWood Ridgewood. Galva has scored 42 total points this season. This is the first of back-to-back meetings between Galva and Peoria Heights. Last season, Peoria Heights won 30-14.

title: Illinois-Penn State 'College GameDay' predictions: Who picked Illini, Nittany Lions?
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Here's who the 'College GameDay' crew picked between Illinois and Penn State.
content:
After plenty of talking and pregame drama, the Illinois and Penn State football teams are ready to meet on the field Saturday night.
For coach Bret Bielema and the No. 21 Fighting Illini, Saturday's game will be a chance to assert themselves as a legitimate threat to contend in the Big Ten after a 31-24 overtime win last week against Nebraska. Penn State, No. 8 in the US LBM Coaches Poll, remains a contender for the new 12-team College Football Playoff and in the Big Ten.
Though their game didn't earn the 'College GameDay' treatment — ESPN's popular pregame show was broadcasting from Tuscaloosa, Alabama, ahead of Saturday night's game between No. 4 Alabama and No. 2 Georgia — the matchup between Illinois and Penn State is one of the biggest on the Week 5 calendar. The game is scheduled to kick off at 6:30 p.m. from Beaver Stadium in University Park, Pennsylvania. The game is broadcast on NBC and streams on Peacock.
What did 'GameDay' say about Illinois-Penn State?
Pat McAfee of the "College GameDay" crew was excited about the Illini, pointing out their solid quarterback play behind Luke Altmyer and receivers Pat Bryant and Zakhari Franklin. He said the large point spread put the Illini and Bielema "right where they want to be."
Host Rece Davis brought up Bielema's oft-discussed comment about " White Out energy, whatever the hell that means" (but left out the full context). Fellow panelist Desmond Howard jumped in and said the Illini were about to "eff around and find out," highlighting the Penn State offense behind QB Drew Allar.
'I love what I see from this Penn State offense," Howard said. "It's gonna be a great game tonight in Happy Valley.'

title: Popular comedian and ventriloquist will perform in Peoria. Here's what to know
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Tickets go on sale Monday, Oct. 7, for the Peoria Civic Center performance.
content:
Stand-up comedian and ventriloquist Jeff Dunham will bring his "suitcase posse" to Peoria for an April show at the Civic Center Arena. Tickets go on sale Monday, Oct. 7.
Dunham has been called "the country's most popular stand-up comedian" by Slate.com. He has appeared on numerous late-night TV shows and starred in multiple comedy specials. He holds the Guinness Book of World Records mark for most tickets sold for a stand-up comedy tour, according to his website.
Dunham's ventriloquist career began with a gifted toy dummy at age 9 in Texas. He began dreaming of characters "who could say what nobody else would dare," his website adds.
He has since crafted a stable of such, among them the crusty Walter and the eager and curious Peanut.
His latest tour, "Artificial Intelligence," will include a stop in Peoria on April 12, 2025. Tickets go on sale at 10 a.m. Oct. 7 and can be purchased at Ticketmaster.com.

title: 6 biggest games left on the 2024 IHSA Peoria-area football schedule
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: 12 teams, six games: The biggest matchups left on the IHSA schedule in the 2024 Peoria-area season.
content:
Things have begun to shake out among Peoria-area high school football teams.
The playoff picture is becoming more and more clear as the season heads into Week 6. Several Peoria-area teams — Eureka, Farmington, Macomb, Monmouth-Roseville, Princeville and Stark County — became playoff-eligible this past Friday, but there are many more games of note left on the schedule.
Here are the six of the biggest games remaining on the 2024 IHSA Peoria-area football schedule.
Week 6 | Macomb at Farmington, 7 p.m.
Farmington's win over Elmwood/Brimfield in Week 5 helped put itself in the driver's seat with Macomb for a LincolnLand-Large Division crown. The Farmers haven't forgotten their blowout loss to eventual Prairieland Conference champion Macomb two years ago. Things don't get easier for Macomb, which heads to Elmwood in Week 7.
Week 7 | Stark County at Princeville, 7 p.m.
Princeville and Stark County are on a collision course for the LincolnLand-Small Division championship. The Princes are fresh off beating United in Week 5 with one-win South Fulton awaiting this week. Meanwhile, Stark County has a date with ROWVA/Williamsfield this week after splitting a pair of games last season including a R/W playoff win.
Week 7 | Dunlap at Washington, 7:30 p.m.
Dunlap finds itself in a great spot, having beaten East Peoria in Week 5. The Eagles play Canton this week, giving them a great opportunity to be 5-1 heading into Week 7. If Washington beats East Peoria this week, the Panthers will still be undefeated in Mid-Illini Conference play and welcoming Dunlap to Babcook Field.
Week 8 | Downs Tri-Valley at Eureka, 7 p.m.
After beating Clinton in Week 5, Eureka has a path to become the inaugural champion of the Heart of Central Illinois-Large Division. The Hornets play Colfax Ridgeview/Lexington and Tremont this week and in Week 7, a pair of teams with a combined 2-8 record. Tri-Valley has to beat Clinton this week to set up this de facto championship game.
Week 9 | Peoria High at Normal Community, 7 p.m.
This game could be the de facto Big 12 Conference title game. A look ahead to Peoria High's schedule shows undefeated Bloomington in Week 8 as the only potential obstacle. Normal Community, which suffered its lone loss to nonconference foe Kankakee in Week 4, would need to beat Bloomington this week to setup this meeting.
Week 9 | Pekin at East Peoria, 7:30 p.m.
East Peoria losing to Dunlap in Week 5 starts a gauntlet schedule of traditional Mid-Illini contenders over the next three weeks — Washington, Morton and Metamora. The Raiders could be 4-4 with a must-win situation at home against Pekin. With Pekin beating Morton in Week 5, the Dragons can earn their fourth win against host Metamora in Week 6.

title: Big Ten Basketball 2024 Preseason Team: Purdue's Braden Smith named Player of Year ahead of season
author: John Leuzzi
description: The Big Ten conference announced some preseason basketball awards, including Player of the Year and All-Big Ten team. Here's more:
content:
It's never too early for basketball.
The Big Ten conference reminded the college basketball world of that Tuesday afternoon, as it announced the conference's 2024-25 Preseason All-Big Ten Team and the Preseason Player of the Year with just a little over a month to go under opening day.
Purdue guard Braden Smith was named the Preseason Player of the Year by the media, marking the second consecutive season that the Boilermakers and Matt Painter had one of their players receive the nod.
The upcoming 2024-25 college basketball season will mark the first year that UCLA, USC, Oregon and Washington will compete as members of the Big Ten, as all four programs departed from the Pac-12 this past offseason.
Aside from Smith, headlining the 2024-25 Preseason All-Big Ten Team is Rutgers star freshman guard Dylan Harper, who was ranked the No. 3 player in the 2024 recruiting class by 247Sports Composite rankings. Indiana center Oumar Ballo and Penn State guard Ace Baldwin Jr. were also named to the list among others.
The Big Ten basketball preseason poll was not released on Tuesday. Big Ten Media Day is set for Thursday, Oct. 2 in Rosemont, Illinois. The Big Ten basketball tournament will take place in Indianapolis this year at Gainbridge Fieldhouse from Wednesday, March 12-Sunday, March 16.
Here's a look at who made a spot on the All-Big Ten preseason team, including who was selected as the preseason Player of the Year:
2024 Big Ten basketball Preseason Player of the Year
Purdue guard Braden Smith was named Tuesday the Big Ten basketball preseason Player of the Year.
The 6-foot guard is coming off his best season in a Boilermaker uniform last year, one in which he helped Purdue reach the national championship game alongside Zac Edey. Smith averaged 12.0 points, 7.5 assists and 5.8 rebounds in 39 games last season. His 292 total assists last season was a Purdue and Big Ten record.
As noted by Purdue, Smith joined BYU's Kyle Collinsworth as just the two players in NCAA history to finish with at least 450 points, 275 assists and 225 rebounds in a season last year.

title: Why the Peoria Rivermen got a wave of talent just days before SPHL season opener
author: Dave Eminian
description: The Peoria Rivermen will likely have received 10 players down from ECHL training camps by the time Tuesday night arrives. Opening night is Friday.
content:
PEORIA — Here comes the cavalry.
The Peoria Rivermen received a wave of players from ECHL camps on Monday morning that changed the outlook for their team in the early going. The defending SPHL champions ave nine players down from Double-A training camps and could get more.
They'll have to get them into practices and sort through lineup possibilities in time for their SPHL 2024-25 season opener at Quad City on Friday.
Who did the Peoria Rivermen add?
Rivermen winger Mike Gelatt — a key producer for the team's championship last spring — and defenseman Josh Martin both arrived from ECHL Bloomington. Defenseman Nick Aromatario came down from Trois-Rivieres, while defenseman Chase Spencer was due to arrive Monday night from ECHL Tulsa and goaltender Troy Kobryn was on the way from ECHL Tulsa. Goaltender Colby Muise came in from ECHL Atlanta. Forward Jake Vaughan was expected to arrive some time Tuesday from ECHL South Carolina's camp.
In addition, key Rivermen defenseman Renat Dadadzhanov was scheduled to be in ECHL Maine's camp, but he had issues getting his border paperwork ready in time. He never skated in Maine's camp, and he's believed to be headed now to the Rivermen as a 10th player technically coming down from the ECHL.
"We're excited to have all these guys join us," Rivermen coach Jean-Guy Trudel said. "It will make our camp more competitive. There's a lot of talent, a lot of skill in this group and we have get it all put together in the next few days. So we have work to do."
A pair of newbies
Among the players coming in from ECHL camps were two new players, forward Frankie Trazzera and defenseman Brock Bartholomew, signed by the Rivermen on Monday.
Bartholomew, 23, is a 6-foot-4, 200-pound blueliner down from ECHL Wichita's camp. A project for Rivermen head coach Jean-Guy Trudel, he turned pro in 2022-23 with Alfta GIF in Sweden's tier-2 pro league. He broke out for 23 goals and 40 assists in 53 games last season for the Hull Seahawks in the National Ice Hockey League, Britain's secondary pro level.
Trazzerra, 26, is a 6-foot-4, 225-pound forward coming from ECHL Allen's camp. He played four years of junior hockey for Lone Star in the NAHL, serving as captain in his final season. He moved on to play four seasons for NCAA Div.-III Trine University, then turned pro last season with Elmira in the FPHL (7 goals, 3 assists in 16 games).
Still battling for ECHL jobs
The Rivermen could still get more players as several of their signings are still sticking with ECHL teams in camp.
Trudel's son, winger Tristan Trudel, is with Fort Wayne. Veteran winger Tyler Kobryn is with Florida, winger Cole Crowder is with Worcester and center John Kaljian is at Allen.
ECHL teams open their 2024-25 season this weekend, as does the SPHL.

title: Rockford area animal shelter runs at-capacity, celebrates $2.4 million renovation
author: Cayden Lewis
description: Winnebago County Animal Services adds 4,385 square feet and a number of upgrades to provide better level of care to dogs and cats in need.
content:
Winnebago County Animal Services celebrated the conclusion of long-awaited upgrades to its facility Friday with a ribbon-cutting ceremony.
'It's a great day for Winnebago County to have this expansion officially open.' said Joe Chiarelli, chairman of the Winnebago County Board. 'It's increased by 4,000 square feet, which I learned today is already at full capacity. It's a constant need. We have a lot of animals that come in here for care.'
While the facility at 4517 N. Main St. in Rockford got a 4,385-square-feet addition, the $2.4 million renovation focused heavily on upgrades to existing spaces and making sure the shelter is able to provide adequate accommodations for the animals in need.
The project included the addition of three new dog rooms, new cat enclosures, an exam room, exercise yards, a new intake area and an improved customer service area.
'Currently, we're housing approximately 100 dogs and 70 cats.' Animal Services Administrator Jennifer Stacy said. 'That's more than we want to hold, for them to have double sided cages and the space that they need.'
To help with the constant flow of animals, Winnebago County Animal Services hosts promotions for adoptions and partnerships with several PetSmart locations to help increase the chances of animals getting adopted.
'We have to make sure adoption needs are met.' Chiarelli said. 'We just added 4,000 square feet, and it's already full again.'
The project was funded through the American Rescue Plan and approved by the Winnebago County Board.
Huffman Keel Partners, a development company operating out of Wisconsin, helped manage the project by providing assistance with budgeting, scheduling and coordination.
'Expenses on a project like this include soft costs, such as architectural costs, permitting fees with the city, contractor costs, and fixture costs for all of the cages and equipment that goes into the new space.' said Jeff Duesterbeck, project manager for Huffman Keel Partners.
'I think we're done for now.' Stacy said in reference to future renovations. 'We'll focus now on different workflows and things like that.'
Winnebago County Animal Services cares for an average of 4,000 animals a year. It is the sole government-run animal services organization, serving all of the municipalities in the county.
The public is encouraged to visit animal services to see the updated facility and perhaps adopt an animal. Winnebago County Animals Services is waiving adoption fees on Tuesday, Oct. 15.
Adoption hours are 11 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and 11 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Saturday.

title: 'Could be worse': Hackers replace Illinois history content with hot takes on 'Star Wars'
author: Jeff Kolkey
description: The non-profit Illinois State Historical Society is rebuilding its Facebook audience after hackers took over its page to post about 'Star Wars.'
content:
History lovers saw sudden changes a month ago to the Illinois State Historical Society Facebook page.
Its detailed Illinois history lessons were suddenly gone.
In their place were essays, memes, hot takes and deep dives on the 'Star Wars' movie franchise.
A hacker had somehow seized control of the page, changed the name from " Illinois State Historical Society" to just "Historical Society," and began populating it with content that had nothing to do with history and everything to do with a fictional battle in a galaxy far, far away between good and evil.
After a decade of building an avid social media audience, the not-for-profit Illinois State Historical Society had been locked out of its own Facebook page, Executive Director William Furry said.
" W e had lots of friends who cared about Illinois history, and then all of a sudden they all were receiving these things about 'Star Wars,' which is probably not a horrible hack if you're going to have a hack," Furry said during a phone interview. "It could be a lot worse than what it turned out to be. It's pretty Innocuous and tame content. Nothing to call attention to all the unfactual history they could be posting up there instead."
Accustomed to content describing events in Illinois history like the Chicago Tylenol tampering murders that led to a massive acetaminophen recall in October 1982, the feeds of the Society's more than 7,000 followers were instead flooded with pronouncements like Darth "Vader would be invincible then with Beskar armour."
The Springfield-based Society has established a new Facebook page which carries the name of its original. So far it has about 175 followers. It has been working with Facebook to shut down the old page which remains under the control of a hacker, but it is a slow process.
Furry said he has sent Meta his identification and other information to have the page closed without success so far.
"We've talked to Facebook, and there's just such a bureaucracy involved in trying to get Meta to do anything helpful," Furry said. "It's so much easier to create one than it is to take one down."
Furry said the hackers engineered a "take over, not a hostile take over," making no demands nor asking for any ransom. It's not clear how it happened or where the hacker or hackers are from, though it's possible they are from overseas. Furry has not so far reported the incident to any law enforcement agency.
Furry said the Historical Society is working to rebuild its audience and is hoping its followers find their way back.
"We want to make sure people who love Illinois history can find us," Furry said. "That's really what this is about. Anybody who's searching for real history or wants to find out more about history — we want them to find us. It could be somebody in Illinois or in Colorado or in Beijing."

title: Illinois launches new DMV kiosks for license renewal and stickers. What you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Illinois is making it easier for you to renew your driver's license and get your new license plate stickers. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Need to renew your license but don't want to wait in line at the DMV or go online to do it? Good news, many Illinois residents have a faster way they can get their license plate stickers.
The state launched a new pilot program where residents can renew their license and get their license plate stickers right from a kiosk.
Here's what you need to know.
The kiosks can quickly print vehicle registration renewals and plate stickers. Customers seeking a driver's license or state ID renewal can receive temporary documents from the kiosk while their new card is mailed to them.
There will be 15 Fast-Lane kiosks initially rolled out.
More: Giannoulias reveals program to cut down DMW wait times
Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias announced expanded online services at the DMV in January, aimed at eliminating unnecessary trips to DMV facilities and cutting down wait times for those who still go.
"I'm serious. Don't come unless you are 100% certain that you need to visit one of our facilities," Giannoulias said at an earlier press conference. "The reason is obvious. Most people do not need to go to a DMV facility to get what they need."

title: Will lawmakers and congressional candidates commit to upholding the 2024 results? We asked
author: Sudiksha Kochi
description: USA TODAY surveyed the members of Congress running for re-election, asking if they'd uphold the presidential results.
content:
WASHINGTON ‒ With nearly half of the country's Republicans and a quarter of Democrats questioning whether next month's presidential election will be fair, USA TODAY wanted to know where members of the next Congress stand on the issue.
So, we surveyed all 382 members of the House and 91 Senators who are either running for re-election or would still be in office in January, asking whether they would uphold the 2024 presidential election results, regardless of the winner. (The remaining lawmakers who were not surveyed either lost their primary races, are seeking a different office or are retiring from Congress.)
We also polled 747 candidates running for the House and Senate whose names are on the ballot this year. USA TODAY couldn't find contact information for 23 additional candidates.
Those who agreed without condition to support the results of the election, regardless of whether Republican Donald Trump or Democrat Kamala Harris is declared the winner include:
114 sitting House members, 14 of whom are Republicans and 100 are Democrats;
26 sitting Senate members, 2 of whom are Republicans and 24 Democrats;
228 candidates for House and Senate, including 126 Democrats, 43 Republicans and 59 third-party candidates.
After the 2020 election, when then-President Donald Trump didn't want to accept that he had lost his bid for re-election against President Joe Biden, he tried to convince members of Congress to raise objections to the votes of several state's electors.
Typically, Congress simply witnesses the counting of the electors' votes. Under the Electoral Count Act of 1887, only a single member of the House and Senate was required to object to electors and state the reason for objection in writing.
On Jan. 6, 2021, after rioters were cleared from the U.S. Capitol, 139 Republicans in the House and eight Republicans in the Senate objected to the electoral votes from Pennsylvania and Arizona, hoping to keep Trump in office.
All Democrats in both congressional chambers accepted the 2020 election results. Numerous recounts, reviews and forensic audits have found the election outcome to be legitimate, and Trump himself has publicly acknowledged that he lost to Biden by a "whisker."
Since then, lawmakers passed the Electoral Count Reform Act ‒ a modernized version of the 1887 law ‒ so that objections must be signed by at least one-fifth of the members of the House and one-fifth of the Senators.
The Congress elected this year, which will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2025, will witness the counting of the electoral votes three days later. Whether they will accept the results and the winner is the question.
Formality turned political
One example of how fraught this largely ceremonial practice has become: A Republican lawmaker who once eloquently defended the importance of Congress upholding the election results won't commit to doing so again.
'Congress cannot overrule millions of votes certified by those states. It's a threat to our federalist system and would play into the hands of those seeking to end the Electoral College,' Congresswoman Victoria Spartz, of Indiana, said in 2021.
But recently, Spartz, who held off eight Republican primary challengers, answered USA TODAY's query by saying: 'This question cannot be answered now, since we do not know what is going to happen in November and what the circumstances will be.'
Fairness is in the eye of the beholder
A dozen sitting House members and four Senators said they would only certify the election results if they believed the results to be 'fair,' which they defined in various ways.
'You got to stick to what the law says, what the Constitution says," Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican of Missouri told USA TODAY.
"Look as long as everybody's following election law in the states, I have no problem," said Byron Donalds, a Republican Congressman whose district covers much of Southwest Florida, including Fort Myers and Naples. Donalds voted against certification in 2021.
Notably, two Republican senators who upheld the 2020 election results also attached certain caveats to accepting this year's results.
Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La. said he would want the process of appeals to be exhausted before he would accept any results.
Susan Collins, R-Maine., said she would uphold the results as long as she believed "the election was conducted in a fair way." Collins was one of the main instigators of the Electoral Count Reform Act, which she said would hopefully avoid "another Jan. 6."
Among Democrats, Rep. Frederica Wilson, of Florida, was one of seven sitting legislators who expressed concerns about election fairness.
'Under normal circumstances, I would fully accept and certify the election results without hesitation," she told USA TODAY.
But she and other Democrats were upset about a recent move to hand-count ballots in Georgia, which she said could open the results up to abuse. A Georgia judge blocked the rule Tuesday after USA TODAY conducted the interviews, but Republicans are appealing the ruling.
Still, she said, "should any lawsuits arise, once the U.S. Justice Department has completed the legal process and (reviewed the) election process, I will accept and certify the election results, no matter the outcome."
Rep. Betty McCollum, D-Minn., said that 'any Republican effort to once again impose phony electors to rig the electoral college will be met with my full resistance when the U.S. House is required to certify the election.'
No answer and non-answers
A total of thirty lawmakers and candidates responded but said they couldn't answer USA TODAY's question.
'How can I commit to anything with an election that hasn't taken place yet?' said Rep. Lauren Boebert, a Republican of Colorado, adding she still has the same hesitations about the results that she did in 2020, when she declined to certify.
Republican candidate Randall Arrington, who's running in Louisiana, said he couldn't commit one way or the other but would make a decision based on his "rational assessment of the election process, and whether or not voter fraud has taken place."
Other House and Senate lawmakers declined to respond at all, including 201 Republicans, 100 Democrats and two independents.
One of those, Republican Sen. JD Vance, of Ohio, Trump's running mate, did not answer whether he would challenge this year's election results in the vice presidential debate earlier this month. However, at a campaign stop in Pennsylvania Thursday, Vance said that Trump did not lose in the 2020 election "by the words I would use."
House Speaker Mike Johnson did not reply to USA TODAY's request for comment, but said in a press conference last month that he would follow the Constitution if the election is free, fair and safe. Johnson shepherded an amicus brief in support of a Texas lawsuit aimed at overturning the 2020 election results in four swing states.
Agreeing to certify
Only one lawmaker who voted against certification in 2021 said he would uphold the results this time, regardless of the outcome. Rep. John Carter, R-Texas, told USA TODAY in an interview at the Capitol that 'if Congress does have to certify, I will certify."
Among the candidates, some are making election integrity an issue in their campaign.
About half of the Democrats and third-party candidates are running in deep red states against opponents who objected to the electoral results in 2021.
'I have a problem with any incumbent and any person who was there that voted to not certify the election results,' said Rodney Govens, a Democrat running in Arkansas' first congressional district against Rep. Rick Crawford, a Republican.
Others are running in races where the incumbent could lose. Although it could enable election deniers to come into office, several candidates said they would uphold the 2024 election results ‒ including two Republicans running in toss-up seats in Pennsylvania and Colorado.
Two lawmakers, Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., and Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., spearheaded a bipartisan unity agreement to acknowledge that the election winner is certified on Jan. 6, 2025, and serve as a voice for calm, hoping to avoid a repeat of the violence of Jan. 6, 2021.
"Peaceful transfer of power is a key part as core to our Constitution, our democracy and it's our responsibility to give the American people faith in our electoral process," Gottheimer told USA TODAY.
Twenty-nine other Democrats and five other moderate Republicans up for re-election ‒ many of them running in tight races ‒ signed the pledge.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, from North Dakota, didn't sign but was among 10 Republicans who told USA TODAY they would uphold the 2024 election results regardless of the results.
'Our role is not to determine whether to certify or not, but our role is to certify when the real certification happens at 50 states and some territories," Cramer said. "That's the way I view it … It's really the state's jobs to certify the electors, and then ours is to sort of validate that."

title: Election: Supporters rally for sales tax that helps 'anyone and everyone' in Rockford area
author: Jeff Kolkey
description: Leaders from across the Rockford area showed their support for a 0.5 percentage point mental health sales tax up for renewal on the Nov. 5 ballot.
content:
Supporters are rallying for renewal of a half-percentage point mental health sales tax, saying it is successfully changing the region's mental health and substance abuse treatment landscape.
If a Nov. 5 referendum to renew the tax were to fail, it would threaten the existence of more than three dozen programs it makes possible, referendum advocate and former Winnebago County State's Attorney Paul Logli said during a rally Monday night.
"I hope when people get to that part of the ballot that they will vote in favor of it," Logli said. "It is incredibly important. It is bringing in about $14 million a year. It is now funding dozens of agencies and programs that are providing mental health services for thousands of people — adults and children."
Those programs have benefitted nearly 18,000 Winnebago County residents, including 11,420 who suffer from serious mental illness and 3,527 who struggle with substance use disorders.
The sales tax was first approved in 2020 and is up for a five-year renewal.
A small group of supporters joined the Citizens for a Healthy Community Committee at the Prairie Street Brewhouse on Monday to rally for the referendum's approval and the continuation of financial support for programs that help residents get counseling and treatment, help families care for loved ones and help save lives.
Money from the tax helps support a crisis co-responder program that teams police officers with counselors from Rosecrance who specialize in de-escalating potentially volatile situations involving mental health crisis. It pays for mental health care programming in the Winnebago County Jail.
It also funds expanded substance use disorder treatment services, new counseling services that were never before available for families suffering with mental illness and is providing funding for youth intervention programs that are aimed at helping traumatized and at-risk young people.
The mental health and substance use disorder treatment services that the sales tax helps support are saving lives, said State Rep. Maurice West, D-Rockford. He said other parts of the state are looking at Rockford and Winnebago County as a model of how to combat it.
"Mental health is a nonpartisan issue," West said. "It has no respect for you as a person. It doesn't care if you are a Democrat or a Republican, Black or white, gay or straight, cute or ugly. Mental health can effect anyone and everyone."
Sales taxes are taxes paid on general merchandise. The county's mental health sales tax has been set at 0.5 percent or half a cent on every $100 spent on qualifying purchases.

title: New hearing date set for former sheriff's deputy charged with Massey's murder
author: Steven Spearie
description: The hearing for the former sheriff's deputy charged with Sonya Massey's murder came on the same day as the first Massey Commission hearing.
content:
Family members and friends of Sonya Massey, who was fatally shot in her home by a f ormer Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy on July 6, were still finding seats in a courtroom when Monday's hearing ended.
In the less than 90-second proceeding before Presiding Circuit Judge Ryan Cadagin, Sean P. Grayson, charged with Massey's murder, was given a new status hearing for Dec. 2.
That is expected to be closer to a Fourth District Appellate Court ruling regarding Grayson's ongoing detention in Menard County.
As with his previous hearing, Grayson wasn't in court but appeared by Zoom seated next to his attorney, Daniel Fultz.
Another of Grayson's attorneys, Mark Wykoff, was present in the courtroom and asked for the new date.
Cadagin has ruled Grayson, 30, be jailed in accordance with the Pre-Trial Fairness Act.
At Grayson's July 18 arraignment, Cadagin cited the former deputy's callousness during and after the shooting of Massey, a 36-year-old Black mother of two who had called 911 about a prowler, including not rendering help to her.
The defense appealed the decision.
About 25 to 30 members of Massey's family and other friends attended Monday's hearing, but some weren't even seated when the hearing finished.
After the hearing, family members huddled in the state's attorney's office to debrief.
Among those attending Monday was Donna Massey, Sonya Massey's mother.
"The family is definitely committed (to this trial)," said Teresa Haley of Haley & Associates, speaking for the Massey family afterwards. "We had more family members here than at the first and second hearings."
Haley admitted the Massey family is "struggling," but is getting educated on the court process.
"It's definitely justice being delayed, but it's process," Haley admitted. "We all have to go through something to get to something and we're hoping in the end we receive victory and that (Grayson) is fully prosecuted for first-degree murder."
The hearing came on the same day as the first Massey Commission hearing, which will consider testimony regarding a proposal for an independent review of the Sangamon County Sheriff's department's procedures.
Shadia Massey, a cousin of Sonya Massey's who is serving as a commission co-chair, attended the court hearing as did another cousin and commission, Sontae Massey.
Grayson has pleaded not guilty.

title: Seriously, Stormy Daniels bringing stand-up comedy act to central Illinois
author: Steven Spearie
description: Adult film star Stormy Daniels is coming back to the Springfield area next month as the headliner of a comedy show.
content:
Adult film star and director Stormy Daniels, whose alleged tryst with Donald Trump in 2006 led to the former president being found guilty of 34 felony counts of falsifying business records as part of a conspiracy to unlawfully interfere in the 2016 election, will headline a comedy show at the Backroom Lounge in Riverton on Nov. 11.
A 6 p.m. show quickly sold out and owner Jeb Brown added a 9 p.m. show.
The venue seats 50 people. Tickets are $100.
Trump, in a neck-and-neck race with Vice President Kamala Harris in the Nov. 5 election, paid the actress $130,000 as part of an agreement in which Daniels would keep quiet about the alleged sexual encounter.
Trump has denied the affair with Daniels, whose real name is Stephanie Clifford.
The former president is awaiting sentencing.
In March 2019, Daniels made several stops in Springfield, including at Déjà Vu Showgirls nightclub. She also appeared at the Abraham Lincoln statue at the Illinois Capitol railing against the Live Adult Entertainment Surcharge Tax, or "pole tax" leveled against dancers.
Joining Daniels at the Riverton show will be nationally touring comedians Copenhagen Bandit and Nina Kern.
Brown said the show has received some national attention. On Monday, he did a 15-minute interview with MSNBC host Rachel Maddow about booking Daniels.
Maddow recently reported that a Trump attorney allegedly tried to work out a deal about what Daniels owes Trump over a 2018 failed defamation suit if she agreed not to talk about Trump leading up to the election.
"Some people have let politics completely take over their lives and they've forgotten how to laugh," Brown said. "I'm sure there are going to be some political jokes in her segment. We're glad we can all come together and get some laughs out of the deal."
Brown said he originally had thought about scheduling the show on election night but thought the better of it.
All of the comedians are donating, after costs, proceeds to local veterans groups, Brown said.

title: Los Angeles is Big Ten women's basketball mecca in first USA TODAY Sports Network rankings
author: Dargan Southard
description: USC and UCLA were easy choices atop the first Big Ten women's basketball power rankings. Who comes next? Where does Iowa rank without Caitlin Clark?
content:
The Big Ten's West Coast arrival has had a significant impact on the league's women's basketball landscape, arguably more so than any other sport.
Particularly with USC and UCLA joining — two national-title contenders in 2024-25 — the Big Ten has never had a stronger women's basketball product than it will this year. Just when the league wrapped up its spotlight run alongside superstar Caitlin Clark, here comes player of the year candidate JuJu Watkins to grab the baton. An exciting Big Ten season is ahead.
Unsurprisingly, the Trojans and Bruins are slotted atop the first USA TODAY Sports Network power rankings for women's basketball. Who comes next is where things get interesting.
1. USC
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Ole Miss
What to know: JuJu Watkins terrorized the Pac 12 last season. The Big Ten is likely going to meet the same outcome.
2. UCLA
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Louisville
What to know: Who's the best women's basketball team in Los Angeles? The Bruins certainly feel they have a case with Lauren Betts and Kiki Rice in the fold.
3. Ohio State
What to know: Cotie McMahon is back and ready to dominate in Columbus once again.
4. Indiana
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Brown
What to know: The post-Mackenzie Holmes era begins in Bloomington with plenty of potential for more success.
5. Maryland
Season opener: Nov. 4 at UMBC
What to know: After an uncharacteristically down year for Brenda Frese's squad, guard Shyanne Sellers is determined to lead a Maryland rebound.
6. Iowa
Season opener: Nov. 6 vs. Northern Illinois
What to know: No Caitlin Clark, no Lisa Bluder but still plenty of promise for the Hawkeyes. Transfer Lucy Olsen leads the next wave of Iowa women's basketball under Jan Jensen.
7. Nebraska
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Omaha
What to know: Alexis Markowski is one of the conference's best and will try to put the Cornhuskers among the league elite squads.
8. Michigan State
Season opener: Nov. 5 vs. Oakland
What to know: The Spartans are eyeing a deeper NCAA Tournament after a first-round exit last season. The Spartans have the pieces to do so.
9. Minnesota
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Central Connecticut
What to know: It's been a minute since Minnesota had a squad among the Big Ten's best. A run to the NIT championship game last season could be the catalyst for a turnaround.
10. Illinois
Season opener: Nov. 7 vs. Florida State
What to know: A WBIT title last season softened the blow from a disappointing year. The Illini are hoping to rekindle success from two years ago and make the NCAA Tournament again.
11. Michigan
What to know: There's no easing into this season with an opener against the defending champs. A stunner could ignite a strong Wolverines season.
12. Washington
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Seattle
What to know: The Huskies haven't made the NCAA Tournament since Kelsey Plum departed. Joining the Big Ten will make ending that drought even tougher.
13. Oregon
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. California Baptist
What to know: Oregon, too, is still trying to find its way after its run in the national spotlight with Sabrina Ionescu. The Ducks will be looking for their first win since Jan. 14.
14. Wisconsin
What to know: Can anything substantial develop around defending defensive player of the year Serah Williams?
15. Penn State
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Bucknell
What to know: Makenna Marisa is gone. Who comes next in Penn State's line of standouts?
16. Purdue
What to know: A promising start fizzled quickly last season in West Lafayette. Purdue will hunt more consistency this season in trying to return to the NCAA Tournament.
17. Rutgers
Season opener: Nov. 4 vs. Manhattan
What to know: The Scarlet Knights have fallen on tough times after once standing as a premier women's basketball program. Avoiding the cellar is good starting point.
18. Northwestern
What to know: The Wildcats can only go up after a 9-21 campaign a year ago. Climbing quickly in this league, though, isn't easy.

title: Meet Illinois basketball roster: Breaking down the Fighting Illini ahead of 2024-25 season
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The Journal Star takes a look at the members of the Illinois men's basketball 2024-25 roster.
content:
The Illinois basketball team came together last season under coach Brad Underwood and had one its best seasons in a generation, winning the Big Ten Conference Tournament and advancing to the Elite Eight of the NCAA Tournament.
The Illini lost their top scorers to either the pros or the transfer portal, including superstar wing Terrance Shannon Jr. and crafty point guard Marcus Domask. Athletic wing Coleman Hawkins is now at Kansas State.
Now Illinois has reloaded with a deft mix of talent across the transfer portal, preps and abroad. Here is a look at each player listed on the 2024-25 roster — split by transfers, international players, high school recruits and returnees.
Illinois transfers
Kylan Boswell, No. 4, junior guard
The 6-2, 205-pound native of Champaign is back home after transferring from Arizona, where is started nearly every game for the 27-9 Wildcats, who made the Sweet 16 of the NCAA Tournament. He averaged 9.6 points, 3.6 assists and 2.3 rebounds.
Ben Humrichous, No. 3, graduate student forward
The 6-9, 225-pound Indiana native is a transfer from Evansville who started 24 games last season, leading the Missouri Valley Conference team with 14.7 points per game. The NAIA transfer was second on the team in rebounding at 4.7 per game and was named to the MVC All-Newcomer Team.
Carey Booth, No. 0, sophomore forward
The 6-foot-10, 215-pounder transferred from Notre Dame, where the Colorado native averaged 20 minutes across 33 games. He's a versatile big man with the ability to shoot the 3. He averaged 6.4 points, 4.3 rebounds for ND.
Jake Davis, No. 15, sophomore forward
The 6-6, 205-pound Indiana native transferred from mid-major Mercer, where he was among the team's leaders in scoring (9.0 ppg) and rebounding (4.5 rpg) while starting 25 games. He shot a nearly 40 percent from 3-point range (60-for-155) for the Southern Conference program.
Tre White, No. 22, junior guard
The 6-7, 210-pound Texas native is a transfer from Louisville, where he averaged 12.3 points, 5.9 rebounds and shot 45.6 percent in 26 starts as a sophomore. The four-star recruit, originally recruited by Illinois, played his freshman season at USC.
Tomislav Ivisic, No. 13, freshman center
The 7-1, 255-pound Croatian is a "modern-day 5 man," according to coach Brad Underwood. He averaged 6.4 points, 3.5 rebounds, 0.9 assists and 0.5 blocks with SC Derby, for which he played three seasons. He also played with Croatia in the FIBA U16 world championships.
Kasparas Jakucionis, No. 32, freshman guard
The 6-6, 205-pound Lithuanian is an accomplished international player who averaged 19,2 points, 6.6 rebounds, 5.7 assists and 1.6 steals while playing for FC Barelona's second team. He represented Lithuania at the FIBA U16 and U18 European championships.
Illinois high school recruits
Will Riley, No. 7, freshman forward
The 6-8, 195-pound Canadian is a prolific scorer and one of the most highly touted prep players to sign with the Illini, ranking as the top recruit from Canada and in the top 10 overall. The five-star wing chose the Illini over a group of finalists that included Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas and Kentucky.
Morez Johnson Jr., No. 20, freshman forward
The 6-9, 255-pound freshman from Harvey Thornton won Illinois Mr. Basketball last season, averaging 20 points, 15 rebounds, four assists and three steals. The four-star recruit was tops in Illinois and helped Team USA win the FIBA U18 AmeriCup.
Jason Jakstys, No. 31, freshman forward
The 6-10, 210-pound Yorkville native was the state's No. 4-ranked player in the Class of 2024. The three-star recruit averaged 15.5 points, 9.5 rebounds, 2.5 assists and a 1.7 blocks his senior season.
Illinois returnees
Ty Rodgers, No. 20, junior guard-forward
The 6-6, 210-pound Michigan native is the only returning starter for the Illini. He averaged 6.2 points and 5.3 rebounds in 22.8 minutes per game last season. "Ty is a rockstar as a human being, as a leader," coach Brad Underwood told the Daily Illini. "He's taken that role on and said, 'jump on my back.''
Dra Gibbs-Lawhorn, No. 2, sophomore guard
The 6-1, 185-pound Indiana native is one of four returnees for Illinois. He played in 28 games last season, averaging 2.4 points across 7.1 minutes per game.
AJ Redd, No. 5, junior guard
The 6-3, 170-pound Chicago native is one of only four returnees for the Illini. He averaged 2 minutes across 10 games.
Keaton Kutcher, No. 24, redshirt junior guard
The 6-2, 195-pound native of Iowa spent last season as a redshirt for the Illini. Before that, he played 25 games over two seasons at South Dakota.

title: Predicting the CFP rankings: How will committee handle Ohio State, Georgia, Penn State?
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: The CFP committee gained a greenlight Saturday to load the playoff with Big Ten, SEC teams.
content:
Show Caption
The CFP committee gained a greenlight Saturday to load the playoff with Big Ten, SEC teams.
If BYU wins Big 12 and Miami wins ACC, those conferences could be left with one bid apiece.
Carson Beck's play remains a concern for Georgia.
The Big Ten and SEC became Saturday's big winners.
Losses by Clemson and Pittsburgh in the ACC and Iowa State and Kansas State in the Big 12 increased the chance that those two leagues will be reduced to one playoff bid apiece and widened the path for the "Super Two" conferences to claim four playoff bids apiece.
The College Football Playoff committee will open a window into their thinking when the first playoff rankings are released Tuesday night.
How the committee operates is shrouded in mystery. Here's how the committee describes its rankings process on the CFP's website: The selection committee chooses the 12 teams for the playoff based on strength of schedule, head-to-head results against common opponents, championships won and other factors.
Well, that single sentence clears it up, doesn't it?
The committee's lack of transparency is sure to heighten the controversy over its playoff picks. The public is not even privy to the strength of schedule metric, which SportSource Analytics provides to the committee.
Basically, the committee can make up whatever rationale it wants to justify its playoff field.
"Record matters," CFP executive director Rich Clark said Wednesday, "but we're not trying to pick the most deserving teams. We're trying to pick the best teams. This committee has got to look at (a team's) entire body of work."
Here's my prediction of what the top 12 of the rankings could look like come Tuesday night:
1. Oregon (9-0): This is the easy part. The Ducks are No. 1. The longer the season goes, the more dominant Oregon looks.
2. Ohio State (7-1): The Buckeyes timed their road win at Penn State perfectly, three days before the first ranking. That showing should linger in committee members' minds as they search for a No. 2 team.
3. Georgia (7-1): The Bulldogs' metrics are excellent, but their performance on the subjective eye test might be the difference between No. 2 and No. 3.
4. Miami (9-0): The committee can't ignore the Hurricanes' record, but Miami's vulnerable defense will be the justification for barring it from the top three.
5. Penn State (7-1): The Nittany Lions won't be overly punished for a one-score loss to OSU, and their schedule strength provides some separation with Texas, Tennessee and Brigham Young.
6. Texas (7-1): The Longhorns' offensive and defensive balance helps them on the eye test, despite a middling strength of schedule.
7. Tennessee (7-1): The Vols' dependable defense powers Tennessee's playoff pursuit. The committee always respects Alabama, so Tennessee's win against the Tide will put shine on the résumé.
8. Brigham Young (8-0): The Cougars own a nice win at Southern Methodist, but their strength of schedule trails one-loss teams ahead of them. This ranking will show the committee's hand that they plan to make the Big 12 a one-bid league.
9. Notre Dame (7-1): The Irish's soft schedule should prevent them from being ranked much higher, but the committee can point to wins against Texas A&M and Louisville to justify this ranking.
10. Indiana (9-0): The Hoosiers keep destroying opponents, but their weaker schedule leaves them vulnerable. Slotting Indiana here would give the committee a chance to bump the Hoosiers if OSU trounces them.
11. Alabama (6-2): Find someone who loves you the way the committee consistently loves the Script A. Alabama's schedule strength positions it best among two-loss teams.
12. Boise State (7-1): A close loss to Oregon counts as a quality line on the Broncos ' résumé. They're positioned for the Group of Five's playoff bid, but they must win the Mountain West to snag it.
Here's what else caught my eye in this view from the 'Topp Rope':
What's wrong with Georgia's Carson Beck?
I didn't expect quarterback Carson Beck to be a factor holding Georgia back, but Beck has gone from team strength to liability at warp speed.
He threw three interceptions in Georgia's sloppy 34-20 victory over Florida, giving him 11 interceptions in his past five games. He repeatedly forced passes into coverage. On his second interception, he needlessly threw a pass into triple coverage on first down.
Beck doesn't look like the same quarterback without Brock Bowers serving as a security blanket.
Are we sure Beck gives Georgia a better shot than blue-chip backup Gunner Stockton? This wouldn't be the first time Kirby Smart parked his best quarterback on the bench.
It took multiple JT Daniels injuries for Smart to elevate Stetson Bennett IV to the starting spot in 2021. Bennett went on to lead Georgia to back-to-back national championships, but what would have happened if Daniels didn't get hurt?
Knowing Smart's history – in 2018, he kept rolling with Jake Fromm over Justin Fields – he'll probably stick with Beck. Without seeing more of Stockton, it's hard to know whether that's the right call, but it's also tough to envision Georgia winning a national championship with Beck playing like he has lately.
'I don't think anything's wrong with him,' Smart said before the Florida game.
And I think Smart is the only one who feels that way.
Three and out
1. Hugh Freeze's record dropped to 9-13 in two seasons at Auburn after the Tigers' 17-7 loss to Vanderbilt, Auburn's first-ever home loss to the Commodores. Bryan Harsin was 9-12 when Auburn fired him in Year 2.
Freeze's recruiting class, ranked No. 5 in the 247Sports Composite, is the only argument for giving him a third season. That argument might be strong enough to retain Freeze, but he'd enter 2025 on a piping-hot seat, much like Billy Napier did at Florida this year.
2. Quarterback DJ Lagway's injury gave Florida an excuse for blowing a lead in a 34-20 loss to Georgia, but let's be honest, the Gators would have found a way to lose anyway. Finding ways to lose winnable games remains their speciality under Billy Napier. I'm now going to list the reasons why Florida should bring Napier back for a fourth season: ... .
Actually, I can't think of any.
3. My latest "Topp Rope" playoff projection: Georgia (SEC), Oregon (Big Ten), Miami (ACC), BYU (Big 12), Boise State (Group of Five), plus at-large selections Tennessee, Texas, LSU, Ohio State, Indiana, Penn State, Notre Dame. Next up: SMU, Alabama, Iowa State, Texas A&M, Army.

title: Election Day 2024: Here's when, how and where to vote in Illinois
author: Mike Kramer
description: After months of anticipation, the 2024 general election has arrived. Here are a few tips for Illinois residents headed to the polls.
content:
An Election Day with the United States presidential contest at the top of the ticket only comes around once every four years. Here's what to know about voting in Illinois on Tuesday.
When is Election Day 2024
Election Day this year is Nov. 5, 2024.
Is my vote safe?
Where can I vote near me on Election Day?
Here is where you can vote in the three biggest counties in central Illinois: Peoria, Tazewell and Woodford:
Rather than being restricted to assigned polling places, Peoria County residents have the option to vote at any of the county's 55 polling locations. The Peoria County Election Commission has provided a list and an interactive map of polling locations.
Tazewell County residents will still need to vote at their assigned precinct locations. The Tazewell County Clerk and Recorder of Deeds office has provided maps of the county's 82 precincts and polling place addresses.
A list of Woodford County's 45 polling places is available on the Woodford County government website
When can we expect election results?
Not on election day. Most Illinois districts will report the early vote and early arriving mail-in ballots shortly after polls close. They then report Election Day votes, which are usually all in by 11 p.m. In subsequent days, the state will count properly postmarked mail-in ballots that arrive after Election Day. The bulk of those ballots should arrive within three or four days but are not due until Nov. 19.
When do polls in Illinois open and close?
Polling places throughout Illinois will open at 6 a.m. and close at 7 p.m.
When is the last day to vote?
Nov. 5. All absentee ballots must be postmarked by Election Day.
Is election day a federal holiday?
The short answer is no. U.S. Rep. Anna Eshoo (D-California) introduced a bill to establish Election Day as a legal public holiday in February. The U.S. House of Representatives have referred the action to the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability.
How can I register to vote in Illinois?
For Illinois residents who have not yet registered to vote, the state offers Grace Period Registration on Election Day at all polling locations while the polls are open.
