title: One person has died of West Nile virus in Tazewell County
author: Mike Kramer
description: An unnamed person is Tazewell County's first human fatality from the virus in 2024.
content:
Tazewell County Health Departmen t officials have reported the first human death caused by West Nile virus in 2024.
A undientified Tazewell County resident in their 70s experienced West Nile symptoms in mid-October and died soon after. TCHD is also reporting one non-fatal case of the virus in the county to date this year.
The state of Illinois is reporting nine West Nile-related deaths to date in 2024.
West Nike virus is typically transferred to humans from the bite of an infected mosquito. Most people who are infected do not experience symptoms. If symptoms are present, mild cases may cause a slight fever or headache. More severe cases of the infection may result in a fast-developing high fever with head and body aches, disorientation, tremors, convulsions, and in some cases, paralysis or death.
Anyone experiencing any of the above symptom should consider seeking medical attention. Symptoms typically happen from three to 14 days after a person is bitten by an infected mosquito.
People 50 years of age or older and those immunocompromised are at the highest risk of serious illness associated with West Nile virus. During the months of May through October, the health department conducts regular testing of mosquito pools throughout Tazewell County.
TCHD encourages residents to observe the 'Three R's' for protection against mosquitos and WNV. They include:
These areas are breeding grounds for mosquitoes and for West Nile virus.
Repelling mosquitoes by using proper insect repellents.
More information on West Nile is available at dph.illinois.gov.

title: Why the Illinois basketball roster will have a new look for the 2024-25 college season
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The Illini opened with a big win, but learned a returning starter will sit out for the 2024-25 college basketball season.
content:
Illinois basketball looked good Monday night in its 112-67 season opening victory against Eastern Illinois. The Fighting Illini roster also looked a little different.
Returning starter Ty Rodgers did not play Monday and has decided to redshirt the 2024-25 season, team spokesman Derrick Burson told the Champaign News-Gazette and coach Brad Underwood confirmed in a postgame news conference.
Underwood also said the program is looking into redshirt options for 6-foot-10, 210-pound freshman Jason Jakstys, who was the only Illini to suit up Monday and not play.
Why did Ty Rodgers redshirt?
Underwood said discussions about a possible redshirt took place over the last few weeks, since practice started, and through the exhibition loss to Ole Miss. Rodgers was scoreless in 14 minutes of the 91-74 road loss to the Rebels.
"The thing about young people is, they have goals, things they want to try to reach," Underwood said Monday night. "We feel he could continue to grow ... offensively. ... He has area of his game he wants to work on and we support that development."
Rodgers was by far the most experienced returning player for Illinois. He started every game last season in a run the NCAA Elite Eight, averaging 6.2 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.0 assists. Underwood called Rodgers decision "a loss," but also said he was a winner and a nice young man with a kind heart.
Bradley basketball 2024-25 season prediction, schedule analysis: Valley title chase Bradley basketball roster: How the BU Braves built a contender for the 2024-25 season Illinois basketball 2024-25 season prediction, schedule analysis: Big Ten title chase Meet Illinois basketball roster: Breaking down the Fighting Illini ahead of 2024-25 season
Will Ty Rodgers transfer from Illinois?
This is a similar situation to last season, when Sencire Harris decided to redshirt before the season; he ended up transferring to West Virginia. Underwood hopes the program can keep Rodgers, but knows the transfer portal is a possibility.
"It's the world we're in," Underwood said with a shrug. "I think he's an Illini. I think he's our guy. We love Ty to death, but our world doesn't have any guarantees in it now."
Who will replace Ty Rodgers for the Illini?
If Monday night was any indication, the Illini have some depth on the wing to replace Rodgers. Louisville transfer Tre White started and provided some stability, but freshman Will Riley and sophomore Dra Gibbs-Lawthorn came off the bench and dominated.
Riley, a five-start recruit from Canada, played 25 minutes and scored 31 points — the most by a freshman in an Illinois debut. He was 10-for-13 from the field including 5-for-6 from 3-point range. Gibbs-Lawthorn finished with 21 points in 21 minutes on 5-for-10 shooting.

title: Music titan Quincy Jones, legendary producer of Michael Jackson's 'Thriller,' dies at 91
author: Kristin McGrath
description: The man who made stars collide for 1985's \
content:
Show Caption
Quincy Jones, best known as the architect of Michael Jackson 's " Thriller" and the man who made stars collide for 1985's " We Are the World," had a long career as a composer and trumpeter who broke down racial boundaries in music and film.
Jones died on Sunday, his publicist said. He was 91.
Jones won an astonishing 27 Grammy Awards throughout his career as an arranger and producer, and his legacy intersected with those of Frank Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald, Duke Ellington and Lesley Gore.
Born March 14, 1933, to Sarah and Quincy Delight Jones, he and younger brother, Lloyd, grew up in gang-riddled Great Depression Chicago. His mother suffered from mental illness and was institutionalized when he was 5, and his father moved the family to Bremerton, Washington.
When he was 11, Jones broke into the Armory recreation center in Bremerton to steal food. Inside, he found an upright piano. As he would later say in interviews, this was the moment that led him from a childhood of petty crime to a life of music.
His chance encounter with the piano led Jones to try a medley of instruments before settling on trumpet. By age 14, he was playing the club circuit with 16-year-old friend Ray Charles, freewheeling from jazz, to big band, to bebop. After high school, Jones toured the world with jazz greats Lionel Hampton and Dizzy Gillespie.
This whirlwind life as a traveling musician deposited Jones back in the States, broke in 1961. He repaid his debts working at Mercury Records, where he was eventually promoted to Vice President at the otherwise white company.
When dreams of scoring films lured Jones to Hollywood in 1965, executives were shocked to learn he was Black after they'd hired him for Gregory Peck film "Mirage." He soon racked up two Oscar nominations (best original song for "The Love of Ivy" and best original score for film "In Cold Blood") in 1968 and became the first Black musical director of the Academy Awards in 1971. He would executive produce the show in 1996.
Yet Jones suffered from health problems. He had two nearly fatal brain aneurysms in 1974. The resulting metal plate in his head ensured he would never play trumpet again. Yet he continued making music, scoring "The Bill Cosby Show," "Sanford and Son" and 1977 miniseries "Roots," for which he won an Emmy.
Then, while scoring the film "The Wiz," Jones met Michael Jackson. He produced Jackson's "Off the Wall" album in 1979, ascending to music royalty alongside the King of Pop in a partnership that also generated mega-sellers "Thriller" and "Bad." In 1985, the pair collaborated for the star-studded charity song "We Are the World," which won three Grammys.
He co-produced "The Color Purple" and helped introduce Oprah Winfrey to a national audience (He also produced the Broadway version). In 2013, Winfrey induct Jones into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
His name appears as a producer, composer, conductor, arranger or performer on more than 400 albums. He composed roughly 35 film scores.
Jones leaves behind seven children: Jolie Jones Levine (with former wife, actress Jeri Caldwell), Martina Jones and Quincy Jones III (with second wife, model Ulla Andersson), Kidada Jones and "The Office" actress Rashida Jones (with third wife, "Mod Squad" actress Peggy Lipton), Rachel Jones (with Carol Reynolds) and Kenya Julia Miambi Sarah Jones (with actress Nastassja Kinski).
In his later years, the force that propelled Jones from jazz musician to music mogul never seemed to die out. He formed the production company responsible for " Fresh Prince of Bel-Air." He published an autobiography in 2001. And he partnered with Lionel Richie for a second installment of "We Are The World" after the Haiti earthquake in 2010.
In 2018, daughter Rashida and director Alan Hicks chronicled Jones' generation- and genre-spanning career in Netflix documentary "Quincy." Rashida called the 2-hour film "a starter pack," saying she shot 800 hours of footage and worked through 2,000 hours of archives.
Netflix's Quincy Jones doc can barely contain his shockingly accomplished career
"He's lived such a big life," Rashida told USA TODAY in a joint interview with Jones at the time. "I just cannot believe all of this experience is contained in this one human being who just happens to be my dad."
Jones, who admitted to tears every time he's seen the film, said the message of his life comes through in the movie: family, love and keeping perspective.
"Don't never give up," he said. "Keep the humility with the creativity. And grace with the success. Just because you're behind a No. 1 record does not make you better than anybody."

title: Celebrity chef set to host charity event next year in Peoria. Here are the details
author: Christina Avery
description: Celebrity chef Amanda Freitag, known for her work on multiple Food Network shows, will host EP!C's Bon Appétit event in March 2025 in Peoria, Illinois.
content:
A celebrity chef is slated to bring her culinary expertise to Peoria next spring.
Food Network's Amanda Freitag will host the 14th annual Bon Appétit event March 20, 2025. Put together by local advocacy organization EP!C, the event raises money for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
"The work they do to keep the community strong and all of you in the room are the reason we are here: to raise funds that are critical for EP!C's mission," Frietag said in a video shared on EP!Cs Instagram page Sept. 20. "Your support of this signature event of EP!C changes lives."
Freitag has been in the culinary industry for more than 30 years and has served as head chef at Michelin-star restaurants in New York along with various other cooking roles around the world. Freitag competed in season two of Food Network's "The Next Iron Chef," and has been a frequent judge on the reality game show "Chopped" since 2009.
Past Bon Appétit chefs have included Omaha Steaks Executive Chef David Rose in 2024, Top Chef fan favorite Fabio Viviani in 2023 and Chopped's Maneet Chauhan in 2022.
EP!C Director of Marketing Ashley Schreck said guests will enjoy a 4-5 course meal during the event with a variety of dishes showcasing Freitag's skills. Freitag will also hold a meet-and-greet where attendees can purchase copies of her book "The Chef Next Door: A Pro Chef's Recipes for Fun, Fearless Home Cooking."
Tickets are currently on sale for sponsors only. Sponsorship levels start at $600 and go up to $15,000. Sponsors giving $3,000 or more will also receive reservations to a VIP event with Freitag before the main event. Tickets for the general public will go on sale in January, Schreck said. Those who are interested can stay updated on EP!C's website, Facebook and Instagram.

title: Predicting the top Illinois high school football games in Peoria area for 2024 IHSA quarterfinals
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Peoria High, Princeton and Farmington play this weekend in the IHSA football quarterfinals. Here is what you need to know and Adam Duvall's picks.
content:
It's the quarterfinals of the Illinois high school football playoffs, and predictions for the IHSA games around the Peoria area are in. All games are Saturday.
Last week, the picks in this space went 5-4 (.556) and are 138-41 (.771) on the season. This year's team records are in parentheses.
CLASS 5A
(6) Joliet Catholic Academy (8-3) at 2 Peoria High (9-2), 2 p.m.
Joliet Catholic 42, Peoria High 26: Peoria High will look to continue its dominant offensive output, scoring 49.1 points per game. The Lions have scored 44 points or more in their nine victories, but only scored 18 in their two losses. Quarterback Breon Green accounted for four touchdowns including three passing scores behind 158 yards in last week's second-round win. He added 72 yards and one rushing TD. Running backs Detaurion Pollard and Kendall Netters combined for 243 yards and three TDs last week. JCA beat Peoria High, 40-16, in last season's first round en route to the state championship game. The Hilltoppers have made 20 state title games, having won 15 championships including two since 2018. Don't look for QB Lucas Simulick to throw much, handing off to Nate Magrini (148 rushing yards, two TDs in second round) and Larry Stringham. Defensively, JCA is giving up 14.3 points a game including three shutouts led by defensive end Ian Campbell. This game will be played at Peoria Stadium.
CLASS 3A
(9) Lombard Montini (9-2) at (4) Princeton (10-1), 1 p.m.
Lombard Montini 48, Princeton 15: This is Princeton's fifth successive quarterfinal appearance with three consecutive losses in the Elite Eight. Montini beat Princeton, 27-9, in last season's Class 3A quarterfinals. Princeton gained 398 total yards last week including 304 on the ground; RB Casey Etheridge rushed for 217 yards and three TDs. Princeton's defense has been stout, giving up 13.6 points a game and 20 points or less during its current six-game win streak. Tigers QB Will Lott threw for 94 yards and two TDs including a 24-yard scoring strike to Etheridge. Northwestern recruit Noah LaPorte caught six balls for 70 yards highlighted by a 21-yard TD. Montini stopped reigning state champion Byron on a two-point conversion for a 14-13 win in the second round. Broncos RB Jeremiah Peterson rushed for 110 yards on 17 carries with two scores. Montini has a strong postseason tradition with nine state title appearances and six championships since 2004.
CLASS 2A
(1) Farmington (11-0) at (12) Dwight/Gardner-So. Wilmington (8-3), 1 p.m.
Farmington 28, Dwight 8: The Farmers are back in the quarterfinals for the fifth time in program history including two of the last four seasons. Farmington utilized an aggressive, tough defense to shutdown Taylor Ridge Rockridge, 14-10, in the second round. Three times the Farmers defense halted Rockridge at or inside Farmington's 15, along with five possessions of three-and-out. The Farmers defense has allowed 94 total points this season including four shutouts. RB Logan Utt's 72 yards led the ground game for Farmington, which got 116 total yards out of QB Lane Wheelwright. Dwight is in the quarterfinals for the first time in program history. A 6-yard TD pass to RB Evan Cox from QB Collin Bachand with 2.8 seconds gave the Trojans a 12-6 second-round win over Elmwood/Brimfield, spoiling a rivalry rematch. Dwight was able to hold the Elmwood run game in check as it gave up just 156 rushing yards. Cox led the Dwight rushing attack, which totaled 258 yards of offense, with 89 of its 232 yards.

title: IHSA medal winners and football heroes: Vote for Journal Star high school athlete of the week
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Trips to the IHSA Final Four and state medalists among the nominees for Journal Star high school athlete of the week for Nov. 11-16.
content:
After plenty of solid fall postseason sports performers over the last week, here are the Journal Star high school athlete of the week nominees for Nov. 11-16.
Head to pjstar.com/sports to vote. The poll closes at noon Friday. Information about the nominees is below.
If you have a nominee for the honor, email us at sports@pjstar.com or tag us on Twitter @pjstarsports. Last week, Jerett Fauser of the Farmington football team was named JS athlete of the week.
Lane Wheelwright, Farmington football
Wheelwright seems to be rounding back into form following a late-season injury. The senior quarterback completed 74 percent (17 of 23) of his passes as Farmington beat Dwight/Gardner South Wilmington, 42-7 in a Class 2A quarterfinal on Saturday. He guided the Farmers offense to 372 yards from scrimmage including his 200 passing yards. The all-stater also threw two touchdowns, finding Landon Crawford and Boston Smith for scores. The Farmers (12-0) host Palos Heights Chicago Christian (11-1) at 2 p.m. Saturday.
Ella Karmenzind, Limestone volleyball
Karmenzind put together a quite memorable last week of her prep career. The senior was instrumental in Limestone finishing as the Class 3A state runner-up last Saturday. She posted six kills and 2.5 blocks as the Rockets suffered a 22-25, 25-22, 25-18 championship loss to Mahomet-Seymour. Her seven kills, four digs and 1.5 blocks in the 25-18, 25-22 state semifinal win over Crystal Lake Prairie Ridge helped put the Rockets in the state title match. Karmenzind's week began with a team-high eight kills in Limestone's 25-23, 25-23 supersectioinal win over New Lenox Providence Catholic.
Aubrey Phillips, El Paso-Gridley volleyball
Phillips put together a pair of memorable matches in helping the Titans make program history. The senior pounded down a match-high 13 kills, while adding five digs and an ace in Friday's Class 2A state semifinal loss to eventual state champion Breese Mater Dei, 25-16, 25-17. She then put together a four-kill, five-dig performance in a , 25-20, 25-15. third-place loss Elmhurst Timothy Christian. The fourth-place finish was the highest in the program's history.
Amelia Heinze, Washington girls swimming and diving
Heinze captured four state medals in the athlete with disabilities competition at the Illinois High School Association girls swimming state finals on Saturday. The senior was the second-place finisher in the 50-yard freestyle (29.8 seconds) and the 100-yard breaststroke (1:22.33). Her other races saw Heinze clock in at 2:42.16 in the 200-yard freestyle, while taking 1:06.74 in the 100-yard freestyle for two third places.

title: From SEC to Big 12, college football doesn't need divisions. It needs smarter tiebreakers
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: College football functions just fine without conference divisions, but some tiebreaker rules we can actually understand would help. Here's an idea.
content:
Show Caption
College football functions just fine without conference divisions, but some tiebreaker rules we can actually understand would help.
Lane Kiffin's suggestion makes sense: Incorporate CFP rankings to break messy ties in conference standings.
Kenny Dillingham quote about Big 12 championship game shows coaches don't even understand how these tiebreakers work.
Conference divisions, don't you dare plot a return. College football functions fine without them.
I hereby declare elimation of conference divisions a smashing success.
If you disagree, tell me whether you enjoyed Ohio State at Oregon, or Georgia at Texas, or Penn State at Southern California.
Games such as those would occur less frequently if conference divisions persisted, because teams in those matchups almost certainly would have been placed in opposite divisions.
Television ratings suggest you very much enjoyed those games.
Georgia-Texas recorded the highest television audience of any game this season, logging 13.2 million viewers, while Ohio State-Oregon (9.6 million viewers) remains the second-highest rated Big Ten game.
True, eliminating divisions meant Missouri and Kentucky didn't face off in an SEC East "clash," and we had to miss out on Florida State-Syracuse (on, no!), but lo and behold, the world kept spinning.
Conferences threaded a needle by dumping divisions while preserving the most important league rivalries. All in all, pretty good deal. So, all's well that ends well, yeah?
Well, not exactly.
Progress often comes at a cost. The price of axing divisions? Logjammed conference standings means that, in some cases, messy tiebreaker rules will be needed to determine conference championship matchups.
Within the SEC, a six-way tie for first place remains in play. The SEC's complex tiebreaker rules include the phrase 'capped relative scoring margin' as a factor that could be considered.
Now, we just need to find someone with four Ph.D.s and a quarter-million dollars in school loans to explain for us what 'capped relative scoring margin' means.
A battle royale takes place toward the top of the Big 12 standings, too, where winning the conference championship likely will be the only avenue to playoff entry.
Asked about the Big 12's tiebreaker scenarios, Arizona State coach Kenny Dillingham admitted, 'I literally have no clue.'
'Somebody was telling me, if we win and somebody else loses, and then ranch dressing falls on a wing, I don't really know,' Dillingham said. 'Just, play the very best you can play, … and don't get lost in the sauce.'
A solution to the conference tiebreaker dilemma
Some in and around the sport have mused that these oversized conferences and muddy tiebreaker rules prove that divisions ought to be restored.
Forget that idea.
No need to rekindle the past. Don't sacrifice the quality of the regular season just to make the conference championship matchup more straightforward. Instead of reviving divisions, come up with a set of tiebreakers that normal people can understand.
I propose this simple three-step system for determining conference championship matchups:
1. Conference records.
2. Head-to-head record among tied teams.
3. If teams with identical conference records remain tied after applying the head-to-head tiebreaker, use the College Football Playoff rankings to decide the conference championship matchup. The highest-ranked team among the tied teams earns the nod.
Would that be controversial? Sure.
At least we could understand it, though.
And, if we trust a committee to choose playoff teams, why shouldn't that committee be qualified to settle a deadlock in the conference standings?
I've got company in this line of thinking.
'All this seems really complicated,' Mississippi coach Lane Kiffin said of the SEC's tiebreaker procedure. '… I would think it would have been a lot easier to say, 'What are the top two teams in the (CFP) rankings?''
Divisions within conferences started as a business opportunity. Roy Kramer, after becoming the SEC's commissioner, seized on a little-known NCAA rule that allowed a conference to conduct a football championship game if that conference included at least 12 teams and split into divisions.
So, the SEC hatched a plan, and in 1992 it launched its revolutionary conference championship.
A championship game meant more conference exposure and more revenue. Other conferences followed the SEC's lead by expanding, splitting into divisions and hosting conference championships.
Decades later, the NCAA modified its rules, and now conferences of any size can conduct a conference championship game without splitting into divisions.
By changing the rules surrounding conference championships, the NCAA eliminated the reason why divisions were created. Once conferences gained permission to conduct championship games without divisions, most leagues unified the conference. Starting this season, the Sun Belt is the only Bowl Subdivision conference still split into divisions.
I don't miss divisions. I do miss the clarity they brought to conference championship matchups, but that can be solved by a solution right in front of our face. The CFP rankings are there in plainsight. Use them.
Here's what else I'm mulling in this 'Topp Rope' view of college football:
Name to watch in 2025 coaching carousel
This shapes up as a quiet Power Four coaching carousel. That points to the carousel kicking into overdrive next season, with several high-profile jobs potentially coming open.
Who will emerge as a top commodity on the 2025 hiring circuit? Monitor SMU's Rhett Lashlee. He's steered the Mustangs to unabated success in their ACC debut. They're in the thick of the playoff hunt.
While Indiana's Curt Cignetti earned every bit of the fanfare he's received for this Hoosiers uprising, Cignetti mania overshadows Lashlee's feat.
Lashlee built on predecessor Sonny Dykes' success with three consecutive winning seasons, this year ranking as his best yet.
By ACC standards, Lashlee enjoys a good gig. He's positioned in rich recruiting terrain. SMU benefits from a formidable NIL collective, making it a player in the acquisition circuit.
SEC and Big Ten jobs are a siren's call, though, and those two conferences unlock the path to the national championship. The ACC projects as a one-bid playoff league.
Lashlee played quarterback at Arkansas, and he was Auburn's offensive coordinator when its 2013 team reached the national championship game.
Arkansas and Auburn could become two of several "Super Two" conference jobs open next year.
Emails of the week
Mike writes: When I look at teams like South Carolina, Florida and Alabama, I see teams that have clearly improved as the season progressed. These teams now barely resemble what they were at the beginning of the season.
But when I look at Tennessee, I see a team that is no better now than it was in late August. The offense might even be worse.
My response: You'll hear no disagreement from me, and, apparently, the CFP selection committee shares your view of the Vols' stagnant progress. That's reflected in Tennessee ranking behind fellow two-loss SEC teams Alabama, Ole Miss and Georgia in the latest rankings.
Lar writes (in response to my column that the CFP committee overvalues Notre Dame): Shush now, 'Baby Cakes'. Try to put on a 'Happy Face.' Goodness me, even after the new playoff expansion format, you still have all those tears about who, why and where. Or maybe it's just your bias showing? Poor thing, you.
My response: 'Baby cakes,' now that's one I haven't heard. Kudos for originality.
Jim writes (in response to my Notre Dame column): I agree, my Notre Dame is way overrated. We just cannot get the top recruits. The SEC is the toughest conference. I enjoyed your article.
My response: Careful, Jim, I wouldn't want your fellow Irish fans to accuse you of SEC bias.
Three and out
1. Deion Sanders dismissed speculation that he's got a foot out the door at Colorado, saying he's got " a kickstand down.' Unrelated (or possibly related), I seem to recall my kickstand buckling and my bike toppling over every now and again when I was a kid. Kickstands aside, the more important indicator came Thursday, when blue-chip quarterback Julian Lewis committed to Colorado. Lewis, at least, believes Coach Prime will stay put.
2. Would coaches of playoff-positioned teams prefer to not earn selection for their conference championship game? My read on the situation: Most coaches would rather not risk the loss and instead head straight to the playoff. Most players would prefer to put it on the line and try to win the conference crown.
3. A low-key odd development from Tuesday's CFP rankings: Alabama leapfrogged Miami, following the Tide's blowout win over Mercer, while the Hurricanes had an open date. If you had Mercer influencing the playoff rankings on your bingo card, come claim your prize.

title: College football rankings: Big Ten teams in updated Coaches Poll, AP Top 25 after Week 13
author: John Leuzzi
description: Here's a look at where Big Ten appear in the Coaches Poll and AP Top 25 after Week 13 of the college football season:
content:
The Big Ten football standings saw a bit of a shakeup in Week 14, with the conference's Cinderella team being brought back down to earth.
In its biggest game of the week, No. 5 Indiana (10-1 overall, 7-1 in Big Ten) saw its College Football Playoff odds take a hit as Curt Cignetti and the Hoosiers fell to Ryan Day and No. 2 Ohio State (10-1, 7-1) 38-15. The Buckeyes overcame an early 7-0 lead by Indiana to shut down the Hoosiers over the course of the first and second halves, scoring 31 straight points before Indiana got on the board again.
No. 4 Penn State (10-1, 7-1) handled business on Saturday, though the Nittany Lions had to put in some extra effort to beat Minnesota 26-25 the road. No. 1 Oregon (11-0, 8-0) was idle this week, as was Washington.
With newly named commit Bryce Underwood in attendance, Michigan football (6-5, 4-4) defeated Northwestern 56-6 at The Big House thanks to a big day from running back Kalel Mullings. Elsewhere, Wisconsin will have to wait another week to challenge for bowl eligibility as the Badgers (5-6, 3-5) fell to Nebraska (6-5, 3-5) 44-25 on the road. The Cornhuskers ' win helped them reach their first bowl game since 2016.

title: Which Peoria-area restaurants offer carryout on Thanksgiving? Here are some options
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: Looking for a quick and easy meal to enjoy at home this Thanksgiving? Try these Peoria-area restaurants.
content:
Thanksgiving Day is quickly approaching − falling on Thursday, Nov. 28.
If you are searching for a quick and easy meal to enjoy at home, here is a look at which Peoria-area restaurants are offering to-go orders on Thanksgiving Day.
Do you have another restaurant to add to the list? Email CWaigand@gannett.com.
Bob Evans
Placing to-go orders: https://www.bobevans.com/menu/thanksgiving.
What's on the menu? The restaurant will offer a limited menu with Thanksgiving specials.
The holiday celebration platter and premium celebration platter each include slow-roasted turkey, dressing, mashed potatoes and gravy, cranberry relish, buttered corn, green beans with ham, dinner rolls and a slice of pumpkin pie. The premium celebration platter also includes hickory-smoked ham.
Customers will also find a holiday hot family meal for six people. The meal includes slow-roasted turkey, hickory-smoked ham, dressing, mashed potatoes and gravy, cranberry relish, buttered corn, green beans with ham, a dozen dinner rolls and a pumpkin pie.
The menu also features various breakfast options.
Hours: 8 a.m. until 7 p.m.
Address: Three Bob Evans locations operate in the Peoria-area. Restaurants are situated at 8821 N. Allen Road, Peoria; 304 N. Main St., East Peoria and 3440 Court St., Pekin.
Cracker Barrel
Placing to-go orders: Customers can call (309) 263-2103 or order online at https://www.crackerbarrel.com/menu.
What's on the menu? A limited menu with Thanksgiving specials will be available.
This includes the homestyle turkey n' dressing meal for $17.99. The meal features turkey and dressing with gravy, green beans, sweet potato casserole with pecans, cranberry relish, dinner rolls and pumpkin pie.
Customers will also find chicken n' dumplings with two sides and dinner rolls for $10.49 and a country vegetable plate − which consists of four sides and dinner rolls − for $10.59.
Hours: 7 a.m. until 10 p.m.
Address: 150 E. Ashland St., Morton
Holy Crab
Placing to-go orders: Customers can call (309) 966-1145 or place a to-go order in person.
What's on the menu? The restaurant's regular menu will be available. Customers can find shrimp, catfish, crab, crawfish, lobster tails, raw oysters and more.
Hours: 11 a.m. until 9:30 p.m.
Placing to-go orders: Customers can call (309) 689-8890 to place a to-go order.
What's on the menu? A Thanksgiving dinner special will be available at IHOP on Thanksgiving Day. The meal includes turkey, pineapple glazed ham steak, stuffing, mashed potatoes and gravy, garlic butter green beans, lingonberry sauce, pumpkin cheesecake and a fountain drink.
The meal is $24.99, but those who order four or more will receive 20% off.
Hours: 7 a.m. until 12 a.m.
Hong Kong Buffet
To-go orders: Customers at Hong Kong Buffet can get their food to go. These orders are charged by the pound.
What's on the menu? Along with the restaurant's regular buffet, turkey will be available during dinner.
Hours: 11 a.m. until 9 p.m.
Perkins American Food Co.
Placing to-go orders: Customers can call the restaurant at (309) 306-2257 or order online at https://www.perkinsrestaurants.com/
What's on the menu? Perkins will offer its regular menu on Thanksgiving Day.
Hours: 6 a.m. until 10 p.m.
Address: 1810 W. War Memorial Drive, Peoria
Washington Family Restaurant
Placing to-go orders: Beginning at 10:30 a.m., customers can place to-go orders by calling (309) 444-1690.
What's on the menu? Customers can order a Thanksgiving meal with baked ham or roast turkey with stuffing for $14.95. The meal is served with mashed potatoes, a vegetable, a choice of soup or salad, a dinner roll and a slice of pumpkin pie.
Hours: 6 a.m. until 2 p.m.

Coaches: L-W — Ric Arand (260-66 in 28 years). BAC — Austin Frazier (33-19 in 5 years).

title: Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith proposes to dismiss Jan. 6 case against Donald Trump
author: Bart Jansen
description: Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith's request to dismiss the charges against Trump was expected after he won the presidential election.
content:
WASHINGTON – Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith asked Monday to dismiss the criminal case against President-elect Donald Trump for allegedly trying to steal the 2020 election.
The request was expected after Smith asked U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan to halt all deadlines in the case. A longstanding department policy bars prosecuting sitting presidents, so Smith was expected to wind down both federal cases against Trump after he won the Nov. 5 election to return to the White House.
"It has long been the position of the Department of Justice that the United States Constitution forbids the federal indictment and subsequent criminal prosecution of a sitting President," Smith wrote in his six-page filing. "That prohibition is categorical and does not turn on the gravity of the crimes charged, the strength of the Government's proof, or the merits of the prosecution, which the Government stands fully behind."
Trump spokesperson Steven Cheung said the American people demanded an end to the weaponization of the Justice Department reflected in Trump's election victory.
"Today's decision by the DOJ ends the unconstitutional federal cases against President Trump, and is a major victory for the rule of law," Cheung said.
Chutkan didn't immediately rule on the request, but Trump's lawyers didn't oppose it.
Smith also dropped his appeal of the dismissal of charges that Trump mishandled classified documents after leaving the White House at the end of his first term.
U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon dismissed the charges by ruling Smith was appointed illegitimately. Smith appealed the decision to the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals but withdrew the appeal Monday.
The charges in the election-interference case had accused Trump of conspiracy for urging state lawmakers to replace the state's presidential electors with Republicans despite Democrat Joe Biden winning the state. Trump was also charged with obstruction of Congress for encouraging a mob of supporters protest at the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, when lawmakers were counting Electoral College votes to certify Biden's victory.
Chutkan was in the midst of weighing whether Trump was immune from the federal charges under a Supreme Court ruling in July. The high court decided former presidents are presumed shielded from criminal charges for official acts in office but vulnerable to charges for private acts.
Trump has argued he was acting in his official role when he urged then-Vice President Mike Pence to reject Democratic electors from key states and replace them with GOP electors, and when he encouraged federal and state officials to pursue baseless claims of election fraud. But Smith has argued he was acting privately for his own benefit through electioneering to remain in office.
What happens to the other criminal cases against Trump?
Trump still faces uncertainty about two state level cases in New York and Georgia, but neither case is expected to interfere with his presidency.
In New York, Judge Juan Merchan has postponed sentencing indefinitely for Trump's conviction on 34 counts of falsifying business records.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg asked Merchan to postpone sentencing until after Trump's presidential term is completed. But legal experts have said that could violate Trump's right to a speedy trial. Trump's lawyers have asked Merchan to dismiss the convictions entirely.
In Georgia, the Court of Appeals canceled its scheduled hearing Dec. 5 for Trump's argument that Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis should be removed from the case because of her romantic relationship with another prosecutor.
Fulton County Superior Judge Scott McAfee hasn't set a trial date in that case while awaiting the appeals decision. But McAfee is not expected to hold a trial for Trump while he serves in the White House.

title: Meet the 22 top football players around Peoria
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Farmington's Lane Wheelwright leads the 2024 Journal Star all-area football team. Meet the 22 best IHSA players around Peoria.
content:
Illinois High School Association football state champions across all eight classes will be decided Friday and Saturday at Hancock Stadium on the Illinois State University campus. This marks the second consecutive year that we're announcing our annual all-area teams on state championship weekend.
Below are the offensive and defensive picks for the 2024 Journal Star all-area football team, including 22 on the first team and 22 honorable mention — led by our player of the year in Farmington all-state quarterback Lane Wheelwright.
2024 Journal Star all-area football first-team
Lane Wheelwright, Farmington, QB
The 6-foot-1, 190-pound senior is the third from his school to be named player of the year, leading Farmington (12-1) to the Class 2A state semifinals for the first time in program history. He threw for 2,097 yards on 128-of-214 passing (60 percent) with 25 touchdowns, while rushing for 10 TDs and 323 yards despite missing the last two regular-season games with an injury. Wheelwright was named the LincolndLand Conference-Large Division Offensive Player of the Year, all-LincolnLand-Large Division unanimous first-team quarterback and Illinois High School Football Coaches Association Class 2A first-team all-state.
Hunter Reed, Washington, RB
The 5-foot-11, 185-pound senior ran for 1,591 yards on 222 carries with 27 touchdowns for the Panthers, who finished 8-3 overall, won the Mid-Illini Conference and made it to the Class 6A second round. He was named all-Mid-Illini first team and IHSFCA Class 6A first-team all-state.
Jack Gronewold, Farmington, WR
The 6-foot-3, 200-pound junior hauled in 51 balls for 1,050 yards and 13 TDs for the Farmers, who finished 12-1 and made the Class 2A state semifinals for the first time in program history. Gronewold, who missed two playoff games with an ankle injury, also played defensive back, recording 29 tackles, four interceptions and returning two punts for touchdowns. He was named all-LincolnLand-Large Division unanimous first-team wide receiver, all-LincolnLand-Large Division first-team defense back and IHSFCA Class 2A honorable mention all-state.
TQ Webb, Peoria High, WR
The 5-foot-10, 170-pound senior caught 51 balls for 964 yards and 12 TDs, while rushing for 83 yards and another score for Peoria High, which went 9-3 and made a run to the Class 5A quarterfinals. He was named all-Big 12 Conference first-team receiver.
Mack Sutter, Dunlap, TE
The 6-foot-6, 225-pound junior had 35 receptions for 505 yards and seven touchdowns for the Eagles, who finished 6-4 and made the Class 6A playoffs. Sutter filled in one game at quarterback, throwing for 119 yards. The four-star prospect also played linebacker with 29 tackles, six sacks, four forced fumbles and a pick-6. He was named all-Mid-Illini Conference first team.
Carter Lambin, Farmington, TE
The 6-foot-1, 190-pound senior caught 39 balls for 559 yards with seven touchdowns for the Farmers, who went 12-1 and made the Class 2A semifinals. Lambin also played linebacker, recording 110 tackles including 11 tackles-for-loss. was named all-LincolnLand Conference-Large Division unanimous first-team tight end and unanimous first-team linebacker.
Josh Hoffer, Washington, OL
The 6-foot-2, 215-pound junior is a three-year starter and played offensive tackle, paving the way for 2,597 rushing yards and 42 TDs for the Panthers (8-3), who won the Mid-Illini Conference and made the second round of the Class 6A playoffs. He was named all-Mid-Illini Conference first team.
IHSA football state championships: Schedule | Preview and predictions | How to watch
Caden Mowen, Farmington, OL
The 6-foot-4, 320-pound senior anchored the Farmington offensive line, opening the way for 1,794 rushing yards and 25 touchdowns en route to a Class 2A state semifinal appearance and a 12-1 record. Mowen was named all-LincolnLand Conference-Large Division unanimous first-team offensive lineman.
Jaquarius Green, Peoria High, OL
The 6-foot-3, 385-pound junior was a big presence on the offensive line, which saw the Lions run for 3,923 yards and score 47 TDs. Green is a three-year starter for Peoria High, which won nine games on their way to a Class 5A quarterfinal berth. He was named all-Big 12 Conference second-team offensive lineman.
Aaron Brown, Elmwood/Brimfield, OL
The 6-foot-3, 330-pound senior cleared holes for the Trojan offense that produced 4,328 rushing yards and 57 TDs for E/B, which went 9-2 and made a Class 2A second-round playoff appearance. Brown was named all-LincolnLand Conference-Large Division first-team offensive lineman.
Hunter Lamberson, Pekin, OL
The 6-foot-1, 305-pound senior was responsible for protecting the Dragons backfield, while producing 3,831 yards from scrimmage (2,301 rushing, 1,530 passing) and 47 total TDs. He was named all-Mid-Illini Conference second team.
2024 Journal Star all-area football defense first-team
Noah Bell, Washington, DL
The 6-foot-1, 255-pound senior plugged up a lot of holes for the Washington defense, which allowed 17 points a game including 8.9 points a game in Mid-Illini play. Bell posted 49 tackles, six tackles-for-loss, five sacks, three fumble recoveries and one forced fumble. He was named all-Mid-Illini Conference first team.
Aiden Shepherd, Farmington, DL
The 6-foot, 235-pound senior was the backbone of the Farmers d-line, which allowed 10.4 points a game including nine games giving up 10 points or less, highlighted by four shutouts. He record 74 tackles including 14 tackles-for-loss. Shepherd was named all-LincolnLand Conference-Large Division unanimous first-team defensive lineman.
Carter Prina, Washington, DL
The 6-foot-4, 220-pound senior was a two-way player, making his bones as a defensive end for the Mid-Illini Conference champion Panthers. Prina, who caught a TD as a blocking tight end, recorded 46 tackles, seven tackles-for-loss, five sacks, one forced fumble and a blocked kick. He picked up all-Mid-Illini Conference first-team honors.
Dorsey Doss, Peoria High, LB
The 6-foot-2, 198-pound senior covered sideline to sideline for the Lions, who made the Class 5A quarterfinals and went 9-3. Doss had a pair of defensive TDs this season including a strip-sack and recovery in the end zone to open the playoffs. He was named all-Big 12 Conference first-team linebacker.
Bo Windish, Elmwood/Brimfield, LB
The 5-foot-11, 175-pound senior seemed to never leave the field for the Trojans, who went 9-2 and played in the Class 2A second round. He had 48 tackles including six-for-loss, one interception and one fumble recovery. Offensively, he ran for 1,822 yards and 26 TDs, hitting 100-plus yards in 10 of the 11 games. Windish added 226 receiving yards and four TDs. He was named all-LincolnLand Conference-Large Division unanimous first-team running back and first-time running back. Windish was also named IHSFCA Class 2A first-team all-state.
Bradley Hoover, Pekin, LB
The senior played nearly lights-out defense for the Dragons, who made a run to the Class 7A playoffs and finished second in the Mid-Illini Conference standings. He recorded 99 tackles, three tackles-for-loss, one interception, forced one fumble and recovered a pair of fumbles. He was named all-Mid-Illini Conference first team.
Lawson Alwan, Peoria Notre Dame, LB
The 5-foot-11, 185-pound senior did a little bit of everything for the Irish, who went 6-5 and made it to the Class 4A second round. Alwan recorded 56 tackles with two sacks. In the backfield, he produced 954 rushing yards with 12 TDs, catching five balls for 123 yards. On extra points, he was 38-for-42, plus hitting a game-tying field goal in an overtime playoff win over Rochester. He was named all-Big 12 Conference second-team linebacker, second-team kicker and honorable mention back.
Tory Kupferschmid, Eureka, LB
The 6-foot, 165-pound senior proved to be a tackling machine during Eureka's 9-2 season and run to the Class 3A second round. He posted the second-most tackles in program history (126), while adding 6.5 tackles-for-loss, one sack, two pass breakups, one recovered fumble and one interception. Offensively, he caught 32 balls for 653 yards and five TDs. He was named all-Heart of Central Illinois Conference-Large Division unanimous first-team linebacker as well as all-HOCIC first-team tight end. Kupferschmid was also named IHSFCA Class 2A first-team all-state.
Jack Hanley, Peoria Notre Dame, DB
The 5-foot-10, 175-pound senior was able to play several different spots on the defensive side of the ball for the Irish, who knocked off Class 4A reigning state champion Rochester to make the second round of the playoffs. Hanley made 32 tackles and one tackle for loss. Offensively, he ran for 1,494 yards and 24 TDs, while adding 65 receiving yards and a TD. He was named all-Big 12 Conference first-team defensive back along with picking up all-B12 first-team running back honors. Hanley was named IHSFCA Class 4A first-team all-state.
Dereon Mays, Peoria High, DB
The 6-foot, 170-pound junior made life very difficult for every opponent's top receiver as the Lions made the Class 5A quarterfinals. Mays was glued to Normal Community senior and all-Big 12 first-team wide receiver Marqun Gary, who had just four catches for 25 yards in the meeting. Mays was named all-Big 12 Conference first-team defensive back.
Dylan Anderson, Pekin, DB
The 5-foot-11, 168-pound sophomore was a dynamic two-way player, especially in the Pekin secondary, which finished as the Mid-Illini Conference runner-up and made the Class 7A playoffs. He recorded 66 tackles, three interceptions and recovered two fumbles. Anderson also played wide receiver, catching 32 balls for 719 yards and 14 TDs. Also, he added 266 rushing yards and two TDs. He was named all-Mid-Illini Conference first team.

title: 'Broken': Lopsided IHSA football state championship games spark public-vs-private debate
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Half of the field at the IHSA football state championships is private schools. And they dominated on the first day of games in Normal, Illinois.
content:
The dominance of Illinois private school football programs is on display this weekend at the 2024 high school state championship games.
Private schools went 4-for-4 in title games Friday at Hancock Stadium in Normal, each defeating public schools to win the four smallest classifications by a combined score of 193-28 — an average margin of 48-7.
On Saturday, two private schools meet in the Class 5A championship and two public schools in the 6A final. It's public vs. private in the final two games, as Catholic powers Chicago Mount Carmel and Wilmette Loyola Academy are favorites to win the 7A and 8A championships against public schools Batavia and Elmhurst York.
In Illinois, private or non-boundary schools can procure students who live within a 30-mile radius of the school's location, giving programs in dense population centers like Chicago, St. Louis metro, Peoria, Rockford and Springfield a large student pool from which to draw. Public schools draw students from their geographic boundaries.
Over the years, there are been calls to "fix" the system by, for example, placing private schools in their own playoffs brackets or elevating them to the largest enrollment classes regardless of how many kids walk the halls. Any such changes would need to be proposed by member schools and gain support before being voted into the rulebooks.
The IHSA uses two ways to combat private schools' advantages, including enrollment multipliers (taking a school's true enrollment times 1.65) and implementation of a "success factor," which takes into account a program's postseason finishes when determining enrollment classification.
'The current IHSA system is broken'
Chicago Sun-Times high school reporter Michael O'Brien posted the private vs. public running points and yardages totals to social media on Friday, after each of the final three games, prompting dozens of comments and hundreds of interactions.
O'Brien, a longtime advocate of high school sports, again took to X.com near halftime of the Class 4A game as a another private school, Chicago DePaul College Prep, led public school Mount Zion 20-0 on the way to an eventual 40-6 win.
"If someone WANTED to devise a system to guarantee blowouts in 8 state championship high school football games, it might be difficult to achieve this kind of success," O'Brien wrote. "There are several significant teams moving up in class next year, but the current IHSA system is broken."
The administrator of the Monticello football X.com account was having some fun Friday despite the on-field loss, poking fun at the private-vs.-public debate late in its eventual 49-8 loss to Montini.
"STORYLINE OF THE DAY: Thanks to our late touchdown we have narrowed the gap for today's State Championship games," wrote @SagesFootball. "Private Schools - 153 Public Schools - 22 Good luck to @mtz_football 98% of the state is pulling for you."
'I think that's a problem'
The public vs. private debate is perpetual, but really began to build late in the playoffs when Loyola quarterback Ryan Fitzgerald said public school semifinal opponent Frankfort Lincoln-Way East didn't "get to play the best competition" while Loyola was tested this season in the Chicago Catholic League.
'Guys were saying that it doesn't matter that they weren't battle-tested. And it showed that they hadn't played a four-quarter game all year. And I think that's a problem,' the Iowa-bound QB told shawlocal.com after a 27-24 win over East. "... Playing St. Francis, Mount Carmel, Brother Rice and Marist, playing teams that are playing for semifinals and championships shows how battle-tested we are.'
And Loyola is far from alone in flexing its tough schedule. In all, private schools make up half of the field on IHSA championship weekend — the most since the playoffs expanded to eight classes in 2001.
The previous high was seven in the 2018 finals, according to IHSA playoff guru Steve Soucie, pointing out a "marked disparity that will probably draw a lot of conversation heading into championship weekend."
Soucie said only 49 non-boundary or private schools play 11-man football, not counting the Chicago Public League. That's about 10 percent of teams statewide. Yet, those schools made up 50 percent of state finalists in 2024.
Is help on the way?
The IHSA system will soften the blow by pushing most of these teams up a class because of the enrollment multiplier and the success factor, but other traditional private powers are on the sidelines ready to take their place.
Soucie provided some cheeky commentary to Friday's blowouts by private schools, letting fans know that these small-school champs will be jumping up in classes next season.
"Just for clarification, and I know it doesn't help anything right now, but Althoff's last game in 1A is today," Soucie wrote. "They will be at least a 3A team next season." Later, as Montini began its blowout win, he wrote: "This game's public service announcement: Montini will be in 5A next season. I know, I know ..."
Finally, as DePaul opened a lead in the 4A final, Soucie wrote: "This game's public service announcement: DePaul Prep will likely be a 7A (possibly 8A) team next season."
Friday's champions Althoff, Christian, Montini and DePaul will be pushed up to larger classes the next two seasons. Also moving up regardless are 5A finalists Joliet Catholic and Nazareth, and Class 7A finalist Mount Carmel.
Yet other private powers like Chicago Brother Rice, Chicago Marist, Springfield Sacred Heart-Griffin, Chicago St. Ignatius, Elmhurst IC Catholic, Decatur St. Teresa and Oak Park Fenwick will lose their multipliers over the next two seasons and drop a class or two.
Let the debate ... continue.

title: CFP bracket bubble watch: As Alabama, South Carolina try to inch in, how to view Buckeyes?
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: Did South Carolina do enough in win over Clemson to win over CFP selection committee? Maybe, if they forget about losses to Alabama and Ole Miss.
content:
Did South Carolina do enough in win over Clemson to win over CFP selection committee? Maybe, if they forget about losses to Alabama and Ole Miss.
Miami's loss kept Clemson alive and threw open the door to discussion about a three-loss SEC team entering the field.
Ryan Day's latest loss to Michigan cast a pall over Ohio State, but maybe a ray of hope still exists.
Let's play a game of yes, no, maybe so.
In this little exercise, we'll assess teams' playoff stock.
Technically, no bids have been awarded, but we don't need a committee to tell us No. 1 Oregon has earned a spot regardless of what happens in the Big Ten championship game.
The Ducks are more exception than rule, though, by avoiding pitfalls that other contenders kept getting sucked into.
I won't tell you everyone on this list has earned a playoff spot, in the conventional sense, but playoff expansion combined with a wacky season full of upsets forces us to rewire what a playoff team looks like.
Yes, these teams are playoff bound
Oregon: The only question for the Ducks is whether they'll be seeded No. 1 or No. 5. A game against Penn State will determine that.
Notre Dame: The Irish used their conference independence to perfection. They took advantage of their soft schedule and will rolll into the playoff red hot after recovering from a Week 2 loss to Northern Illinois. While other playoff teams beat up on each other in conference championship games, Notre Dame enjoys weekend off before a home playoff game.
Texas: Pair Texas winning the SEC with Penn State capturing the Big Ten, and you'd probably get the Longhorns snagging the No. 1 seed. Lose the SEC to Georgia, and the Longhorns would remain a strong candidate to host a first-round playoff game.
Tennessee: Beating Vanderbilt secured a spot for the Vols, and now the only question is whether they'll be seeded high enough to play a first-round game at home (where they're quite good) or the road (where they're vulnerable).
Penn State: Ohio State's dud against Michigan forced Penn State into the Big Ten championship game, where the Nittany Lions will risk their seed, but not their bid.
Georgia: The Bulldogs nearly lost to Georgia Tech. If they had, this game against Texas would have had the power to eliminate Georgia. As it is, the Bulldogs are safe, regardless of outcome. Uncomfortable with a three-loss SEC runner-up in the playoff? Then shrink the playoff.
Ohio State: It takes a true victim of the moment to think the Buckeyes jeopardized their bid by losing to Michigan, but they damaged their seeding. They'll probably hover around the No. 8 or No. 9 seed line, which is the difference between hosting in Round 1 versus going on the road.
Indiana: The Hoosiers ' blowout win of Purdue, combined by losses from Miami and Clemson, solidified Indiana's playoff footing. The No. 10 seed projects as the likeliest landing spot.
Maybe, they'll be in the CFP bracket
SMU: The committee has been slow to recognize the Mustangs, winners of nine straight, but they can zoom to the No. 3 seed by winning the ACC crown. They still might qualify if they lose to Clemson, but that could depend on how the loss presents. SMU's best win came against Louisville, casting a bit of doubt on its at-large résumé.
Clemson: The Tigers lost to South Carolina but managed to keep their playoff hopes afloat thanks to Miami's loss to Syracuse that elevated Clemson into the ACC title game. A loss to SMU would eliminate Clemson. A win would unlock a bid, but likely not a bye.
Arizona State: Win the Big 12 championship, and the Sun Devils are in the playoff and vying for a bye. Lose the Big 12 championship, and it's off to an also-ran bowl, despite an impressive turnaround season.
Iowa State: See above description for Arizona State. The same applies to the Cyclones.
Boise State: The stakes for Boise State couldn't be higher. Beating UNLV would not only button up a playoff spot, it would thrust the Broncos into conversation for a bye, while a loss quite likely eliminates them.
UNLV: Upset the Broncos, and UNLV probably heads to the 12-seed. Lose, and that's that.
Miami: Miami's utter lack of a defense caught up with it in a loss to Syracuse. With a résumé pinned to victories over Louisville and Duke and losses in two of its last three games, Miami perhaps threw away its playoff bid. That probably depends on how the committee views a 10-2 ACC team compared to a three-loss SEC team.
South Carolina: Unranked in the initial CFP rankings, the Gamecocks stormed to the finish line with a lights-out defense and an improving freshman quarterback, LaNorris Sellers. Beating Clemson gave South Carolina more momentum than either Alabama or Ole Miss, but a bid for the Gamecocks would require the committee to overlook losses to Alabama and Ole Miss.
Alabama: Hard to imagine a three-loss team that lost to Vanderbilt and got trounced by Oklahoma would remain in the mix, but here we are. If strength of schedule and brand bias tip the scales, then Alabama will snag that final spot. Wins against Georgia and South Carolina bedrock Alabama's case.
Ole Miss: The Rebels' case nearly parallels that of Alabama: Wins against Georgia and South Carolina are mixed around perplexing losses. The trouble is, the committee valued Alabama ahead of Ole Miss last week, so the Tide seem to have Ole Miss blocked.
No, they're not making the playoff
Everybody else: The 18 teams listed above account for the remaining playoff contenders. If Tulane hadn't lost to Memphis on Thursday, you could have made an argument for two Group of Five qualifiers if three-loss Clemson won the ACC, but that avenue closed with Tulane losing on Thanksgiving.
Some closing thoughts in this "Topp Rope" view of college football:
1. The clouds haven't parted yet in Columbus, Ohio, but if the Buckeyes desire a ray of hope, here's one: Two years ago, Michigan clubbed Ohio State at the Horseshoe. The next we saw of the Buckeyes, they were a field goal away from upsetting Georgia in the CFP semifinals.
Point being, Ryan Day wilts against Michigan, but he's pretty good against most everyone else. Of course, that 2022 Michigan team I'm referencing was much better than the squad that beat the Buckeyes on Saturday. Still, there's only one team in this field that beat OSU, and that loss came by a single point. The Buckeyes are down, but not out.
2. I predict the top 13 of Tuesday's CFP rankings: 1. Oregon, 2. Texas, 3. Penn State, 4. Notre Dame, 5. Georgia, 6. Ohio State, 7. Tennessee, 8. SMU, 9. Indiana, 10. Boise State, 11. Alabama, 12. South Carolina, 13. Arizona State. First team out: South Carolina, because the Big 12 would claim an auto bid.
3. My latest "Topp Rope" playoff projection: Oregon (Big Ten), Texas (SEC), SMU (ACC), Arizona State (Big 12), Boise State (Group of Five), plus at-large selections Notre Dame, Penn State, Ohio State, Indiana, Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama. Next up: South Carolina.

title: Unlabeled food and soiled ceilings: Tazewell County's best, worst restaurant inspections for November
author: Mike Kramer
description: Nine Tazewell County restaurants had no violations during Tazewell County Health Department inspections in November. Three had five or more.
content:
The Tazewell County Health Department inspects a variety of local establishments identify issues that could contribute to the spread of foodborne illness and to ensure their general cleanliness and maintenance.
In November, the Health Department conducted about 40 routine inspections on restaurants, mobile establishments, and bars in Tazewell County. The Peoria Journal Star lists establishments based on the number of violations observed during routine inspections. Nine Tazewell establishments had no violations in November, and three had five violations or more.
Terminology used by the Health Department
Foodborne Illness Risk Factors: Risk factors are practices and procedures identified as the most prevalent contributing factors to foodborne illness.
Public Health Interventions: These are control measures meant to prevent foodborne illness or injury.
Good Retail Practices: Preventive measures to control the addition of pathogens, chemicals, and physical objects into food.
October inspections: Soiled equipment and expired food
Establishments receiving no violations
Boardwalk Inc. — 435 Court Street, Pekin
Countryside Banquet — 659 School Street, Washington
Culver's — 121 E. Courtland Street, Morton
Kep's Sports Bar Inc. -- 313 Muller Road, Washington
Prep Freeze Cook -- 1320 Washington Road, Washington
Scrolls the Sweet Room — 321 S. First Street, Morton
Striketown Bowl — 1690 Edgewater Drive, North Pekin
The Red Barn — 32597 Hay Road, Mackinaw
Tropical Smoothie Cafe -- 200 W. Washington Street, East Peoria
Establishments receiving five or more violations
Beck's, 317 Derby Street, Pekin
Seven violations: Discrepancies included a handwashing sink that was blocked by several buckets and boxes, employees without head coverings and jewelry on their wrists, and no sanitizer solution available while active food preparation and service were occurring. The Health Department also observed raw food stored above ready-to-eat food and several areas of soil and debris accumulation. Beck's was cited for a repeat violation for unlabeled food in the walk-in refrigerator.
September inspections: Pitted floors and soiled surfaces
Fast Dragon Pekin, 321 Court Street, Pekin
Six violations: The Health Department found several food items being stored directly on the floor of the walk-in freezer, a leaking faucet in the three-compartment sink, and a scoop that was completely buried in a container of corn starch. Additionally, the racks in the walk-in cooler were worn and beginning to rust, restroom doors that did not close properly, soiled ceilings in the walk-in cooler and women's restroom, a peeling floor in the walk-in cooler, and a hand sink that was not secured to the wall.
Subway, 1304 N. Eighth Street, Pekin
Six violations: There was no Certified Food Protection Manager present. Other violations included food stored directly on the floor, several soiled non-food contact surfaces, no soap at the handwashing sink, and no thermometer in the two-door refrigerator.

title: Nation's oldest brewing company finally bringing its beer to Illinois. What to know
author: Mike Kramer
description: Pennsylvania-based brewing company D.G. Yuengling & Son has plans to bring its beers to Illinois in 2025.
content:
The nation's oldest brewery is expanding into central Illinois.
The Pennsylvania based brewing company D.G. Yuengling & Son, Inc. announced Wednesday it will distribute its beers across Illinois in early 2025. Yuengling beers will initially be available on draft in Illinois at the end of January. The company will roll out more distribution and packaging in the following weeks.
"For years we have seen an overwhelming desire for our portfolio from our most loyal fans in Illinois that have been eagerly awaiting the brand's arrival," said Wendy Yuengling, the D.G. Yuengling & Son chief administrative officer. "We are incredibly proud to announce our expansion into a great beer market such as Illinois in the new year and, as the Oldest Brewery in America, we look forward to upholding our commitment of delivering high quality beer drinking experiences across the entire state."
D.G. Yuengling is family-owned and has been in operation since 1829. Principal beer brands include Yuengling Traditional Lager, Light Lager, Black and Tan, Golden Pilsner, Premium, Light, Bock, Dark Brewed Porter, Lord Chesterfield Ale, Oktoberfest, Yuengling, and Bongo Fizz.
Production of the beer is supplied by two breweries in Pottsville, Pennsylvania, and one in Tampa, Florida. More information is available at Yuengling.com.

title: Cheer up, Ohio State fans. At least Ryan Day isn't USC coach Lincoln Riley
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: Ohio State fans don't want to hear this, because losing four in row to Michigan cuts deep, but it could be worse. You could do worse than Ryan Day.
content:
Ohio State fans don't want to hear this, because losing four straight to Michigan cuts deep, but it could be worse. Just ask USC about Lincoln Riley.
Buckeyes retain lofty odds to win national championship, even after losing to Michigan.
NIL changed college sports forever, but didn't change recruiting rankings.
Ohio State fans don't want to hear this, because losing four consecutive games to your hated rival feels as unpleasant as pepper spray to the eyes, but it could be worse.
You could be a Southern California fan, stuck with Lincoln Riley.
Ryan Day, at least, offers upside during the 364 days a year he's not coaching against Michigan.
This past week reiterated the roller-coaster experience of employing Day.
On Saturday, Day seemed doomed. He lost, at home, to the worst non-COVID team forged in Ann Arbor since Brady Hoke ran the program, then watched dumbfounded as his Buckeyes players got into a postgame donnybrook with the Wolverines.
Day looked lost, befuddled, stupefied, choose your adjective.
By Wednesday, he'd transformed into Dr. Jekyll, signing a national top-five recruiting class for the sixth year in a row.
Day's haul included Tavien St. Clair, a five-star quarterback from Ohio, the type of quarterback who could help the Buckeyes maybe beat Michigan again someday.
Day and Ohio State form a combination that always will produce one of the nation's most talented rosters. He'll win nearly all of his games, and he'll break fans' hearts in the worst way, once or twice a season. Jekyll, meet Hyde, and Ohio State fans are sick of getting their hopes up only to watch Michigan men plant their flag in the Horseshoe.
But, the Buckeyes' hopes aren't dashed just yet, because the 12-team playoff affords Day the opportunity to win the national championship without beating Wolverines. Throughout most of the first 11 games, the Buckeyes looked like national championship material, and oddsmakers give Ohio State the third-best odds of winning the title.
Not bad for a team that mustered 252 yards against Michigan.
Two years ago, Day came as close to winning a national championship as he ever has. The Buckeyes lost by 22 points to Michigan in 2022, slipped in through the playoff's back door, then lost to the nation's best team, Georgia, in a game decided on the final play. If the Buckeyes convert their last-second field goal that night, they go on to beat TCU in the national championship.
That's not an excuse for Day, but rather a reminder that the Buckeyes are down, but not out.
Not with this roster.
'We have plenty of good enough players to (still win the national championship)," Day said this week.
Ohio State's talent isn't under the microscope, but Day will be if he can't achieve something of substance with this group.
Oh, because I mentioned Riley, how about the Big Ten's other $10 million-a-year man?
Riley's signing class ranks No. 13 nationally, which checks in behind Oregon, Ohio State and Michigan within the conference. Riley's recruiting couldn't maintain the pace of his first two ballyhooed classes, back when most of us thought he'd be a boon for the Trojans and that USC would capitalize on NIL.
You won't find national championship odds next to the Trojans, who are 6-6.
Of course, disgruntled Ohio State fans don't want to swap Day for Riley. They just want to swap him for someone else, anyone else who might beat Michigan.
Tread carefully.
Maybe, Ohio State would hire the next wunderkind, like Oregon did with Dan Lanning, or, perhaps, a big name would be interested.
Former NFL coach and Buckeyes alumnus Mike Vrabel is without a head coaching job. Notre Dame coach Marcus Freeman also played for Ohio State.
Would either say yes?
Hard telling, but, Ohio State remains an elite job, and the Buckeyes would attract good candidates if the job opened this winter. Ohio State blesses Day with great resources. The next coach would be well-resourced, too.
Ohio State fans aren't wrong to expect more than Day's 1-4 record vs. Michigan, and if Day can't beat the Wolverines or reach the national title game with a roster that reportedly earned $20 million in NIL money, then it's absolutely fair to ask whether it's time to try something else.
Riley's experience at USC, though, shows there's no such thing as a slam-dunk hire. As Day signs another premier recruiting class and heads to the playoff, the Trojans march on in mediocrity, strapped to a $10 million-a-year bust.
Here's what else I'm musing in this 'Topp Rope' view of college football:
NIL came, and recruiting rankings stayed the same
Well, that narrative died on the vine.
Three years ago, amid the first year of NIL, Texas A&M shot in like a comet soaked in oil money and signed the nation's No. 1 recruiting class.
Also that year, No. 1 overall recruit Travis Hunter – ever heard of him? – signed with Jackson State of the Championship Subdivision to play for coach Deion Sanders.
Those were peculiarities, although it wasn't entirely out of left field that Texas A&M signed a good class. Even before NIL, the Aggies had been gathering recruiting momentum. And Hunter had his reasons beyond NIL to want to play for the magnetic Sanders, the former two-sport star who allowed Hunter to play on both sides of the ball.
In any case, let's check out this year's top 10 signing classes, as ranked by the 247Sports composite: Texas, Alabama, Georgia, Oregon, Ohio State, Auburn, Michigan, LSU, Texas A&M, Tennessee.
Dial back the clock 10 years ago, and seven of those 10 schools signed top-10 classes, while Texas A&M signed the No. 11 class, and Oregon's class ranked 16th. Michigan was the only team signing a top-10 class this year that did not rank within the top 20 a decade ago. That's because the Wolverines had undergone a coaching change.
Point being, NIL changed everything for athletes profiting off their abilities and their fame. For recruiting rankings, it changed very little.
Email of the week
Rick writes: Speaking of 'elite' teams, who would you say is elite in the SEC, Blake? I would argue no one. Georgia and Tennessee might come the closest – but I would call them far short of elite, especially Georgia.
My response: Let's extend this exercise beyond the SEC's borders. I've compiled the list of elite college football teams this year, and the list is as follows: .
Did I miss anyone?
Parity rules this season – or, at least, more parity than we're used to in college football. Highly entertaining, and the perfect season for a 12-team, four-round playoff.
Paul writes: Alabama earned its status as a ' benefit of the doubt getter ' by a hundred years of winning national championships. ... As usual, the winners laughed and told jokes while the losers cried.
My response: Yes, even if the exploits of yesteryear's stars have little to do with this particular team, the events of the past wield power over decisions in the present.
Three and out
1. For the second consecutive year, Oklahoma will lose its starting quarterback to the transfer portal, with Jackson Arnold headed for the exit, The Oklahoman reported. Sooners coach Brent Venables contends for the No. 1 spot on a crowded SEC hot-seat list entering 2025.
2. As I mull whether to place Colorado's Hunter or Boise State's Ashton Jeanty atop my Heisman Trophy ballot, here's another question: Who goes third? I'll monitor Oregon quarterback Dillon Gabriel in the Big Ten championship game Saturday for an opening on my ballot that remains up for grabs.
3. Big 12 commissioner Brett Yormark recently bemoaned that the CFP selection committee values 'logos versus résumés.' Welcome to college football, Mr. Yormark. You still seem new here. And, by the way, the Big 12 would be a one-bid league even if the committee valued résumés over logos.
