There are a number of criteria the NCAA Tournament selection committee looks at in order to make its assessment in addition to subjective assessments like the 'eyeball test.' Among them:
Record: The team's overall record, conference record, and nonconference record.
Strength of schedule: The strength of the teams the team played against.
Head-to-head results: The results of games between the teams being compared.
Conference championships: Whether a conference championship was won in the regular season, or tournament.
Common opponents: The results of games against common opponents.
Adjusted Net Efficiency (NET): The NCAA's preferred metric measuring a team's overall performance during the regular season.
Team Value Index: A results-oriented component of the NET that ranks teams based on who they beat and where they played.
: A formula that ranks teams using a team's winning percentage, opponents' success and opponents' strength of schedule.

title: Presidential inauguration fact check: Analyzing claims from and about Trump
author: Chris Mueller
description: The USA TODAY Fact Check Team analyzes claims from Donald Trump's presidential inauguration.
content:
President-elect Donald Trump will be sworn in today at the U.S. Capitol, returning to the White House after winning a second term in the 2024 election.
The USA TODAY Fact Check Team will be monitoring the inauguration ceremonies and reactions from around the country. Follow along as we sort fact from fiction and add context where it's needed.
Our team uses primary documents, trustworthy nonpartisan sources, data and other research tools to assess the accuracy of claims.
Donald Trump claim: He won young voters in a landslide in 2024
'We won the youth vote by 36 points.'
Trump made this claim at a pre-inaugural rally on Jan. 19 while touting the resumption of TikTok's services in the U.S. The basis for Trump's claim wasn't clear, but exit polls from the 2024 election show he lagged behind Vice President Kamala Harris in support from young voters.
Exit poll data from CNN found Harris garnered 54% of the vote from voters age 18-29, compared to 43% for Trump. Harris also led 51% to 47% among voters 30-44.
A Tufts University analysis found Trump made gains among young voters compared to his performance in the 2020 election, but it similarly showed Harris beating Trump 51% to 47% among voters ages 18-29 and 50% to 47% among voters ages 30-44.
Harris defeated Trump 54% to 43% among voters ages 18-29 and 51% to 47% among voters ages 30-44, according to exit poll data from 10 key states published by NBC News.
-Andre Byik
Donald Trump claim: Crime rate has soared in the US
'Crime has gone through the roof.'
Trump's claim at Sunday's Washington, D.C., rally doesn't align with the most recent data.
A report by the FBI released in late September 2024 found violent crime in the U.S. fell for the third straight year in 2023, including murder, rape and assault, as USA TODAY reported. Overall, violent crime went down by 3% compared to 2022, while murder decreased more than 11% and rape dropped by about 9%.
A study by the Council on Criminal Justice examined monthly rates for 12 violent, property and drug crimes in 39 U.S. cities through the first half of 2024 and found there the rate dropped in 2024 for 11 of the 12. The study reported there were 7% fewer reported aggravated assaults and 18% fewer gun assaults compared to the first half of 2023.
The declines follow a sharp increase in crime that happened during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, when the country's murder rate jumped in its largest single-year increase on record. Violent crime then went down slightly in 2021 and again in 2022, according to the FBI.
The Justice Department's National Crime Victimization Survey for 2023 found the rate of violent victimization in the U.S. was 22.5 victimizations per 1,000 people 12 or older, similar to the 2022 rate. It also notes the 'overall decline' in the last three decades of violent victimization, which includes rape or sexual assault, robbery, aggravated assault, and simple assault. In 1993, the rate was 79.8 victimizations per 1,000 people.
-Chris Mueller
Where to find our fact checks
In addition to live events like today's inauguration, the USA TODAY Fact Check Team publishes about 100 checks each month on the most viral and significant claims circulating online. Here's how to find our work.
Subscribe to our Checking the Facts newsletter to have get the latest updates in your inbox each morning.
Follow our Facebook page to get our latest work in your feed.
This landing page always has our most recently published work.
A few of our latest fact checks:
President-elect Donald Trump's choices for his Cabinet have been lauded by his supporters, including many Republican lawmakers. But with Senate confirmation hearings underway, many have already faced tough questions about their qualifications for the high-level roles in Trump's administration.
Trump's pick for defense secretary, Pete Hegseth – a former Fox News host and Army National Guard veteran – was the first to endure a confirmation hearing. He was criticized by multiple Democratic senators who said he wasn't qualified for the role because of a lack of experience and accusations of sexual assault and alcohol abuse.
Pam Bondi, Trump's choice for attorney general, said if confirmed it would be her job to 'not only keep America safe but restore integrity to (the Justice Department).' Her confirmation hearing included heated exchanges with Democratic senators when she repeatedly refused to acknowledge that President Joe Biden won the 2020 election, though she did say she accepted that he was the current president.
Bondi wasn't Trump's first choice for the role – that was former Florida Republican Rep. Matt Gaetz, who dropped out after facing accusations that he paid women for sex and had sex with a minor.
Trump's selection of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to lead the Department of Health and Human Services prompted criticism of Kennedy's history of spreading health-related misinformation, including the long-debunked claim that vaccines are linked to autism.
Throughout the confirmation process, misinformation has spread online about Trump's nominees – both about who they are and what their policies might be if they're confirmed.
Here are some of the claims USA TODAY has debunked about Trump's nominees:
Claim: Pete Hegseth said 'I'm not a perfect person' in response to sexual assault question at confirmation hearing (False)
Claim: RFK Jr's only statement on vaccines is that they need to be studied (False)
Claim: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said all GMOs will be banned in the US on Jan. 20 (False)
Claim: Lindsey Graham announced he wouldn't confirm Matt Gaetz as attorney general (False)
Claim: Trump nominated Kash Patel as CIA director (False)
Claim: Trump nominated Amber Rose for education secretary (False)
Claim: Trump named Lauren Boebert as his education secretary on Nov. 13 (False)
Claim: Image shows Trump statement naming Tucker Carlson as White House press secretary (Altered)
-Chris Mueller
Donald Trump claim: Biden's 2020 election victory was 'rigged'
'If only the election weren't rigged, all the things that would have happened that would have been so good, but it was. We're not going to let that happen again.'
President-elect Donald Trump won the 2024 election, but that hasn't stopped him from making false claims about his prior loss. Speaking to supporters at a rally Sunday at Capital One Arena in Washington, D.C., Trump once again falsely claimed his 2020 election defeat to President Joe Biden was 'rigged.'
However, an overwhelming amount of evidence shows Biden won the presidency that year with 306 electoral votes. There have been lawsuits, recounts and forensic audits, but no credible evidence of widespread voter fraud has ever been uncovered.
In a statement released shortly after that election, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said it was "the most secure in American history," and there was "no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes or was in any way compromised."
William Barr, Trump's own attorney general, also said in early December 2020 that the Justice Department had "not seen fraud on a scale that could have effected a different outcome in the election."
Sen. Mitch McConnell, the Senate's top Republican at the time, pushed back on Trump's claim too, saying, 'Nothing before us proves illegality anywhere near the massive scale, the massive scale that would have tipped the entire election.'
The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, when Trump supporters tried to disrupt Congress' certification of the presidential election results, was predicated by the misguided belief that widespread voter fraud swayed the election in Biden's favor.
-Chris Mueller
How we pick and research fact checks
Ever wonder how fact-checkers do their work? We've got you covered.
Check out our process explainer to see how we pick claims, research them and edit them. This includes a rundown of how we cover live events like tonight's debate.
And if you've ever wondered who fact-checks the fact-checkers, you might want to read this op-ed explaining our emphasis on transparency. Because the answer is you! We use the format and approach precisely so that everyone has the ability to check our work.
-Eric Litke
Inauguration background: Our latest fact checks about Trump
A swirl of misinformation has surrounded President-elect Donald Trump in the lead-up to his inauguration.
Social media users, for instance, have spread false and misleading claims about his ideas for U.S. takeovers of Greenland and the Panama Canal, the attempt on his life at a Pennsylvania rally in July 2024 and the first actions he'll take when he becomes president for the second time.
Here are some of USA TODAY's recent fact-checks related to Trump:
Claim: Investigators haven't accessed Trump rally gunman's phone (False)
Claim: Trump said the US, Italy have been allies 'since the time of ancient Rome' (False)
Claim: Denmark announced interest in buying US after Trump floated idea of purchasing Greenland (False)
Claim: Panama banned Trump family from country for 100 years (False)
Claim: Image shows Elon Musk posted 'cool' image of himself sitting at Oval Office desk (Manipulated media)
Claim: Image shows Trump post saying he'll ban porn on day one of new term (Manipulated media)
Claim: Video shows Trump post about giving Staten Island to New Jersey (Manipulated media)
Claim: White House will appear on sex offender registry after Trump takes office (False)
-Andre Byik
Catch up on our debate, convention fact-checks
We fact-checked key moments throughout the 2024 election cycle, including debates and the Republican and Democratic conventions. Catch up here on what was false, what was true and what was in between from Kamala Harris, Donald Trump, JD Vance, Tim Walz and a host of others.
-Eric Litke
Inauguration background: Claims about the election

title: Forget loyalty, Ohio State's Jeremiah Smith should enter transfer portal to cash in after national title
author: Matt Hayes
description: This isn't about loyalty, it's about financial security: Ohio State star wide receiver Jeremiah Smith should enter transfer portal to cash in.
content:
It's unshakeable and unmistakable, this rare and real lifelong bond of college football championship teams. There is no greater truism.
Yeah, well, money changes everything.
Money is the very reason Ohio State star freshman wide receiver Jeremiah Smith – the best player on the field in Monday's national championship victory over Notre Dame – should enter the transfer portal and test the open market.
The engraving isn't set on the national championship trophy, but the writing couldn't be more on the wall in the now age of get yours. Millions are available in NIL deals, why ignore it?
More to the point: with the NFL still two years away for Smith, why risk a potential career-defining injury without earning as much as you possibly can?
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
This isn't about staying true to your school. It's about financial security in a physically-demanding business, where the end is always one play away.
'I've got two, three years left of college,' Smith said. 'I'm just focused on college right now.'
And that's the point. That's where this uncomfortable but necessary conversation must begin.
Because football, at the college or NFL level, has always been a game of what can you do for me now? And when you can't do it anymore, for whatever reason, it's next man up.
If you think college football has moved closer to the NFL in every aspect over the last four years of the NIL boom, it's obvious what ugly reality comes next. The NFL uses players until they're not physically able to play at an elite level, and once that happens, they cut players loose.
Thanks for your help, we're moving on. That's not college football, you say. It's not a cold, cutthroat business.
College football is not only a business, it's more player-friendly than anything the NFL Players Association could dream of demanding. It's free player movement every single season.
It's outperforming your contract in one season, and jumping into the portal and finding another team to pay you more. The NFL, for first-round picks in the annual draft, may as well be a career sentence.
The team has players guaranteed for the first five years of their career (if it picks up the option year of the first contract), and has exclusive negotiating rights thereafter. In other words, if players can't come to an agreement on a deal, the team can use a franchise tag to force a one-year deal ― a tag that can be used as many as three times.
And if players sustain a career-defining injury during that one-year franchise deal, they're out of luck. Guess who's moving on?
This is how Smith must see his next two seasons of college football. It would be fiscally reckless to see it any other way.
Former Ohio State star wideout Marvin Harrison Jr. was the first wide receiver selected in last year's draft, going No.4 overall to the Cardinals. He signed a fully-guaranteed $35.3 million contact.
Smith would not only be the first wide receiver selected in this year's draft, he would likely be picked in the Top 5. In other words, a near identical deal.
That's what a transfer portal move means for Smith. No matter what he's earning from Ohio State now, he has outperformed it.
He can enter the portal and return to Ohio State with a better deal, and we can all still talk about loyalty and lifelong bonds of championship teams. The grand statement can be made that at least one player still values school and money.
But by entering the portal, he can also see what the market will bring — then go back to Ohio State and see if the Buckeyes will match it. And if they don't or can't, he moves on with a championship and memories that will still last a lifetime.
Maybe he returns to Miami, where he grew up and won three state titles at Hollywood Chaminade-Madonna. That's four titles in four seasons, and the best player on the field in each season.
'It just shows that I picked two great schools,' Smith said.
Now it's time to choose again, to hit the open market and see what it brings. Be it at Ohio State, or somewhere else.
This has nothing to do with chasing money, or a lack of loyalty or leaving teammates behind. It has everything to do with financial future.
Again, it's fiscally reckless for Smith, or any elite college player on a one-year deal, to not see what else is out there. If college football truly is a mini-NFL, there's one truism that really is undeniable.
They'll use you until they can't, and then move on. The only difference is college players control movement and money.
And money changes everything.

title: Peoria, Boyd Gaming have discussed potential locations for a land-based casino
author: JJ Bullock
description: Huge Savings: Subscribe today to enjoy sports, entertainment, life, money, tech, and travel news along with videos, apps, and more.
content:
Peoria officials presented representatives from Boyd Gaming multiple locations in the city they think could be plausible spots for a new casino to be built.
The future of the Par-A-Dice Casino, which is operated by Boyd Gaming, has been in flux for months after Boyd indicated last year that it has intentions to build a new land-based casino, replacing the riverboat casino in East Peoria.
Officials from Peoria have been trying to entice Boyd Gaming to build a new facility on their side of the river in accordance with a 1991 agreement signed between East Peoria and Peoria that dictated any new land-based casino would have to be on Peoria's side of the river.
More: 'David vs Goliath': How East Peoria won the riverboat casino battle three decades ago
No final determination has been made yet on Boyd Gaming's plans, but the city did discuss potential locations near interstates where a new casino could fit with Boyd Gaming, according to city officials.
Boyd Gaming's Vice President of Communications David Strow declined to comment Thursday when reached by the Journal Star via email.
The revelation was noted by city councilmember and mayoral candidate Chuck Grayeb during a mayoral debate Wednesday night in which he said in a response to a question from moderators about the casino that Peoria had shown Boyd Gaming potential sites for a casino.
Grayeb told the Journal Star after the candidate forum on Wednesday night that he believes Boyd Gaming will be interested in doing a land-based casino in Peoria.
"Just removing itself from our area entirely, you start bumping into other gaming markets," Grayeb said. "So, we want to make it a great place, show them some of the locations where we think it would work well relative to our interstate highway links. There are a couple of sites we are sharing with them, and our staff is working with them very closely."
Grayeb said the city hopes to hear a decision soon.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali said Wednesday that she still feels that Boyd Gaming should adhere to the 1991 agreement, but she told the Journal Star on Wednesday night after the forum that the "jury is out" on what Boyd Gaming's plans will be.
Peoria City Manager Patrick Urich said Thursday the city will continue to have conversations with Boyd Gaming and will "hopefully find something that is amenable to everyone."
Ali, Grayeb and Urich declined to disclose the potential locations.
"I do feel strongly that we should enforce that agreement," Ali said Wednesday.
On Thursday, Ali confirmed that talks have been held between the city and Boyd Gaming on potential casino locations in Peoria. Ali said the parties involved agreed not to share what the locations were.
She did say, however, that the locations were suggested by the city.
"Casinos usually like locations that are near an expressway or highway," Ali said. "They like that visibility for people who might be passing through and they see a big sign and it draws them in. So, this is just standard for most casinos where they choose to locate because of visibility."
More: 'Forever strained'? Latest casino battle tests Peoria, East Peoria relationship
Ali said the locations have been discussed at several different meetings beginning last summer.
"They were open to the discussion," Ali said of Boyd Gaming's interest. "I can't really gauge their level of interest, but they were open to continued discussions."
Urich said conversations with Boyd Gaming have been "very professional."
While Boyd Gaming's plans for a casino still remain up in the air, Peoria's interest in drawing it across the river has been very much in the open.
In December, the Peoria City Council took its first official step in its efforts to lure the casino to Peoria, approving a plan to hire an attorney and investment firm to help it formulate a plan to woo Boyd Gaming.
Peoria will pay the attorney, John Elias, an hourly fee of $395 for the work and the investment firm, Innovation Capital, will be paid a minimum of $10,000 a month while working for the city.
The attorney and investment firm have been "helpful members of the team," Urich said, and the city has been "very happy to have them on board."

title: Opinion: It's not too late to restore civility
author: Carol Merna
description: Civility is the ethical glue of society and it starts and ends with us, this letter writer says.
content:
Who amongst us does not genuinely want to be treated with kindness and respect? It is the whole principle of the Golden Rule. Be nice to others and others will be nice in return; choose for others what they would choose for themselves; put yourself in someone else's shoes, and so on. I allege that this kind of civility represents the actual quality of our behavior. Civility requires us to control our impulses for the sake of others, freeing ourselves from self-centeredness, putting ethics into practice in our day-to-day encounters. Civility is, in a sense, ethical glue.
Civility represents a long tradition of moral virtues. Virtues like kindness, empathy, humility, integrity, honesty, and respect for others are standards of being good humans in open engagement. Without civility a society can erupt into verbally abusive, accusatory, and offensive attacks on one another, which is the way things appear to have been headed in the U.S. for quite a few years.
During the 105th Congress in 1997, Peoria's then member of the United State Congress, Ray LaHood (R-IL) and then Congressman David Skaggs (D-CO) hosted the first 'Civility Retreat' for their fellow members, designed to restore a bit of fellowship to a Congress whose poisonous partisanship had reached what was considered then to be a critically destructive level. That year, 200 members of the U.S. House of Representatives, 165 spouses and 100 of their children attended a three-day gathering to seek a greater degree of civility, mutual respect and, when possible, bipartisanship, proving that debate and mutual respect could coincide. Building relationships, developing trust, mutual respect and fostering civility really mattered to representatives LaHood and Skaggs, both of whom have long since left public life.
Realizing that putting effort into creating civility is an idea whose time has come around … again: It can only help us, as a nation, reclaim the honorable high ground. It goes without saying that all levels of government could benefit, but so could communities at large, the workplace, schools, and especially social media, where so much discord seems to be born.
Last year, the Center for Prevention of Abuse's outstanding Prevention Education team taught important lessons to 41,599 students in nearly 150 schools and other educational settings. CFPA offers plenty of essential age-appropriate, evidence-based, comprehensive courses on things like body safety, healthy relationships, anti-bullying, and peaceful conflict resolution. This important programming encourages civility and ways to stop abuse before it starts. We want everyone to feel safe and secure in their relationships, in all settings, in all circumstances. At CFPA we believe this learning should start at an early age so that young people grow up to understand healthy boundaries and how to keep themselves happy and out of harm's way while working to help others achieve the same.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
When one person is rude, others tend to follow, creating a society that does not care about the well-being of others. For the same reason, when one person is kind and thoughtful, others tend to follow, encouraging a caring culture. According to a recent study by the American Bar Association, 85% of U.S. residents believe civility is worse today than a decade ago. Can civility still be found? Of course it can. And if we really want it, we can rebuild what we have lost at a remarkable rate of speed. The first step to righting such wrongs starts in our own homes, and we must work to grow it where we can. We are in control of our own actions, and we can all play a part in creating a more civil and desirable society. This can only benefit our common humanity. It starts and ends with us.

title: 'We got Illinois going again': Legendary Illini basketball player dies at age of 61
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Chicago native helped Illinois basketball to a Big Ten Conference title and national prominence in the mid-1980s.
content:
Former Illinois men's basketball standout Efrem Winters died Monday morning, according to the Champaign News-Gazette. He was 61.
The 1984 all-Big Ten Conference first-team selection grabbed a then program-best 853 rebounds during his four-year career, from 1982 to 1986. Winters was living in Arizona after retiring from the Pepper Construction Company.
"He the nicest guy I ever played basketball with," former Illini teammate Doug Altenberger told the News-Gazette.
Winters was a McDonald's All-American at Chicago King before he played in 129 of 130 games during four consecutive 20-win seasons with the Illini. The 6-foot-9, 240-pound power forward left Champaign as the No. 3 all-time leading scorer with 1,487 points.
Illinois basketball: How the Illini beat Northwestern
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Winters was instrumental in helping Illinois win the Big Ten Conference championship during the 1983-84 season, ending a 21-year Big Ten title drought as part of the team that help put Illinois on the national radar. That season, Illinois finished one game short of the Final Four, losing to Kentucky, 54-51, in a regional final.
'I always think about the Kentucky game," Winters said in 2009 when that Illini team was honored during a 25-year reunion. 'People bring it up all the time. The Kentucky game? What happened? What if you would have won that game?"
Illinois eventually made the Final Four in 1989 and again in 2005. Winters said his 1984 squad stands alongside. 'We'd won the Big Ten," Winter said in 2009. "We were the thing that got Illinois going again."
Winters was selected by the Atlanta Hawks in the fourth round of the 1986 NBA draft. He didn't make the Hawks, and never played in the NBA.

title: Illinois football continues in-state push, lands commitment from three-star edge rusher
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Illinois added its sixth recruit from the Class of 2026 and its second from the state — this one from a Class 8A power.
content:
The Illinois football program received another in-state commitment for the Class of 2026.
Defensive end Jacob Alexander of state power Frankfort Lincoln-Way East committed to coach Bret Bielema and the Illini on Monday, according to a post from his high school's X.com account.
The 6-foot-4, 240-pound edge rusher chose Illinois over more than a half-dozen other Big Ten Conference offers, including Michigan, Michigan State and Wisconsin.
"Just a great atmosphere and the people here," Alexander told Illini Inquirer on Sunday. "That's what's important: the people here in the building. I know I can be great here."
Alexander is the sixth high school prospect to commit to the Illini's Class of 2026 and the second from the state, joining receiver Davon Grant of DeKalb. The Illini continue their push for the state's top talent and are in the mix for about 10 three- and four-star recruits in Illinois, according to Illini Inquirer.
The Illini also have received commitments from offensive lineman Landen Van Seggern of Nebraska, and three Florida players in quarterback Michael Clayton and receiver Kenyon Alston of Orlando and linebacker Kingston Shaw of Apopka.

title: Trump White House rescinds freeze memo on federal grants, ending feud with Congress
author: Bart Jansen
description: The Trump administration reversed its policy to freeze grants and loans while officials evaluated whether spending met the president's priorities.
content:
WASHINGTON − The Trump administration rescinded a memo describing a freeze Wednesday on federal grants and loans after setting off a firestorm in Congress and at least two lawsuits disputing who controls spending priorities, according to White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.
The Office of Management and Budget aimed to review grants and loans to ensure they complied with his priorities, which lawmakers and legal experts blasted as unconstitutional, Leavitt told reporters on Tuesday.
But congressional Democrats insisted the Constitution gives Congress the power to control spending decisions. A federal judge on Tuesday had temporarily blocked the Trump administration policy.
In a statement to reporters on Wednesday, Leavitt said "in light of the injunction" OMB is pulling back its memo "to end any confusion on federal policy created by the court ruling and the dishonest media coverage."
Trump's other executive orders on federal funding issued since Inauguration Day will "remain in full force and effect and will be rigorously implemented by all agencies and departments," Leavitt added.
"This action should effectively end the court case and allow the government to focus on enforcing the President's orders on controlling federal spending. In the coming weeks and months, more executive action will continue to end the egregious waste of federal funding," Leavitt said.
The Trump administration's decision came shortly before a federal judge in Rhode Island was set to consider a request by 22 mostly Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia for a temporary restraining order blocking a policy that they said could have a devastating effect on their budgets.
Chief U.S. District Judge John McConnell in Providence could have issued an opinion that was longer in duration than the temporary pause U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan imposed on Tuesday in a separate case brought by a group of nonprofits in Washington, D.C.
On Capitol Hill, top Republicans and Democrats both endorsed the Trump White House's move.
'While it is not unusual for incoming administrations to review federal programs and policies, this memo was overreaching and created unnecessary confusion and consternation,' said Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, the chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee.
Collins' Democratic counterpart on the powerful Senate panel, Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, called the Trump administration's decision "an important victory for the American people."
"Still, the Trump administration − through a combination of sheer incompetence, cruel intentions, and a willful disregard of the law − caused real harm and chaos for millions over the span of the last 48 hours which is still ongoing," Murray said in a statement.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the Trump White House's reversal should justify withdrawing Russell Vought's nomination to head the Office of Management and Budget. A hearing on Vought's nomination is scheduled Thursday.
'Americans fought back and Donald Trump backed off,' Schumer said in a statement. 'Now Donald Trump needs to rescind Russell Vought's nomination.'
Skye Perryman, CEO of Democracy Forward, which led the legal challenge to the policy for nonprofits, health agencies and small businesses, said millions of people can "breathe a sigh of relief."
The Department of Veterans Affairs announced late Tuesday that all its grant, loan and financial assistance programs were approved to continue under a White House memo that threatened to halt the aid.
"Our team will continue to bring swift legal actions to protect the American people and will use the legal process to ensure that federal funding is restored," Perryman said.
In the meantime, the department said it determined 44 financial assistance programs would continue uninterrupted even if the memo is reinstated.
'This will have no impact on VA health care, benefits or beneficiaries,' Veterans Affairs Acting Secretary Todd Hunter said in a statement.

title: Freezing rain expected for much of Illinois on Wednesday. Here's what you need to know
author: Tom Ackerman
description: It may have felt like summer for some Illinoisians in recent days, but slick roads will soon remind us that winter has not gone yet.
content:
It may have felt like summer for some Illinoisians in recent days, but slick roads will soon remind us that winter has not gone yet.
Central Illinois can expect some freezing rain during their morning commute Wednesday, while northern Illinois is predicted to see freezing rain Wednesday night, according to the National Weather Service. Southern Illinois will see only rain.
Here's what you need to know for Wednesday's forecast.
Central Illinois outlook
The Springfield area can expect to see patches of freezing drizzle by 5 or 6 a.m. Wednesday.
Rising temperatures there should be just warm enough to change the freezing drizzle to simply rain in the late morning, said Chris Geelhart, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
One degree of temperature could make a significant impact when it comes to the slickness of the roads and sidewalks. Areas just north of Springfield like Peoria and Bloomington may still have slick roads by the afternoon commute, Geelhart said.
Springfield will reach a balmy high near 38 Wednesday.
Predictions only call for a few hundredths of rain in Central Illinois, but 'when it comes to freezing rain, it really does not take much to start causing significant issues,' he added.
There is a 90% chance of precipitation.
Northern Illinois outlook
North of Illinois 74 and towards Illinois 80, slick conditions are more likely later into the afternoon Wednesday and into the evening.
In Rockford, for example, snow, freezing rain and sleet will happen before midnight with a 90% chance of precipitation. Wednesday night will see a low around 29.
Slippery commuting is possible Thursday morning because the temperature will be below freezing. Thursday ultimately will reach a high near 41.
Friday will cool off and see and high around 29.
Southern Illinois outlook
Places south of Illinois 70 in the southern part of the state will not see freezing rain in the coming days because it will be too warm.
What should a winter safety kit include?
IDOT recommends that motorists turn on interior lights and call for help if they get stuck on the roads. Stay with the car and try not to over-exert themselves. Also, keep a winter safety kit handy in case of being stuck for long periods.
The kit should include:
Jumper cables
Flares
Windshield washer fluid
An ice scraper
Traction material
Blankets
Non-perishable food items
A first-aid kit
Water

title: 9 romantic restaurants to visit on Valentine's Day in Peoria
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: From steakhouses to seafood spots, these Peoria restaurants could be an ideal dinner date on Valentine's Day.
content:
Show Caption
A time for romance is almost here, as Valentine's Day is drawing near.
You may get cards, candies or a flower bouquet, and then go out to dinner to round out the day.
So as you're getting the whole thing planned, the Journal Star is here to lend a hand.
I've created a list of restaurants here, where you can celebrate with the person you hold most dear.
As a note, only restaurants with Valentine's Day seating still available as of Thursday, Jan. 30 have been included. Seating times may be limited to early or late-night dinners.
The Bar at BLACK BAND
Diners will step into a moody, rustic industrial atmosphere with large wooden beams and warm brick walls. The establishment's upstairs seating area provides a cozy, intimate setting which is especially perfect for a romantic outing.
The Bar at BLACK BAND is serving a five-course prix fixe menu with two cocktail pairings on Valentine's Day. Tickets are $150 each and seatings are available at 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. Customers can select a soup or salad, one of three starters and their main course. Entrée options include:
Filet with potato and asparagus
Seafood linguine with clams and mussels
Vegetarian mushroom risotto
The restaurant's regular menu will be available at the bar.
Details: 1000 SW Adams St., Peoria; (309) 680-1233, https://www.thebaratblackband.com/
Cyd's in the Park
Tucked away in Donovan Park, Cyd's in the Park offers a welcoming and comfortable space to escape and unwind with the person you love. The dining area and Star Bar boast large windows which frame the park's scenic views. Or, couples can cozy up near a warm fire in the enclosed patio.
A five-course prix fixe menu is available for $110 per person on Valentine's Day. The meal includes an appetizer, bread and salad, a pasta dish, an entrée and a dessert trio. The full menu can be viewed at https://www.cyds.biz/VALENTINES2025/.
https://reservations.getwisely.com/cyd-s-in-the-park.
Rizzi's Italian Restaurant
Italian cuisine is widely considered an ideal choice when it comes to romantic dining. So, if you're searching for the finest pastas in Peoria, Rizzi's has been named best Italian restaurant for multiple years running.
Inside, couples will find a cozy, white tablecloth restaurant.
The menu features pasta dishes such as capellini marechiara, hand-rolled manicotti, fettuccine carbonara, butternut squash ravioli and tortellini & steak. Seafood, veal and chicken dishes are also available, along with various soups, salads and starters.
The restaurant is not taking reservations and will operate on a first come, first served basis.
Joe's Original Italian & Martini Bar
Situated along Prospect Road in Peoria Heights, Joe's Original Italian & Martini Bar includes patterned tablecloths, warm wood accents and homey décor.
The establishment's menu features Italian-focused fine dining dishes, such as:
Blue filet – which is a 9 oz filet mignon wrapped in bacon and topped with blue cheese butter and port wine reduction.
Seared tuna
Pan seared Maine diver scallops
Lobster ravioli
Pasta compamare – which includes sauteed chicken, shrimp and crabmeat in a cayenne cream sauce. The pasta also includes broccoli, mushrooms and tomatoes.
Seatings for Valentine's Day are limited, and reservations are recommended.
Johnny's Italian Steakhouse
With sparkling chandeliers and an upscale menu, Johnny's Italian Steakhouse may offer an ideal space to celebrate with that special someone.
But don't just take my word for it. The restaurant was a finalist in the romantic restaurant category of the 2024 Official Community's Choice Awards – and was a finalist during the 2023 awards, as well.
The establishment serves a variety of pastas, such as the Johnny's Chanel No. 5. The dish features cheese ravioli served in a garlic cream sauce and topped with lobster, shrimp, prosciutto, artichokes, spinach and sun-dried tomatoes. Customers can also find aged steak, seafood, specialty entrees and more.
Valentine's Day seatings are limited, and reservations are highly recommended.
Details: 101 Holiday St., East Peoria; (309) 692-3887, https://johnnysitaliansteakhouse.com/east-peoria/
Jonah's Seafood House & 2601 Oyster Bar
Perhaps seafood seems suitable for a special occasion like Valentine's Day. If so, Jonah's Seafood House & 2601 Oyster Bar serves an extensive seafood selection.
The restaurant's dinner menu features entrees such as:
South African lobster tail and filet
Jumbo Alaskan king crab
Sesame crusted Hawaiian ahi tuna #1
Devil bronzed ora king salmon
Gulf shrimp scampi alla crema
Spicy Louisiana jambalaya
Couples can also dine at the 2601 Oyster bar, which serves a variety of starters, entrees and drinks.
Reservations are highly recommended.
Details: 2601 N. Main St., East Peoria; (309) 694-0946, https://www.jonahsseafood.com/
Reservations
Reservations opened in Peoria earlier this year. The restaurant's menu features distinct, elevated dishes perfect for special occasions or romantic outings. Some of the entrees include:
Lamb chops
Butter salmon
Lobster tacos
Poblano lime cream pasta
Asian kale salad
For Valentine's Day, chef Jeremy Washum expects to serve stuffed salmon, as well as steak and lobster, as specials.
Those planning to visit are strongly encouraged to RSVP. Reservations can be made on the restaurant's website.
Details: 718 W. Glen Ave., Peoria; (309) 966-9121, https://www.reservationsfoodgroup.com/
'Something for almost anybody': New Peoria restaurant will offer distinctive dinner menu
Rhythm Kitchen Music Cafe
How about dinner followed by a night of jazz?
The Contemporary Art Center of Peoria is hosting a live musical performance featuring Peoria jazz vocalist Judy Page at the Preston Jackson Gallery. The event is scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m. and tickets can be purchased at https://309tix.com/events/st-valentines-live-at-the-five-spot-featuring-judy-page-2-14-2025.
On the building's first floor, Rhythm Kitchen will welcome guests on a first come, first served basis beginning at 5 p.m. Couples can dine before the event begins or can bring their food and drink with them.
Diners at Rhythm Kitchen can find entrees such as:
Gumbo ya-ya
Salmon berry salad
Grilled ahi tuna
Crawfish Etouffee
Tandoori chicken salad
Smoked gouda cheeseburger
Details: 305 SW Water St., Peoria; (309) 676-9668, https://rhythmkitchenmusiccafe.com/
Saffron Social
With glowing chandeliers, stylish accents and an intricate, built-in bar area, Saffron Social boasts a high-end atmosphere in Downtown Peoria which is perfect for those getting fancied up for Valentine's Day. The restaurant serves steaks, seafood, sushi, pastas and other dishes.
Valentine's Day seating is limited, and reservations are highly recommended.

title: Gov. Pritzker pokes fun at President Trump, jokes he's renaming Lake Michigan
author: Jeff Kolkey
description: In new video, Gov. JB Pritzker pokes fun at President Donald Trump's recent efforts to rename the Gulf of Mexico and buy Greenland.
content:
Taking a humorous shot at President Donald Trump, Gov. JB Pritzker on Friday posted an "important announcement" on social media, declaring with a straight face that he plans to rename Lake Michigan and annex Green Bay, Wisconsin.
The Great Lake will henceforth be known as "Lake Illinois," Pritzker announced with a straight face. Mississippi River — Pritzker is looking at you next.
"The worlds finest geographers, experts who study the Earth's natural environment have concluded a decades long council and determined that a Great Lake deserves to be named after a great state," Pritzker said. "So today I am issuing a proclamation declaring that hear in after, Lake Michigan shall be known as 'Lake Illinois.'"
The Pritzker proclamation comes after Trump recently signed an executive order requiring the federal government to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on official maps. Google has said it is going to follow the order once updated on official government sources.
Pritzker said he is forwarding his declaration on Lake Michigan's new name to Google as well.
"In addition, the recent announcement that to protect the homeland the United States will be purchasing Greenland, Illinois will now be annexing Green Bay to protect itself against enemies foreign and domestic," Pritzker said. "I have also instructed my team to work diligently to prepare for an important announcement next week regarding the Mississippi River. God bless America and Bear down."

title: Visits, offers and NIL money: Whirlwind start to 2025 for elite Dunlap college football recruit
author: Adam Duvall
description: Huge Savings: Subscribe today to enjoy sports, entertainment, life, money, tech, and travel news along with videos, apps, and more.
content:
DUNLAP — January was a whirlwind 31 days for Mack Sutter.
The 6-foot-6, 225-pound four-star Dunlap tight end navigated the live period as a revolving door of college football coaches visited him, a slew of new scholarship offers came his way — and for the first time he experienced dealing with NIL.
In January alone, Sutter picked up 11 scholarship offers including Notre Dame, USC, Florida State, North Carolina and Colorado. He now has 45 overall offers over the last calendar year.
'It was pretty crazy,' Sutter said Monday. 'It was getting a little stressful for my parents, but we were enjoying it. It was an unreal experience.'
Sutter estimates "almost every coach I've been talking to popped in." The coveted Class of 2026 recruit saw faces both new and familiar. Head coaches James Franklin (Penn State), Bret Bielema (Illinois), Kirk Ferentz (Iowa) and Barry Odom (Purdue) all made in-person appearances at either Sutter's basketball games or practices.
'He'll play in the NFL': Illinois coach heaps praise on downstate football recruit after visit
'I didn't think it was going too busy,' the second-ranked junior in the Illinois said, 'because I narrowed it down to a top 12.'
Sutter, ranked No. 2 statewide, narrowed his list to 12 finalists in August: Alabama, Auburn, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, Ohio State, Ole Miss, Penn State and Tennessee. Despite not making the original cut, schools like Indiana, USC, UCLA, Texas A&M and Texas came on strong during the first part of 2025.
What's more, schools not on that list are using NIL to try and lure themselves back into the mix. NIL — or "Name, Image, and Likeness" — deals have become common place in college athletics with some football players getting six-figure contracts through endorsements.
'Money's a big thing now,' the 6-foot-6, 225-pounder said, 'so they're trying to win me over with that … Some schools I've said no to are still trying to get in the race because they know they can swing things with (NIL).'
Right now, though, the two-time Journal Star All-Area player is focused on cutting his finalists to five, while making his official visits to those schools.
One school already has made the cut: Penn State. Sutter has plans to visit University Park, Pennsylvania, on the weekend of June 6, 2025.
'I'll be setting the other four here, soon,' Sutter said, noting that will happen in the next week or two. He expects to make a final decision around the first week of June.
Another four-star tight end in the Class of 2026 is Mt. Zion tight end JC Anderson, who is good friend of Sutter's. The fellow Illinois high schooler saw a similar string of coaches spend January coming through the school, located about 90 miles south of Peoria.
In fact, the 6-foot-7, 235-pound Anderson recently finalized his official visit schedule: Illinois, North Carolina, Auburn and Notre Dame made Anderson's wish list.
These two would give opposing defenses big time problems.
'Our families are really close,' Sutter said, 'so we're always just sharing stuff about the recruiting process and all that. We always talk about how it would be really cool if we went to the same school together, because we're the package deal that everybody would want — the X and Y that are tight ends that would be pretty cool to have.'
Another unique aspect of last month's live period was getting an offer from UNC head coach Bill Belichick, the legendary NFL coach with six Super Bowl rings with the New England Patriots. Tar Heels general manager Mike Lombardi and UNC offensive coordinator Freddie Kitchens met with Sutter in person to make the pitch.
Sutter's dad, Eddie Sutter, played for the Cleveland Browns from 1993-95 when Belichick was head coach and Lombardi was the director of player personnel.
Bill Belichick: Peorian's connection to Bill Belichick came full circle in son's college football recruitment
'That just was cool to see what my dad's coaches were like,' the younger Sutter said, 'because he's always had stories about how good they were, and stuff. It was cool finally meet them in person and see what it was like for my dad when he was going through the (NFL) process, too.'

After plenty of solid winter sports performers over the last week, here are the Journal Star high school athlete of the week nominees for Feb. 3-8.

Tucker Sennett, Princeville boys basketball - Class 1A
Sennett helped Princeville come out of its four-game losing streak in a big way. The senior guard hit six 3-pointers and scored 26 points in a 77-69 double-overtime win against Peoria Christian on Saturday. He began his week last Tuesday with a game-high 18 points in a 56-43 loss to Annawan.

Meiss helped give the Titans a pair of victories last week. Kitt makes back-to-back appearances on the ballot following another big week. The sophomore's 34 points on Saturday night was instrumental in helping EP end Morton's 17-game win streak with a 72-69 overtime victory. He began his week last Wednesday with a double-double (20 points, 12 rebounds) to beat Washington, 54-46.
Joley McLaughlin, Lewistown girls basketball - Class 1A
McLaughlin bookended her week with two big games for Lewistown. The junior went for 22 points and eight rebounds in Saturday's 74-16 win over Riverton. McLaughlin began her week last Monday with a 26-point, eight-rebound performance in a 69-38 victory against Payson-Seymour.

The senior helped lead the Washington, East Peoria and Morton co-op to the Mid-Illini Conference Tournament on Saturday. He won the 500-yard freestyle in 4:58.29, while swimming on the winning 400-yard freestyle relay (3:28.82). Walliker also took second in the 200-yard IM with a time of 2:06.80. title: SEC tries to revise College Football Playoff bracket, but Greg Sankey faces pushback
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: The SEC helped rearrange conference alignment in a blow to the 12-team playoff's vision. Now, it's time for SEC boss to slurp what he crumbled.
content:
The SEC helped rearrange conference alignment in a blow to the 12-team playoff's vision. Now, it's time for SEC boss Greg Sankey to slurp what he helped crumble.
Removing byes for conference champions would help SEC and Big Ten, but other conferences could throw up a short-term road block.
12-team CFP bracket format could stay the same for 2025 season, even though SEC hungry for change.
Greg Sankey enjoys philosophical musings. I wonder whether the SEC commissioner knows this one: You slurp what you crumble.
Or, what about this one? Self-made problems become the toughest to solve.
Sankey wants to reconfigure the 12-team College Football Playoff, which he helped create, after just one season.
Sankey's modification wish list includes stripping away protection of first-round playoff byes for conference champions.
In such a universe, first-round byes would go to the top four teams in the final College Football Playoff committee rankings, with no built-in protections for conference champions. In theory, then, all four byes could go to teams from the same conference – say, Sankey's SEC.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Sankey says this change became necessary because conference affiliation no longer looks how it did when commissioners, including Sankey, devised the 12-team playoff format.
Hmm, I wonder why conference alignment changed.
Ah, yes, it changed after Sankey steered the SEC's plunder of Texas and Oklahoma, the Big 12's top brands. The SEC's heist started the realignment carousel's ignition, and then the Big Ten sprang into action and raided the west coast. In turn, the Big 12 and ACC shopped the Pac-12's discount rack, and that conference became an unrecognizable husk.
'It's not the same reality that existed when the 12-team model developed, and I've opined what I believe is the need to adjust,' Sankey said on 'The Paul Finebaum Show' last week.
'And, the seeding issues, particularly moving teams into the top four, need to be looked at deeply.'
Let's not forget, Sankey already engineered a change to the 12-team playoff before its launch. Originally, the playoff had been devised for six automatic bids and six at-large bids. After the Pac-12 buckled, Sankey successfully spearheaded the switch to five automatic bids and seven at-large berths.
His latest effort to bend the bracket to the SEC's desires encounters a roadblock, though.
Changing the playoff before next season would require unanimous approval from the other conference commissioners, plus Notre Dame. Sankey knows he's unlikely to gain the full support necessary to trigger a change. Commissioners from leagues like the Big 12, Mountain West and ACC have little incentive to give up byes for conference champions.
Big 12, ACC have little reason to rework College Football Playoff
The first-round bye carries more value than bracket positioning. It also triggers additional financial compensation to the league represented in the quarterfinals.
Conference commissioners aren't in the business of turning down paydays.
'I do not have the appetite to give up any financial reward that comes with a bye,' Big 12 commissioner Brett Yormark recently told Yahoo! Sports.
As ACC commissioner Jim Phillips told Yahoo! Sports, earmarking byes for conference champions is 'not some exotic structure.'
Indeed, a professional league might call that common sense.
If at-large playoff qualifiers become eligible for byes, college football would become America's only sport in which a team could finish fourth in its conference standings and earn a playoff bye.
The commissioners reportedly will meet in Dallas later this month to discuss the playoff's future. If even one rival conference commissioner tells Sankey, 'No thanks, bucko. We like the playoff as is,' the format will remain the same next season.
In other words, grab a straw, SEC.
You too, Big Ten.
Those 'Super Two' conferences puffed up during realignment by weakening other conferences, but now it's time to grab a straw and slurp what they crumbled – for one more year, anyway.
SEC, Big Ten will get their way, but question is how soon?
Impeding the 'Super Two' in their playoff revision would be a short-lived roadblock to the playoff becoming a de facto SEC-Big Ten Invitational. Starting with the 2026 season, unanimous commissioner approval no longer will be required to change the format. At that time, the SEC and Big Ten gain additional authority over the bracket. Hard to imagine that'll be good for the "little guy" conferences.
So, changes very likely are coming, but why should rival commissioners capitalate to Sankey and Tony Petitti, Sankey's Big Ten cohort, any sooner than required?
If teams were seeded based off ranking this past season, Big Ten and SEC teams would have seized all the byes.
I don't fault the SEC for snapping up Texas and Oklahoma and triggering realignment, and Sankey's just doing his job by seeking an avenue to more byes for SEC teams. The SEC endured two consecutive seasons without advancing a team to the national championship game, so the conference could use a boost. But, the Big 12, ACC and others have no reason to fork it over.
Yormark and Phillips would be doing their jobs by telling Sankey to spend the next year slurping up the beautiful 12-team playoff vision that he helped crumble into realignment soup.

title: 'The right thing for us:' Couple keeps longtime Morton space alive with new restaurant
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: The business owners refreshed the vintage space and reopened at a popular Tazewell County spot in December.
content:
Show Caption
Amy and Joe Erickson worked to put their own touch on the space, which formerly housed Kemp 208 Main Street Grille.
Co-owner Amy Erickson said she wanted to create a place where everyone can "come in and be comfortable."
The menu features steaks, seafood, salads and more.
After nine years spent serving Morton, Kemp 208 Main Street Grille announced its time in business was coming to an end.
Yet, as former owner Cathy Kemp bid farewell to the community, she announced the beginning of a new chapter for the space.
The previous restaurant gave way to The 208 House late last year, as Kemp passed the torch to longtime employee Amy Erickson and her husband, Joe Erickson. After refreshing the space, the couple opened The 208 House on Dec. 17 to a tremendous turnout.
'The very first night we opened – without taking any phone calls of reservations — just me setting people up, and we were full from top to bottom,' Amy said, estimating that the restaurant served over 70 people its first night.
Since then, the Ericksons said they have continued to receive a warm welcome from the community.
What's on the menu at The 208 House?
The former restaurant's chef has remained, and Amy said The 208 House utilizes many of the same vendors for products. Having spent many years at Kemp 208, Erickson said she wanted to offer similar options while also expanding the menu to include items customers consistently asked for.
'We always had customers kind of asking for a (little more) diversity in the menu, which can be hard with us being such a small restaurant,' Amy said. 'But that's basically what we tried to do.'
The 208 House serves various starters, salads, seafood, pastas and entrees. This includes dishes such as:
The 208 House salad, which combines apples, candied walnuts, crumbled feta, dried cranberries and mixed greens with an herb dressing. A half salad is $6, and a full salad is $12.
Lobster flatbread with bacon, creamy alfredo, Romano and a ranch drizzle for $16.
Bourbon peppercorn New York strip for $42. The 16 oz steak is marinated in a bourbon peppercorn sauce.
Balsamic bacon scallops for $48. The dish features scallops which have been pan-seared with a balsamic bacon jam.
Steaks have been a popular menu item so far, according to Joe. Amy said customers have also been drawn to the restaurant's seafood dishes. She said, often, diners will order a steak during their first visit before branching out to try something new.
Amy said the restaurant typically runs two to three features per week, and she expects to update the menu seasonally, as well.
'That's always kind of a nice way to go,' she said. 'People get to try new things, and you get to use new products that kind of come in as the seasons change.'
Moving into the warmer months, Amy hopes to add more casual items to the menu. She would also like to launch wine dinners and burger nights.
At The 208 House, customers can also find a seasonal cocktail selection. The menu currently includes drinks such as:
The 208 White Russian – which combines vodka, Kahlua and RumChata
Apricot old fashioned – which features bourbon, apricot brandy, apricot syrup and bitters
Frosty margarita – which includes tequila, lime juice, pineapple juice and coconut cream. Amy Erickson said the drink, 'looks like winter but tastes like summer – that's for sure.'
Amy Erickson said new wine selections are also available.
'Come in and be comfortable'
While The 208 House offers various high-end menu items, Amy wants everybody 'to be able to come in and be comfortable.'
Diners do not have to fancy up for their visit, she said, or order the most expensive dishes available. She said guests are welcome to order a lighter option or even stop by to enjoy a few drinks.
'We want it to be somewhere where people can still pop in and just feel like it's still pretty casual,' Amy said. 'But then again come in and celebrate something really important like an anniversary.'
The restaurant is broken into various spaces – which gives guests multiple seating options. There is the main dining room, an enclosed porch and two rooms on the second floor which work well for private dining.
Overall, Amy said customers will find different atmospheres 'depending on where you're sitting.'
While they tried to preserve the comfort Kemp 208 offered, Amy and Joe Erickson said they worked to put their own touch on the space, as well. They freshened up the paint, brought in new lighting and décor, set up a new host stand, rearranged the tables and added tablecloths.
'Being in a 1918 Craftsman home, the structure itself is just very charming …' Joe said. 'There isn't a lot that can or should be done to the structure itself to make changes. It's really just kind of changing that aesthetic and freshening it up.'
'The right time for us to take a chance'
Amy knew Kemp eventually wanted to step away from the restaurant to focus on family. So, about a year ago, Joe said they began talking to Kemp about the possibility of taking over the space.
There was a lot to consider. Joe said they realized owning and operating a restaurant would have a big impact on their family and finances. The couple met while working at a restaurant, so each understood how challenging the industry can be.
However, Joe noted that the location had long housed various eateries. Moreover, Amy had spent years connecting with the community at that very establishment.
'We really just decided it was the right thing for us and the right time for us to take a chance,' Joe said.
Getting open took longer than anticipated, but Amy said the extra downtime allowed them to 'be in a better position' when it came to welcoming the community.
While there is never a perfect time to open a restaurant, Amy said opening in mid-December proved to be hectic with the holiday season. So, she was grateful for the community's patience and support.
'Everybody so far has been really kind and coming in. And, you know, not really taking it easy on us, but just being very supportive,' Amy said. 'So, it's been nice.'
Connect with The 208 House
Address: 208 N. Main St., Morton
Hours: 4:30 p.m. to 9 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Closed Sunday and Monday.

title: Watch: Illinois high school rivalry decided by half-court buzzer-beater
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: LaGrange Lyons snapped the 25-game win streak of rival Hinsdale Central with a running half-court heave to win an IHSA basketball game Tuesday night.
content:
Two suburban Chicago boys basketball teams added a chapter to their schools' rivalry Tuesday night.
LaGrange Lyons Township snapped the 25-game win streak of rival Hinsdale Central when guard Owen Carroll splashed home a running half-court shot to win the game 58-55 in LaGrange.
Hinsdale missed a shot with under 7 seconds left, and the rebound bounced to Carroll. The junior corralled it in the lane with just under 3 seconds remaining, dribbled around two defenders and rose up beside a third to launch a leaping two-handed shot from well beyond half court.
2025 IHSA boys basketball brackets: Peoria-area postseason schedules, scores and pairings
The shot was captured in all its glory on LTTV, the LaGrange Township student television station.
"Shot is up ..." the announcer called, leaving a long pause before the ball splashed into the net. Lyons students rushed the floor and mobbed Carroll as the call continued: "Oh my goodness! ... LT wins it! LT wins it! ... Unbelievable. One of the greatest things you'll ever watch on LTTV."
The 2-minute clip then cuts immediately to a slow-motion clip of the shot and then another angles from under both baskets — incredibly impressive production value all around.
Hinsdale (28-3) came into the game ranked No. 4 in Class 4A and on a 25-game win streak. Lyons is 13-15 after the upset win. The schools are longtime rivals located less than 5 miles apart in suburban Chicago.
The two teams are in the same IHSA Class 4A regional, and if they both win semifinals, could meet again next week for the championship.

title: What to know about a Peoria Rivermen trade, waiver claim, call-up and even more moves
author: Dave Eminian
description: Huge Savings: Subscribe today to enjoy sports, entertainment, life, money, tech, and travel news along with videos, apps, and more.
content:
PEORIA — And now they welcome goaltender No. 8 and players 43 and 44.
The Peoria Rivermen on Monday sorted through their 11th trade, the SPHL waiver wire, acquired their eighth goaltender of the year, lost another player to ECHL call-up and made several other moves they hope will keep them in first place in the SPHL.
"Everyone in the league has holes to fill on their roster, and we're no different," Rivermen coach Jean-Guy Trudel said. "We go to work, every day, and try to do everything we can to make our team better.
"It's a challenge, but we succeed because our guys buy in to the culture here."
Rivermen hockey: Historic win record goes well beyond the ice for Peoria Rivermen hockey coach
The Rivermen now have rostered 44 players in 38 games this season. They have rostered eight goaltenders after a trade Monday. Yet they have patched and re-patched that roster enough to build a 27-6-5 record good for first place — based on the highest pointsmaking percentage in the SPHL.
Trudel finds six regulation losses all season to be stunning under these circumstances. Peoria was 14-0-3 on the road and the only pro team in North America without a regulation road loss this season until Evansville caught the Rivermen coming off a seven-day layoff and beat them Sunday in Indiana.
Here is a look at the trade, the waivers, the call-ups and other roster notes after another shakeup:
The Rivermen got goaltender Dysen Skinner in a trade with Macon for future considerations. He was signed Thursday by ECHL Atlanta, so it's unclear if he's on the way back down or if he'll remain stashed there.
He played 17 games for Macon, compiling a 6-7-1 record with a 2.60 goals-against and a .921 saves rate. The 6-foot-1, 190-pound 25-year-old from Billings, Montana, played four seasons at University of Wisconsin-River Falls.
The rookie pro played three games for Carolina in the low-A FPHL, and 17 for Macon in the high-A SPHL. He is the eighth goaltender the Rivermen will roster this season. How he fits isn't certain yet.
More: 'Something special': How the Peoria Rivermen are a winning team amid unprecedented churn
The Rivermen have SPHL No. 1-ranked goaltender Colby Muise on call-up to ECHL Adirondack, where he's seen just 79 minutes in the last seven days.
Peoria also has veteran goaltender Nick Latinovich, who led them to the SPHL President's Cup last spring. He has been out two months, recovering from a broken foot, and is due to come back soon. Now they have another ECHL goaltender in Skinner, plus FPHL call-up Jack Bostedt.
The Rivermen picked defenseman Timur Gavrilovich off waivers from Knoxville. He's massive, at 6-6, 230 pounds. The Minsk, Belarus, native played four seasons for Buffalo State College. This is his rookie pro season, and he was on brief call-up to Knoxville from FPHL Blue Ridge.
Rivermen top-pair defenseman Renat Dadadzhanov was called-up by ECHL Bloomington on Monday. He had two goals, eight assists, a plus-9 rating and 81 penalty minutes in 33 games with Peoria, delivering a physical, steady presence on the blueline.
More: 'Diamond in the rough': How a full-blooded Cree became a rising star for Peoria Rivermen
The Rivermen have defenseman Chase Spencer (Kansas City), right wing Tyler Kobryn (Worcester) and goaltender Colby Muise (Adirondack) all up in the ECHL.
Spencer has two goals, two assists and a plus-6 rating in 16 ECHL games. He might not return to Peoria. Likewise, Kobryn was just traded from ECHL Florida to Worcester. He has four goals and two assists in 21 ECHL games.
The Rivermen released goaltender Ricky Gonzalez on Monday. He was 3-1-0 with a 2.27 goals-against and .922 saves rate.
His departure leaves only Bostedt, which indicates either Latinovich is coming off IR or Skinner or Muise are returning from the ECHL.
Peoria also released big winger Jake Vaughan, who had four goals and five assists in 22 games here.
The Rivermen play a three-games, three-nights series against Quad City this weekend, with home games Friday and Sunday at Carver Arena. If they sweep those, Peoria clinches an SPHL playoff spot. … Rivermen winger Tristan Trudel was ejected with an attempt to injure penalty in Sunday's game, which means a suspension is coming from the SPHL. … Last-place Pensacola fired head coach Gary Graham on Monday. Pensacola owner Greg Harris brought back three-time SPHL championship winner Rod Aldoff to serve as interim head coach for the 14-22-6 team. … The SPHL suspended Evansville's Matthew Hobbs one game for his major boarding penalty in a game against the Rivermen on Feb. 8. … The league suspended Evansville's Grayson Valente one game for a crosscheck that went unpenalized in that same game. … Former Rivermen defenseman Jake Hamilton was suspended five games by the SPHL for pulling out a chunk of hair from Macon's Jacon Schnapp during a fight Feb. 7, then skating with it on his own head (which is bald) in celebration.

title: East Peoria building a basketball culture not seen at the school since the 1990s
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: 'We're right there': Talented and confident East Peoria basketball team has its first 20-win season in almost 30 years.
content:
EAST PEORIA — This season's edition of East Peoria has its boys basketball fans reminiscing about the mid-1990s.
For the first time in 27 years, the Raiders have a 20-win season and are in a good position to end a regional title drought spanning the same amount of time. EP's 1996-97 team went 24-5, losing to the eventual Class AA four-peat state champion Manual by three points in the Peoria Sectional final.
'We're right there,' East Peoria junior Jackson Ahrens said. 'We're creating a new culture here that hasn't been here for a long time.'
Peoria basketball renaissance? This generation's elite talent makes the case
East Peoria (22-8) heads into Friday's regular-season finale against Urbana (13-17) having won six of its last seven games. This included a 77-72 overtime victory against Pekin on Tuesday night that locked up sole possession of third place in the Mid-Illini Conference at 9-5, the program's second nine-win league season in three years.
'It's happened,' East Peoria coach Jarrett Brown said of his team's success, 'because we have talented players, but we're razor thin on margin for error. Razor thin.'
Learning from the past, building the future
Brown isn't being negative, rather emphasizing that all the little things play a factor.
'If we're not really, really, really good in all phases, all areas, then we don't win,' he said. 'They just don't know what it takes daily. That's been the cultural change ... accepting who we are more than anything.'
Ahrens teams with super sophomores Quinton Kitt and Cole Dubois to give EP just three years of varsity experience. Kitt, who recently picked up a scholarship offer from Bradley, and Dubois recently both went over the 1,000th career point scoring mark.
Now, the trio has an opportunity to continue to build off lessons learned from past players. Ahrens was a freshman when Justin Page, who is currently a sophomore at Niagara, was a senior. That season helped Ahrens in all aspects of his game. He says he models his game after Page, who worked out daily with Ahrens. Also, learning how to lead was huge for Ahrens.
'He's a dude that I looked up to every day,' the 5-foot-11 guard said. 'He truly made me better.'
Unique season structure has EP rolling
One unique aspect of East Peoria's season was the Raiders didn't play in a holiday tournament over the Christmas break. Brown says he was intrigued by the possibility of not participating in one and it is something he always wanted to do.
So, the second-year coach gave his team four days completely away from the game. East Peoria also got a chance to restart its season with a 'preseason thought' of development work.
'We loved it,' Brown said. 'The kids loved it. I know it was good for us, so we'll continue to do it as long as we can. … It offered us an opportunity to talk about two sprints instead of a big marathon.
'We are trying to be the best team we can be by Dec. 23. If you're playing a Christmas tournament, you just can't have that talk.'
East Peoria went 9-2 in its first leg, then got nine days to prepare for Peoria High, which was coming off winning the State Farm Holiday Classic-Large School tournament.
The result? A 71-66 double-overtime win over the state-ranked Lions.
'It really gave us an opportunity to grow together,' Ahrens said. 'Over that break while teams were playing games, we were in here getting better and working on what we were going to do for the second half of the season.'
EP then made a long weekend January trip to Moline, plus a trek down to Pinckneyville. During EP's current stretch, the Raiders picked up another resume-boosting victory when it beat state-ranked Morton, 72-69, in overtime on Feb. 8.
'It's a statement win, for sure,' Ahrens said. 'I think teams even after we've beaten Peoria High and Morton still doubt us. We have more to do. … We already knew we could win at a high level, but we've proven it twice now and there's more to come.
'Our goal is to be the best we can be in March.'

title: One arrested in Pekin after months-long investigation turns up cocaine, AR-15
author: Mike Kramer
description: An unidentified man is in custody after a search last week by Pekin detectives turned up 3 kilograms of cocaine, cash and guns.
content:
A three-month narcotics investigation has led to the arrest of an unidentified adult male in Pekin.
Detectives with the Pekin Police Department's Special Services Division searched an unspecified property last week, the PPD announced Tuesday night. During the search, detectives found and seized more than 3 kilograms of cocaine, more than $20,000 in suspected narcotics money, a loaded handgun and a loaded AR-15 " ghost gun," which are often assembled from kits purchased online or 3D-printed. They don't require the typical background checks for purchase and do not have serial numbers, according to a story from USA TODAY.
The adult male was arrested and currently remains in the Tazewell County jail.
"The Pekin Police Department is committed to the relentless pursuit of drug traffickers in and around our city," the department said in a Tuesday social media post.
The Pekin Police Department did not release the suspect's name or what charges he will face. The Drug Enforcement Administration Resident Springfield Office, the Peoria Metropolitan Enforcement Group and the Marquette Heights Police Department assisted Pekin police in the investigation.
