title: After winning CFP, Ryan Day should head to NFL and leave toxic Ohio State fan base
author: Matt Hayes
description: Now that he has won a national championship at Ohio State, it's time for Ryan Day to leave for the NFL to escape the toxic environment in Columbus.
content:
ATLANTA — Chip Kelly was talking last weekend about his friend of nearly 30 years, emphasizing the importance of family for Ohio State coach Ryan Day.
'Every decision he makes,' said Kelly, Ohio State's offensive coordinator, 'revolves around his family.'
It is here where we introduce Nina Day, Ryan Day's wife of 19 years — and why the coach with the highest active winning percentage should walk away from Ohio State after Monday night's win over Notre Dame in the College Football Playoff national championship game.
Ryan and Nina met in Manchester, New Hampshire, when they were 6, and have traveled life together, in one form or another, since.
If ever there were a doubt that Ryan Day would execute the ultimate walk-off and leave Ohio State after winning it all, consider Nina's recent interview last week with WBNS-TV in Columbus — where she reflected on life in Columbus since late November, after the program's fourth straight loss to bitter rival Michigan.
Since they had to put an armed guard outside the family home for protection.
'The weeks between the Michigan and (CFP) Tennessee game were brutal,' Nina told WBNS. 'I was very upset by what was happening to some of our players, my children. It just wasn't right.'
It was then that Nina explained a family ritual during the season, one that – more than anything – underscores the severity of what the family has dealt with since Ryan was named head coach in December 2018.
'Before he leaves (for games),' Nina said, 'he says, 'No matter what, we always have each other.''
It's a game. You throw the ball, you catch the ball.
Never, under any circumstance, should the coach at any university leave his home, his safe solitude from high-level stress, and reassure his family that – no matter what – they always have each other because some lunatic fan base isn't happy that Michigan has the upper hand in a rivalry.
Forget about what Day said in November about the rivalry, how he compared the game to war. How there are casualties and consequences for the loser.
That's a desperate man tossing chum to a rabid fan base, a group of unreasonable and unapologetic fans doling out the unthinkable to young men playing a game.
A game, everyone.
The Days have three children under the age of 16, three kids who clearly have been impacted by the 24/7, 365 nonsense of "Ohio Against The World." Or whatever strange soliloquy the scarlet and gray mob spout these days.
This is the same fan base that once protected former coach Urban Meyer, and his history of poor personal decisions, at all cost. All because he was 7-0 vs. That Team Up North.
Meanwhile, the wife of the coach who just lost his fourth straight to Xichigan (they refuse to use the 'M' in Columbus), told WBNS that she had to see a therapist because of the absolute insanity surrounding the program.
And when Nina Day was done pouring her heart out on local television – what coach's wife in their right mind would publicly pour their heart out unless it had truly hit a breaking point? – the bobblehead anchors on local Columbus television applauded her for perseverance through 'tough times.'
Tough times? Tough times?! What world are we living in?
I have some advice for Ryan Day, 45, who earns $10 million annually to be the caretaker of this zoo: leave.
Now.
Walk away with your pride, your dignity and your wife's and family's safety and security. Drop the mic after reaching the mountaintop of college football, and leave with no regrets.
Now it's all coming into focus. Now we know why Day looked dazed and confused in late November after the Michigan loss, why he stood and watched his players fight Michigan players at midfield in the aftermath and did nothing.
He must have been imagining just how bad it would get with the wacko fan base. The same fan base that nearly 15 years ago, forced Kirk Herbstreit – ESPN's college football analyst and a former Ohio State quarterback – to move his family from Columbus to Nashville to escape the madness.
A beloved alum, the definition of ambassador for the university and all it holds sacred, Herbstreit walked away because he feared for his family's safety. Now Day, after winning the school's first national title since 2014, should do the same.
Walk away and coach somewhere else, or don't coach at all.
Take a job in the NFL, where he spent time with the Eagles (2015) and 49ers (2016) as quarterbacks coach, before arriving at Ohio State as Meyer's offensive coordinator. Leave for the (mostly) sane professional process of the NFL, where the Saints, Cowboys, Jaguars, Raiders and Jets are looking for new direction.
Where the league that values the vertical passing game – Day has developed some of the best quarterbacks and receivers for the NFL draft – would embrace his elite track record.
A record that, prior to the 2023 season at Ohio State with first-year starting quarterback Kyle McCord, had produced quarterbacks who averaged 41 touchdown passes per season.
A record that saw quarterbacks Dwayne Haskins, Justin Fields and C.J. Stroud selected in the first round, and wide receivers Terry McLaurin, Garrett Wilson, Chris Olave, Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Marvin Harrison Jr. join the elite of the league.
More than anything, Day should walk away from the nonstop circus inside the Ohio State bubble. It's not worth it mentally, physically and emotionally.
'When you go through difficult times," Nina Day told the Ohio State cheer squad at WBNS, 'you hold on tight to the ones you love.'
And you do what's right for them, and protect them.
No matter what.

title: Ryan Day is selling Ohio State toughness. Will anyone buy it? Yes, if Buckeyes win title
author: Dan Wolken
description: Ohio State football coach Ryan Day likes to talk about his team's toughness. But is anyone buying what he is so overtly selling?
content:
ATLANTA — Ryan Day talks about Ohio State 's toughness like an overzealous TV salesman trying just a little too hard to convince you how sharp the picture is. In the end, we're either going to see it or we're not.
The depth of that obsession emerged a little more than a year ago, moments after Ohio State defeated Notre Dame, 17-14. In an on-field interview with NBC, then then again with reporters after having a chance to cool down, Day lashed out at former Irish coach Lou Holtz, who had said on the Pat McAfee Show earlier in the week that all of Day's high-profile losses to the likes of Michigan, Alabama and Georgia had occurred because opponents "are more physical than Ohio State."
It was obviously a deep cut for Day, the former quarterback at New Hampshire and high-flying offensive coordinator whose teams up to that point had not exactly been the embodiment of smash mouth, old school Big Ten-style football.
Because after expressing his disbelief that Holtz would say such a thing, Day stomped into the press conference and declared that it was 'not even close to true,' that any suggestion of softness was about 'one bad half' against Michigan in 2021 and that the narrative 'ends tonight' after winning a close September game in South Bend.
It all felt a little, well, manufactured. A narrative in college football doesn't end because the coach said so, and it certainly doesn't go away because of a non-conference game in September. It's also worth nothing that Ohio State would go on to lose to Michigan two more times after that moment, including an inexplicable performance this season that, at minimum, put Day within range of the proverbial hot seat.
But on the eve of anther matchup with Notre Dame — this time for the national championship — Day's ultimate redemption is very much rooted in his distaste for the idea that Ohio State was more of a track team than a football program.
While the desire to continually prove how tough they are has backfired in the Michigan matchup, where Ohio State strays too far from its strengths and ends up playing the Wolverines' game, it is now unquestionably a net plus when you look at the totality of where the Buckeyes are now and how they got here.
'I think it's kind of cool to see the maturation of Ryan Day and to see how he's adjusted and how he now sees the game,' said Greg McElroy, the former Alabama quarterback who is now one of ESPN's top commentators. 'Look, if you're an offensive coordinator, the lens through which you saw the game forever was, 'Alright, I'm in charge of that side of the ball and I have to maximize that side's output. That's how we win.' You're wired that way. It's been a really cool adjustment to see how he's deviated ever so slightly from tempo, deviated away from trying to create explosive plays, to being a little bit more patient. And I think the great depiction of how he's evolved was the Texas game.'
When Ohio State beat Texas in the semifinals, 28-14, what McElroy saw was a team that played offensively within the structure of the game and didn't try to force plays that weren't there. He also saw a defense that, at one time earlier in Day's tenure, might have relied on exotic looks and blitzes to make up for the fact that they just weren't physical enough to win those line-of-scrimmage battles against the best programs in the country and often struggled to tackle in space.
But against Texas, when Ohio State had to stop a first-and-goal from the 1-yard line to retain the lead in the game's final few minutes, America saw the Buckeyes do pretty much what they've done a lot of this season. Just like they did against Penn State earlier in the season when they sealed the game with a goal-line stand, Ohio State stuffed the run inside and forced the Longhorns to try something on the perimeter. That also failed spectacularly, setting up Jack Sawyer's strip sack of Quinn Ewers and touchdown return to put an exclamation point on the game.
Yes, Ohio State can still win a track meet. But when they need to win another way, as the situation presented itself against Texas, there has been real growth in the toughness and physicality department. It might be what wins the Buckeyes a national title.'
'There was some narrative that came out that we weren't a tough team and this and that,' Ohio State safety Lathan Ransom said. 'Obviously we block out the outside noise, but all the stuff we do in the offseason behind closed doors, it's all for toughness. And when you hear that we're not tough, it definitely might trigger somebody.'
Despite Day's public protests, it's no mystery how he's evolved the program since that 'one bad half' in 2021 when Michigan physically mashed the Buckeyes, 42-27.
After that season, Day upended his defensive staff, most notably getting rid of coordinator Kerry Coombs. He also parted ways with offensive line coach Greg Studrawa.
Fast forward to 2024, and Ohio State is one of the best defenses in the country under Knowles and has an offensive line that has survived and thrived despite some brutal injuries including center Seth McLaughlin.
'Top-five defense, that's basically what he expected and that's what I expected,' said Knowles, who took the job after four seasons at Oklahoma State. 'You come to Ohio State, you expect to be the best and play against the best and have coaches who expect the best. I don't know what it was like before I got there, and I didn't spend much time with it. I just knew that from the time I arrived, this is what we were going to be and that's how I drove it."
Of course, to do that requires more than just saying it. These days at Ohio State, everyone talks about the Tuesday and Wednesday practices when they put the pads on and play good-on-good, which hasn't always been so fashionable in this era of protecting players' bodies but is often the necessary element to build a team that can function against punishing opponents.
'It's a mindset,' linebackers coach and former Buckeye All-American James Laurinaitis said. 'Coach Day has said it — there's a certain callous that builds up when you put the pads on and you do it over and over.
'I think even in the NFL, everything goes in ebbs and flows. There was a whole thing about physicality — pads, pads. And then there's a new wave of just like, we're going to do walkthroughs and save their legs and then all the sudden you see missed tackles go up and now we're all back to pads. It comes and goes. There's always a fine line there of, like, you've got to work hard but you also want to have a fresh team. If there was a perfect science to it, someone would just bottle it up and make a lot of money. There's no perfect formula to any of it.'
But Ohio State seems to have the right mix at the moment. Though Day stops short of saying his program wasn't tough enough a few years ago, he allows that they are now better built to win different styles, which is what you need to win a coast-to-coast Big Ten and the College Football Playoff.
'Every year you learn, and to be honest every year I learn and grow and figure out what needs to be done to get it fixed and identify the issues and be honest and call it for what it is,' Day said. "That's what leaders do. They look out on the horizon and see what's coming. We all have to continue to learn, and I think I've done that as well.'
And if Ohio State wins one more game, Day won't have to keep telling the world how tough his team is because it will be as self-evident as the shine on their gold trophy.

Notre Dame finished second after losing Monday night to the Buckeyes, but its position wasn't completely unanimous among voters. And there were significant variance among the teams that didn't make the national championship game or the College Football Playoff.

title: What to make of the middle nine in latest Big Ten women's basketball power rankings
author: Dargan Southard
description: Check out the latest USA TODAY Sports Network Big Ten women's basketball power rankings.
content:
Show Caption
Each night is an adventure inside the Big Ten. The conference women's basketball scene is as deep as ever, and the results reflect that with all kinds of interesting storylines.
Right now, there appears to be a solid top four and bottom five inside the league. UCLA, USC, Maryland and Ohio State in some order at the top. Penn State, Wisconsin, Rutgers, Purdue and Northwestern in some order at the bottom. That leaves a fluctuating middle nine that all feel the NCAA Tournament is possible.
Here are the latest USA TODAY Sports Network Big Ten women's basketball power rankings. Rankings are reflective of games through Jan. 21.
1. UCLA (18-0)
Previously: No. 1
What to know: The Bruins had convincing wins over Penn State (in Los Angeles) and Baylor (in New Jersey) at the Coretta Scott King Classic on MLK Day. The East Coast swing continues with games at Rutgers and Maryland.
2. USC (17-1)
Previously: No. 2
What to know: After having their midweek game vs. Northwestern postponed, USC returned to action with a nice road win at Indiana. The Trojans play at Purdue Wednesday.
3. Maryland (16-2)
Previously: No. 4
What to know: While it might seem strange to see a team move up following a 38-point loss, Maryland's MLK Day stumble vs. Texas isn't indicative of the Terrapins' place in the Big Ten. Maryland further cemented that with last Tuesday's win over Minnesota. Thursday's trip to Ohio State is even more pivotal.
4. Ohio State (17-1)
Previously: No. 3
What to know: Quite the head scratcher for Ohio State to give Penn State its first Big Ten win Sunday afternoon. But the Buckeyes have a great rebound chance Thursday vs. Maryland.
5. Michigan State (15-3)
Previously: No. 6
What to know: The Spartans picked up two road wins over Rutgers and Illinois and will look to make it three wins in a row Wednesday vs. Penn State.
6. Nebraska (15-4)
Previously: No. 8
What to know: A nice road win at Iowa spilled into a convincing MLK Day win over Wisconsin. Nebraska now waits for Sunday's big home showdown vs. Ohio State.
7. Minnesota (17-2)
Previously: No. 5
What to know: The Golden Gophers drop after falling at Maryland last Tuesday, though a road win over Northwestern came Sunday to soften the blow. Minnesota hosts Michigan Wednesday night.
8. Michigan (13-5)
Previously: No. 9
What to know: The Wolverines have won three straight to get back on track ahead of an important week. Michigan plays at Minnesota Wednesday before hosting Michigan State on Saturday.
9. Illinois (13-5)
Previously: No. 10
What to know: Despite a tough home loss Sunday against Michigan State, last Thursday's road win at Indiana shows Illinois isn't fading despite key injuries.
10. Indiana (12-6)
Previously: No. 7
What to know: Following back-to-back home losses to Illinois and USC, the Hoosiers head out west to face Oregon on Friday and Washington on Monday.
11. Oregon (14-5)
Previously: No. 13
What to know: This rare thee-game home swing in the middle of conference play has started right for Oregon with wins over Purdue and Iowa. The Ducks host Indiana on Friday before a two-game swing in the state of Michigan.
12. Washington (13-6)
Previously: No. 12
What to know: The Huskies were swept in the state of Michigan but responded with Saturday's win over Purdue. Washington hosts Iowa Wednesday and Indiana Monday.
13. Iowa (12-7)
Previously: No. 11
What to know: The Hawkeyes are free-falling with five consecutive losses. Another Wednesday at Washington would mark Iowa's first six-game losing streak since 1999.
14. Penn State (10-9)
Previously: No. 15
What to know: It's likely that Sunday's stunning win over Ohio State will finish as a fluke, but what a way for Penn State to secure its first conference win. It ended a seven-game losing streak in the process.
15. Wisconsin (10-9)
Previously: No. 14
What to know: The Badgers have dropped seven straight following losses to Ohio State and Nebraska.
16. Rutgers (8-11)
Previously: No. 16
What to know: Rutgers hasn't won since Dec. 21, and it doesn't get any easier Thursday vs. UCLA.
17. Purdue (7-11)
Previously: No. 17
What to know: The Boilermakers also haven't won since Dec 21, and they, too, have a huge challenge this week vs. USC on Wednesday.
18. Northwestern (7-10)
Previously: No. 18
What to know: After the Los Angeles fires postponed Northwestern's West Coast games, the Wildcats returned to action Sunday with a home loss to Minnesota.

title: Ryan Day shuts up critics with Ohio State title. 'What they gonna say now?'
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: Team meeting with Ryan Day after Ohio State lost to Michigan galvanized the Buckeyes for their college football championship run.
content:
Ryan Day becomes third active college football coach to win a national championship.
Team meeting with Ryan Day after Michigan loss galvanizes Ohio State.
Buckeyes players take up for Ryan Day, who won his first national championship in Year 6, same as Kirby Smart.
ATLANTA – Ryan Day stood at the back of the stage behind a wall of his jubilant players, beaming like a kid while a confetti cannon blasted paper into the air.
Ohio State's coach earned that grin. He deserved that joy, after a season that brought unrelenting pressure, unapologetic blowback and, finally, triumph. Day is a national champion, one just three active coaches with that distinction.
"What they gonna say now?" Ohio State senior safety Lathan Ransom said, before exalting his coach.
The critics can't say squat now, after Ohio State's 34-23 win against Notre Dame, and the trolls crawled back into their caves. Day shut them up after his Buckeyes laid waste to the field in this College Football Playoff.
"Seeing Coach Day hoist up that trophy after seeing all the flak he got, all the, excuse my language, (crap) he's gotten, it's just amazing as a player to see our coach in the position that we know he should be," senior offensive lineman Donovan Jackson said.
And what of Ohio State's " lunatic fringe," as Kirk Herbstreit dubs them? Those Bucks nuts probably will pretend they never wanted Day's head on a platter just two months ago and chanted for his ouster after he suffered his fourth straight loss to Michigan.
"It's funny now, right?" Ransom said, when a reporter reminded him of those angry chants after the Michigan loss. "We never stopped believing in Coach Day. We always had Coach Day's back, and he always had our back."
Don't confuse this as the story of a plucky eighth-seeded underdog getting off the mat. Nobody could match Ohio State's talent. This is the story of an embattled coach and a two-loss team realizing their potential.
"We stuck together," Day said. "We hung in there like a family does when things get hard."
Ohio State plays to billing after team meeting with Ryan Day
The annals of history might indicate that Ohio State's loss to Michigan became a turning point, but Buckeyes players point to a team meeting that occurred days after that result as the fork in the road.
Day joined his players for a meeting that became an open forum to clear the air, offer critiques and unify behind a common goal.
Ransom won't detail the specifics of what was said within those four walls, but he'll tell you this much: Day let himself be vulnerable in that meeting. The Buckeyes respected him that much more because of that.
"Anything that anyone wanted to say, they got a chance to say it," Ransom said. "Coach Day took some critiques from the players. That shows how great of a leader he is. That's why we go out there and we play so hard for him."
Try to imagine Nick Saban or Kirby Smart, for that matter, opening himself up to player critiques throughout a meeting. Yeah, I'm not seeing it. There's more than one avenue to becoming a championship coach, although the common thread between Saban, Smart and Day is that all are elite recruiters who magnetize talent.
"Coach Saban was a more stoic person. Coach Day has a different type of relationship with the players, and I respect him for that," said Buckeyes safety Caleb Downs, an Alabama transfer who touts the virtues of both coaches. "You've got to run your organization as who you are."
Outside the program, the pitchforks came out after that Michigan loss. The headlines got spicy, the hot boards filled with potential replacements for a job not open, and an athletic director, for perhaps the first time in the sport's history, needed to offer a vote of confidence for a coach who'd lost just 10 games throughout six seasons.
Inside the Woody Hayes Athletic Facility, the confidence remained strong in Day.
"We trusted in him," senior defensive end JT Tuimoloau said.
The Buckeyes trusted, too, that despite two regular-season losses, they possessed a national championship team.
"Getting an opportunity to get in the playoffs, that's all we needed," Jackson said. "We just needed our foot in the door."
Ryan Day nears Kirby Smart territory
Day, 45, is a year younger than Smart when the Georgia coach won his first national championship. Day's first national title arrived in Year 6, just as Smart's did, but Smart never faced an onslaught of criticism like that directed at Day after Michigan stunned the Buckeyes in November.
Couple of explanations for that that. Georgia does not define its self-worth based on the result of one game. Also, Smart wasn't replacing Urban Meyer, and, even before his first national title, he lifted Georgia to heights Mark Richt never reached.
Day, in contrast, got shackled with the reputation that he started the job on third base, inheriting a blue blood in fine shape from Urban Meyer, and he couldn't advance the remaining 90 feet to home.
Truth is, Day's become a home-run hire, and if we conducted a draft of active college football coaches tomorrow, who would come off the board before Day, other than perhaps Smart? This list is short. It's getting shorter.
Day built, developed and retained an unmatched level of talent. Yes, Ohio State's NIL war chest helped, but the Buckeyes didn't win this crown with an army of mercenary rent-a-players. The roster's tentacles trace to Day stacking one elite recruiting class after another. Senior standouts found throughout Ohio State's offensive and defensive starting units trace to Day's 2020 and '21 recruiting classes, before NIL came aboard.
The coordinator combo of Chip Kelly and Jim Knowles highlighted an elite coaching staff that schemed up a beautiful plan for this playoff romp, after Ohio State's perplexing offensive approach against Michigan.
Day, in the offseason, completed the roster puzzle with portal prizes like Downs and quarterback Will Howard. As Howard peaked in the postseason, Day served a reminder of his deft hand developing quarterbacks.
Howard was a decent player at Kansas State, but he transcended into an ace throughout this playoff run, bringing his A game in four straight games while the Buckeyes averaged more than 36 points against four of the nation's top defenses. That culminated with Howard completing his first 13 passes throughout a master class of quarterbacking against a Notre Dame team that failed to defend Ohio State's vaunted assembly of wide receivers.
The Buckeyes buried Tennessee, routed Oregon, held firm against Texas and bent Notre Dame with a stretch of dominance that relegated the Michigan loss to a curious footnote in the story of a national champion.
"We're resilient, man," Jackson said. "At the beginning of this run, everyone had us dead. Everyone had us thrown aside."
They'd thrown aside the coach, too, but what are they saying now?
Nothing left to say, except that Day persevered, and now he can smile the way champions do, while confetti blasts into the air.

title: Buzzer-beaters and win streaks: Vote for Journal Star athlete of the week for Jan. 13-18
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Nominees from East Peoria, Pekin, Brimfield and more. Vote now for high school athlete of the week around Peoria.
content:
After plenty of solid winter sports performers over the last week, here are the Journal Star high school athlete of the week nominees for Jan. 13-18.
Head to pjstar.com/sports to vote. The poll closes at noon Friday. Information about the nominees is below.
If you have a nominee for the honor, email us at sports@pjstar.com or tag us on Twitter @pjstarsports. Last week, Remi Joesting of the Peoria Notre Dame boys wrestling team was named JS athlete of the week.
Gavin Walder, Peoria Christian boys basketball - Class 1A
The senior was instrumental in leading PCS to its third Inter-County Athletic Conference Tournament in four seasons. His 21 points and five rebounds were key as the Chargers beat Illini Bluffs, 68-41. PCS ran off 23 consecutive third-quarter, plus added a 18-3 stretch in the final eight points. Walder made sure the Chargers would be playing for title thanks to a 28-point, five-rebound and three-assist effort to beat Elmwood, 82-52 in the tourney semifinals.
Ryan Kaiser, Tremont boys basketball - Class 2A
Kaiser contributed in a big way as the Turks continued their winning ways last week. After helping Tremont post 90 points in a win last Tuesday, the senior scored 21 points to beat El Paso-Gridley, 77-56. This included a third-quarter buzzer beater from the other free-throw line. The Turks had a quick turnaround, being Fisher, 77-67 to open play in the Heart of Illinois Conference Tournament. Kaiser scored 17 points including 10 in the second quarter.
Quinton Kitt, East Peoria boys basketball - Class 3A/4A
Kitt shook off an early week illness to produce a pair of big games over the weekend. The sophomore scored a game-high 28 points on Friday as the Raiders beat Pekin, 67-64. Kitt then poured in 19 points on Saturday to beat Taylor Ridge Rockridge, 60-45 for EP's third win in a row. He had the flu last Wednesday, missing EP's 72-59 win over Illinois Valley Central.
Ava Heinz, Brimfield girls basketball - Class 1A
The senior continues to be on of the area's most consistent, yet dominant players. Her three games last week proved that. Heinz opened her week last Monday by single-handedly outscoring Farmington in a 41-20 victory. She almost posted a triple-double with 21 points, 10 rebounds and nine blocks. Heinz came back with 24 points, 15 rebounds and four blocks to beat North Fulton, 44-34 on Thursday. Her week ended Saturday with 19 points and six blocks in a 62-42 loss to Monmouth-Roseville. Heinz also went over 1,500-career points.
Mya Edwards, Eureka girls basketball - Class 2A
The super sophomore made sure Eureka continued its winning ways last week. Edwards scored 17 points as the Hornets won their fifth in a row, 59-38 to open Heart of Illinois Conference Tournament play on Saturday. She had scored 21 points in beating Downs Tri-Valley, 59-50 on Thursday. Her week started by turning in a 22-point game as the Hornets cruised over Le Roy, 61-24.
Cadence Covert, Pekin girls basketball - Class 3A/4A
The junior has played a big role in Pekin having won seven in a row. The Dragons started 0-4 in Mid-Illini Conference play before reeling off four straight. This culminated Thursday by Covert and teammate Zoe Kormah each scoring 10 to beat Dunlap, 44-38. Last Tuesday, Covert put up 12 points as Pekin knocked off East Peoria, 48-35.
Bradlee Ellis, Farmington co-op boys wrestling
As a member of the Farmington-hosted co-op, the North Fulton junior won the 144-pound division at the Kewanee Invitational on Saturday. In the championship match, Ellis scored a fall in 2:49 over Caleb Modglin from Morrison. This was proceeded by a 17-2 tech fall over Rockford Auburn's Xzavier Lindhe in the semifinals. Plus, Ellis, who is 28-3, has already posted 100 career wins.
Karen Canchola, Morton girls wrestling
The senior grabbed her second tournament title of the season by winning the 140-pound bracket at the Canton Invitational on Saturday. The senior won a title bout victory over Kelly Ladd of Macomb thanks to a pin in 2:51. Canchola made her way to the finals by pinning semifinal opponent Ava Weatherford from Ottawa in 4:56. This came after Canchola pinned Erie's Dena Cox in 3:39 during the quarterfinal match.
Ryan Tapper, Galesburg boys swimming and diving
The senior was a three-event winner as Galesburg won the eight-team Grayhound Invite on Saturday at Burlington, Iowa. His individual victory came in the 100-yard backstroke, clocking in a 57.34 seconds. Tapper then teamed with Travis Henry, Carson Olson and Nathan Nelson to win the 200-yard medley relay in 1:39.88. Tapper and Nelson paired with Anders Bergren and Brayden McGuire, swimming to victory in the 200-yard freestyle relay (1:31.61). Tapper also took second place in the 100-yard freestyle (51.15 seconds).

content:
Football fans are one Sunday away from knowing which two teams will compete at Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans.

Shop Eagles vs. Commanders NFL playoff tickets
AFC Championship Game tickets
Kansas City Chiefs vs. Buffalo Bills
Mahomes and Allen have played against each other eight teams during their careers, with each quarterback winning four times. That said, Mahomes and the Chiefs are 3-0 in the playoffs against Allen and the Bills.
This is the playoff game most football fans wanted in the AFC, and it's a bit surprising that the cheapest ticket price to the AFC Championship Game is less than half the price of the cheapest ticket to the NFC Championship Game.

title: Illinois high school basketball state rankings: Peoria-area schools in sixth poll
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Here is how Peoria-area basketball teams rank in the the sixth regular-season AP top 10 poll for Class 1A, 2A, 3A and 4A in 2024-25.
content:
Washington is now the sole No. 1-ranked Class 3A girls basketball team, while Metamora and Morton are headed for a top-five Class 3A boys meeting as the latest high school poll was released by The Associated Press on Wednesday afternoon.
After spending last week tied with Quincy Notre Dame for the top spot, Washington regains the No. 1 ranking thanks to nine first-place votes. Morton maintained its spot at No. 4, while Galesburg slid a place to No. 8.
In the Class 2A poll, Peoria Notre Dame is now ranked No. 4 following an overtime loss to Class 3A No. 3 Chicago St. Ignatius. Deer Creek-Mackinaw moved up a spot to No. 7, while both Tremont and Eureka were among those receiving votes.
Abingdon-Avon stayed steady at No. 1 in Class 1A for a second straight week. The Tornadoes are joined in the poll by No. 9 Monmouth United along with Wethersfield and Roanoke-Benson, which both received votes.
Lisle Benet (Class 4A) and Breese Central (Class 2A) are the other two top-ranked girls teams.
On the boys side, Class 3A No. 3 Metamora and No. 4 Morton will meet next Tuesday in a key Mid-Illini Conference matchup. Peoria High fell out of the top 10 and was the first team receiving votes, which also included East Peoria.
Manual fell four spots to No. 7 in Class 2A, which saw Fieldcrest and Tremont receive votes. Princeville was the lone local team to receive votes in Class 1A.
Pecatonica (Class 1A), Auburn (Class 2A), Chicago DePaul Prep (Class 3A) and Quincy (Class 4A) all were voted No. 1 in their respective classes by the statewide media.
The next AP poll will be released Jan. 29.

title: Former central Illinois man among Jan. 6 rioters who were pardoned by Donald Trump
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The former Marine was found guilty in 2023 and had been awaiting sentencing.
content:
A former Bushnell man and former U.S. Marine living in Ohio who had been convicted of storming the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, was among thousands pardoned Monday by newly reelected President Donald Trump.
Donovan R. Crowl, 54, was convicted in July 2023 of conspiracy to obstruct an official proceeding and aiding and abetting civil disorder for his role during the insurrection in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 6 that delayed certification of the Electoral College count confirming then-former-Vice-President Joe Biden's victory in the 2020 presidential election for several hours.
Crowl was a 1988 graduate of Bushnell-Prairie City High School before joining the U.S. Marine Corps. According to the initial criminal complain t filed with the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, he was living in Champaign County, Ohio, at the time of the insurrection and was a member of a militia group affiliated with the Oath Keepers, a right-wing paramilitary organization.
The organization, according to one of Crowl's eight superseding indictments, places a high priority on recruiting people who have served in the military, such as Crowl, and their founder, Stewart Rhodes, had called upon its members to take up arms on Jan. 6, 2021.
The complaint said that a leader of the Ohio militia had posted a picture of Crowl dressed in military attire to the social media site Parler and were able to confirm his identity by comparing pictures of him at the Capitol with those from DMV records and from the militia's social media accounts.
Crowl did an interview with The New Yorker on Jan. 14, 2021, in which he claimed that he hadn't committed any acts of violence, but admitted that he had injured three people during the insurrection, telling the reporter that he had dragged someone off of a wall and assaulted them.
A video obtained by ProPublica in the aftermath of the insurrection also shows the leader of the Ohio militia and Crowl bragging about how they had overran the Capitol before taking a selfie. The FBI arrested Crowl on Jan. 17, 2021, after he and one other person had turned themselves into local police.
Court documents reveal Jan. 6 accusations
Crowl had been indicted on eight separate occasions along with other members of the Oath Keepers, with him being accused of coming to Washington, D.C., in November 2020 and bringing firearms and ammunition in response to Rhodes' call to action and planning to travel by car from Ohio to Arlington, Virginia, to the events on Jan. 6.
According to the last of the eight superseding indictments, Crowl had been in attendance at Trump's rally on the Ellipse prior to the march on the Capitol. He entered restricted Capitol grounds at 2:21 p.m. that afternoon as both the House of Representatives and the Senate were deliberating an objection against Arizona's results.
Crowl and a group of other Oath Keepers members pushed their way into the Capitol rotunda and continued to fight law enforcement for at least 30 minutes before being pushed out.
After two years of delays, Judge Amit Mehta found Crowl guilty on two counts of what was initially an eight-count indictment, with sentencing set for November of that year. However, the sentencing was continued multiple times before being set for Jan. 22.
On Jan. 13, one of the charges – that of obstructing an official proceeding – was dropped after Mehta granted a request from Crowl to take that charge off due to a Supreme Court decision in 2024 that narrowed the definition of obstruction to criminalizing actions only if government records were impaired. The outgoing U.S. Attorneys did not have any objection to this request, but did say that the second conviction was unaffected by the court's ruling.
Sentencing remained set for Jan. 22 until Trump made his decision to pardon Crowl and thousands of others Monday night. According to the Washington Post, Trump had intended to pardon many of the Jan. 6 rioters who had been previously convicted during his ultimately-successful campaign to return to the White House, saying that those convicted were "political prisoners" and "hostages."

Record: The team's overall record, conference record, and nonconference record.

Team Value Index: A results-oriented component of the NET that ranks teams based on who they beat and where they played.
Rating Percentage Index (RPI): A formula that ranks teams using a team's winning percentage, opponents' success and opponents' strength of schedule.

title: Some Illinois residents are able to file taxes for free this year. Here's what to know.
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Tax season is officially upon us and some Illinois residents will be able to file their taxes for free this year. Here's what you need to know.
content:
Tax season is officially upon us.
Illinois residents can start filing taxes Jan. 27.
Some Illinois residents will be able to file their 2024 federal tax returns for free.
Here's what you need to know.
Who can file their federal taxes for free?
Check to see if you are eligible by visiting https://directfile.irs.gov.
How can it be free?
Illinois is participating in the Internal Revenue Service's Direct File program this year. Through the program, the eligible taxpayers would be filing their federal returns directly with the IRS.
"It offers a range of benefits for taxpayers, including free federal tax return filing, step-by-step guidance, and real-time online support," a spokesperson wrote.
Direct File has no income limits for filers.
For those who choose to file a federal return using Direct File, the program afterwards will connect taxpayers to Illinois' free state income tax filing system, MyTax Illinois, where people can file and complete their Illinois state returns.
Do I have to file with Direct File?
No, people can still choose to file using tax-prep software, a tax professional, or the paper Form IL-1040.
How quickly can I receive a refund?
Taxpayers who file an Illinois return electronically with no errors should receive a direct deposit refund in about four weeks. The Where's My Refund? tool, which is updated each night, is the simplest way to track your refund within 24 hours of e-filing. For taxpayers who filed a paper return, refund information is normally available after four weeks.
When is the tax filing deadline?
April 15, 2025.
What is the deadline to file an extension?
The deadline to file for an extension is April 15, according to the IRS. That gives taxpayers until Oct. 15 to file without penalties.

title: Man hit and killed by vehicle in East Peoria has been identified
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The 43-year-old suffered multiple blunt-force injuries after being hit on West Muller Road.
content:
A Creve Coeur man was killed Monday after a vehicle collided with him in East Peoria.
Adam Harbison, 43, died after he was hit by a vehicle in the 800 block of West Muller Road. According to Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood, police in Tazewell County responded to the scene at 6:20 a.m., finding a man down at the scene.
Harwood said that Harbison was unconscious and wasn't breathing when he was transported to OSF HealthCare Saint Francis Medical Center in Peoria, in addition to not having a pulse. Despite the best efforts of physicians to revive him, he died at 1:09 p.m. Monday.
An autopsy conducted Wednesday revealed that Harbison suffered multiple blunt-force injuries that caused his death.
A toxicology report remains pending from the coroner's office.

title: These 11 Peoria-area softball teams are state ranked in the preseason coaches poll
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Illini Bluffs and Metamora lead Peoria-area schools in the Illinois preseason high school softball poll. See the rankings here.
content:
Illini Bluffs and Metamora will each enter the high school softball season with a No. 2 ranking, according to the Illinois Coaches Association preseason poll released Friday.
IB is behind Biggsville West Central in the Class 1A poll, while Metamora trails reigning state champion Pontiac in Class 3A. These two programs are the highest rated among the 11 Peoria-area teams appearing in the polls.
Illini Bluffs finished as the Class 1A state runner-up the past two seasons after winning back-to-back state titles in 2021 and 2022. The Tigers were also the state runner-up in 2019 before the pandemic cancelled the 2020 campaign.
The Redbirds, who lost to Pontiac in the sectional final, are joined in the Class 3A poll by fellow Mid-Illini Conference foes East Peoria (No. 7), Dunlap (No. 10), Washington (No. 17) and Limestone (No. 20). Since the four-class split, Mid-Illini teams have made five Class 3A state title games, winning three (Limestone, Metamora, Washington) and finishing as runner-up twice (Washington, East Peoria).
Other Class 1A ranked teams include No. 14 Henry and No. 16 Putnam County, while Olympia is in the Class 2A poll at No. 8 along with St. Bede and Tremont each receiving votes.
The No. 1 teams in the other two classes are reigning state champions Carterville (Class 2A) and St. Charles North (Class 4A).
Softball practice begins March 3 with first games being held two weeks later on March 17.

title: Once a gold standard, Michigan football's response to NCAA violations shows it's just a common cheat
author: Matt Hayes
description: The once proud Michigan football program is now your average NCAA cheat. And its excuses for breaking rules are laughable.
content:
The curtain has been pulled back in Ann Arbor, and one of the nation's most respected institutions of higher education has reduced itself to a childish defense of its embattled football program.
The NCAA: We know you cheated and how you cheated, and how it gave your football program a competitive advantage.
Michigan: No we didn't, and even if we did, it's not as bad as you say it is.
How embarrassing for hoity-toity Michigan, once the gold standard for all that was pure and holy in college athletics.
How embarrassing for the university and storied football program, and all the proud Michigan Men of the past – the leaders and best, no less – to stand behind this legal pretzel response to NCAA allegations of scouting future opponents.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Have they no shame?
Michigan's formal response to the NCAA's official allegations of illegal advanced scouting and sign stealing was obtained by Yahoo Sports earlier this week, and it's remarkably stunning in its abject disdain and mockery of the investigation.
The Michigan response obfuscates, argues semantics, and degrades the investigatory process. All signs, any prosecutor worth his weight in all-nighters will tell you, of those who are guilty.
In the response, the university says it respects confidential sources, but the NCAA can only present evidence and infractions from former staffer Connor Stalions' scouting scheme based on 'information that can be attributed to individuals who are willing to be identified.'
At one point in the response, Michigan says Moore's reason for deleting 52 texts – fifty-two – between himself and Stalions on the day the scouting scheme was uncovered by Yahoo in October of 2023, was that Moore was 'angry' because he didn't want one person (Stalions) credited for 'all the work' put into the 2023 season.
The university also claims the texts, which were recovered once Moore handed over his phone to NCAA investigators, were 'innocuous and not material' to the investigation.
It's here where I need to remind everyone that the Big Ten, in unprecedented cooperation with the NCAA during the investigation of a member institution, suspended former Michigan coach Jim Harbaugh three games for the scouting scheme during the 2023 season.
The Big Ten decided that Michigan conducted "an impermissible, in-person scouting operation over multiple years, resulting in an unfair competitive advantage that compromised the integrity of competition." Such activities, it said, compromised sportsmanship and affected the "integrity of the competition.'
The 13-page Big Ten report, which used information from NCAA investigators – pictures, video, electronic money trails – called the Michigan penalties, 'A sanction against the University that, under the extraordinary circumstance presented by this offensive conduct, best fits the violation.'
Less than a year later, Michigan – 2023 national championship in hand – has moved into deny, deny, deny mode.
Because We're Morally Better Than You Michigan can't have an NCAA cheat as head coach. Can't have a national championship stained by NCAA violations, or a former coach and beloved alum run out of town by the NCAA sheriff — only to take refuge in the NFL.
Here's all you need to know about Michigan's impermissible future scouting scheme: Stalions allegedly use his minions — he sent friends to future opponents to film games from the stands (which Michigan denies) — to allegedly scout Georgia during the 2023 season.
That's two-time defending national champion Georgia, which beat Michigan by 23 points in the College Football Playoff during the 2021 season. That's Georgia, the 2023 playoff favorite — and Michigan's biggest obstacle to winning its first national championship since 1997.
Georgia wasn't even on Michigan's 2023 regular-season schedule.
If that doesn't do it for you, think about what Michigan is truly trying to sell with this utterly comical response to the NCAA.
We're supposed to believe that Harbaugh, an obsessively organized and detailed coach, who controlled everything in nine seasons and more than 100 games at Ann Arbor, didn't ever think to ask what in the blue blazes Stalions was doing in coaches meetings, and on the field during game day.
Harbaugh isn't going to stand on the sideline against Ohio State – the team he famously said Michigan would finally beat or die trying – and allow some flunky with an advance scouting scheme on his sideline without knowing everything about that system.
You say system, I say scheme.
Harbaugh isn't going to accept, willy-nilly, where that scheme came from, how it operates, and if it wasn't double- and triple-checked, before even contemplating changing a call mid-game in the biggest moment of every single season. There's a level of trust that's undeniable on the field of play.
You're not simply relying on word of mouth, or an understanding of generalities. Nothing is left to guess.
Not when you're playing Ohio State. Not when you're trying to win it all.
If you think Harbaugh – and by proxy, the rest of the coaching staff – didn't know exactly how Stalions received his information and what it took to get it, your blood runs Maize and Blue.
No coach at any program allows anyone on the sideline – within the inner sanctum of the coaches and players box – without knowing exactly why they're inside, and what they do to contribute to winning. Period.
Because that's all it's about in big-time college football: winning. And there's nothing wrong with that.
Just don't try to sell it as something else when you're caught cheating.

title: Fed warns NCAA could violate Title IX with expected revenue sharing model, NIL payments
author: Nick Wilson
description: Schools are setting aside funds for revenue sharing ahead of the House vs. NCAA settlement. The fed says those funds are still regulated by Title IX.
content:
Show Caption
College athletics is experiencing an unprecedented influx of cashe.
Between conference realignment plus the massive TV deals that followed and Name, Image, and Likeness agreements, there has never been more money floating around college sports.
Most of that comes from college football, which drives a majority of revenue for athletic departments across the country. Universities have recognized that football is the key revenue generator, and have reinvested into those programs ahead of the House vs. NCAA settlement.
As revenue sharing with student-athletes becomes the norm after the settlement, schools are starting to evaluate what percentage of their revenue will go toward paying football players. Under the proposed model, schools will be allowed to distribute up to 22 percent of the average Power-5 annual athletic revenue with a cap of $20.5 million dollars. While these numbers are not finalized, the cap is expected to rise to $30 million in the next 10 years.
Most schools were expecting to set aside more than 70 percent of their allotted revenue sharing to go back into football. The federal government is now saying that could be a violation of Title IX compliance.
The U.S. Department of Education's Office of Civil Rights (OCR) added a 'fact sheet' to their policy guidance portal two weeks ago reminding schools that revenue sharing still falls under the purview of Title IX. This means that any school that receives federal financial assistance is required to provide equal athletic opportunity based on sex – including publicity, support services, opportunities, treatment, and most importantly according to the Department of Education, "that schools not discriminate in the provision of athletic financial assistance."
The federal government signaled that NIL payments are considered "athletic financial assistance", and broke down in four parts how colleges are expected to operate in this evolving landscape as it relates to Title IX compliance.
Here is a breakdown of what the federal government is saying about how Title IX affects NIL payments.
How does Title IX involve NIL?
Name, Image, and Likeness payments are the new standard in college athletics. As the revenue-sharing model takes over, schools are setting percentages of the NIL funds aside for different athletic programs – with the lion's share being set aside for football.
The federal government said last month that dividing these funds disproportionally across men's and women's sports is a violation of Title IX. More specifically, Title IX regulations require schools to "provide reasonable opportunities for such awards for members of each sex in proportion to the number of students of each sex participating in interscholastic or intercollegiate athletics."
Does Title IX require equal NIL payments between men's and women's programs?
The short answer is no. The federal government is not saying schools have to pay men and women student-athletes the same amount of money on the same number of deals. Schools are not required to divide up resources 50/50 between men and women but in a proportionate manner.
When seeing whether or not a school is Title IX compliant, the OCR evaluates whether or not the sum of athletic financial aid is equitable. The OCR also says they include other financial assistance outside of NIL payments when evaluating Title IX compliance but that NIL opportunities must be as "proportionately" available for women's sports as well as men's sport.
How does Title IX affect social media and publicity?
Schools have leveraged their large alumni bases and social media followings when negotiating deals with athletes, and often schools use their social media to promote individuals and teams. When a student-athlete's social media presence rises, so does their NIL evaluation.
Knowing this, the OCR made clear that publicity and promotion also fall under Title IX regulations. A school can be considered non-compliant if the availability and quality of sports information personnel is lacking, access to publicity resources is inequivalent, and/or if the quantity and quality of promotional devices favors a men's team over a women's team.
There are reasons that publicity and promotions may be disproportionate and still be Title IX compliant. Teams can still promote teams and individuals more often than others for nondiscriminatory factors and unique circumstances like if a student-athlete is also an Olympic athlete, promoting national champions, or publicizing competitive events like national or conference competition.
Can schools use a third party as a loophole around Title IX compliance?
The fed does not see compensation from a third party as athletic financial assistance that must comply with Title IX regulations.
However, the OCR still understands that this is a rapidly changing issue. So they make clear in this fact sheet that schools are not relieved from their Title IX obligations just because specific funds from private sources (like boosters and alumni) are not regulated by the OCR.
The OCR essentially said that things are changing too fast for them to make a specific rule regarding third parties, so no such guidance can be given at this time other than a school can still trigger non-compliance by using third parties in a discriminatory manner – like using a third-party to create NIL agreements so that a disproportionate amount of money is going to the football team while using a school's official NIL collectives to remain Title IX compliant.
"OCR has long recognized that a school has Title IX obligations when funding from private sources, including private donations and funds raised by booster clubs, creates disparities based on sex in a school's athletic program or a program component," the OCR said in their policy guidance.
"It is possible that NIL agreements between student-athletes and third parties will create similar disparities and therefore trigger a school's Title IX obligations. Because these NIL agreements vary widely and continue to evolve and because the application of Title IX's equal athletic opportunity requirements is a fact-specific inquiry, this Fact Sheet does not offer specific guidance on Title IX's application in the context of compensation provided for the use of a student athlete's NIL by a third party, including an NIL collective."
The OCR likely added this section of guidance as a warning to schools that this fact sheet is not a rulebook, but a reminder that the absence of a rule does not create a Title IX loophole.

title: Iconic thrift store to close one of its central Illinois locations
author: Mike Kramer
description: With the opening of a large store in Galesburg, Goodwill of Central Illinois has decided to close a neighboring location next month.
content:
Goodwill announced Thursday it will close its location in Kewanee on March 8.
The non-profit organization Goodwill of Central Illinois announced all Kewanee store employees will be eligible for rehire at another location. These employees will also qualify for unemployment benefits. All of Goodwill's free employment, youth and veterans services will still be available to area residents.
Goodwill in December opened a larger store in Galesburg, located about 40 miles southwest. It is three times the size of its previous store.
Goodwill chief executive officer Don Johnson said "sustainability must always be our first consideration."
"To maintain that ability, we must be as strategic as possible," Johnson said. "With the opening of our new, larger Galesburg store, we are strengthening our sustainability and thus our ability to serve even more individuals. title: Illinois, Chicago sued by Trump administration over immigration laws that 'thwart' feds
author: Tom Ackerman
description: The Trump administration has sued Illinois and Chicago, alleging its laws are impeding on federal efforts to enforce immigration laws.
content:
The Trump administration, DOJ sues Illinois and Chicago over some of its immigration laws.
The lawsuit argues that the government has authority to regulate immigration, but it needs to work with state and local partners.
Chicago and Illinois have some of the strongest protections for immigrants in the nation.
The Trump administration and the U.S. Department of Justice sued the State of Illinois and the City of Chicago Thursday, including several of its officials, alleging that its sanctuary city designation and other protections for immigrants are impeding on federal efforts to enforce immigration laws.
The lawsuit takes issue with state laws that prohibit Illinois law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration agents. The suit also cites laws and ordinances in Chicago like the Welcoming City Ordinance that limits Chicago police officers from arresting on the basis of immigration status.
'The conduct of officials in Chicago and Illinois minimally enforcing — and oftentimes affirmatively thwarting — federal immigration laws over a period of years has resulted in countless criminals being released into Chicago who should have been held for immigration removal from the United States,' according to the lawsuit that has been filed in Chicago's federal court.
The administration argues in the suit that the U.S. has authority to regulate immigration matters, per the Constitution, numerous acts of Congress, and U.S. Supreme Court precedent. Further, they say that consultation and communication between federal, state, and local law enforcement officials is necessary for federal officials to carry out federal immigration law.
Gov. JB Pritzker who has been highly vocal and critical about President Trump, said the state has always complied with the law.
'Unlike Donald Trump, Illinois follows the law,' Pritzker's office said in a statement. 'Illinois will defend our laws that prioritize police resources for fighting crime while enabling state law enforcement to assist with arresting violent criminals. Instead of working with us to support law enforcement, the Trump Administration is making it more difficult to protect the public, just like they did when Trump pardoned the convicted Jan. 6 violent criminals. We look forward to seeing them in court."
Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson has defended the city's sanctuary laws. He and other may plan to testify next month at a congressional hearing on sanctuary cities, according to Associated Press.
Chicago in recent months has helped host trainings for people to learn their rights when it comes to immigration agents and publicized the information at public transit stations.
President Donald Trump has often singled out Chicago and Illinois, which have some of the strongest protections for immigrants in the nation, AP reported.

title: College basketball ref goes viral for accidentally 'playing defense' vs. Illinois
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: College basketball official Jeffrey Anderson paused, smiled incredulously and said 'my fault' after the uniquely viral play.
content:
College basketball official Jeffrey Anderson inadvertently went viral during a game Wednesday between Illinois and Rutgers.
The longtime ref appeared to "play defense" when he found himself sandwiched between Rutgers ballhandler Ace Bailey and Illinois defender Ben Humrichous as Bailey drove the baseline for a short jumper.
Anderson at first attempted to remove himself from the play, but then bumped Humrichous and somehow got pulled into the play even more. Anderson even then appear to set a screen on Illinois post player Morez Johnson.
After Bailey scored, the referee paused, smiled and incredulously shook his head. As Armstrong headed down court on the next play, he smiled again and appeared to say "my fault" to the Illinois bench.
The X.com account @itsAntWright, a basketball content creator, posted two photos of play with the comment: "I've been in tears all morning." By Thursday afternoon, the post had been seen by half a million users and had 7,000 engagements.
"The slow mo version is the best," wrote X.com user @JacobDivens77, sharing video of the play. The official "legit set 2 moving screens during the play."
And this isn't the first time Anderson got into precarious positioning this season. Just a couple weeks back, the ref appeared to defend an Oregon State player during its game against Gonzaga.
Who is the 'High Knees Referee'?
Anderson was a bit of an online celebrity even before this incident in the Illinois-Rutgers game.
The longtime college basketball official has the nickname "high knees" because he sometimes will kick his knees skyward as he runs down court. The "Jeffrey Anderson Fan Account" @highkneesref on X.com has nearly 20,000 followers. It posts short video clips of Anderson doing high knees and making various calls as he officiates games.

title: Illinois football lands four-star linebacker as Class of 2026 grows in national prominence
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Illinois football's Class of 2026 is growing in national ranks after it got a commitment from a 4-star linebacker Cam Thomas from Ohio.
content:
The recruiting wins keep coming for Illinois football and coach Bret Bielema.
Four-star linebacker Cam Thomas from Ohio announced his commitment to the Fighting Illini on Thursday, the latest to join the program's Class of 2026 that is now approaching the national top 10.
The 6-foot-2, 217-pound linebacker is from Lakota West in West Chester, Ohio. He chose Illinois over Michigan, Oregon, Indiana, West Virginia and Kentucky.
Thomas is the eight commit in the Class of 2026 and second from Ohio in the last few days, joining four-star defensive back Victor Singleton from Toledo — the highest-ranked high school commit under Bielema.
Thomas also joins to state of Illinois recruits in Jacob Alexander of Frankfort Lincoln-Way East and receiver Davon Grant of DeKalb. The Illini also have received commitments from offensive lineman Landen Van Seggern of Nebraska and three Florida players in quarterback Michael Clayton and receiver Kenyon Alston of Orlando and linebacker Kingston Shaw of Apopka.
The Illinois recruiting class has climbed to No. 13 overall in the nation, according to 247Sports. The Illini are coming off a 10-win season and a victory in the Citrus Bowl. They return 18 of 22 starters for the 2025 season.

title: Illinois congressman questions purpose of Musk group's access to NOAA systems
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Before entering politics, 17th District Rep. Eric Sorensen was a TV meteorologist for various stations.
content:
An Illinois congressman – and former TV meteorologist – is looking for answers from the Trump administration after reports that a group associated with Elon Musk had gained access to IT systems at the headquarters for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Rep. Eric Sorensen, who represents the 17th Congressional District containing much of Peoria, sent a letter, along with North Carolina congresswoman Deborah Ross, to President Donald Trump on Monday asking him to clarify the purpose of allowing members of Musk's Department of Government Efficiency access to NOAA's systems.
In addition, both want further clarification as to whether DOGE was able to access sensitive data, if Trump wants to alter NOAA's mission, restrict public access to NOAA data and if there are any safeguards preventing Musk in particular from abusing his access to the data.
The letter says that Musk's varied business interests – including aerospace, telecommunications and artificial intelligence through companies like Tesla, X (Twitter) and Starlink – provide him with conflicts of interest that may impact the integrity of the agency's operations, which include weather forecasting through the National Weather Service.
The pair extolled the virtues of NWS and its mission, saying that the work done by their forecasters provides life-saving information and helps farmers, fisherman and other "hardworking Americans" protect their livelihoods. They also noted that NWS helps ensure the safety of the nation's airspace, saying that any threat to NOAA and NWS would "pose a great danger" to the United States.
The pair had been acting on reports published last week that DOGE members had gained access to NOAA and had gained access to the agency's computer systems, which contained confidential information only available to department staffers. The Musk-backed group had entered several other government agencies, such as the Treasury Department, where they reportedly gained access to payment systems that contained personal data for millions of American citizens, according to the New York Times.
Sorensen was a meteorologist for over 20 years before entering the political sphere. A native of Rockford, he had served as a meteorologist for one of the city's major TV stations – the NBC-affiliate WREX from 2003-2014 – before heading to the Quad Cities and ABC-affiliated WQED from 2014-2021. First elected in 2022 in the 17th District, Sorensen is currently in his second term in office.
Sorensen and Ross ask that the Trump administration provide answers to their inquiry by Feb. 21.

title: How much snow will Illinois see this week? Here's the forecast
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A snowstorm this week is predicted to bring around at least four inches of snow to a sizable part of Illinois. Here's what to know.
content:
A snowstorm this week is predicted to bring at least four inches of snow to a sizable part of Illinois.
Most places near and west of Illinois 55 are expected to receive at least four inches of snow Wednesday, according to latest predictions from the National Weather Service.
The storm could also bring a mix of rain and freezing rain to central Illinois.
Here's the outlook for throughout Illinois.
Northern Illinois
The northern part of the state largely sees strong probabilities of receiving at least three or four inches of snow Wednesday, which will start around noon and stop around midnight.
While the weather is always subject to change, that prediction for the northern part of the state should remain fairly accurate, said Mike Albano, who is a meteorologist with the NWS.
Light snow will start around noon and the snow is expected to be falling heavily by the evening commute time.
Chicago, Peoria and Rockford all fit within the storm's path traveling from southwest to northeast that could bring three to five inches.
Central Illinois
Places in central Illinois currently are predicted to see anywhere from one inch to four inches on the low end.
Central Illinois sits in the transition zone of the storm that is especially subject to change as it gets closer, Albano said. That could mean variations of snow, freezing rain, sleet, and rain alone, in moving south.
Areas in that transition zone are from Quincy to Kankakee, including Springfield.
Southern Illinois
Areas along and south of I-70 could see freezing rain and the further south will see only rain.

title: Bracketology: Kansas, Kentucky continue tumble down projected NCAA Tournament field
author: Eddie Timanus
description: This week's bracketology looks at some big names are struggling as the men's college basketball season nears one month before Selection Sunday.
content:
In theory, a basketball team's recent results are supposed to count the same as those from earlier in the campaign. In practice, however, evaluators entering the bracketology fray must also account for trends, and right now some would-be contenders are moving in the wrong direction.
Our latest bracket projection has a couple of name-brand programs slipping outside the top 16, which could mean early upset exposure come March Madness. Kansas and Kentucky picked up important quality victories prior to conference play that will help come Selection Sun day, but the Jayhawks are now in fifth place in the Big 12 and the Wildcats have fallen behind the upper tier in the highly competitive SEC with just a 5-5 league record. Those usual powers find themselves as No. 5 regional seeds in our projection with Selection Sunday just over a month away.
On the other side of the conference coin, Arizona has used its strong start in the Big 12 to overcome some early setbacks and has moved comfortably into the upper quadrant of the bracket as a No. 3 seed, while Purdue rides a Big Ten hot streak to the No. 2 seed line. The projected No. 1's remain unchanged this week with Duke and a trio of SEC squads still at the head of the class.

PEORIA — The Bradley Braves are in Iowa on Sunday afternoon to take on the Missouri Valley Conference's first-place team at the Knapp Center in Des Moines.
Bradley fell behind by nine points in the opening minutes of the first half.

They kept on going, adding a dunk from Christian Davis and a 3-pointer from Darius Hannah to build a seven-point lead with 4:26 left.
Bradley (20-6, 11-4) is tied for second in the MVC with Northern Iowa and just reached its sixth 20-win season in 10 years under head coach Brian Wardle.
Drake comes in at 23-2 overall and 13-2 in the conference, and has won 11 straight games, all in the Valley. It's the third longest active win streak in the nation (Akron 13, Towson 12).

title: Opinion: David Horowitz's ‘Fight Back' legacy still resonates in Peoria
author: Fraser Engerman
description: Opinion: The Bradley grad and Emmy winner left a lasting impression as a consumer advocate.
content:
In the fall of my senior year at Bradley University, I received a letter from David Horowitz congratulating me on being the first student awarded the journalism scholarship he had just established in his name. It was one of the highlights from my time on the Hilltop. I was honored to have the financial help to complete my last year, but at the time I did not grasp the importance Bradley held for David nor the passion and commitment he felt toward the university and Peoria.
I did know the basics; he graduated Bradley with honors in 1959, became a distinguished reporter breaking major stories for NBC and CBS and Vietnam where he opened the NBC Saigon Bureau in 1963. And of course, there was the work that brought him his widest recognition — creating and hosting the decades long Emmy Award winning ' Fight Back! With David Horowitz.'
Through his TV show, his syndicated radio show, his newspaper column and personal appearances on programs like "The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson," David became known as our national consumer advocate investigating defective products and false claims, while at the same time empowering American consumers to stand up for their rights.
Horowitz once said, 'I don't want anyone to take me for a sucker, and I don't want to see anyone else taken either.'
Thus, I knew why David was successful, but what I came to understand later was his path to success went directly through Peoria. He was born into poverty in New York City, as his daughter Amanda Horowitz told me, 'My dad grew up so poor in the Bronx that he played with cardboard boxes because my grandparents couldn't afford toys.'
David came to Bradley which became a turning point in his life. It was the late Bradley professor Dr. Paul Snider who taught David the fundamentals of journalistic ethics and professional standards. Those same qualities Dr. Snider instilled in me and countless other students over the years.
Long after he left the Hilltop, David continued to help the next generation of students by hosting Bradley communications professor emeritus Dr. Ron Koperski's Entertainment Industry Seminar Expedition course in his Los Angeles Fight Back! national office, giving up-close, firsthand experience to hundreds of students. 'In addition to sharing inside, real-world information, he graciously answered their questions. The students were always so thankful to be in his presence,' said Koperski.
Bradley bestowed about every honor possible on David including Distinguished Alumnus, Centurion, and the highest award recognizing world-class achievement: Honorary Doctor of Humane Letters. And in return, for his lifetime of giving back to Bradley, the main lecture hall in the Caterpillar Global Communications Center was named in 2004 the David C. Horowitz Auditorium.
Since that time students, faculty, scholars, professional guests, and community members have attended the many classes, lectures, performances, and special events in the space everybody knows as the Horowitz Auditorium. As retired dean of the Slane College of Communications and Fine Arts Dr. Jeffrey Huberman said at the dedication ceremony, 'David's professional life is a world-wide convergence of teaching, informing, creating, and advocating.'
On the sixth anniversary of his passing, that advocacy is getting a new life thanks to Amanda, who now carries on her father's role of the 'Fight Back!" message. Amanda, who grew up testing products on his show, has created @WatchFightBack! where a new generation can engage with legacy clips as well as new content. In fact, the same month she launched Fight Back! her own consumer focused campaign received 9.5 million views on social media. 'What makes Fight Back! unique is its cross-generational appeal — some people remember the show, while others are discovering it for the first time. Fight Back! is for everyone because navigating life as a consumer is an experience that we all have in common,' said Amanda.
Amanda also hopes David's legacy will continue to grow with the next generation of Bradley students. One of the two most recent recipients of the Horowitz Scholarship is Caden Sexton, a junior who runs the Braves Vision program, (the student-led club that broadcasts all Bradley athletics events) and says he hopes more students will begin to understand the man whose name is on the lecture hall.
'I wish I could reach out to David and thank him for the scholarship. I wouldn't be at Bradley if it weren't for the kindness of people like him. His personal help in my education means the world to me, and strengthens my pride as a Bradley Brave,' said Caden.
Bradley University and Peoria have had their share of producing national figures in all fields. David Horowitz is a giant among them and that has become all the more clear to me since I opened that letter from him all those years ago.
