title: The state of Illinois might be sending you a check in the mail. Here's why
author: Mike Kramer
description: The Illinois State Treasurer's Office is distributing almost $13.2 million in Enhanced Money Match program funds to nearly 140,000 residents.
content:
Show Caption
Nearly 140,000 Illinois residents soon will be getting checks through the Enhanced Money Match program, and state lawmakers are encouraging those who receive the checks to cash them. More than $13 million is expected to be distributed.
What is the Enhanced Money Match program?
The Enhanced Money Match Program crossmatches data collected by various state agencies with the Illinois State Treasurer's unclaimed property database. The treasurer's office matches names and mailing addresses and confirms them, then sends a letter to the unclaimed property owner that describes the amount and source of the money. The program allows the treasurer's office to automatically return missing money to residents without the need to file claims.
How much money is ICash paying out? How much can you get?
In the latest round of the program, the Illinois treasurer's office is distributing nearly $13.2 million. Most checks are for amounts ranging from $50 to $100.
'Something that tastes like home': Peoria Mexican restaurant celebrates 10 years
How do I see if I have unclaimed money in Illinois?
Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs said residents can determine whether they have unclaimed Enhanced Money Match funds by visiting illinoistreasurer.gov.
Is ICash Illinois legit?
Apparently, concerns about identity theft can make recipients uneasy about cashing their checks.
Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs, Illinois State Sen. Sara Feigenholtz, and Illinois State Rep. Stephanie Kifowit held a presentation Tuesday at the State of Illinois government offices in Chicago to remind residents to redeem their uncashed property/I-cash checks when they arrive in the mail.
'One of the toughest parts of my job is giving away money,' Frerichs joked. 'We have done such a good job of convincing people there are identity thieves out there trying to steal their identities that when we tell people we have money for them, they frequently don't believe it.'

title: Lifelong Rockford Republican defends Kamala Harris against plagiarism charges
author: Jeff Kolkey
description: Former Winnebago County State's Attorney and lifelong Republican Paul Logli is defending Kamala Harris against unfair charges of plagiarism this week.
content:
A lifelong Republican, former Winnebago County State's Attorney Paul Logli found himself this week coming to the defense of Vice President Kamala Harris against charges of plagiarism.
The Democratic presidential nominee was accused in a story Tuesday by The Washington Free Beacon of plagiarizing 2007 testimony that Logli had given before the Senate Judiciary Committee. He was there as the president of the National District Attorneys Association representing more than 4,000 local and state prosecutors across the country. Harris, then the district attorney of San Francisco, was a board member.
Logli testified in support of a bill that would have created a student loan repayment program for prosecutors and public defenders to encourage more to enter the profession. Several news outlets picked up on the story including CNN and Newsweek.
Long passages of testimony Harris gave a couple months later in April 2007 before a House Judiciary Committee were 'strikingly similar' to testimony Logli had given, 'but not because she was copying me,' Logli said Wednesday.
'I do not believe that she in any way, shape or form is guilty of plagiarism,' Logli said. 'She just did the same thing I did, which was to rely on staff to do the research on this particular issue.'
Logli said his opening statement before the Senate committee was largely prepared by staff of the NDAA. He has no doubt staff provided Harris with the same material when she later went to testify before the House committee.
It was an effort to provide a consistent message to both chambers of Congress, Logli said.
Several news outlets including CNN reported reviewing testimony given by Logli and Harris, determining that "Harris lifted language from a Republican attorney.' CNN also quoted a plagiarism expert as saying this was "not a serious case of plagiarism, to put it mildly.'
Logli was contacted by several national and international news outlets seeking comment.
'Most of the fun of those committee hearings was the question-and-answer period,' Logli said. 'That's where I really inserted much more of my own opinions, and I could respond to other people on the panel who may be for or against the legislation. I'm sure that what the staff did was they copied and pasted what they had prepared for me two months earlier and gave it to Kamala.'

description: Nearly 140,000 Illinoisans will be receiving a check in the mail as the state tries to return more than $13 million to residents. What to know.
content:
Thousands of Illinois residents may have some free money coming their way.
Illinois Treasurer Michael Frerichs said 138,561 residents have checks coming in the mail for unclaimed property.
In total, the state's treasurer's office is trying to return $13.2 million to residents.
Here's what you need to know.
Where are the checks coming from?
The checks are from the latest round of the Enhanced Money Match program, which allows the Treasurer's Office to automatically return missing money to people without the need to file a claim.
How much are the checks worth?
The majority of the checks in this round are for $50 to $100.
How do the checks get sent to the right people?
The program leverages data already collected by the state and crossmatches it with the State Treasurer's unclaimed property database. The Treasurer's Office then sends a letter to the unclaimed property owner after confirming their identity.
What is the Enhanced Money Match program?
The program focuses on simple claims, or cash owed to a single person. This does not include cash owned by multiple parties, including a joint holding of a parent and minor child, as well as shares of stocks and bonds, escrow accounts, and the contents of bank safe deposit boxes. The program is part of the state's Unclaimed Property program, also known as I-CASH.
Why are checks being mailed?
The state treasurer is legally required to return unclaimed property to its owners or heirs, no matter how long it takes.
How much money has been returned through the program?
Since 2018, the Illinois Treasurer's Office has returned more than $102 million to nearly 422,000 people through the Enhanced Money Match program.
Do I have unclaimed property?
Residents can check to see if they have any unclaimed property at icash.illinoistreasurer.gov.

title: Great Lincoln's ghost! Study names Illinois the second-spookiest state in the U.S.
author: Mike Kramer
description: Illinois is the country's second-spookiest state based on its haunted attractions and ghost sightings, according to a study conducted by High 5 Casino.
content:
Being one of the spookiest states in the country is probably not a persuasive selling point most of the year.
But during the Halloween season, it makes Illinois one of the best destinations in the United States for October fright-seeing.
Illinois captured second place behind Ohio in a recent study of the spookiest states in America, according to the gaming company High 5 Casino. The study weighed four factors in compiling the results of the spookiest states in the U.S.:
Haunted attractions
Horror-themed escape rooms
Ghost sightings
Average haunted house rating.
Illinois has 106 haunted attractions; the third-highest number behind Ohio and California; 28 horror-themed escape rooms and 14 ghost sightings. Its average haunted house rating, based on a scale of 1 to 10, was 8.88.

title: Man identified as victim of Tazewell County shed fire
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The 43-year-old man died of smoke and soot inhalation, according to the coroner.
content:
A 43-year-old man from rural Mackinaw was killed Monday following a shed fire.
Nathan Robertson was pronounced dead at 8:15 p.m. Monday night, according to the Tazewell County Coroner's Office. They were asked to respond to the scene of a shed fire in Mackinaw at 6:43 p.m. after receiving an alert of a fatality at the scene.
Coroner Charles Hanley said that an autopsy conducted Tuesday revealed Robertson died due to inhalation of smoke and soot coming from the blaze.
The coroner's office and the Tazewell County Sheriff's Office is investigating what led to the fire, along with Illinois State Police and the .

title: These are Donald Trump's key allies for a possible post-election fight
author: Josh Meyer
description: Here are some of the more prominent people in MAGA World who could be at the center of a post-election fight over the results.
content:
WASHINGTON − Former President Donald Trump has said he had ' every right' to "interfere" with the 2020 election he lost in an effort to overturn it. He has refused to say that he'll accept the outcome of the 2024 election.
Being out of office, Trump cannot ask officials in the Justice Department to help him try to nullify the results, as special counsel Jack Smith says he did last time. But there remains a group of supporters who stand ready to assist Trump, including some who have been investigated, charged and even convicted in connection with his unsuccessful effort to overturn the 2020 election.
Some of Trump's most stalwart alleged co-conspirators from 2020 are playing less of a role, if any, this time around, including former administration officials like then-White House chief of staff Mark Meadows and advisor Peter Navarro, who went to prison for refusing to cooperate with the congressional investigation into the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol. Some of Trump's lawyers and legal advisors like Sidney Powell and Jenna Ellis have pleaded guilty to criminal charges in connection with the plot and are cooperating in ongoing prosecutions of Trump and other alleged co-conspirators.
But other Trump acolytes old and new have rallied to his cause and indicated they will fight a Trump loss at the precinct level, in Congress and the courts − and on the social media platforms that influence public opinion.
Here are some of the more prominent people in MAGA World who could be at the center of a post-election fight over the results:
'The fixer' - Boris Epshteyn
A longtime Trump political advisor, legal strategist, fixer and campaign operative, Epshteyn has been described as Trump's ' wartime consigliere ' by former Trump White House official Steve Bannon. He was one of 18 people indicted in Arizona for trying to overturn Trump's loss there in 2020. He has pleaded not guilty.
Epshteyn also matches the person identified as unindicted Co-Conspirator No. 6 in the federal insurrection case against Trump led by Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith, according to The New York Times and other media outlets and legal analysts. Prosecutors allege that Co-Conspirator No. 6 played a key role in a plan to use fake pro-Trump electors to try to overturn Biden's victory in as many as seven battleground states, and to pressure then-Vice President Mike Pence to go along with the plan. (Smith secured a new Jan. 6 indictment against Trump aiming to satisfy a recent Supreme Court ruling saying some of his acts as president granted him immunity.)
Epshteyn, currently counsel and senior advisor to Trump among other roles, had no comment when asked about his role in the 2024 campaign and any plans to contest a loss to Trump's Democratic rival Kamala Harris. He also had no comment to USA TODAY on whether he was, or was not, Co-Conspirator No. 6 in the Smith filing.
'The Billionaire Booster' - Elon Musk
Musk, the world's richest man and founder of SpaceX and other ventures, has gone from merely being a supporter of Trump to a full-blown campaign surrogate − and financial backer. In recent months, he has used his influential social media platform, X, to boost debunked conspiracy theories smearing Harris and to spread false or misleading claims about the election.
Musk was a speaker at Trump's Oct, 5 rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, at which the mega-billionaire donned a black "Make America Great Again" hat and described himself as " Dark MAGA." Now appearing on Trump campaign billboards along with the candidate, Musk also has been repeating Trump's threat that, "If Trump loses, this is the last election" that Americans will get.
Musk did not respond to requests by USA TODAY to comment on his role in the election in posts sent to his account on X and via email.
'The Dirty Trickster' - Roger Stone
A longtime Trump adviser, political consultant and self-proclaimed "dirty trickster," Stone has been deeply involved in promoting election conspiracy theories. As a founder of the "Stop the Steal" movement, his alleged participation in efforts to disrupt the certification of the 2020 election results drew deep scrutiny from the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection at the Capitol.
Stone was convicted in 2019 of lying under oath to congressional lawmakers to protect Trump's campaign from the investigation by special counsel Robert Mueller into Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. election. Trump later commuted his sentence and eventually pardoned him. A frequent guest at Mar-a-Lago, Stone told USA TODAY in May that he still speaks with Trump occasionally but doesn't have a formal role in the current campaign. That's a similar arrangement to past campaigns.
'Everything I do is on a voluntary basis and I kind of pick my shots,' said Stone, who continues to claim that Trump can only lose in 2024 if the election is stolen.
In a new video, Stone is seen saying he wants to send armed guards to dispute the election in Detroit. He also wants to imprison former Attorney General Bill Barr if Trump returns to power. Stone did not respond to requests seeking comment.
'The Field General' - Michael Flynn
Trump pardoned Flynn, his first (and short-lived) national security adviser, after the retired Army lieutenant general pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his contacts with Russian officials in late 2016. After Trump lost in 2020, Flynn suggested he declare martial law to 'redo' the election because it was stolen from him. He was involved in efforts to overturn the election results, including raising money for an election audit in Arizona.
However, Flynn was not among those charged in the Arizona election case.
Since then, Flynn has continued to spread conspiracy theories about the election and other "deep state" cabals such as thoroughly discredited QAnon accusations of Democratic pedophiles and child traffickers.
In 2024, Flynn has been traveling the country in support of his autobiographical documentary "Flynn." He recently told an interviewer that if the result isn't known by Nov. 6, "I feel like people are going to go to these locations where there's counting, and there could actually be violence, because people are gonna be − people so upset after 2020 and what is very clear in terms of a fraudulent election in certain states − and they're just not gonna put up with it any more."
A March 28 movie screening and pool-side reception at Trump's Palm Beach, Fla. club Mar-a-Lago sold out. And Trump has suggested several times that he intends to find a role for Flynn in his administration if he wins in November.
Flynn did not respond to requests seeking comment.
'The Operative' - Michael Roman
A longtime Republican operative and opposition researcher, first for the Koch Brothers and then Trump, Roman was a senior campaign official responsible for Election Day operations in 2020. In that role, Roman allegedly was central to the Trump "alternate' electors scheme that sought to subvert the Electoral College results by recruiting fake electors in battleground states to prevent certification of President Biden's Electoral College victory, prosecutors say. Trump then appointed Roman as a White House special assistant to the president and director of Special Projects and Research.
Roman was among the 18 people indicted in Georgia in addition to Trump, Meadows and others for election fraud. It was Roman's court motions that forced lead prosecutor Nathan Wade off the case for having an affair with Fulton County, Ga. District Attorney Fani Willis. He has pleaded not guilty.
In 2020, DOJ special counsel Smith alleged, a Trump official matching Roman's description urged Republican operatives to make Trump supporters riot outside a Detroit polling facility to stop the vote count when it began trending in Biden's favor.
Roman also was the Trump campaign official who delivered false elector certificates to a Pennsylvania congressman's chief of state in an attempt to get them to Vice President Mike Pence, Politico reported in 2022.
A source familiar with Roman said he is not working for Trump or related organizations this election.
'The Propagandist' - Steve Bannon
A former White House official and chief strategist for Trump, Bannon has for years fueled the political movement behind Trump's false claims of election fraud and rigged voting systems, encouraging public protests and resistance – by force if necessary.
On his last day in office in 2021, Trump pardoned Bannon, who had been charged with fraud unrelated to the election. But he remains in prison, serving a four-month sentence for contempt of Congress after defying a subpoena from the House committee that investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol attack. Even so, Bannon's influential 'War Room' podcast reaches millions and has been increasingly riling up Trump's base with more bogus claims of another rigged election in 2024 and the need to rise up and fight back.
The former investment banker-turned-populist also was involved in the infamous meetings at a Washington hotel where Trump supporters like Stone, Flynn and others gathered to coordinate efforts to overturn the election in the days before the Jan. 6 Capitol attack. And he told associates in October 2020 that Trump would falsely claim election victory even if he lost the following month, which he did.
Asked recently if he keeps in touch with Trump, Bannon told the Guardian, 'I don't want to talk about all the conversations, but I stay in contact with the president enough that there is no separation between the War Room and President Trump. If you watch the War Room, you'll see a lot of stuff pop up in the speeches and what he's put up on Truth Social."
'The Architect' - Rudy Giuliani
In 2020, Giuliani, the former New York mayor and personal attorney for Trump, was the legal architect and public face of Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 election. In that role, he led many of the legal challenges and efforts to promote unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud. He was later indicted in Arizona and Fulton County, Ga., for his alleged role in the election subversion case, and was socked with a separate $148 million civil judgment for defaming two election workers whom he falsely accused of election fraud. He has pleaded not guilty and denied wrongdoing.
Giuliani was recently disbarred in the District of Columbia based on his misrepresentations of election fraud when serving as Trump's campaign lawyer in 2020. He was also disbarred in New York.
On Sept. 11, he appeared with Trump, Republican vice presidential nominee JD Vance and others at a memorial event at Ground Zero in Manhattan honoring those who died in the 2001 terrorist attacks.

title: Ahead of Election Day, officials prepare for protests and possible violence
author: Sarah D. Wire
description: Election officials and emergency management agencies have spent months planning how to keep counting ballots once polls close, no matter what happens
content:
The bushes in front of city hall in Green Bay, Wisconsin, have been removed. On election night, the street out front will be blocked off. These "hardening" measures were suggested by the city police chief to protect the ballots being counted inside, said Celestine Jeffreys, Green Bay's city clerk.
As threats against election workers have grown more violent, election officials across the country have spent months coordinating to protect voters, ballots and poll workers at an unprecedented level with emergency management agencies. Amid that coordination, the centralized locations where ballots are counted on election night have emerged as a key place needing protection. More than a dozen county and city election officials spoke with USA TODAY about what they are doing to make sure they can count ballots at central ballot counting locations once polls close, no matter what happens outside.
Election officials have built new warehouses where ballots will be counted under increased security. Local and state law enforcement have run through multiple scenarios for large crowds descending on the ballot counting locations. Some jurisdictions have reduced the number of observers allowed to attend and required them to obtain credentials far in advance.
Despite polls showing a tossup race in key swing states, former President Donald Trump is already saying he can only lose if there is massive fraud. He has without evidence named Detroit, Milwaukee and Philadelphia as places where fraud could occur.
Some prominent pro-Trump Republicans are already saying supporters will go to ballot counting locations if the winner of the presidential election isn't clear on Election Day, Nov. 5.
Former Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn, Trump's first White House national security advisor who played a central role in 2020 efforts to overturn the election results, said on Oct. 20 on right-wing podcast American Truth Project that the results should be known on election night.
Otherwise, Flynn warned, "I do feel like people are going to go to those locations where there's counting and there could actually be violence, because people are so upset after 2020."
Jim Burch, president of the National Policing Institute, a nonprofit research organization, told USA TODAY the central ballot counting facilities have become an "incredible point of potential risk and concern."
The Trump campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
'Stop the count'
Election officials are responding to fears of what could occur in 2024 and to the reality of what happened at the central counting location in Detroit in 2020.
The day after the 2020 election, a crowd of Michigan Republicans − primed by months of Trump's baseless claims of massive voter fraud and that he'd won the election − hurried to the convention hall in downtown Detroit where mail-in and military votes were being counted, argued with police and election officials and banged on windows while they chanted 'stop the count.'
On X, formerly known as Twitter, Flynn's associate Ivan Raiklin, a former Green Beret, and retired Army Reserve lieutenant colonel, said last Monday that Americans should be"planning to descend on states and counties where they do not finish the election count by midnight Nov. 5 in order to document, audit and livestream every movement and breath of every single poll worker, election official, to ensure they are motivated to guarantee a free fair and transparent election."
Lawrence Norden, vice president of the Elections & Government Program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said his biggest fear about post-election violence is if one candidate declares victory before the ballots have all been counted and while it is still unclear who won.
"That is the period of time where there's an information void, and emotions are running extremely high," Norden said. "That's when you get the crowd showing up, threats against election workers, election officials, who are doing their jobs."
In 2020, Trump declared victory hours after the polls closed, even though it was too close to cal l and neither candidate had secured the 270 electoral college votes needed to win and ballots were still being counted across the country. Days later, Biden secured the electoral college votes needed to win.
'You have to have contingency plans in place'
In Chester County, Penn., about 40 minutes from Philadelphia, Voter Services Director Karen Barsoum has been meeting with representatives of county agencies for months.
'This is not a clerk − me − sitting in an office like maybe 20 years ago. This is a big operation that needs everyone from this county almost to be helping with and on standby, from the (district attorney) to the sheriff to the Department of Emergency Services," she told USA TODAY.
All 300 county staffers have been trained on what happens at the central ballot scanning facility, including emergency training by the Department of Emergency Services, she said.
'God forbid you're at a station, and there is an envelope that has white powder... this is how we are going to conduct ourselves. This is how we're segregating it. This is how we segregate a person. This is how we evacuate,' Barsoum said, paraphrasing the training.
Local elections officials nationwide have changed procedures or built new facilities in anticipation of people potentially trying to interfere with counting ballots. Jurisdictions of all sizes expect intense public scrutiny of election administration.
Paulina Gutierrez, the Milwaukee Election Commission executive director, said every person going into central counting now has to go through security and is only allowed to carry one bag. Posted signs will explain the rules in preparation for large crowds and city attorneys will be on site. They've also reduced the observation space so it will be harder for a large crowd to gather, she said.
'Any member of the public can show up to any of our polling sites and central count, and we are expecting large crowds,' Gutierrez said.
In Washoe County, Nevada, home to Reno, election workers are now monitored by overhead cameras as they count ballots, with panic buttons installed in case of emergency, and security badges to limit access. And because election observers have sometimes tried to harass workers counting ballots, the county installed a soundproof glass-fronted "penalty box" to keep them separate.
The new election facility in Fulton County, Ga., home to most of Atlanta, was specifically built to have wide windows where the public can view every part of the process, in an effort to be as transparent as possible, said Nadine Williams, director of registration and elections. The fire marshal will keep a close eye on how many people enter the building, she said.
"We are concerned about the large crowd that we can possibly get on election night," she said. "We've been doing scenario trainings and things of that nature to prepare."
In Maryland, Baltimore County's new central building for election administration was designed with transparency and security in mind, said Election Director Ruie Lavoie.
'If anyone wants to come and watch us till four o'clock in the morning while we upload the results, they're more than welcome to do so," she said.
Santa Fe County, N.M., Clerk Katherine Clark said tabletop exercises with local law enforcement, the FBI and the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency have been useful.
'There's always going to be things that happen, and because that election has to happen no matter what − absolutely no matter what − you have to have contingency plans in place," she said.
The National Policing Institute is one of several election advocacy and law enforcement groups that have held meetings with law enforcement across the country on how they can help elections officials protect not just staff, but ballots and the ability to count them. Safety of the central ballot counting locations have been a focus, Burch, the group's president, said.
Law enforcement is being asked to think about elections in a way they never had to before, he said. They are preparing for protests and civil disobedience, along with providing security for months of campaign stops, weeks of early voting locations, polling places on Election Day and at the ballot count locations for days afterward.
Detroit has changed
Changes to procedures in Detroit and state law in Michigan should make it harder for a large, upset crowd to gather and disrupt the count, Daniel Baxter, Chief of Operations for Detroit, told USA TODAY.
In 2020, challengers − a person who is appointed by a candidate or political party to observe the process on their behalf − just had to sign a piece of paper to enter the tabulation area. Now, they have to provide credentials showing they pre-registered with one of a dozen groups that signed up weeks in advance to have challengers in Wayne County, which includes part of Detroit and the surrounding counties. Everyone entering will have to present identification, be credentialed in advance and pass through metal detectors manned by Detroit Police officers.
An initiative petition passed by Michigan voters in November 2022 also allows local election administrators to start pre-tabulating absentee ballots before the election and limits how many challengers can be present during pre-tabulation and on election night.
Ballot counting was moved from the basement to a new hall within the convention center where there is more space to work 'and there are no windows to bang on," Baxter said.
Baxter, who has worked in the office since the mid-1980's, said election officials have always talked with law enforcement about protection and security, but this year is different. It includes lessons learned from the last presidential election, what state and federal law enforcement are hearing and the threats other election officials have faced.
"Everything that we're doing for the 2024 presidential election is rooted from what our experience was in 2020,' he said.
Law enforcement will also help ensure that ballots and the memory cards holding ballot data make it to the central count location from the precincts.
"Everything that we do will be under police escort to ensure a tranquil and smooth operation and transition of all of those items," Baxter said.
Officers will be visible on every street around the convention center, and will be in parking areas to keep ballot-counting staff from being hassled or an aggressive crowd from interfering with counting the ballots.
"We just want to make sure that every area is covered. While we hope for the best, we plan for the worst," Baxter said.
Planning in Green Bay
Jeffreys, Green Bay's clerk, said she began thinking about contingency plans a year ago. She took the job in 2021.
"My clerkship is in a post-January 6 environment. I have always been concerned, and I've always worked closely with the police department on our security,' she said.
So Jeffreys quickly agreed when the police chief suggested removing bushes at city hall and closing off the street out front while ballots are counted.
"That came about as a result of some information the police chief had received and also his professional judgment that we needed to, quote, unquote, harden where central count takes place,' she said. 'I leave the intelligence gathering to the police department. And I trust them."

title: 18 things to do in Peoria in November: Holiday traditions, music and comedy shows and more
author: Josh Jenke
description: November begins the holiday season, and there are many fun traditions and other events to enjoy in central Illinois.
content:
The holiday season is just around the corner in central Illinois, and the calendar is full of fun parades and activities, big music and comedy shows and more.
Here are 18 things to do in the Peoria area in the month of November.
1. Nitro Circus Live
The gravity-defying thrill-seekers of Nitro Circus will bring their live sports entertainment show to the Peoria Civic Center Arena at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 30. The show will feature world-class athletes and daredevils performing a variety of high-flying stunts. Tickets start at $33.50 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.
2. 137th annual Santa Claus Parade
The longest-running holiday parade in the country, the Peoria Santa Claus Parade, will be held at 9:15 a.m. Friday, Nov. 29, in downtown Peoria. The theme of this year's parade will be "Hometown Holidays." The parade will feature costumed characters, decorated floats, marching bands, Santa Claus and more. For more information, visit www.peoriaevents.com/events/santa-claus-parade.
3. East Peoria Parade of Lights
The East Peoria Festival of Lights will kick off the holiday season with the 2024 Parade of Lights at 6:30 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 23, along the streets of East Peoria. The parade will have several floats shaped by bright, colorful LED lights and will run from the intersection of Washington Street and Dolans Lane to the intersection of Taylor Street and Springfield Road. For more information, visit www.cityofeastpeoria.com.
4. Thanksgiving Riverfront Market
The 7th annual Thanksgiving Peoria Riverfront Market will take place from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 23, at the Riverplex, 600 NE Water Street. The market will feature fall produce, baked goods, cheese, popcorn, honey and local arts and crafts. Admission is free. For more information, visit www.visitdowntownpeoria.com.
5. 'Bored Teachers' comedy show
The comedians of the Bored Teachers comedy group will bring their "The Struggle is Real Tour" to the Peoria Civic Center Theater at 7:30 p.m. Friday, Nov. 22. Tickets start at $45 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.
6. Illinois CancerCare fundraiser
"A Royal Affair," the 15th Annual CUREageous fundraising evening supporting the Illinois CancerCare Foundation, will be held at 7 p.m. Friday, Nov. 22, at the Par-A-Dice Hotel & Casino, 21 Blackjack Blvd., East Peoria. Doors open at 6 p.m. Dress in your finest attire and enjoy an evening full of live music, a raffle and silent auction, as well as the 2024 Rock Doc & AMP Champ Awards. For tickets and more information, visit https://cureageousevent.com/details/.
7. Crittenton Centers Festival of Trees
The Annual Crittenton Centers Festival of Trees will be held Nov. 21-23 at Holiday Inn and Suites, 7601 N. Orange Prairie Road. The event will feature over 80 designer pre-decorated trees and wreaths, centerpieces and other holiday decor items on display and for bidding to take home. Thursday night will be a Jingle & Mingle Cocktail Party from 5:30 to 9 p.m. for adults ages 21 and over. Saturday events will include Senior Day from 9:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., Cookies with Santa from 3 to 5 p.m. and Paint Night from 7 to 9 p.m. Sunday event will include Brunch & Bubbly from 9:30 to 11:30 a.m. and Family Day from 1 to 4:30 p.m. For more information and tickets for all events, visit https://crittentoncenters.org/event/festival-of-trees/.
8. German American Society Kristkindlmarkt
The Peoria German American Society will host its annual Kristkindlmarkt from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 16, and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 17, at Expo Gardens, 1601 W. Northmoor Road. Vendors will be showcasing various arts, crafts, jewelry, toys, clothing, collectibles, woodworking items, Christmas cards, ornaments, household items and fashion accessories. Food and beverage will also be available for purchase, including bratwurst, schnitzel, German potato salad, sauerkraut, glühwein, hot chocolate, hot cider, Bavarian pretzels and German beer. Admission is free.
9. An evening of comedy with Steve-O
Stunt performer, actor and television personality Steve-O will bring his Super Dummy Tour to the Peoria Civic Center Theater at 7 p.m. Friday, Nov. 15. Tickets start at $35.75 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.
10. A Motown Christmas
Experience a Motown Christmas at 7 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 13, at the Peoria Civic Center Theater. The concert will feature a world-class vocal group, assembled from past and present members of Motown's most legendary groups, Ali Woodson's Temptations, The Miracles and The Contours, and will combine Motown's greatest hits with everyone's favorite holiday classics. Tickets start at $53 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.
11. Kansas in concert
Legendary progressive rock band Kansas has extended their 50th anniversary Another Fork in the Road Tour and will make a stop at the Peoria Civic Center Theater at 7:30 p.m. Friday, Nov. 8. Tickets start at $54 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.
12. Peoria Players presents 'The Sound of Music'
Peoria Players will present its run of "The Sound of Music" at 7:30 p.m. Nov. 8-9 and Nov. 14-16, and 2 p.m. Nov. 10 and Nov. 17, at the theater, 4300 N. University St. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit www.peoriaplayers.org.
13. Chillicothe Players present 'A Christmas Story'
The Chillicothe Players Theater will presents its run of the holiday classic, "A Christmas Story," at 7:30 p.m. Nov. 7-9 and 2:30 p.m. Nov. 10 at Shore Acres Park, 6588 E. Park Blvd., Chillicothe. For tickets and more information, visit www.chillicotheplayers.org.
14. Jeremy Camp in concert
Christian music singer/songwriter Jeremy Camp will bring his Deeper Waters Tour to the Peoria Civic Center Theater at 7 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 7. The show will also feature special guests Andrew Ripp and Rachel Lampa. Tickets start at $29 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.
15. The Snow Queen ballet
The Grand Kyiv Ballet will present their performance of "The Snow Queen" at 7 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 5, at the Peoria Civic Center Theater. This adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen's classic fairy tale is sure to enchant audiences of all ages. Tickets start at $39 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.
16. Dancing with the Local Stars fundraiser
The annual CASAblanca: Dancing with the Local Stars will take place from 6 to 9 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 2, at the Par-A-Dice Hotel & Casino, 21 Blackjack Blvd., East Peoria. CASA's primary fundraising event of the year will feature local celebrities dancing with local dance instructors and competing against each other. Tickets are $300 per person or $2,500 for a table of 10 and can be purchased online at www.casaofthetenth.org.
17. Annual Itoo Supper
The Itoo Society will host its 97th annual Itoo Supper from 3 to 6 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 2, and 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Sunday, Nov. 3, at the Itoo Hall, 4909 Farmington Road. The menu will include cabbage rolls, chicken with rice, baked kibbeh, green beans, Lebanese salad and pita bread. Cost is $20 per meal. Saturday will be drive-thru pick-up for pre-orders only. Orders must be placed by the end of the day on Friday, Nov. 1, at https://itoosupper24.square.site/. Sunday will be dine-in and carry-out and will also include a bake sale.
18. Barenaked Ladies in concert
The Barenaked Ladies will bring their In Flight Tour to the Peoria Civic Center Theater at 7:30 p.m. Friday, Nov. 1. The concert will also feature special guest Toad the Wet Sprocket. Tickets start at $41 and can be purchased at www.peoriaciviccenter.com.

title: Gary's Tom Harmon won Heisman at Michigan and was shot down during World War II — twice!
author: Gregg Doyel
description: Tom Harmon, the only Indiana schoolboy to win a Heisman, was even more remarkable in the skies of World War II than on the football field of Michigan.
content:
The first time he parachuted out of a burning plane during World War II, on the night five men around him died — American soldiers, all of them — Tom Harmon landed in the dark of a South American jungle. The sounds of the rainforest followed him as he thrashed through vines and swamp grass.
Back at home in the Midwest, the parents of the greatest college football player ever to come from Indiana — Harmon played at Michigan, where in 1940 he became the first and still only Indiana schoolboy to win the Heisman Trophy — had received the bad news via telegram from the U.S. War Department. Louis and Rose Harmon spent much of the next five days at church, praying for his return, and had just arrived home from mass when a reporter called with the good news, as headlined in the Indianapolis News on April 17, 1943:
Tommy Harmon is Safe in Plane Crash
The second time he parachuted out of a burning plane during World War II, on the night two men around him died — both Japanese fighter-pilots, shot down by the 1940 Heisman Trophy winner — Tom Harmon floated above the Yangtze River in Japanese-occupied China. His legs were badly burned after a Japanese Zero had blown up the fuel tank of his Lockheed P-38 Lightning, and Japanese planes in the area were trying to finish the job, shooting at Harmon as he descended toward the Yangtze.
For a month, Louis and Rose Harmon waited for the impossible, news their son had survived a second crash during World War II. Their prayers were answered, as headlined in the Indianapolis Star on Nov. 30, 1943:
Tommy Harmon is Safe Second Time
After Being Missing Month in China
None of that made the movie.
Neither did his triumphant return to the NFL, where he'd been the No. 1 overall pick by the Chicago Bears in 1941 but didn't make his debut until 1946, with the Los Angeles Rams. Neither did his post-playing career, or marrying actor and World War II pin-up model Elyse Knox in 1944, or broadcasting the first televised Rose Bowl in 1948.
Harmon and Knox had three kids: Mark Harmon, who played quarterback for UCLA before becoming one of the most well-known actors in Hollywood; Kristin Harmon, an actor and artist who married rock star Ricky Nelson in 1963; and Kelly Harmon, an actor and model who married John DeLorean in 1969.
Ricky Nelson and John DeLorean didn't make the movie, either.
'Harmon of Michigan' was released in 1941 — before he won his Silver Star and Purple Heart in World War II — to capitalize on his fame as one of the most popular athletes in America.
Who played the starring role? He did.
Only Tom Harmon could do the Tom Harmon story justice.
Tom Harmon, best athlete in Indiana HS history?
He could've gone pro in three sports, and perhaps competed in the Olympics in a fourth.
Harmon earned 14 letters at Horace Mann High in Gary, where he threw no-hitters for the baseball team and was leading scorer for the basketball team — he played one season at Michigan, and was named to the Indiana Basketball Hall of Fame's 1962 Silver Anniversary team — and won state track championships in the 100-yard dash and 220 hurdles, setting records.
Hard to know if football was his best sport, but it was the one that earned him the most acclaim. Harmon was a two-time all-state quarterback, scored seven touchdowns in a game twice, and led Horace Mann to the mythical Indiana state title in 1936 when he led the country in scoring with 150 points. He chose Michigan but found himself at the center of controversy weeks before his first game when a coach from Tulane sent him a telegram — published by the Michigan student newspaper — asking him to transfer to Tulane.
Harmon stayed at Michigan, obviously, where he led college football in scoring in 1939, finishing second in Heisman Trophy voting that year to Iowa's Nile Kinnick.
Harmon opened the 1940 season on his 21 st birthday, at California, by producing five touchdowns and kicking four extra points. He returned a kickoff 95 yards for one TD, returned a punt 70 yards for another, threw a 7-yard TD pass and scored on runs of 86 and 8 yards. On the 86-yarder, according to the Indianapolis Star on Sept. 29, 1940 — Headline: Tom Harmon Beats Bears in Coast Tilt — 'an unidentified spectator endeavored to help the California tacklers by rushing out to stop the Michigan wraith, but Harmon also was too fast for California's '12 th man'. He had touched the ball down and was walking back to kick his conversion before the would-be tackler reached the end zone.'
After that game, with Harmon well on his way to leading the country in scoring again, the 1940 Heisman Trophy was his as long he stayed healthy. And he did despite suffering another broken nose, one of 13 times it was broken.
After that season, Michigan retired his No. 98 jersey — and Tom Harmon retired from football.
Larger than life in life, death
Between the first and second time Tom Harmon parachuted from his burning plane during World War II, the 1939 Heisman Trophy winner was killed in action: Nile Kinnick of Iowa.
Kinnick had turned down chances to play in the NFL and for the Brooklyn Dodgers to enter law school, then enlisted in the U.S. Navy. He was flying a training mission off the coast of Venezuela when his plane experienced a catastrophic oil leak, and Kinnick had to parachute into the Caribbean Sea. Neither he nor his plane was ever found, only an oil slick off the coast of Venezuela.
Times were different back then, with pro sports offering middle-class wages, which is why Tom Harmon chose Columbia Pictures over George Halas and the Chicago Bears in 1941. Soon he was in the U.S. Army Air Forces, enlisting after the draft board in Lake County, Indiana, turned down his request for a permanent deferment to take care of his parents. He flew with the 449 th Fighter Interceptor Squadron in a plane nicknamed 'Old 98,' and went down twice in seven months. The first time, flying with five fellow U.S. soldiers, the engine failed; he was the only survivor, parachuting into a tree near the wreckage of the plane in a swamp, where he found the bodies of two of his colleagues. The other three were never found.
That was April 1943. Two months later, Kinnick went missing. Five months after that, another Big Ten football star — All-American quarterback Don Scott of Ohio State — was killed in a bomber crash near England.
One month later Tom Harmon went down again.
The first time, he'd walked himself to safety in the coastal nation of Suriname. The second time, after shooting down two Japanese planes before going down over Japanese-occupied China, he wasn't walking anywhere.
Tom Harmon, burned badly on his legs and face, his mouth swollen shut, was probably going to die had he not been discovered by Chinese sympathizers and carried via stretcher for hundreds of miles. Little is known about that four-week stretch where Harmon was MIA and his parents were praying at a Catholic church in Ann Arbor, Mich. Harmon never said much about it, but he did come home from China in January 1944 with the silk parachute he'd used to float toward the Yangtze.
His wife was married in a dress made from the white silk and cords of that parachute.
One more, from 2015: The amazing life of IU football trailblazer George Taliaferro
Harmon returned to football after the war, but his body — ravaged by burns and infection and dysentery, he'd lost 52 pounds in a month — was never the same. He had an occasional glimpse of greatness, including an 84-yard run that was the longest play from scrimmage in the 1946 NFL season, but in his other 46 carries that year he gained just 152 yards. He retired after the 1947 season at age 28.
By then he'd starred in his own movie and been among the most decorated U.S. aviators in World War II. At Michigan he'd been so popular, he'd hired a secretary to handle fan mail that exceeded 200 pieces each week. After the war he remained in demand, playing a sports announcer in two Dean Martin and Jerry Lewis comedies and doing that job for real for ABC and CBS. At one time his nightly sports show was syndicated to more than 400 stations.
That's according to his obituary in the Indianapolis Star on March 17, 1990 — Headline: Tom Harmon, 70, former football hero — written shortly after Harmon had played in a two-man golf tournament at Bel-Air Country Club. Harmon died hours later of a heart attack.
He won the golf tournament.

title: Meet the 6 players named top boys golfers around Peoria
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: East Peoria's Connor Watson leads the 2024 Journal Star all-area boys golf team. Meet the 6 best IHSA golfers around Peoria.
content:
Show Caption
Here is the 2024 Journal Star boys golfer of the year, who leads the six-player JS all-area team. The POY is listed first, followed by the five all-area picks in alphabetical order:
Connor Watson, East Peoria
Watson is once again the Peoria-area's top prep golfer, being named the 2024 Journal Star boys golfer of the year for a second successive season. He becomes just the fifth golfer to win the award multiple times, joining a list that includes Tommy Kuhl (2014, 2016, 2017), Trevor Gold (2011, 2013), Jordan Fahel (2009, 2010) and Jonathan Hauter (2006, 2007). Watson was steady all season, wrapping up his high school career tied for fourth at the Class 2A state finals. He shot a final-round 2-under 69 at Normal's Weibring Golf Club course, joining David Perkins (2013 Class 2A fourth place) for the best individual finish in program history. In the sectional, Watson, who was regional runner-up, took home medalist honors with a a 6-under 72 at the U of I Golf Course in Savoy. He had seven birdies — 1, 4, 8, 11, 12, 13 and 17 — in his round.
Brock Brown, Richwoods
Brown came up big in helping the Knights win the Big 12 Conference Tournament. He shot a 1-over 73 at the Kellogg Golf Course, coming in as a runner-up after losing on the fifth playoff hole. This helped Richwoods to a five-stroke victory. He birdied the third, fourth, 15th and 17th holes. During the postseason, the senior advanced to the Class 2A sectional after taking a tied for seventh finish. He missed qualifying for state by three shoots.
Jack Coulter, Peoria Notre Dame
Coulter was a Class 2A regional individual champion, edging East Peoria senior Connor Watson by one stroke, 70 to 71 at Kellogg Golf Course. The sophomore went on to finish as the Class 2A sectional runner-up, shooting a 1-under 71. In the Class 2A state finals, Coulter shot a first-round 1-over 72, then carded a final-round 10-over 81 to finish tied for 21st. He took eighth at the Big 12 Conference Championships with a 78.
Nolan Eccles, Dunlap
Eccles followed up a stellar freshman season with no sophomore slump. He tied for seventh at the Class 2A state finals, shooting a final-round 4-over 75. This came on the heels of Eccles carding a 3-over 75 to take a top-10 finish at the sectional. His postseason began by helping the Eagles win a Class 2A regional championship, taking a third-place individual finish. Eccles was also the second-place finisher in the Mid-Illini Conference Championships.
Crew Fortin, Illini Bluffs
Fortin is the lone Class 1A golfer on the all-area team. The sophomore became the first IB golfer to capture a state medal, finishing tied for 10th with a final-round 1-under 71 at Bloomington's Prairie Vista Golf Club. Fortin's 71 also set the Illini Bluffs program record for 18 holes. His postseason run began by taking fourth with an 80 at regionals in Jacksonville, then placing eighth by shooting a 78 in the sectionals at Quincy Notre Dame.
Gavin Schreurs, Washington
The junior was the Mid-Illini Conference individual champ in a four-hole playoff over Dunlap sophomore Nolan Eccles. His finish helped the Panthers hoist the Mid-Illini team crown. Schreurs was not only won a Class 3A regional title, but also was the individual sectional champ. Both of those victories came with postseason plaques for the Panthers. He wrapped up his season by carding an even 72 to tie for 24th at the Class 3A state finals.

title: Your guide to 2024 Veterans Day activities around Peoria: Parades, ceremonies and more
author: Mike Kramer
description: November 11 is a day to recognize veterans living and dead for their service and patriotism. Here are a few Veterans Day events in the Peoria area.
content:
Unlike Memorial Day, which is a day to remember and honor military personnel who died in the service of their country, Veterans Day is a time to thank all veterans for their service, sacrifice and contributions to national security. The holiday always falls on November 11, the date World War I ended. Veterans Day was originally called Armistice Day.
Here are some Peoria-area events that will occur on or around Veterans Day, which falls on Monday this year.
Veterans Day 2024 is near! What restaurants offer freebies, free meals or deals in Illinois?
Saturday's events
East Peoria: East Peoria VFW Post 2078 is hosting the city's 93rd annual Veterans Parade at 1:30 p.m. on Nov. 9. This year's parade will feature an air show by the Lima Lima Flight Team consisting of four Navy pilots.
Pekin: Pekin Community High School District 303 will place flags at Lakeview Cemetery on Nov. 9. The flags will fly at the cemetery until Nov. 16.
Monday's events
Marquette Heights: Georgetowne Middle at 51 Yates Road, Marquette Heights will host a Veterans Day celebration Nov. 11. The event will begin at 12:30 p.m. and will include a coffee and cake social, a Veterans Day program, and a roll call of veterans.
Chillicothe: St Edward's Catholic School at 1221 N. Fifth Street, Chillicothe will hold a Veterans Day celebration from 8 to 11 a.m. on Nov. 11. The program will include a veteran uniform display, Veterans Day cards and crafts, a flag-folding ceremony, and a fitness event. The City of Chillicothe will host a Veterans Day event at the Chillicothe Veterans Memorial, 1619 N. Santa Fe Avenue.
Peoria: Peoria's annual Veterans Day Parade kicks off at 10 a.m. Nov. 11 at William Kumpf Boulevard and Monroe Street in Downtown Peoria. The parade will continue on Adams Street, then will turn left towards Hamilton Boulevard. and conclude at the World War I and World War II monuments at the Peoria County Courthouse.

title: Racist text messages spamming Black Americans across US, including Illinois
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Illinois is the latest state to have Black Americans reportedly receiving racist text messages. Here's what we know.
content:
Illinois is the latest state to have Black Americans reportedly receiving racist text messages.
The widespread messages are being reported in multiple states and screenshots are going viral on social media sites. The messages vary in detail, but follow the same basic script.
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul confirmed students in the state have received some of these text messages.
'Hate has no place in the state of Illinois," Raoul said in a news release. "Full stop. I am outraged by reports of these offensive, racist texts and am particularly saddened to learn these hate-filled messages have even been received by students, including in Illinois.'
Raoul's office did not provide additional information on the text messages.
A spokesperson for the University of Illinois Springfield said there have been no instances reported at UIS. The Illinois NAACP and the Springfield branch of the NAACP were unable to be reached for comment.
The Southern Poverty Law Center, which tracks hate incidents nationwide, is investigating the messages, according to a report from the Columbus Dispatch. So are authorities in Texas, Ohio, Alabama, South Carolina and other states.
At least some of the messages claimed to have come from, "a Trump supporter."
Raoul encouraged residents who may have received a racist text to contact local law enforcement or the Help Stop Hate Helpline at 877-458-4283. People can also file a complaint with the AG's Civil Rights Bureau.

title: With a Republican trifecta in Washington, a new era of college oversight is on its way
author: Zachary Schermele
description: With the GOP set to take control of Congress and a staunch Trump ally slated to lead the Education Department, colleges may be in for lots of change.
content:
WASHINGTON – There's an irony to how some Republicans are thinking about policing the nation's colleges.
On the one hand, conservatives believe in small government and fewer regulations. An executive order issued by President Donald Trump in 2017 directed every federal agency, including the U.S. Department of Education, to 'alleviate unnecessary regulatory burdens.' Before he secured a second term this month, Trump called for the Education Department to be dismantled.
On the other hand, Republicans have become increasingly critical of "liberal indoctrination" on campus and are pitching big ideas about reforming how colleges work. But some of those proposals would likely require more government intervention, not less.
The president-elect, for instance, wants to create a new tuition-free university funded entirely by taxes on the richest schools. Others in his party have demanded that the feds intervene to curb diversity, equity and inclusion positions and programs while doing more to address antisemitism on campuses. Several far-reaching GOP-sponsored bills in Congress – proposing to reshape the student loan system and end "wokeness" on campus – would dramatically change the rules governing colleges and the students they serve.
With the Republican Party set to control all the levers of power in Washington on Jan. 20, its plans to overhaul higher education are on a collision course with other GOP efforts to limit the federal government's authority. Big changes may be hard to effect given Republicans' slim margins on Capitol Hill and recent Supreme Court rulings limiting government intervention. But all indications in Washington point to a new era of college oversight.
'It's our job to expose what's happening' on college campuses, Rep. Virginia Foxx, the outgoing chair of the committee overseeing education in the U.S. House of Representatives, told USA TODAY in an interview this week. 'That's what oversight does.'
Still, the North Carolina congresswoman agrees with Trump that federal overreach must be curbed.
'It is going to be difficult to get the federal government out of its role in education,' she said.
Leading that effort within the Trump administration will be Linda McMahon, whom the president-elect tapped Tuesday as his nominee for secretary of the Education Department (the same agency he has said he wants to abolish). A staunch Trump ally and the co-founder of World Wrestling Entertainment, she served as the head of the Small Business Administration during his first term.
Though McMahon has relatively little education experience compared to a typical nominee for the job, Trump said she would bring a "deep understanding of both Education and Business" to the role.
"We will send Education BACK TO THE STATES," Trump wrote in a social media post, "and Linda will spearhead that effort."
GOP's competing visions for higher ed
Andy Smarick, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, a conservative think tank, said two different visions could shape how the newly empowered Republican Party will approach higher education policy.
One of those blueprints would involve 'getting the federal government out of education as much as possible,' he said. If Trump chooses that path, he could inhibit the Education Department's ability to make rules and issue guidance. Or he could try to abolish the agency as he has pledged (though experts say such a proposal would likely face an uphill battle in Congress, even with Republican control.)
Another approach, according to Smarick, would be to issue more conservative regulations.
'Traditionally, Republicans have done the former,' he said. 'It appears that Donald Trump doesn't come from that school.'
Civil rights enforcement, student loans could change
During Trump's first term, the Education Department rescinded many Obama-era rules and wrote its own versions of them. One that received lots of attention concerned Title IX, a federal statute that prevents sex-based misconduct at schools that receive federal funding. Under Betsy DeVos, Trump's first education secretary, the Education Department raised the bar on how much evidence was necessary for investigations, prompting critics to say she'd bolstered the rights of people accused of sexual assault and harassment.
The agency reversed course under President Joe Biden, eliminating the Trump-era rules and attempting to expand the definition of sex-based misconduct to include discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. The Biden administration's new policies have since been halted in dozens of states amid legal challenges.
Shiwali Patel, who worked as an attorney in the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights during the Obama administration and resigned during Trump's first term, said she worries about the plans Republicans have for her former workplace.
'They clearly have an agenda to roll back any sort of progress made under the Biden administration on Title IX,' she said, 'and to go even further and weaponize Title IX to engage in further discrimination against students.'
If Trump rescinds the Biden administration's guidance, students who identify as LGBTQ+ and those who experience sexual misconduct may feel less safe on some campuses, according to Brendan Cantwell, a higher education professor at Michigan State University.
'It is going to feel like your campus is providing you fewer protections,' he said.
The federal government's student loan system could also see big changes in Trump's second term. Although Biden approved billions in student loan relief for millions of Americans, his attempts to launch new repayment programs and fix existing ones have been met with more unfavorable court battles.
It's likely that the incoming administration will reverse some of those programs or shrink them, said Karen McCarthy, the vice president of public policy and federal relations at the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators.
'There are lots of ways to kill something,' she said. 'You can just not prioritize it."
Republican overhaul of student loan borrowing could come up for vote
Much remains unclear about what the Republican trifecta could ultimately do to change the nation's colleges. For clues, some Washington experts are turning to a conservative bill that Foxx, the Republican congresswoman from North Carolina, introduced this past January.
The 224-page College Cost Reduction Act would impose sweeping – and controversial – reforms to the higher education system. The proposals in the bill include stricter caps on student loan borrowing and a program that would effectively force colleges to cosign loans. While some have argued the bill would prevent certain groups from attending college and leave more Americans saddled with debt, Foxx and her GOP colleagues say it would make the system fairer and unburden taxpayers.
Foxx said she's consulting with congressional leadership about bringing the bill to the House floor before the end of the year.

title: How Central Illinois became a hotbed for esports on high school, college levels
author: Bill Welt
description: With a new computer arena for the Springfield high schools' championship-level esports program, as well as more players at Glenwood and Illinois College, the video game competition is growing by leaps and bounds locally.
content:
Chatham Glenwood junior Nikash Madanagopal appreciates all that esports has to offer in high school.
The excitement, adrenaline and camaraderie rival any other sport.
'It does feel pretty intense when you're in the game when the rounds are really close," Madanagopal said. 'At the end of the day, everyone wants to win, so it gets pretty intense, especially when you're playing with all your friends.
'When someone has a huge play, everyone will get excited, so it's just really fun. You can really feel the intensity, especially when it's in the playoffs. You need to win this to go on.'
Esports has been teaching life skills beyond the classroom as well.
It's dispelling old notions long associated with video games that Glenwood coach Rashid Bibb and Springfield Capitols interim coach Adam Martin perhaps grew up with.
Bibb said he has seen kids break out of their proverbial shells in his four years at the helm.
All-state football stars: Here are the 10 all-state football players from around Springfield
'I had to adjust my mindset to what this was,' Bibb said, ''Oh, competitive video games. How competitive could it be?' You get in there and see these kids are as determined to win this game as a football or a basketball player.'
Skeptics may think esports is just kids playing video games, Bibb said, 'but there's also a lot of strategy that goes into it.'
Teamwork is imperative. It's something that becomes especially visible in an esports arena.
The Capitols, a co-op between Springfield High, Southeast and Lanphier that began in 2019, recently settled into its decked-out arena at Lanphier last winter. Part of the school's $93.5 million renovation, it resembles a computer lab, but the space is exclusive to the Capitols.
Springfield High senior Christian Schneider said it promotes a stronger team environment.
'The difference between preparedness and coaching staff from the other schools and having everyone in the single room, you can tell,' Schneider said. 'There are a couple times their captains won't even be there on time, it's just a real blessing that we have this and we're able to go somewhere to actually compete.'
What is the high school esports experience?
Schneider, who also participates in the SHS marching and pep bands, has been with the Capitols since he started high school.
He has competed in a variety of games through the Illinois High School Esports Association and the Illinois High School Association. The former looms the largest.
The IHSEA serves up a fall and spring season. Each spans eight weeks with a different array of games that culminate in the state finals at Northern Illinois University in DeKalb or remotely. The IHSA subsequently hosts sectionals and state finals toward the end of the school year in April and May.
Each participating team typically ranges between 4-6 players, depending on the game's parameters.
A player may dabble in multiple games simultaneously, perhaps occasionally competing and practicing on the same day. Schneider, who acted as the captain of the Fortnite team this fall, intends to play both Pokémon Unite and League of Legends in the spring.
The practice schedules are typically flexible, but they certainly still require time commitment.
The Capitols alternate games each day — each practicing twice a week — and have the advantage of being able to huddle together and strategize over a whiteboard and large-screen TV in their new accommodations.
Due to the medley of esports titles across different platforms, Martin's staff includes four other coaches.
Martin emphasized these players are held to the same academic standards as any other student-athlete.
'It's not necessarily that we're coaching the games,' said Martin, who has a proclivity for Call of Duty. 'We're coaching the students as well to kind of come into their own and fill those spots in the game.'
Cross country state champs: Gillespie's Chaz Oberkfell, Williamsville girls capture Class 1A cross country state glory
Players assume leadership roles
Captains also point the way.
That includes Glenwood students Madanagopal in Valorant and Brady Daniels in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate.
Madanagopal, who also plays tennis, first started esports as a freshman.
'As a captain, I'm kind of the in-game leader,' Madanagopal said, 'so when we're playing, I kind of direct the strategy that we're taking. When we're having matches against other teams, I talk to them to set up the time. It's a good aspect to be able communicate with other people, it kind of helps.'
Daniels, a senior, said it was a little intimidating when he first came aboard as a sophomore.
He now instructs teammates on the nuances of the aforementioned Nintendo Switch game, which Daniels described as more fast-paced and intense than chess.
'You can study it down to one specific interaction between your opponent and what move beats out this other move, or how you can avoid one move to counterattack back,' Daniels said.
Glenwood sophomore Szymom Dynda, who also assists the football team, not only wants to reach the Overwatch 2 varsity lineup this spring, he also harbors state title ambitions. Last year's Overwatch team took third place in the IHSEA finals.
'Through esports, I've gained friends who are a lot better than me and they've given me some tips,' Dynda said. 'I've also learned to have a wide variety of characters to play.'
A few of these students said they may pursue esports in college.
Illinois College figures most prominently in the region. It launched its program and Meraki Gaming Center in 2016. It's directly funded by the athletics department and offers scholarships.
It's a prospect that so many high school students overlook, according to IC coach David Seering.
Seering was a former player himself at IC before taking the reins in 2023. Esports may still be relatively new ground, but Seering has seen improvements on the recruiting front with more resources available such as the web site Stay Plugged In.
It's just a matter of growing the world of esports from the bottom up.
'I think the momentum is building the same as it's been since 2016,' Seering said. 'IC has been consistent with it the entire time. We have done what we've needed to do to make sure we're a competitive team.
'It's more so just seeing other high schools invest in esports. That's what I'm looking forward to because the more people who get into it and realize there are scholarships available, competitions are going to be more fierce and I think that's just going to make everything more fun in the long run.'
Players can also take the intramural route at University of Illinois Springfield, which has a sleek, new arena at Founders Residence Hall. The UIS teams compete in the National Esports Collegiate Conference, separate from IC's Midwest Valley Esports Conference and Midwest Esports Conference.
It may be more relaxed, but that's only true to an extent.
'Definitely this semester I've noticed some players have shown frustration from losing, so I'd say it's very competitive for some of these students,' UIS coach John Nguyen said. "When you're competing in something, everybody wants to win. Everybody's competitive in their own mindset.'
Nguyen was a former player at UIS before becoming a coach at the start of the fall semester, primarily Valorant and Overwatch 2.
The workload took the 2024 alum by surprise balancing multiple teams, practices and matches all in a week's effort. And not unlike Seering, Nguyen sees plenty of room for growth. These games, after all, are global in scope.
'It's definitely different than as a player for sure,' Nguyen said. 'I didn't do any research as a player, so whenever it was match play, I just played to the best of my ability. As a coach, you look at the other team — what they play and how they play it — and then try to prep your players as best as possible.'

title: Deputy in fatal Sonya Massey shooting to be released with conditions
author: Steven Spearie
description: The ruling by the appellate court comes out just before Grayson's scheduled court appearance on Monday.
content:
The Fourth District Appellate Court late Wednesday afternoon reversed the detention order of former Sangamon County Sheriff deputy Sean P. Grayson, charged in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey, meaning Grayson will be released with conditions soon.
The ruling asks for the circuit court "to promptly set the case for a hearing to determine the least restrictive conditions of defendant's pretrial release."
Grayson already has a hearing set for 9 a.m. Monday. Circuit Court Presiding Judge Ryan Cadagin, who had twice ordered Grayson to be detained under the Pre-Trial Fairness Act, will set a date with attorneys to consider conditions of his pre-trial release.
Those conditions may include home confinement or some sort of monitoring system.
The appellate court didn't weigh in about what those conditions might be.
Grayson's attorney, Daniel Fultz, had argued in the past that Grayson wasn't a flight risk and that he was dealing with complications from a diagnosis of Stage 3 colon cancer.
Cadagin had cited the former deputy's callousness during and after the shooting of Massey, including not rendering help to her.
Grayson is being held in the Macon County Jail in Decatur.
Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman, was shot in her home after she had called 911 about a possible prowler around her home in an unincorporated area of Woodside Township.
The shooting, captured on the bodycam of Grayson's police partner, sent shock waves throughout the nation.
Earlier in November, the U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation against the sheriff's office, noting "serious concerns about (the sheriff department's) interactions with Black people and people with behavioral health disabilities," along with a host of practices and procedures.
Fultz said a number of other issues need to get ironed out before Grayson's release, including whether the State decides to file a petition for leave to appeal to the Illinois State Supreme Court.

What bowl game will Illinois make? Projecting Fighting Illini matchup possibilities

title: 'Zest for life': Longtime college football coach and Illinois assistant dies at age 62
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Dana Dimel was in his first season as an assistant at Illinois. He spent 20 years under Bill Snyder at Kansas State.
content:
Longtime football coach Dana Dimel, an assistant on the Illinois staff, has died, according to the school. He was 62.
The Columbus, Ohio, native was a 35-year coach most recently in his first season as a senior offensive assistant for the Illini, who just completed a 9-3 season and are headed to a bowl game.
Illinois was the sixth coaching stop for Dimel, who was head coach at Wyoming (1997-99), Houston (2002-02) and UTEP (2018-23). The former Kansas State all-American offensive lineman began his coaching career at K-State in 1997 as a graduate assistant and spent 20 years in various roles under coach Bill Snyder, who called Dimel a "special friend and coaching companion" who had a passion for helping players and fellow coaches.
"Dana was an exceptional person, husband, father, friend, and football coach," Illinois coach Bret Bielema said in a release. "He affected the lives of countless coaches, players, and staff members for more than three decades in college football."
What bowl game will Illinois make? Projecting Fighting Illini matchup possibilities
Bielema said Dimel's influence on the Illini was incredible, and his "infectious positive energy had a major impact on everyone in the program." In his 32 seasons as head coach or assistant, Dimel mentored 37 players who went on to the NFL.
"He will be dearly missed," Bielema said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with his wife and family."
Sports agent Pete Roussel posted a tribute to Dimel on X.com on Tuesday, calling him "one of the most positive people I knew, and he was unafraid of any challenge. He had an incredible zest for life, one that would make those around him smile time and time again.
"I will miss Dana more than words can express."
Illinois, Houston and Kansas State were among programs to post tributes to Dimel on Tuesday morning, along with a host of former co-workers and players. Dimel is survived by his wife, Julie, and children, Winston and Josey.

title: Illinois high school basketball state rankings: Peoria-area schools in first poll

content:
Manual and Washington each garnered No. 1 rankings by The Associated Press in the first statewide poll released on Wednesday afternoon.
The Rams are the top-rated boys team in Class 2A, while Washington claims the No. 1 spot among Class 3A girls programs. Reigning state champion Peoria Notre Dame is the next highest ranked Peoria-area team coming in at No. 2 on the girls side in Class 2A.
Peoria High is the fourth-ranked Class 3A boys team, while Morton is No. 8 and Metamora checks in at No. 10 in Class 3A. Among the boys teams receiving votes include Richwoods (Class 3A) and Peoria Christian (Class 1A).
In the girls polls, Morton is No. 7 in Class 3A, while Galesburg is No. 10. Abingdon-Avon is the lone small-school ranked, checking in at No. 6 in Class 1A.
Roanoke-Benson and Illini Bluffs both received votes in the Class 1A girls poll.
