title: An 'A' list player: Rivermen sign veteran defenseman, designate him an assistant captain
author: Dave Eminian
description: The Peoria Rivermen signed veteran former SPHL Defenseman of the Year Zach Wilkie and named him assistant captain for their championship defense.
content:
PEORIA — Zach Wilkie is on the "A" list with the Peoria Rivermen again.
The defending SPHL champions brought back the veteran and former SPHL Defenseman of the Year on Wednesday and named him assistant captain, as their priority to build their leadership group for the 2024-25 season continued.
"We are so excited to have the best defenseman in the league back with us," Rivermen coach Jean-Guy Trudel said. "He brings the energy and effort needed every day that allows us to be successful. He is absolutely phenomenal on and off the ice for the Peoria Rivermen and he is becoming the face of the culture we built here.
"I can't say enough about the kid. We are lucky to have him."
Wilkie is a colorful character who plays with a high level of emotion. He shows joy in playing the game, even in his traditional exit from the ice after pre-game warmups, when he charges through the bench and down the tunnel full-speed to the locker room.
Wilkie told his teammates during the 2021-22 SPHL President's Cup Finals at Roanoke, as they sat in the locker room after the third period, waiting for overtime: "Boys, when we come back in here, we're going to be champions."
And they were. Peoria won it in overtime to bring home the franchise's first championship in 22 years.
A history of success
Wilkie is physical, skilled and has been among the league's elite defenders since he came in as a rookie in 2021-22.
The 6-foot, 200-pound 27-year-old from Villa Park was named to the SPHL All-Rookie Team in that Rivermen championship season.
In the title defense of 2022-23, Wilkie led all SPHL defenseman in scoring (43 points), all players in plus-minus (+42), was an SPHL All-Star first-team selection and chosen SPHL Defenseman of the Year.
He scored 13 goals and added 30 assists in 53 games that season, but suffered a significant knee injury in the final days and missed all but one game of a playoff run in which the Rivermen fell short in the finals.
He returned last season to score 10 goals and add 31 assists in 49 games with a plus-32 rating, plus two goals and four assists in seven playoff games.
Wilkie played his junior hockey for Niagara and Sudbury in the Ontario Hockey League, then spent four seasons in the Canadian University system playing for Laurentian University before turning pro with Peoria.
He has 26 goals, 85 assists and a plus-101 rating in 152 regular-season games with the Rivermen over parts of three seasons. In addition, he has three goals and eight assists in 18 playoff games with Peoria.
Wilkie is the second returning veteran from Peoria's championship team last spring, following center Alec Baer, who was signed and named the Rivermen's new captain on July 17.
Dave Eminian is the Journal Star sports columnist, and covers Bradley men's basketball, the Rivermen and Chiefs. He writes the Cleve In The Eve sports column for pjstar.com. He can be reached at 686-3206 or deminian@pjstar.com. Follow him on X.com @icetimecleve.

title: This national clothing brand has reopened its store in Peoria mall
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: The national retailer, which had filed for bankruptcy, revived its first Illinois location in Peoria.
content:
On Aug. 2, rue21 returned to Peoria under new ownership.
The opening comes just over two months after the Northwoods Mall store shuttered as the national clothing brand filed for bankruptcy for the third time since 2003.
Tim Keller, operations and leasing director at Northwoods Mall, said mall staff learned YM Inc. bought the rue21 brand in June. Other YM Inc. brands include Charlotte Russe, Urban Planet and more.
A message on rue21's website notes: 'We're thrilled about our recent acquisition and are diligently working to revitalize the rue 21 brand.'
Mall news:What is going on at the old Sears Automotive Center near the Peoria mall?
Keller said a district manager from YM Inc. requested to see the former Northwoods Mall space. He said she liked the space, and it was soon working to reopen.
Currently, Northwoods Mall is the only Illinois location listed on rue21's website.
According to an Instagram post from the business, grand opening weekend will include a buy two, get one free sale.
Keller visited the storefront on opening day and said, 'it looks great in there.' He said the store is working to bring in fresh items at affordable prices.
'People hear that name and they're familiar with it,' Keller said. 'So, it helps bring them in (and) it helps the locals because then they see what local businesses we have. So having another national store here – having (rue21) back here – is huge for us. We're very excited.'

title: East Peoria man dies after suffering severe injuries in I-74 motorcycle crash
author: Zach Roth
description: The 20-year-old's friends have set up a GoFundMe page that has already raised over $8,000 for the family.
content:
An East Peoria man died Sunday after sustaining severe injuries in a motorcycle crash along Interstate 74 near the Knoxville Avenue exit.
Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood said that Carson E. Guymon, 20, died at 1:59 a.m., six days after he was found injured off of his motorcycle along eastbound I-74 at the North Knoxville Avenue off-ramp.
Illinois State Police said that they were called to the scene at 3 p.m. July 29 in response to a single-vehicle motorcycle crash. Harwood said that Guymon was found 20 feet from his motorcycle and was transported to OSF HealthCare Saint Francis Medical Center in critical condition, unresponsive and with labored breathing.
Guymon received intense treatment for six days, including "aggressive resuscitative efforts," but he eventually succumbed to his injuries.
Harwood said that Guymon sustained multiple blunt-force injuries, with a toxicology report still pending. He noted that it wasn't clear if he was wearing a helmet at the time of the crash.
Friends of Guymon have set up a GoFundMe page to help his family with funeral expenses. As of Monday afternoon, over $8,000 have been raised, with a goal of $12,000 now in effect.
The GoFundMe said that Guymon was a "loving, helpful and kind-hearted person" who loved his family and friends. He also was said to have a passion for sport bikes, with his social media names all being some variation of "speediskey."

title: Riverfront concert, Ignite Peoria and more: Here are 6 things to do in Peoria this weekend
author: Josh Jenke
description: August is full of activities. Here are six events you might want to check out in the Peoria area this weekend.
content:
August is full of activities. Here are six events you might want to check out in the Peoria area this weekend.
Brimfield Old Settlers Days
The 134th annual Brimfield Old Settlers Days festival will be held from Aug. 8-10 in downtown Brimfield. The event will include food and beer tents, carnival rides and more. There will be live entertainment from Taylor Bruninga and the Bandits at 7 p.m. Friday and The Joe Stamm Band at 8 p.m. Saturday. Activities for Saturday will include breakfast at the American Legion from 7 to 10 a.m., a 5K walk/run at 8 a.m. and parade at 1 p.m.
Ignite Peoria 2024
Ignite Peoria, presented by ArtsPartners, will be held from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday, Aug. 10, at the Peoria Civic Center. This one-of-a-kind festival boasts over 65 hands-on creation station booths where attendees can learn about singing, writing, dancing, building, acting, painting, drawing, coding, 3D printing, robotics and more. Admission is free.
Wizard of Oz festival
Hollis Park will present the 14th annual Illinois Wizard of Oz Festival from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday, Aug. 10, at Butler Haynes Park in Mapleton. Festivities include meet and greets with all your favorite Oz characters, trolley rides and story time with Auntie Em, live entertainment, contests, children's activities, a vendor market and more. Admission is $6 for adults, $4 for children age 3-12 and free for children ages 2 and under.
Concert on the riverfront
Grammy Award-winning artist Blues Traveler and platinum-selling rockers Big Head Todd and the Monsters will bring their Blue Monsters Tour 2024 to CEFCU Center Stage at Riverfront Festival Park at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, Aug. 10. To purchase tickets, visit https://bluestraveler.com/tour/.
Flea market at Peoria Speedway
The Central Illinois Flea Market will be open from 9 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. Sunday, July 14, at Peoria Speedway, 3520 W. Farmington Road. Items for sale include antiques, collectibles, boutique clothing, books, yard decor, home decor, art, plants and more. Several food trucks will also be onsite with a variety of food for purchase. Admission is $2 and half of the admission proceeds will benefit Sophia's Angels Kitchen.
Italian Society Festa
The Italian American Society's 93rd Festa Picnic will be held from noon to 5 p.m. Sunday, Aug. 11, at Hickory Grove Park, 12403 N. Hickory Grove Road, Dunlap. The picnic will include authentic Italian food and desserts, Italian and domestic beer and wines, Italian t-shirts and gift items, live music by Vince Amore and Jack Miuccio, children's activities, local artisans, a bocce tournament and more. For more information, visit www.italianamericansociety.com.

title: Pritzker signs 3 bills to enhance abortion protections in Illinois. What you need to know
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: The bills Gov. JB Pritzker signed into law come a little more than a week after Iowa saw abortion restrictions go into effect.
content:
A little more than one week after a neighboring state saw abortion restrictions go into effect, Gov. JB Pritzker signed a slate of bills expanding reproductive rights in Illinois.
The new fetal heartbeat law in Iowa, signed into law by Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds in July, bans most abortions in the state six weeks into a pregnancy. It went into effect on July 29 and drew swift condemnation from pro-abortion groups throughout Illinois.
Responding to Midwestern states enacting restrictions and the platform of the Republican presidential ticket, which he claims will take those restrictions nationwide, Pritzker said the three bills he signed into law on Aug. 7 would help protect the state's status as an abortion haven for years to come.
"They're under attack," Pritzker said of reproductive rights during a press conference in Chicago. "We see it every day from the other side of the aisle from the presidential and vice presidential candidates for the Republicans and from Project 2025 that outright says that they want to ban abortion in the United States.
"I think that frightens many people across the country."
Here's what you need to know about the bills the governor signed.
House Bill 581
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear a case against Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act, or EMTALA in June, which permits doctors to provide abortion services during medical emergencies.
Democratic lawmakers pushed the legislation that would codify the federal law in case the nation's high court overturned EMTALA. With Pritzker's signature, the state is now prepared if the challenge was heard by the Supreme Court at a later date.
The bill led by Rep. Dagmara Avelar, D-Bolingbrook, also grants the Illinois Department of Public Health the right to investigate hospitals for violations and could issue penalties starting at $50,000.
House Bill 5239
Another bill adds additional protections in the state's interstate shield law.
Already having protections for patients and providers that travel to Illinois for reproductive health services, the new law prohibits state and local jurisdictions from disclosing information, or providing resources, to assist any out-of-state agency conducting an investigation into someone receiving legal abortion services in the state.
House Bill 4867
Pritzker also signed a bill expands the list of protected parties in the Illinois Human Rights Act. The new law prohibits discrimination against people for their reproductive health decisions, including abortion, in vitro fertilization and fertility treatment.
It comes after the governor recently signed a bill to ensure insurance companies provide coverage for infertility treatments that are recommended by a physician.

title: Sneak peek: New East Peoria restaurant will serve up authentic Mexican fare and drinks
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: The restaurant features hand-carved, wooden designs on the chairs and bar front. The menu will include Mexican seafood, soups and more.
content:
Two tables are situated against the walls at Tacos El Gallo in East Peoria. A handful of chairs are found at each. It's a cozy restaurant that serves dishes such as tacos, tortas and burritos.
Just a few months after opening in 2022, José Reteguin Jr. saw the need to expand.
He said some guests wanted to sit and enjoy their meal – which sometimes wasn't possible with the restaurant's limited dining area. So, his father and co-owner José Reteguin Sr. said customers asked them to open a space with more seating.
'We give to our customers, you know, whatever they want,' Reteguin Sr. said.
El Gallo Bar & Grill expects to hold its soft open Thursday, Aug. 15, the younger Reteguin said.
The new establishment is situated just a few units away from Tacos El Gallo. Despite being nearby, the father-son team said the new storefront will operate alongside the original restaurant, rather than replace it.
'100% Mexican food'
Reteguin Jr. said El Gallo Bar & Grill will feature a different menu from what customers can find at Tacos El Gallo. He said the menu will center around authentic Mexican cuisine.
'We're gonna have a different flavor than other (places),' Reteguin Jr. said, with his father adding, 'It's gonna be 100% Mexican food – not a 50/50.'
Reteguin Sr. said the menu will be around three times larger than the one at Tacos El Gallo. The father and son said customers will find dishes such as:
Barbacoa
Caldo de Camarón – which is Mexican shrimp soup
Caldo de Res – which is a Mexican beef soup
Mexican seafood – which Reteguin Jr. said includes octopus
Steaks
El Gallo Bar & Grill will also feature a variety of alcoholic beverages, which Reteguin Sr. looks forward to serving. Reteguin Jr. expects to offer a variety of margaritas, as well as beers and other standard drink options. He said the menu will also feature Micheladas and a seafood cocktail.
Fire, flood and 'over 100 leaks'
Formerly home to IHOP, Reteguin Jr. said the unit – at 214 W. Camp St., East Peoria – needed a near total overhaul.
'We basically had to gut the whole thing out since IHOP had a fire before, and then they had a big like leak so it flooded in here,' Reteguin Jr. said. 'So, we had to renovate pretty much everything.'
Work included moving walls, removing the drop ceiling, updating the unit with paint and wallpaper and bringing in a custom bar and seating, according to the father and son. Electrical and plumbing work needed to be done, as well, to bring the space up to code.
The primary challenge, Reteguin Jr. said, was addressing the plumbing issues. He said, 'we had over 100 leaks everywhere – all over the building.'
After months of work, however, the space was transformed.
'A dream come true'
Inside, Reteguin Jr. said they wanted to create a dark, modern atmosphere for guests.
Burnt wood tabletops feature the restaurant's name prominently in the center, and barrel-themed lights add to the unique, elevated ambiance.
Customers will find elaborately carved seating – including high-chairs – with leather cushions. Custom carvings are also found on the long, wooden bar front, and in the center, the establishment's name is accented with green and red paint.
'We got a lot of our stuff done in Mexico …' Reteguin Jr. said. 'It's all hand carved.'
Some of the carvings feature roosters, which plays into the business's name. Gallo is Spanish for rooster.
A variety of designs can be found, however, as Reteguin Jr. said they wanted to bring 'more Mexican culture' to the space. Reteguin Sr. said some of the restaurant's drinks will be served in cantaritos, which are clay cups.
The father-and-son team said multiple TVs will allow customers to watch various sporing events. In the future, both said they also hope to add an outdoor dining area.
Reteguin Jr. said neighbors and others who have seen the progress have been astounded by the results. He described the completed space as 'a dream come true.'
'It was a vision before and now it's here, you know,' Reteguin Jr. said. His father said, 'Yeah, it was real bad, and now it looks beautiful.'

title: Man found dead in wrecked vehicle in Peoria County, police say
author: JJ Bullock
description: The vehicle with the 31-year-old inside was found flipped over about 40 yards from the roadway.
content:
A 31-year-old man was found dead in a crashed vehicle Tuesday morning in Peoria County.
Officers from the Peoria County Sheriff's Department responded to a report of a damaged culvert in the 10300 block of Smithville Road around 11:26 a.m. Tuesday morning.
Before police arrived on the scene a nearby property owner discovered a car flipped onto its top in a wooded area about 40 yards from the road.
Officers from the Peoria County Sheriff's Department had to cut through brush to reach the wrecked vehicle and located a dead 31-year-old Mapleton man inside.
Authorities are not sure when the crash occurred, but residents nearby told investigators they heard trees falling at around 9 p.m. Monday night.
Speed does appear to be a factor in the crash, according to the Peoria County Sheriff's Department.
The wreck remains under investigation.
Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood will release the identity of the driver at a later time.

title: Pekin man receives prison sentence for attempted enticement of minor
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The man had previously been convicted of aggravated criminal sexual abuse in 2001.
content:
A Pekin man was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison Wednesday for attempting to entice a minor to have sex with him on several occasions over a nine-month period.
Kenneth W. Holobaugh, 43, pled guilty to one count of attempted enticement of a minor in April for contacting someone who he believed to be a 13-year-old girl and telling her that he wanted to meet and have sex multiple times over a nine-month period from April 2023 to January 2024.
Central District of Illinois Senior Judge Joe Billy McDade handed down the sentence Wednesday, which included a 15-year term of supervised release.
According to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of Illinois, prosecutors provided evidence at Wednesday's sentencing hearing that Holobaugh used social media to try and communicate with this person, expressing multiple times his desire for sexual activities. In January, Holobaugh made arrangements to meet with her in Peoria for sex, only to be greeted by FBI agents who arrested him upon arrival.
A federal grand jury indicted Holobaugh in February on the single count, with the guilty plea coming on April 1. He had previously been convicted of aggravated criminal sexual abuse in 2001, receiving a sentence of 30 months in prison and requiring him to register as a sex offender for the remainder of his life.
He had been facing life in prison on the charges, along with five years-to-life of mandatory supervised release.

title: Attorney: SAFE-T Act 'failed to stop' former sheriff's deputy accused of Massey's murder
author: Steven Spearie
description: Sonya Massey's uncle calls the retirement of Sheriff Campbell a "great first step" in rectifying the "multiple systems" that failed Sonya.
content:
Attorneys for the family of Sonya Massey want a national database for police officers to prevent "ticking time bombs" like former Sangamon County Sheriff's deputy Sean Grayson, charged in the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey.
Grayson's hiring by the sheriff's department, particularly because of some of his record with the Logan County Sheriff's Office prior to coming to Springfield, and his two DUIs before he became an officer have continued to raise questions.
Massey family members applauded the retirement of Sheriff Jack Campbell, who is leaving office by Aug. 31.
While calling Illinois' SAFE-T Act "one of the most comprehensive police reform bills" passed, Antonio Romanucci, an attorney who has worked with the Massey family's attorney, Ben Crump, said the act "needs a little bit of help."
Romanucci said a more comprehensive national database would include infractions such as DUIs, driving excessive speeds during a police chase and incidents of excessive force or unnecessary profane language on a citizen.
It also would create a waiting period, "some quiet time," Romanucci said, in between officers going from job to job, in order for "a thorough and comprehensive background check (to be) completed."
Romanucci said the act failed to stop Grayson "until he literally exploded and caused a needless life to be lost in Sonya Massey."
"There has to be mandatory reporting," Romanucci added. "Illinois has been a great leader. We just need to caulk the SAFE-T Act."
Grayson, 30, worked for six different agencies, including several on a part-time basis, in four years.
Raymond Massey said his niece, Sonya Massey, was "failed by multiple systems and multiple people. By the sheriff stepping down, I think it's a great first step."
"We have to catch the warning signs," Crump said, "before they become homicides. That's why we have to have accountability at the department level.
"The blood is the hands of the system as well as Sean Grayson."

title: Man faces a traffic charge after crash in Peoria that killed Dunlap HS student
author: JJ Bullock
description: The Peoria Police Department investigation into a deadly crash yielded a traffic citation against the man driving the wrong way.
content:
PEORIA – A Stark County man has been cited for driving the wrong way on a divided highway in connection with the head-on collision in May that killed a Dunlap High School student.
Levi Dietz, 25, was scheduled to appear in court Tuesday for what is categorized as a petty offense, but Judge Katherine Legge moved his first appearance. A review of the case is scheduled for Oct. 1.
On the night of May 4, Dietz's vehicle collided head-on with the car of 18-year-old Nevaeh Mitchell on Orange Prairie Road in Peoria. She was pronounced dead in the early hours of the next day.
Results of toxicology tests
The toxicology report for Dietz came back clean, according to the Peoria Police Department. That means drugs or alcohol were not detected in his system.
Mitchell also had a clean toxicology report, according to Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood.
Peoria Police spokesperson Semone Roth said there is nothing left on the police end of the investigation now that Dietz's toxicology report has been returned. There are no charges against Dietz aside from the traffic charge, Roth said. Dietz was hospitalized after the crash but was released on May 14.
Mitchell, of Princeville, was two weeks away from graduating from high school when she died. She was set to attend Loyola University Chicago and had earned a scholarship, according to her obituary.
'Frustration is mounting'
Shaun Cusack, an attorney representing Mitchell's family, said he expected the toxicology report for Dietz to come back negative and will be investigating other potential causes of the wreck.
"Preliminary toxicology reports are pretty accurate, so what we heard preliminarily is that it was negative, so we expected this," Cusack said. "Now it's looking into other causes of the accident. If alcohol wasn't a factor, then we need to find out what was."
Cusack said the release of investigative materials in this case has been far slower than usual for a death investigation. He said materials are usually available between two weeks and two months after a death. Mitchell was killed over three months ago.
"This has been way longer than any death case — and we've handled a ton of death cases — and we've never had to wait this long, so it's kind of a 'what gives' situation," Cusack said.
Cusack said Mitchell's family is being patient but "frustration is mounting" with the delays in information coming out.
"They're frustrated but they've got good heads on their shoulders and good support around them," Cusack said. "They're willing to be patient and they'll wait this out. Their daughter is gone, so they're in it for the long haul, but the long haul shouldn't be this long in this case."

title: Supermarket store brands are more popular than ever. Do they taste better?
author: Daniel de Visé
description: Store brands have evolved from inferior generic alternatives into private-label offerings that can compete with name brands on both quality and price.
content:
When the Washington Post ran a blind taste test last year to find the best bottled marinara sauce, the winner was Rao's Homemade, the gourmet brand, at $10.59 a bottle.
The big surprise, though, was the runner-up: Trader Joe's Tomato Basil, at $1.99.
Store brands have evolved from inferior generic alternatives into private-label offerings that can compete with name brands on both quality and price. And in today's supermarkets, store brands are surging.
Private label products made up 20.7% of all grocery sales in 2023, in terms of units sold, a record high. Store brands reaped $236 billion in sales last year, another record, according to the Private Label Manufacturers Association. Through mid-July, the trade group reports, 2024 sales are on track to exceed $250 billion.
Younger shoppers, raised on private labels, have never known a time when store brands bespoke culinary misery.
'I think the store brands are filling a fundamental need for the consumer right now,' said Elizabeth Hasle, 31, of Seattle, who is partial to Costco's Kirkland Signature brand.
'Their olive oil, you can get three liters for twenty bucks, and it's actually good quality,' she said. 'That alone makes me happy.'
'The flavor's better. The carbonation's better.'
Taylor Harms, 28, of Fresno, California, discovered store brands in college and never looked back. His favorite item at the moment: Walmart's store-brand seltzer water.
'They're priced, like, 89 cents for a liter,' he said. 'And for something comparable from a big name, like Schweppes or Perrier, it's so much better. The flavor's better. The carbonation's better.'
Decades ago, analysts say, store brands occupied the proverbial bottom shelf of the grocery industry. Yes, they were cheaper. They were also distinctly second-rate: Anemic, flavorless alternatives to superior (and pricier) name brands.
Today, many store brands compete not only with name brands but also with upmarket gourmet selections, such as Rao's.
'I just think store brands have become hip for people,' said Phil Lempert, a grocery industry analyst. 'It's always great to find something that you love, that you can save money on, that's high quality. That's a magic formula for store brands.'
In another recent taste test, held by the New York Times's Wirecutter, store-label frozen pizzas held their own against the nation's best name brands. Top pepperoni picks included a $6 wood-fired pizza from Trader Joe's, and a $7 Good & Gather pie from Target.
The evolution of store brands: 'It's a huge change.'
'Our research has told us that 85% of consumers view private brand quality as equal to or greater than the national brands. It's a huge change,' said Jim Griffin, president of Daymon North America. Daymon helps supermarkets develop private brands.
Back in the inflationary 1970s, store brands offered relief from spiraling prices, but often at a grievous cost to your palate.
'Those were the yellow and black labels,' Lempert said, often rendered in Soviet-style type on labels bereft of art. 'This was the worst-quality food that you could get, but it was really cheap.'
The turnaround began with pioneering chains such as Loblaw in Canada and A&P in the United States, Lempert said, offering store brands that rivaled name brands in taste and beat them on price.
When Loblaw rolled out chocolate chip cookies under its President's Choice label, the company insisted on using real butter, and twice as many chocolate chips as the leading brand. Loblaw's Decadent brand became the best-selling cookie in Canada.
Trader Joe's and Whole Foods Market grew into national chains in the 1990s, featuring store brands that promised gourmet flavors at a discount.
Nearly every grocery store chain seems to offer a private label
Nowadays, seemingly every respectable grocery-store chain offers a private label. Here are a few of the best, in addition to several brands mentioned above, according to Real Simple magazine:
ALDI Simply Nature: 'Not only inexpensive, but also organic, non-GMO, and free of artificial preservatives.'
Kroger Private Selection: 'Its goal is to give shoppers the best culinary experience at reasonable prices.'
Albertsons Signature Select: 'Some customer favorites include the mac n' cheese, bacon, wine, pasta sauce (shout out to the black truffle pasta sauce, which routinely sells out), and ice cream.'
Increasingly, Griffin said, grocery-store chains offer store brands on multiple tiers. Walmart, for example, offers a Great Value line that competes with national brands. Starting this year, Walmart also offers bettergoods, a gourmet label that caters to connoisseurs.
With the new brand, 'they're attracting a more affluent shopper than they would have four of five years ago,' Griffin said.
That is not to say that every store brand is a commercial and critical hit. Washington Post taste-testers bemoaned that Walmart's Great Value Marinara sauce ($1.59), while indisputably a bargain, 'didn't cling to noodles properly.' Wirecutter reviewers found Costco's Kirkland Signature Pepperoni Pizza 'overly sweet' and imbued with a 'slightly acrid taste.'
Inflation provides a new incentive to seek out store brands
Nonetheless, elevated inflation in the past two years has given consumers a new incentive to seek out store brands, analysts say, in much the same way diners hunt for value meals at fast-food chains.
'Today's consumers are savvy, and most have grown up with store brands,' said Peggy Davies, president of the store brand association, in an email.
'A consumer who tries a store brand product and has a positive experience tends to stick with that brand,' she said. 'It's that stickiness by the consumer, and the increased competition among retailers' own brands to capture store loyalty, that's fueling the continued growth."
Some supermarkets offer almost nothing but the store brand. At ALDI, for example, 90% of items are private label. That emphasis puts extra pressure on the chain to keep quality high.
'For us, it really is the only option in the store,' said Scott Patton, vice president of national buying at ALDI. 'It has to be good.'
For a grocery chain, a popular store brand can build customer loyalty in a way that a national brand cannot, Lempert said.
Trader Joe's, for example, offers store-brand Chili & Lime-Flavored Rolled Corn Tortilla Chips that perennially rank among the store's most popular items. And only Trader Joe's carries them.
'Retailers look at those name brands, and what they want to do is have a better-quality product at a better value,' Lempert said, 'because you can't get it anyplace else.'

title: 89 faculty, staff lose jobs: What led to Western Illinois University's most recent cuts
author: Tilly Robinson
description: Another round of layoffs is WIU's latest effort to stabilize its budget, which has been hit hard by heavy enrollment declines.
content:
In a bid to cut costs amid an ongoing financial crisis, Western Illinois University has announced that it will be laying off 89 employees — 57 faculty members and 32 staff — this school year.
The announcement came just days before the beginning of a new fall semester at the Macomb, Illinois, public university and less than two months after 36 contingent faculty were informed that their contracts would not be renewed.
WIU has found itself struggling with a shrinking student body, the fallout of the 2015-17 budget impasse and state appropriations that haven't kept pace with inflation. Now, the university is trying to shrink its budget deficit and escape a cash crunch — and WIU officials say there aren't many options left.
During an Aug. 6 WIU Board of Trustees meeting, Interim President Kristi Mindrup said she was committed 'to minimizing the number of layoffs that we actually have to make.'
The cuts so far this year amount to nearly 8 percent of WIU's fall 2023 workforce.
The latest round of layoffs includes 40 tenure-track faculty, who will continue to teach for the 2024-25 academic year. The 17 contingent faculty who were laid off in this latest round will remain on contract through the fall semester. Civil service employees received 90-day notice.
The hardest-hit departments include Accounting, Finance, Economics & Decision Sciences, which lost eight faculty, and Kinesiology, which lost 5. The library system lost eight faculty. Staff were cut from across the university.
The university will also move 16 faculty and staff positions from the Quad Cities campus to Macomb.
WIU English professor Merrill Cole, president of the University Professionals of Illinois local representing WIU faculty and technical support staff, slammed the layoffs in a statement.
'Layoffs are not a plan,' Cole said. 'They are a desperate attempt by this administration to appear as if they are taking bold action.'
Budget woes
Like many regional public universities, WIU has suffered from dwindling enrollment.
At the start of the fall 2014 semester, more than 11,000 full-time students attended WIU. A decade later, projected enrollment for fall 2024 is 6,000.
Meanwhile, the university is running out of cash.
Mindrup said WIU currently faces a $22 million budget deficit. In a presentation to trustees, WIU's executive director of financial affairs, Ketra Roselieb, said the university has run deficits since fiscal year 2022. WIU's income fund, made up of students' tuition dollars, dipped below zero in 2023. As of June, the university has less than $5 million in unrestricted funds.
'With deficit spending in fiscal year 2023 and 2024, the cash balances at the university have declined to critical levels,' Roselieb said.
A university spokesperson declined to provide information on how much the university expected to save as a result of the layoffs.
According to a press release announcing the layoffs, WIU's HR department will offer counseling services and a job fair to affected employees.
Administrative turnover
At the Aug. 6 Board of Trustees meeting, it was hard to escape the sense that WIU's current leaders felt they had been dealt a bad hand.
The university has churned through three different administrations since its longtime president, Jack Thomas, resigned in 2019 amid budget struggles and tensions with faculty.
Mindrup assumed the interim presidency in April following the sudden resignation of her predecessor, Guiyou Huang. The interim provost, Mark Mossman, took office in November.
'Over the past few years, our institution has engaged in short term fixes and patches to our finances based on the promise of more students,' Mindrup told trustees. 'These strategies were not sustainable.'
Mindrup said that previous administrations had tried to shore up WIU's budget using strategies — like amped-up advertising and recruiting — that ultimately relied on increasing the size of the student body. In the face of a declining local population and competition from other universities, that approach was bound to fail, she said.
'This is the day that we make the conscious decision to not pass the buck to future students and current and future faculty, staff and administration,' Mindrup said. 'With all other options exhausted, this is the work that has been handed to us.'
Waves of layoffs
Layoffs aren't a new strategy at Western.
In May 2016, the university cut 147 employees, including 30 faculty. In 2018, WIU laid off 24 faculty members and two academic affairs employees. Then in 2019, the university laid off another 132 employees.
During the layoffs, enrollment continued to decline — by almost a thousand students each year.
Several faculty argued at the Board of Trustees meeting that the layoffs promoted a vicious cycle. In his Friday statement, Cole wrote that past layoffs 'made matters worse by lowering enrollment and decimating educational programs and student services.'
At the meeting, Board of Trustees chair Carin Stutz said WIU should be open to raising its student-to-faculty ratio, which is currently 11:1, noting that many of its peer schools have higher ratios. (Southern Illinois University, in Carbondale, also has an 11:1 student-to-faculty ratio.)
Mindrup said 80 percent of WIU's budget currently goes toward personnel.
She told meeting attendees that her administration had taken a voluntary 15 percent pay cut compared to their predecessors, axed two vice president positions and left several other administrative posts temporarily unfilled. In March, the trustees approved a 3 percent tuition increase along with hikes to fees, room and board.
John Smith, who serves as WIU's interim leader of both facilities management and finance and administration, said he was doing his best to save on facilities costs. That involves closing off unoccupied dorm floors and reducing the frequency with which buildings are cleaned.
But trustees voted down a resolution to explore selling off the University Residence at 2001 Wigwam Hollow Road, a columned estate that's typically home to the WIU president.
Mindrup has stayed in the University Residence on occasion but does not live there full-time.
An uncertain future
University leaders described the layoffs as a move to reset WIU's finances and 'right-size' the school for a future with fewer students.
Agriculture Science major Cody Cornell, the student representative who sits on WIU's Board of Trustees, said in an interview that WIU students have been greeted with a dismal view of campus: deteriorating buildings, cracked sidewalks and parking lots, and a two-week wait for counseling services.
He said the layoffs — which he voted to authorize last week — will help WIU focus more resources on its student body.
'Ultimately, what this will allow is for us to put money back towards what matters at our university, and that's our students,' he said.
Mindrup said she hoped WIU would be able to focus on offering professional development and certification programs to attract adult and online learners, improving retention and easing the experience of transfer students.
Still, she described the layoffs as 'heartbreaking.'
John Nichols, a College of Arts and Sciences graduate student, said at the Board of Trustees meeting that help from WIU faculty allowed him to study Czech in Prague and take a field course on Darwin's finches in the Galápagos Islands.
'My horizons were dramatically expanded by my interaction with faculty inside and outside of the classroom,' he said.
Math and philosophy professor Tom Blackford said in an interview that he wondered what exactly WIU's future will involve.
Would Western become a small liberal arts school, a community college, a regional campus of the University of Illinois, or something else?
He's heard administrators say WIU is finally seeing the light at the end of the tunnel, he said. 'But they don't tell us what's going to be waiting for us at the end of the tunnel.'

title: What these Grammy nominees had to say ahead of Blues Fest in Peoria
author: Mike Kramer
description: The two-day Peoria Blues and Heritage Music Festival will feature a weekend of highly-acclaimed performers, including two artists from Alligator Records.
content:
In addition to three-time Grammy winner and Blues Hall of Famer Bobby Rush, the Peoria Blues and Heritage Music Festival will feature two artists with 11 Grammy nominations between them.
The festival is a two-day event on the Peoria Riverfront. Soul blues and Americana vocalist Shemekia Copeland will perform Aug. 30, and pianist Marcia Ball will play Aug. 31. For more information, visit peoriabluesandheritagefestival.com.
We interviewed the pair ahead of their shows later this month in Peoria. Here is what the had to say.
Who is Shemekia Copeland?
Copeland is on tour to promote her new album 'Blame It on Eve.' The Washington Post newspaper has hailed Copeland as 'the greatest blues singer of our generation.' A six-time Grammy nominee, she has shared venues with artists like Bonnie Raitt, Keith Richards, Carlos Santana, and Dr. John. In 2012, she performed at the White House for President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama; along with B.B. King, Mick Jagger, Buddy Guy, Trombone Shorty, and Gary Clark, Jr.
Copeland has performed in Peoria on several occasions and has always been impressed with both the welcome she has received and the greater Peoria area's music scene.
'Any time you have a town where people come out and support music, it's a beautiful thing,' she said. 'You can tell that the people are big music fans who are ready to come out and have a good time.'
Who is Marcia Ball?
Over a career spanning six decades, Ball has collected five Grammy nominations, 11 Blues Music Awards, and a 2024 Living Blues Award for Most Outstanding Musician — Keyboards.
She was named the official Texas State Musician in 2018 and the Texas Songwriters Association named her its 2023 'Texas Music Legend.' She is also an inductee in the Gulf Coast Music Hall of Fame, the Louisiana Music Hall of Fame and the Austin City Limits Hall of Fame.
Both she and Copeland have shared a stage with Rush in the past, and she is looking forward to both playing in Peoria and again performing with Rush.
'He's got a great rhythm and he's a really nice person to interact with,' Ball said. 'People coming to the festival should see some great shows.'

title: Here's how Illinois Cash App users can get up to $2,500 after a security breach
author: Claire Grant
description: A heads up to Cash App users: you can be part of a $15M payout after a security breach. See if you qualify.
content:
Cash App users could be seeing a boost in their bank account after the popular money transferring app was ordered to pay $15 million in damages in a lawsuit settlement following a security breach dating back three years.
Some of that cash could be set aside for Illinois users, who've had fraudulent withdrawals to their app accounts.
Here's what you need to know.
How many users were impacted?
According to a class-action lawsuit obtained by USA TODAY, Cash App Investing and Block Inc, the companies behind the app were sued by plaintiffs for "failure to exercise reasonable care in securing and safeguarding consumer information."
In the lawsuit, the data breach in December 2021 resulted 'in the unauthorized public release of the personally identifiable information of 8.2 million current and former Cash App Investing customers.'
A former employee additionally gained access to Cash App users' personal information during their employment and downloaded the data without the users' knowledge, the lawsuit said.
Was my data compromised?
Cash App users should check to see if they had unauthorized or fraudulent withdrawals or transfers of funds from their Cash App account between Aug. 23, 2018, and Aug. 20, 2024.
How much money can I receive?
Eligible users who found a fraud withdrawal can submit a claim to the Cash App website, with claims going up to $2,500 in return for fraud.
How to qualify for a claim
Cash App users who will be able to file a claim must have had an account on Aug. 23, 2018, and before Aug. 20, 2024. The users who will qualify have not already been reimbursed by Block Inc., Cash App Investing or a third party, the mobile payment service said.
According to Cash App, a user can submit a claim for the following:
Out-of-Pocket Losses: Users can submit a claim that shows their Cash App account was involved in the data breach. If a user is eligible for a reimbursement, after submitting the required documentation to the company they could receive up to $2,500.
Lost Time: Cash App users who submit a claim may be eligible for reimbursement for lost time. Users can submit a claim for up to three hours at a rate of $25 per hour for time spent regarding the unauthorized users and data breach.
Transaction Losses: If a user experienced a monetary loss and has not been reimbursed, they will be able to submit the Transaction Losses claim.
It's important to note users with more than one account can only file a single claim form; the mobile payment service recommends users to list each of their Cash App user tags and information about their claims on a single claim form.
Filing a claim settlement
To file a claim, Cash App users can submit a completed claim form by Nov. 18, 2024, for consideration.
You can submit the claim form at cashappsecuritysettlement.com/submit-claim.

title: DNC speakers schedule tonight: See who is speaking Thursday, including Kamala Harris
author: Mike Kramer
description: Presidential nominee Kamala Harris is expected to speak on final day of 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Illinois.
content:
Thursday is the fourth and final day of the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago. U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris' expected acceptance speech of the party's nomination will headline the primetime lineup.
Here is what to expect on Day 4 of the DNC in Chicago.
DNC speaker schedule Day 4: Who is speaking tonight?
Kamala Harris will be this evening's headline speaker, as her acceptance speech will be the climax of the four-day convention, which closes tonight. Other notable speakers will include North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healy, and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. The program will also include one Republican: former U.S. Rep. Adam Kinzinger, who used to represent his native Illinois.
Who is performing at the DNC tonight?
Grammy-winning pop singer Pink is scheduled to perform just before Kamala Harris' acceptance speech.
What time does the DNC start tonight?
Official programming of DNC Chicago 2024 will begin at 5:30 p.m. Primetime television coverage will begin at 7 p.m.
What time does the DNC end?
This is the final day of the Democratic National Convention. The DNC is scheduled to end tonight's session at 10 p.m.
DNC Chicago 2024 dates
The Democratic National Convention runs from Monday, Aug. 19 to Thursday, Aug. 22 in Chicago, Illinois.
DNC live stream: How to watch
The Democratic National Convention is available on multiple live streams and TV channels:
How to watch the DNC convention
ABC News will air two hours of primetime coverage tonight from 8 to 10 p.m. ABC News Live, the network's streaming news channel, will stream primetime coverage from 7 to 11 p.m. all four days of the convention.
C-SPAN will broadcast all four days of the Democratic National Convention without interruption.
CBS News ' primetime coverage of the convention will air from 7 to 10 p.m. and be anchored by "CBS Evening News" anchor and managing editor Norah O'Donnell.
CNN will broadcast almost the entire Democratic National Convention and will have a nightly primetime show airing from 7 to 11 p.m. called "CNN Democratic National Convention."
Fox News will air a show each night of the convention beginning at 9 p.m. hosted by Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum called "Fox News Democracy 2024: The Democratic National Convention."
MSNBC Rachel Maddow will host coverage of the Democratic National Convention from 7 to 11 p.m. each night of the convention.
NewsNation anchors Chris Cuomo, Elizabeth Vargas and Leland Vittert will host primetime coverage of the convention called "Decision Desk 2024: The Democratic National Convention." It will air from 7 to 11 p.m. each night of the convention.
PBS will air primetime coverage of the DNC every night of the convention from 7 to 10 p.m. ET. Amna Nawaz and Geoff Bennett will host.
DNC schedule 2024
Day 1: The first day on Monday was highlighted by speeches from President Joe Biden and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton endorsing vice president Kamala Harris as the party's nominee for president.
Day 2: Tuesday night featured former President Barack Obama and former First Lady Michelle Obama, second gentleman Doug Emhoff, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, and Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker. The speaker slate also included two Republicans: former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham and Mesa, Arizona mayor John Giles.
Day 3: Wednesday's headliners included former U.S. president Bill Clinton and vice presidential candidate Tim Walz, who accepted the party's nomination. Other DNC Day 3 speakers were U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. Former Trump administration official Olivia Troye also addressed the DNC.

title: Locally owned Tazewell County coffee company closing one of its locations
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Three other coffee shop locations in Tazewell County will continue to operate.
content:
With "sincere gratitude" and "the heaviest of hearts," the owners of Eli's Coffee Shop have announced the closure of their Mackinaw location. The final day of service will be Sept. 6.
The company announced the closure in a Friday Facebook post.
In a statement on the company's website, owners Rachel and Weston Berchtold wrote, "We close our doors in two weeks resting in the knowledge that we were able to be a bright part of this building's story and this community for the time we were able."
The Mackinaw location opened in 2022 at 116 S. Main St. in a building that used to be home to Heartland Bank.
It was the company's fourth site in the Peoria area. The locally owned Eli's also operates coffee shops in Morton, Tremont and Metamora. Those sites remain open.
Eli's Coffee shops are known for their distinctive locations, including the renovated Mackinaw bank. The Morton shop, which opened in 2005, is in a former home at 205 W. Jefferson St. The Tremont location opened in 2014 at 105 W. Pearl St. in the historic Tremont Depot. The Metamora shop, which opened in 2017, is in a 140-year-old building at 101 W. Partridge St. on the village square.

title: Rental, restaurant and riverfront views for sale in East Peoria
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Charlie's at Sunset Cove, a waterfront restaurant, closed on July 16 and is now for sale along with a house, land and marina.
content:
In East Peoria, Charlie's at Sunset Cove abruptly closed on July 16.
The restaurant, situated right along the Illinois River, opened in February 2023. Later the same year, the business said it would close at its one-year anniversary before reversing course and announcing, ' the adventure continues.'
A recent Facebook post, however, stated that the owner 'decided to sell the property and take a job offer elsewhere.'
The restaurant space is now included in a larger commercial property listing that includes 1111 Sunset Drive and 1109 Sunset Drive in East Peoria. Described as an 'exceptional 26.8-acre waterfront property,' the property was listed for $2.7 million in early August.
Aside from the restaurant, the description said the property includes:
A 'luxurious' 4,839-square-foot house that typically rents for $475 each night on Airbnb
A 7,500-square-foot barn that could provide storage or additional income
A marina that could be used for boat parking
Ten acres of additional land which offers 'many possibilities for development'
Charlie's at Sunset Cove earned a profit of nearly $300,000 in 2023, according to the listing. The description went on to note:
'It boasts a nicely furnished dining area, a perfectly situated bar, and a back patio with stunning views of the marina and river.'

title: Illinois high school rule change caused confusion and controversy. How the IHSA fixed it
author: Dave Eminian
description: All-star games involving Illinois high school athletes were in limbo this summer after an IHSA rule went into effect. Here's what happened.
content:
Illinois' underclass high school athletes are back in the lineup for all-star events after an adjustment made this month by the state's athletic association.
The Illinois High School Association has clarified — via a new definition — a by-law change that triggered confusion among those involved in its team sports, especially baseball and softball organizations in the midst of all-star season.
Illinois high school football previews: Ultimate guide to Peoria-area high school football for 2024
The by-law was passed by IHSA member schools via a December vote of 547-136 (43 no opinion). It went into effect July 1, prompting the IHSA to spotlight it on their website. It reads:
"No student at a member school shall participate on an all-star team in any IHSA sport during the student's high school career until completing their interscholastic athletic eligibility in that particular sport. A student may participate in no more than three (3) all-star contests in a sport."
IHSA By-law 3.120: 'ALL-STAR PARTICIPATION'
Why the IHSA rule caused confusion
That new wording caused panic among showcases like the McDonald's All-Star Classic and other special baseball and softball events that traditionally were open to seniors and underclassmen at the outset of summer.
"It was badly conceived and badly written," said Ben Diggle, a former junior college coach, summer developmental team recruiting coordinator and founder of Diggle's Diamonds, a program that promotes high school baseball players in the form of mentorship, advice, recruiting news and promotion via social media.
"I felt bad for the IHSA guys in a way. They were stuck enforcing a bad law," Diggle said. "I don't think anybody had a damn clue what they were voting on. It reads like stereo assembly instructions.
"To the credit of the IHSA, they fixed it. I don't ever recall another instance where the IHSA has made a common-sense adjustment."
But that's exactly what happened, as IHSA executive director Craig Anderson explains.
IHSA executive director 'was a bit surprised' rule passed
Anderson saw the bylaw pass and knew it might be problematic, but it was not directed at just baseball, softball and basketball. It was designed to simply bring all IHSA team sports into alignment so they were all treated equally. The rule change just happened to go into effect at a time when baseball and softball were staging summer showcase events, which prompted confusion and controversy.
"Honestly, I was a bit surprised that it passed in favor of the change," Anderson said. "So on July 1, the new by-law was implemented. These non-school teams and leagues were culminating at that time in selecting their all-stars to play one last time at the end of summer. Our by-law indicated that wasn't permitted unless you were a graduated senior."
The reaction was, in some places, panic, according to longtime Morton baseball coach Jesse Crawford. He feared the rule could affect his players' future IHSA eligibility.
"That kind of directly impacted some of the kids who played for me," said Crawford, who also is on the Greater Peoria Baseball Coaches Association board — headed up by Metamora's Tony Riddle — which operates the annual McDonald's All-Star Game.
"PBR (Prep Baseball Report) was hosting a showcase in Indianapolis when that bylaw was announced," Crawford said. "Team Illinois was there, and got pulled off the field because of the bylaw. There was concern kids' eligibility could be impacted."
Where IHSA by-law 3.120 came from
So why does IHSA by-law 3.120 exist? Anderson said an all-star limitation has long been in place for football, soccer, volleyball and basketball, preventing underclass players from participating in all-star contests during their seasons.
"They had to be seniors with eligibility in their sport finished," Anderson said. "It's been in place over 40 years, dates back a long, long ways and long before there were non-school sports the way we know it today."
Last fall, one of IHSA member schools proposed to expand that limitation to all team sports — including baseball and softball — and it passed. Hence, the confusion. "We quickly discovered," Anderson said, "there's all kinds of these non-school organizations in baseball and softball that meet our (definition) of an all-star game or tournament."
How the IHSA board altered the bylaw and notched a save
Faced with mounting confusion from the team sports showcase ranks about the revised by-law on his hands, Anderson found a solution. The executive director met with his board and changed the IHSA's definition of an all-star event.
"Our office didn't do this by-law change," Anderson said. "Our school membership made this change. ... So the board put together a new definition of what an all-star event should be. Fortunately, it withdrew a lot of concern and backlash we were getting.
"All team sports are covered. And the bottom line is, there are no all-star contests or showcase limitations for baseball, softball and basketball during the summer. This has broad application."
IHSA all-star games: The 180 players selected for 2024 McDonald's all-star high school baseball and softball games
The clarifications on the bylaw from the IHSA leave the door open for continuation of the annual McDonald's All-Star Game with seniors in its traditional format. If underclassmen are involved, then the above-mentioned restrictions apply, in addition to one more — no score can be kept at the event.
How the new definition reads
The IHSA handbook now defines "All-Star Team" as the following for all team sports:
"All-Star Team — A team of students who are selected to participate in a non-school contest or tournament based on athletic ability, performance or reputation when representing the member high school the student attends or previously attended. Students represent their school by using the school's name, being selected or nominated by the school, or by wearing any part of the school's athletic uniform.
Illustration: By-law 3.120 applies during the school year (from Monday of Week 8 through Saturday of Week 49 of the IHSA standardized calendar)."
Anderson released a statement on Aug. 9 after the board re-worked the all-star definition.
'When the new IHSA by-laws went into effect on July 1, 2024, the changes to the All-Star Participation by-law created a significant number of questions from member schools amidst the changing landscape of non-high school participation in the summer.
"The Board felt it was prudent to produce the updated language to the All-Star Team definition and the new by-law illustration to more clearly define the scope and timeline of when 'all-star events' for underclassmen are restricted. The changes to the by-law that were voted into effect by our member schools in December remain intact as written, however, the Board is confident that today's updates will better reflect the initial intent of the by-law change."
Clarification from the IHSA
Here are a few clarifying questions and answers from Anderson about revived IHSA bylaw 3.120:
Can underclassmen play all-star games?"Underclassmen can now play," he said. "Everyone can get in it. I think we shocked them initially."
What is not allowed?"During the IHSA school year, you can't play in all-star events when representing a school, whether by selection or wearing equipment from the school as underclassmen. That's not allowed," Anderson said.
What about AAU?"If players are part of a team, like AAU, that has a full schedule, that's not considered an all-star game and it's OK," Anderson said.
Why does the bylaw exist?"At the heart of why the original by-law limit was in place was to not bog down underclassmen with playing in showcases and all-star events after their season," Anderson said.
Dave Eminian is the Journal Star sports columnist, and covers Bradley men's basketball, the Rivermen and Chiefs. He writes the Cleve In The Eve sports column for pjstar.com. He can be reached at 686-3206 or deminian@pjstar.com. Follow him on X.com @icetimecleve.

title: COVID-19 cases are on the rise. Here's what to know about the latest variants
author: Mike Kramer
description: New sub-variants of the Omicron variant have driven a COVID-19 summer surge. What to know about rise in COVID cases in U.S., including Illinois.
content:
Show Caption
COVID-19 appears to have made a summer surge.
According to data from the Centers for Disease Control (CDC), the percentage of people in the United States reporting positive tests for the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which causes COVID-19, has risen from 3.1 in May to its current 18 percent. Illinois is just above the national average with an 18.2% test positivity rate.
As COVID-19 cases rise nationwide, so does concern and curiosity. Here are some answers to a few COVID-related questions:
What are current COVID symptoms?
Symptoms of the Omicron sub-variants responsible for most new COVID-19 cases in the U.S. do not seem to be different than appeared with earlier variants, says Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg School of Public Health. Typical symptoms are fever, chills, body aches, persistent coughing, loss of ability to smell or taste, chest pain and fatigue. COVID-19 can also cause nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea, says the Mayo Clinic.
Digestive symptoms are more common with the current Omicron variants than they were with earlier waves.
When is COVID most contagious?
People infected with COVID are at their most contagious about two days before they develop symptoms, according to The World Health Organization. People who develop severe cases can be infectious for longer.
How long is COVID contagious for?
People with COVID-19 can be infectious from one to two days before and up to 10 days after symptoms begin, according to the CDC.
How many Americans died from COVID?
Between the start of 2020 and Aug. 17, 2024, COVID-19 has caused nearly 1.2 million deaths in the United States, according to the CDC.
What are COVID quarantine requirements?
The CDC says people with COVID-19 should isolate at home, but can resume normal activities if they have had no symptoms for at least 24 hours. Additional precautions such as masking and social distancing are encouraged for five days after resuming normal activities.
COVID map: Where are the highest and lowest COVID-19 rates in the U.S.?
Region 9 — which includes Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Texas — has the nation's highest COVID-19 positivity rate at 22.3% this week, according to a CDC map. The lowest positivity rate is 13.7 percent in Region 1, which consists of Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont. Region 5, which includes Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Ohio and Wisconsin, is at 18.2 percent, says the CDC.

title: Here's what the Old Farmer's Almanac predicts for winter weather in Illinois this year
author: Dean Muellerleile
description: The Old Farmer's Almanac divides Illinois into three different regions, all of which have very different winter forecasts.
content:
The Old Farmer's Almanac has released its 2024-2025 Winter Weather Forecast, and while the national outlook calls for a "calmer, gentler" season, the prediction for Illinois — especially Peoria — is not so clear.
The almanac divides the Prairie State among multiple regions, all of which have different forecasts. Peoria is roughly on the border between two of those areas — the Lower Lakes and Heartland regions.
The Old Farmer forecasts below-average snowfall for both regions. But temperature-wise, the almanac offers a mixed outlook. Central Illinois temperatures will range from colder than average to above normal, the Old Farmer says. And Peoria is at the center of that range.
Here's what the almanac predicts for Illinois:
Related:Here's what the Old Farmer's Almanac predicts for fall weather in Illinois this year
The Lower Lakes region includes much of the eastern half of Illinois. That part of the Prairie State is expected to see a colder than normal winter. The coldest periods are forecast for early and late November, early December, and from late January into early February.
The Old Farmer predicts below-normal precipitation, including snowfall, in the Lower Lakes region. The almanac expects the most snow in late December, from late January into early February, and from late February into early March.
The Heartland region incorporates most of western Illinois from the Wisconsin border to St. Louis.
The almanac forecasts a warmer-than-normal winter throughout the Heartland. The coldest periods are predicted for late January and early and late February.
The Old Farmer foresees below-normal precipitation and snowfall. The snowiest periods are expected during the January and February cold snaps.
More:'Brace yourself': Wet, snowy weather in forecast for central Illinois this winter
The Ohio Valley region includes roughly the bottom third of Illinois. The almanac predicts a colder-than-normal winter. The coldest days are expected in late January through early February and in late February.
The Old Farmer foresees above-average snowfall for most of the region, including southern Illinois. The region's snowiest periods are predicted for late December, from late January into early February, in late February, and mid-March.
'This winter, temperatures will be up and snowfall down throughout most parts of the United States,' wrote Carol Connare, the Old Farmer's Almanac editor, in a news release. "It will be, by and large, a very temperate, uneventful winter."
The Old Farmer's Almanac claims 80% accuracy in its long-range predictions. It says it employs solar science, climatology and meteorology in its seasonal forecasts. The almanac dates to 1792.

Peoria High 35, Peoria Notre Dame 34: The Irish, who got a blocked punt by Mitch Sager recovered by Tyler Miller for a TD, lost a six-point heartbreaker to Normal West. New Peoria High QB Breon Green found Jaylen Rayford and Kendall Netters for receiving TDs. This game will be played at Richwoods Stadium. Last season, Peoria High won 44-40.
East Peoria (1-0) at Springfield Lanphier (0-1), 7 p.m.
East Peoria 34, Springfield Lanphier 20: EP gave Sam Durley his first head coaching victory, using two TDs by Aidin Hindert, who also got a fourth-down pick to end the game. Lanphier is riding a 12-game losing streak, having not won a game since Week 7 of the 2022 season. These teams did not meet last season.
Pekin (1-0) at Belleville East (1-0), 7 p.m.
Pekin 27, Belleville East 14: Pekin used RB Ty Jackson (150 yards, TD), QB Brogan Benassi (147 yards, TD) and Dylan Anderson (84 yards, TD) to grab a 14-point season-opening victory. Belleville East, which scored 30 points in Week 1, made the second round in the Class 8A playoffs last season. In 2023, Belleville East won 34-14.
Limestone (0-1) at Galesburg (0-1), 7:30 p.m.
Galesburg 35, Limestone 14: Limestone, which is on a seven-game skid, gave up 302 passing yards and 37 points in last week's loss to Mt. Zion. Galesburg looks to rebound from a Week 1 shutout to Dunlap, utilizing RB Jamar Range (51 yards), QB Caden Riley (120 yards) and WR Bradley Eaton (47 yards). In 2023, Galesburg won 41-7.
Coal City (0-1) at Canton (0-1), 7:30 p.m.
Coal City 35, Canton 15: First-year coach Nick McCormick is looking for his first victory, using a late TD from Lakon Otto to avoid a Week 1 shutout against Eureka. Coal City lost to Morris, but came within five points off a 43-yard punt return TD from Jonathan Widlowski. In 2023, Coal City won 41-0.
Dunlap (1-0) at Rock Island (0-1), 7:30 p.m.
Dunlap 56, Rock Island 8: The Eagles put up 48 points in Week 1, getting 206 yards and three TDs from QB John Bargen, who found Mack Sutter, Jackson Oldham and Dawson Marmion for scores. Rocky will counter with QB Jae'Vion Clark-Pugh (152 yards, two TDs) and WR Elijah Venegas (104 yards, two TDs). In 2023, Dunlap won 21-7.
Rochelle (1-0) at Morton (0-1), 7:30 p.m.
Rochelle 33, Morton 28: The Potters, who scored 30 first-half points in Week 1, look to bounce back after giving up 69 points and 593 passing yards and eight TDs to Mahomet-Seymour QB Luke Dyer last week. Rochelle put up 39 points in a Week 1 victory thanks to RB Dylan Manning, who had 107 yards and a 57-yard TD. In 2023, Morton won 27-26.
LaSalle-Peru (1-0) at Metamora (1-0), 7:30 p.m.
Metamora 34, LaSalle-Peru 16: Metamora aired it out in Week 1, getting 283 passing yards from QB Stephen Petri, who found Avery Grebner for 138 yards on five catches including two TDs. L-P, which got two TDs by Adrian Arzola, needed a game-winning missed field goal to escape East Moline United Township in Week 1. In 2023, Metamora won 37-6.
Washington (0-1) at Kankakee (0-1), 7:30 p.m.
Kankakee 20, Washington 18: Washington is looking to give Todd Stevens his first victory during his coaching tenure. The Panthers got a 47-yard score by WR AJ Jones and a 34-yarder from RB Hunter Reed. Kankakee QB Phillip Turner had two rushing TDs in a Week 1 loss. In 2023, Kankakee won 7-3.
Monticello (0-1, 0-1) at Illinois Valley Central (0-1, 0-1), 7 p.m.
Monticello 27, IVC 24: With the running clock in effect last week, backup IVC QB Keegan Schol led the Grey Ghosts on their two scoring drives last, rushing for a score and throwing a TD. Sages QB and Illinois baseball recruit Ike Young threw for 292 yards and two TDs, plus running for 66 yards and two scores. In 2023, Monticello won 52-13.

Elmwood/Brimfield 35, Illini West 6: The Trojans flexed their ground attack muscle, getting three backs to run for 100 yards or more: Bo Windish (184 yards, three TDs), Matthew Glenn (111 yards, two TDs) and Landon Kline (108 yards). Illini West was shutout by Farmington in Week 1. In 2023, Illini West won 34-14.
Farmington (1-0, 1-0) at Warsaw West Hancock (0-1, 0-0), 7 p.m.
Farmington 42, Warsaw West Hancock 15: The Farmers, who got a receiving score by Landon Crawford from Lane Wheelwright, pitched a shutout for the first time since a 2022 Week 4 win against Illini West. West Hancock wide receiver Nolan Gooding scored three TDs with 112 yards in Week 1. In 2023, Farmington won 45-20.
Eureka (1-0) at St. Bede (0-1), 7 p.m.
Eureka 28, St. Bede 13: Hornets QB Austin Gerber made a near flawless debut with 195 passing yards and 95 rushing yards with a rushing score and hit Tony Kupferschmid for a 47-yard TD score. St. Bede RB Grady Gillan rushed for 20 yards and two TDs in a Week 1 loss to Downs Tri-Valley. These teams didn't play last season.
Deer Creek-Mackinaw (1-0) at Trenton Wesclin (0-1), 7 p.m.
Dee-Mack 41, Trenton Wesclin 28: Dee-Mack, which scored 58 points in Week 1, used a big game from running back Max Eccles, who rushed for 136 yards and three TDs. Wesclin, which was a 2023 Class 2A playoff qualifier, lost by six points to Marshall in Week 1. These teams didn't play last season.
Moweaqua Central A&M (0-1, 0-1) at Fieldcrest (0-1, 0-1), 7 p.m.
Fieldcrest 20, Moweaqua Central A&M 13: The Knights nearly grabbed a Week 1 victory, but a late-game interception ended a comeback. Fieldcrest RB Eddie Lorton ran for 101 yards, while QB Kash Klendworth scored four TDs (two passing, two rushing). Central A&M allowed 45 points in Week 1. These teams didn't play last season.
Princeville (1-0, 1-0) at Havana (0-1, 0-1), 7 p.m.
Princeville 42, Havana 38: Princeville scored by pass (Jake Williams), rush (Jack Lied), receiving (Jett Benningfield) and kickoff return (Brady Day) on the way to 38 points in Week 1. Havana, which got four TDs from running back Cayden Green, scored 23 fourth-quarter points in a six-point loss last week. In 2023, Princeville won 36-14.
8-player: Peoria Heights (0-1) at Flanagan-Cornell (1-0), 7 p.m.
Flanagan-Cornell/Streator Woodland 40, Peoria Heights 18: Heights looks to bounce back after giving up 44 points last week. It was their first time getting shut out since Week 6 of the 2023 campaign. F-C got two rushing TDs as well as a game-sealing interception by Logan Ruddy. These teams didn't play last season.
Tremont (0-1) at Carlyle (0-1), 2 p.m. Saturday
Tremont 15, Carlyle 14: The Turks, who tallied 40 points all of last season, scored 22 points last week, putting up 174 yards of offense and getting on the board in the first quarter. Tremont did give up two kickoff returns for touchdowns. Carlyle allowed 52 points in a Week 1 defeat to Nashville. These teams didn't play last season.

title: Festivals, music and shows: Here are 5 things to do near Peoria this weekend
author: Josh Jenke
description: Outdoor festivals, a cat show and a band competition are among the things to do this weekend in the Peoria area.
content:
September is full of activities. Here are five events you might want to check out in the Peoria area this weekend.
2024 Pekin Marigold Festival
The Pekin Marigold Festival is now under way and will continue through Sept. 8 at Mineral Springs Park in Pekin. This year's theme is "Marigold Rockin' The Bicentennial" and the event will include a carnival, parade, festival foods, live entertainment and more. For a full schedule of events and more information, visit https://pekinchamber.com/pekin-marigold-festival.
Elmwood Fall Festival
The city of Elmwood will hold its annual Fall Festival on Sept. 5-7 in on the square in its historic downtown. The event will include carnival rides each night; live music by Press Play from 7 to 10 p.m. Friday, Minivan Morrisey from 4 to 6 p.m. Saturday and Common Ground from 8 to 11 p.m. Saturday; and a Medieval Times-themed parade at 12:30 p.m. Saturday. For more information, visit the Elmwood Fall Festival Facebook page.
Children's Home cattle auction
The 59th annual cattle auction to benefit Children's Home Association of Illinois will be held from 6:30 to 10 p.m. Friday, Sept. 6, at Venue Chisca, 1009 SW Washington St. The live auction will feature luxury trips, uniquely curated experiences and signature favorites. There will also be a BBQ dinner and live music by country music entertainer DJ DU. Tickets are $125 per person and can be purchased online at www.chail.org.
Annual cat show at Expo Gardens
The American Gothic Annual Cat Show will be held from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 7, and 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 8, at Exposition Gardens, 1601 Northmoor Road. Come see over 100 purebred and household pet cats compete for top cat in different judging rings throughout the day. Admission is $10 for adults, $6 for seniors and children ages 5-12 and free for children ages 4 and under.
Washington marching band competition
Enjoy an afternoon and evening of music, competition and fun at the 36th annual WCHS Marching Panther Invitational on Saturday, Sept. 7, at Babcook Field, 115 Bondurant St., Washington. Gates open at 11:30 a.m. and performances start at 12:16 p.m. Twenty-seven high school marching bands from across the state will perform their 2024 marching band field shows in competition. Admission is $10 for adults and $5 for seniors and students.

title: Dunlap high school football recruit goes to Ohio State campus; changes plan for Illini visit
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: One of the nation's top juniors is making the rounds this college football season.
content:
Mack Sutter made his way to the Horseshoe.
The four-star Dunlap tight end, part of the Class of 2026, was in attendance for No. 2 Ohio State's 56-0 win over Western Michigan on Saturday, making an unofficial visit to the Columbus, Ohio, campus. Sutter has Ohio State among his 12 finalists.
The 6-foot-6, 225-pound junior's visit to Ohio State followed previous announcements be would be in Champaign for Illinois' game against Kansas or head south to see Ole Miss, but a change in family travel plans shook up his schedule. Sutter said he plans to attend a Fighting Illinois game at some point next month.
Sutter on Aug. 10 shared a social media from @Recruit2Illini that reported he would visit Champaign on Sept. 7. A week later, Sutter posted on social media he would be at Ole Miss for their Sept. 7 game.
The Ohio State campus visit comes after Sutter attended Auburn's win against Alabama A&M on Aug. 31.
Sutter was coming off last Friday's 41-31 victory over Rock Island in Week 2 during which he caught six balls for 121 yards. After this big game in Week 1, he now has 11 receptions, 198 yards and a touchdown on the season.

Having 'me' swagger
