title: LIVE: Trump says 'he is safe' after shots fired in his vicinity
author: Phillip M. Bailey
description: Donald Trump's campaign says the former president is safe after gunshots were reported in his vicinity on Sunday in Florida.
content:
Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump is safe following gunshots in his vicinity, his campaign and U.S. Secret Service announced on Sunday with no further details provided.
The incident took place at Trump International Golf Course where the former president was golfing, according to the White House.
"The Secret Service, in conjunction with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, is investigating a protective incident involving former President Donald Trump that occurred shortly before 2 p.m.," Secret Service spokesman Anthony Guglielmi said in a statement.
This is a developing story. Follow along with USA TODAY for the latest.
Trump: 'I am safe and well'
In a fundraising email sent out roughly an hour after the incident, Trump said there were gunshots in his vicinity, "but before rumors start spiraling out of control, I wanted you to hear this first: I am safe and well!"
Kamala Harris: 'I am glad he is safe'
Vice President Kamala Harris said she has been briefed about shots being fired near Trump and his property in Florida, adding she is glad he is safe.
"Violence has no place in America," she said.
Hannity: Trump wanted to finish golfing
Fox News host Sean Hannity has developed a close relationship with Trump and conveyed having a brief conversation with the GOP nominee on Sunday. He joined a live broadcast after speaking with the former president.
Trump checked to see if others were OK, Hannity said, but then joked about wanting to finish the round.
"I guess in typical, 'fight, fight, fight' fashion Trump said... 'I really wanted to finish the hole,'" Hannity said.
White House has been briefed on incident
The White House said President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris have been briefed about the incident. security incident at the Trump International Golf Course, where former President Trump was golfing.
"They are relieved to know that he is safe," the statement said. "They will be kept regularly updated by their team."
When was Donald Trump last attacked?
This incident occurs two months after the former president was injured in an assassination attempt in Pennsylvania on July 13. That incident has sparked an investigation and caused the resignation of then Secret Service Director Kimberly Cheatle, who had led the agency since 2022.
In the subsequent weeks, Trump has increased security at his events with him often speaking behind bulletproof glass at outdoor rallies.

title: Upsets, historic seasons and more. Vote in Journal Star poll for IHSA athlete of the week
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Players from Metamora, Dunlap, Pekin and more shined this week in Peoria-area high school sports. Get your votes in for athlete of the week.
content:
After plenty of solid fall sports performers over the last week, here are the Journal Star high school athlete of the week nominees for Sept. 9-14.
Head to pjstar.com/sports to vote. The poll closes at noon Friday. Information about the nominees is below.
If you have a nominee for the honor, email us at sports@pjstar.com or tag us on Twitter @pjstarsports. Last week, Colin Kemp of the Pekin boys golf team was named JS athlete of the week.
Dylan Anderson, Pekin football
The sophomore came up big on both sides of the ball in Pekin's 34-33 upset road victory against state-ranked Dunlap on Friday. Anderson picked off Dunlap's potential game-winning, two-point conversion to seal the win. This came after Anderson scored the go-ahead touchdown on a pass from Brogan Benassi.
Jimmy Lollar, Olympia football
The sophomore running back put on quite the display in Friday's 43-34 win over Pittsfield. Lollar rushed for 225 yards on 25 carries with four touchdowns. His offensive output was a part of 456 rushing yards for the Spartans.
Addison Pacha, Metamora volleyball
Pacha was instrumental in helping the Redbirds win the silver bracket at the Jacksonville Tournament on Saturday. In the title match, the 5-foot-8 senior outside hitter posted eight kills and nine digs to beat Richwoods, 25-15, 22-25, 15-9. She was the team's kill leader in three other matches, highlighted by a 12-kill effort in a three-set loss to Petersburg PORTA and 10 kills to beat West Prairie in straight sets.
Anna McGlasson, Midland volleyball
McGlasson has the Timberwolves heading towards a historic season. The 6-foot-1 sophomore's seven kills and nine blocks came in knocking off previously undefeated Brimfield in straight sets of the Midland Invitational championship match on Saturday. This was the first time Midland has ever won its own tournament. She tallied 32 kills and 19 blocks on the week as Midland is 9-1 over its last 10 matches.
Tucker Hinkle, Eureka boys cross country
Hinkle guided the Hornets to the Class 1A First to the Finish Invitational title on Saturday. He ran the historic Detweiller Park course in 15:24.70, finishing eighth overall. The senior's top-10 placing helped Eureka take the title in the 52-team field, edging out Aurora Central Catholic, 167-169.
Dusti Smith, Stark County girls cross country
Smith was a top-10 individual finisher in Saturday's Class 1A First to the Finish Invitational. The sophomore raced around the 3-mile course at Detweiller Park in 17:59.9, clocking in as the fastest Journal Star-area girls runner regardless of class. She took ninth overall in a field of 424 runners.
Connor Watson, East Peoria boys golf
Watson, the reigning Journal Star Boys Golfer of the Year, won the A Flight at the Redbird Classic by three strokes on Saturday. The senior, who won the 2023 event, started on Friday by shooting a 69 at Coyote Creek, then wrapped up his two-day total by firing a 72 at Weaver Ridge. East Peoria (625) finished second as a team, trailing only Normal U-High (606). This comes off Watson shooting a 31 last Tuesday as EP set a school record with a 2-under 138 as a team.
Sydney Hunt, Dunlap girls golf
Hunt was key in leading the Eagles to a third-place finish Saturday at the Normal Community Invite. The sophomore's fifth-place finish paced Dunlap at Prairie Vista Golf Course in Bloomington.
Logan Walliker, Washington boys soccer
The senior goalkeeper posted a pair of clean sheets last week. He picked up his third and fourth shutouts of the season, blanking Rock Island on Thursday and Pekin last Tuesday. In the 8-0 victory against Pekin, Walliker was helped out by teammate Eric Nolte's three goals and two assists.
Jenna Kozinski, East Peoria co-op girls swimming and diving
Kozinski was a four-event winner in beating Mid-Illini Conference foe and host Pekin, 134-42, on Thursday. She won the 200- and 500-yard individual freestyles. Her final two victories came on the 200 freestyle and 400 freestyle relays.
Maya Baman, Dunlap girls tennis
Baman went 4-0 last week, grabbing two single wins and two doubles victories against Normal U-High and Peoria Notre Dame. In last Tuesday's 6-3 win over U-High, the junior won her singles match in two sets, then teamed with Melaina Humbles in the No. 3 Doubles for a 8-2 doubles win. Baman then didn't drop in a game in either singles or doubles match as the Eagles beat PND, 9-0, on Thursday.

title: Pekin man pleads guilty to infant's murder, will serve 70-year sentence
author: Mike Kramer
description: The Pekin, Illinois, man pled guilty to first-degree murder of his nine-week-old daughter.
content:
A 20-year-old Pekin man has pled guilty to the murder of his infant daughter last year and will serve 70 years in prison.
Hunter Waters was due to go to trial Monday on charges of first-degree murder and aggravated battery to a child, according to a report from Tazewell County State's Attorney Kevin Johnson.
Just before jury selection, Waters pled guilty to one first degree murder charge. The state subsequently dismissed two additional first-degree murder charges and nine aggravated assault including great bodily harm to a child under 13 charges.
Waters was arrested last November after his 9-week-old daughter, Addison Waters, died at a local hospital from numerous severe injuries. He pled not guilty to the charges last December at his arraignment.
According to Johnson, Waters will not be eligible for good behavior credits or parole. He will receive 293 days credit for time already served.

title: 'Surreal': Popular singer regularly visited Downtown Peoria coffee shop during stay
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: The owner said staff kept quiet about the visits and offered the singer "the finest Midwestern hospitality we could."
content:
Charli XCX has garnered a lot of attention this year.
The English singer-songwriter released her new hit album, 'Brat,' this summer, and she and fellow pop star Troye Sivan recently embarked on their Sweat tour. The artists will perform for crowds in Canada, Dallas, New York, San Francisco and many other states throughout the U.S.
Ahead of the tour, though, Charli XCX became something of a regular at Intuition Coffee + Juice in Downtown Peoria.
Owner Ty Paluska said both singers paid the coffee shop a visit during their stay but added that Charli XCX consistently returned to the Peoria establishment.
They became 'obsessed with this place'
Trey Mowder, a staff member and longtime fan, was working during one such visit and was surprised when she ordered two of his favorite items – the nitro cold brew and avocado toast. He described the experience as 'surreal.'
'But what was almost more surreal was that, to me, it all kind of felt really normal,' he said. 'Like it seemed like she had been coming here for years.'
Along with the cold brew and avocado toast, Paluska said Charli XCX ordered other items − such as the Swift Kick in the Grass cold-pressed juice − which match the color scheme of her hit 2024 album.
Paluska said dancers and other team members also visited Intuition multiple times during their stay.
'Their team, in their own words, said they'd become obsessed with this place,' Paluska said. 'Just to be able to come to a small town and find like healthy, quality options. They were just like floored.'
Mowder was excited for the opportunity to highlight Peoria's local coffee scene and 'show a celebrity that like Peoria has some cool stuff.'
Offering 'the finest Midwestern hospitality'
If you hadn't heard about the singer stopping by Intuition until recently, that was by design. Paluska said everyone on staff kept quiet about the visits until after she left the area.
'I think we just all agreed we wanted to show her, like, just the finest Midwestern hospitality we could and respect her privacy,' Paluska said.
Even so, news of her visits got out to an extent.
Paluska said small groups of fans gathered at the coffee shop after the first few days to try and meet the singer. He and Mowder said Charli XCX was kind to each person she met and would often sign autographs or smile for a photograph. She took photos with staff members, as well, and autographed a 'Brat' record cover for an employee's partner.
During one of her visits, Paluska noticed his daughter and her friend left two homemade friendship bracelets with a note asking him to 'Please give to Charli XCX.' So, he brought the green bracelets out to the singer.
'She was like, 'Oh my god, That's so cute,' and she put them on and then she wore them the rest of the time she was here,' Paluska said.
'Making her feel at home'
Paluska said 'it was a joy' to watch employees interact with Charli XCX. With multiple longtime fans on staff, he is proud of the service and experience his team was able to provide.
For employee Deborah Sheppard, the experience felt unreal. She has been a fan of the singer for roughly a decade and plans to see her in concert soon. So, it was both exciting and a bit nerve wracking when Charli XCX visited the shop.
'I'm like, this is the Matrix, like, anything could happen,' Sheppard said. 'If Charlie XCX can walk into my job, anything can happen to me.'
A true fan, Mowder discussed how one of Charli XCX's new songs, 'Rewind,' is about 'missing when her life was more normal.' He felt as though Intuition was able to provide a small sense of normalcy during her time in Peoria.
'I think the fact that she kept coming in every day is like a credit to like Peoria and our staff,' Mowder said, 'and I don't know, I was really proud of us for like making her feel at home the whole time she was here.'

title: A ‘heart the size of Texas': Family grieves young woman who was fatally shot in Peoria
author: Zach Roth
description: Mary Halcomb is remembered as a caring, kind person who was studying to become a nurse.
content:
It was 1:30 a.m. on Sept. 7 and Ashley Halcomb had awoken to hear the sound of a knock at the door. It's not the most convenient time for someone to be asking to come into her house and she felt a sense that something, anything, was awry.
"From the time I opened my eyes to the noise, I had a feeling that something wasn't right," Halcomb, who lives in Mapleton, said. "Both my husband and I knew something was wrong."
Indeed, something terrible had happened to their oldest daughter, 20-year-old Mary Halcomb, and a detective from the Peoria Police Department – along with Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood – had arrived at their home in the dark of night to give them the news no parents ever want to hear.
Mary had been killed earlier that night at a home in the 1400 block of South Griswold Street in Peoria. Upon hearing the news, Ashley went into a state of shock, not quite believing the facts that she had heard from the authorities.
"I went into sheer shock and numbness," Ashley said. "I didn't want to believe any of it was true."
Unfortunately for Ashley, her husband, Luke, her two other children Chloe and Braxton and the rest of her family, it was true. The circumstances surrounding her death were considered"brutal (and) violent" by a Peoria County judge and have the family wondering about the right way to move forward following a tremendous shock.
How it happened
According to the Peoria County State's Attorney's Office, detectives from the Peoria Police Department found Mary's body on the steps of stairs inside the home, with a gunshot wound in her neck. Located in her hands was a firearm with a bloody fingerprint.
Officers began searching the home, when they came across a bedroom soaked in blood. A sticky note was placed to the wall, with a promise that Mary wouldn't break the heart of her boyfriend, 18-year-old Nathaniel Archuleta. If she broke the promise, Archuleta would have no choice but to "euthanize" her.
Archuleta was at the scene that night and spoke with detectives. However, Assistant State's Attorney Terry Muench said that he frequently changed his story, at first telling detectives that the gun used to kill Mary accidentally went off when he was trying to clean it, but changed tack when it was discovered that he had nothing to clean the firearm available to him in the house.
He did tell detectives that he was upset Mary was talking to another man that evening and denied putting the gun in her hands. However, officers found a loaded clip inside his car, and an autopsy from Harwood's office indicated that when the gun was fired, it was 2 to 3 feet from Mary's neck.
Because of the inconsistencies in his story, Muench argued in court that Archuleta had been trying to cover up his alleged actions to frame it as a suicide.
Circuit Judge Mark Gilles ruled last week that Archuleta would have to be held at the Peoria County Jail before his trial on first-degree murder charges. Arraignment is set for Oct. 10 at 1 p.m.
'A heart as big as Texas'
Mary was born when Ashley was 20 years old, and her mother says that the two grew up together, in some ways. By the time she became an adult, the two thought of each other as close friends.
"We did everything together," Ashley said. "She told me everything – sometimes a little bit too much – but I knew she trusted me."
Ashley said that Mary had a "contagious" laugh and was someone who had a "heart the size of Texas."
"She'd do anything for anyone," Ashley said.
Jayne Halcomb, Mary's paternal grandmother, said that she was a "kind, giving" person who cared for people – appropriate considering she was studying to become a nurse at Midwest Technical Institute.
"At first, she wanted to become a doctor," Jayne said. "After she grew up, I think she realized that being a nurse would be best. She worked two to three jobs and was a nurse's aid at several nursing homes and hospitals."
Jayne also mentioned Mary's passion for softball, where she played catcher for several traveling teams. The family would frequently travel with her to watch her play, with Jayne noting that she was a solid teammate to those she shared the diamond with.
"She was a good, team player," Jayne said. "She was always looking out for the other person. She wasn't self-centered."
Trying to explain the unexplainable
Ashley says she didn't know much about Archuleta, the man that Mary was with on the night of her death. She knew that Mary frequented the house in South Peoria, but not much else.
"I knew that she would go to his house and (she) was friends with him," Ashley said. "(But) that's all I know."
Now, she has to figure out a way forward without her eldest daughter and must explain this to her younger children. Chloe is in high school and, according to Ashley, is struggling to comprehend what happened two weeks ago.
"They were best friends," Ashley said. "She is taking it pretty rough, grieving the best way she can, but trying to keep her mind busy through sports and school."
As for Braxton, the youngest of Ashley's three children, he didn't quite understand what happened to his big sister until he saw her body at the visitation held in Bartonville on Sept. 14.
"It's hard to explain with him," Ashley said. "He's only 10, so up until her services, I don't think he fully comprehended the forever-ness of it. But when he saw his sister at the funeral home over the weekend, it really hit him and he's grieving even harder."
Ashley described Mary as a best friend to her younger siblings, which matches the description of her obituary, which noted how she was always ready to lend a hand at home.
"I miss seeing the interactions between her and her siblings," Ashley said.
Even though two weeks have passed, Ashley remains stunned as to what she has witnessed, with her eldest child and best friend gone in a flash for no obvious reason.
"It feels like a really bad dream," Ashley said.

title: 'Let's do this': Female kicker from Pekin makes football history for Monmouth College
author: Dave Eminian
description: Pekin grad Mylee Hansen kicked a PAT for Monmouth College to become first female to score point in program history.
content:
Mylee Hansen kicked a football between the uprights and into history Saturday when she scored for Monmouth College in an NCAA game.
The Pekin High School grad and Monmouth freshman kicker booted an extra point against Lawrence University, her first collegiate football point in a 52-6 victory in front of 2,501 at April Zorn Stadium and Woll Memorial Field.
The 5-foot-5, 140-pound kicker is the first female in Monmouth football program history to score a point.
"This was such an exciting moment," Hansen said. "It's a very new experience. They kind of mentioned something about it, happening, hinted at it. The coaches were calling 'Mylee, Mylee,' and I realized I was going in there. I'm always nervous before a kick. But nerves make me kick better. The whole moment was such a great experience."
Hansen had a busy day, playing for the Scots' women's soccer team Saturday morning against Illinois Wesleyan before her milestone afternoon. With 6:06 left in the fourth quarter, Monmouth running back Nate Wrublik added the final points of the game on a 13-yard scoring run.
Cody Zelc had kicked extra points for the Scots during the game. But the team sent in Hansen after this final TD to attempt her historic point-after kick, and she delivered.
"I wasn't even stretched," Hansen said, laughing. "I thought, 'Oh gosh, let's do this.' I ran out there, and my holder (East Peoria High School grad Gabriel Zeigler-Harris) said, 'No problem, you got this.' "
Piles of points and perfection: What we learned about Peoria-area football in Week 4
And she did, while her mother, Amy, and her father, Dan, and twin brother, Cooper, looked on.
"If you'd told me when I was younger that I'd kick a college point some day, I'd probably tell you I would not believe it," Hansen said, laughing. "It was a crazy experience. I wouldn't change it for anything."
Hansen was the first female kicker in Pekin's program history. She hit the game-winning extra point against Normal Community in the 2022 Class 7A second-round comeback playoff victory. Video of a tackle she made on a Washington kick returner also made headlines last season.
Hansen played soccer in high school as well, a center-back who earned first-team all-Mid-Illini Conference honors. She helped lead the Dragons to a Class 3A regional title match appearance this past spring.
Are there any female kickers in college football?
Women have an expanding presence on college football rosters. Here is a look at a list of women to score in college football:
1997: Liz Heaston played two games as a placekicker for then-NAIA Willamette University, becoming the first woman to play and score in a college game.
2001: Ashley Martin, kicking for Jacksonville State, became the first woman to score in an NCAA Division I-AA game.
2003: Katie Hnida kicked a pair of extra points for NCAA Division I-A New Mexico in 2003.
2003: Tonya Butler kicked a field goal for West Alabama.
2015: April Goss kicked an extra point for Kent State.
2020: Sarah Fuller kicked a pair of extra points for Vanderbilt.
2023: Leilani Armenta joined the Jackson State roster and kicked some extra points.
2024: Mylee Hansen kicked an extra point for NCAA Division III Monmouth College.

title: Who are Pekin's highest-paid city employees? These 20 have salaries over $100K a year
author: Mike Kramer
description: Pekin's city manager is the highest-paid city employee, followed by the highest-ranking members of the police and fire departments.
content:
Illinois statute requires municipalities that participate in the Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund to publicly post a list of all employees making more than $75,000 in total compensation.
The Journal Star is reviewing those public documents and sharing contents of the reports with readers for transparency. Pekin's compensation report includes annual salary; education and other premiums; holiday payouts; allowances for equipment and uniforms; and stipends.
Here are the 20 highest salaries for Pekin employees for 2024-25, according to the city's annual compensation report. The report has not been posted on the City of Pekin website, but copies are available for public viewing at Pekin City Hall at 11 S. Capitol St. or by emailing Pekin city clerk Sue McMillan at smcmillan@ci.pekin.il.us.
1. John Dossey
As Pekin's city manager, Dossey is the administrative head of the municipality and responsible for its day-to-day operations, implementing city policies, preparing and submitting budgets to the City Council, personnel management and delivery of city services. He is Pekin's highest-paid city employee, with an annual salary of $175,100.12, which is also his total compensation, according to Pekin's compensation report.
2. Seth Ranney
Pekin's police chief, Ranney collects an annual salary of $142,139.92, and an annual $1,100 equipment and uniform allowance for a total compensation of $143,239.92. Ranney served as the city's deputy police chief until 2023, when then-police Chief Dossey assumed the city manager role.
3. Trent Reeise
Reeise garners a $142,139.92 annual salary and a $700 equipment and uniform allowance for a total compensation of $142,839.92. Pekin's fire chief is responsible for the Fire Department's administrative, fiscal and operational aspects.
4. Courtney Hutchinson
One of the city's two deputy police chiefs, Hutchinson earns an annual salary of $131,839.76 and a $1,100 uniform allowance for a total compensation package of $132,939.76
5. Brian Willmert
A deputy police chief, Willmert's $132,939.76 total compensation includes a $131,839.76 annual salary and a $1,100 uniform allowance.
6. Anthony Rendleman
The annual salary for Pekin's deputy fire chief is $131,839.76. Rendleman's $700 annual uniform allowance boosts his total compensation to $132,539.76
7. Dean Schneider
The city's public works director, Schneider oversees the day-to-day maintenance of Pekin's infrastructure services. His total compensation consists of a $124,578.48 annual salary.
8. Joshua Bush
A lieutenant with the Pekin Police Department, Bush's annual salary was listed as $121,036.76, with an $1,100 equipment and uniform allowance for a total compensation of $122,136.76.
9. Matthew Damron
Damron's $122,136.76 total compensation as a police lieutenant includes a $121,036.76 annual salary and an $1,100 equipment and uniform allowance.
10. Robert Jones
As a Pekin police lieutenant, Jones' annual salary was listed as $121,036.76, with $1,100 in equipment and uniform allowance for a total compensation of $122,136.76.
11. Matthew Kirk
Kirk is listed as a lieutenant in the Pekin Police Department with an annual salary of $121,036.76. His total compensation is listed as $122,136.76, which includes $1,100 in equipment and uniform allowance.
12. Justin Rabe
With a title of lieutenant in the Pekin Police Department, Rabe's annual salary was listed as $121,036.76. He also receives an $1,100 equipment and uniform allowance, bringing his total compensation to $122,136.76.
13. Josie Esker
As Pekin's city engineer, Esker manages and directs municipal engineer products. Her $117,022.24 total compensation consists of a $116,122.24 annual salary and a $900 allowance, according to the compensation report.
14. Nic Maquet
Pekin's chief building official, Maquet's role is to ensure buildings comply with building codes and regulations. His total compensation consists of his $110,929 annual salary.
15. Craig Zukowski
Zukowski's total compensation in his role as an assistant fire chief was listed as $121,437.34. In addition to his $107,196.70 annual salary, he was set to receive $7,503.77 for education and other premiums, $6,036.87 for police and fire holiday payouts, and a $700 equipment and uniform allowance.
16. Robert Baughman
As assistance fire chief for the city, Baughman's annual salary was listed as $107,196.70. His $119,180.56 compensation included $5,359.84 for education and other premiums, $5,924.03 for police and fire holiday payouts, and a $700 equipment and uniform allowance.

An assistant fire chief, Turner's $119,180 total compensation package includes a $107,196.70 annual salary, a $5,359.84 education and other premiums allowance, $5,924.03 for police and fire holiday payouts, and a $700 equipment and uniform allowance.
18. Sue McMillan
Pekin's city clerk, McMillan's total compensation is her $102,194.82 annual salary.
19. Shelly Costa
Pekin's human resources director collects total compensation in the form of a $101,969.92 annual salary.
20. Brian Franciscovich
Franciscovich is Pekin's street department operations supervisor. His total compensation consists of a $101,351.90 annual salary.

title: Illinois community among best places to live, according to Money. It might surprise you
author: Mike Kramer
description: The only Illinois community on Money magazine's 50 Best Places to Live of 2024 is a conservation community about 40 miles north of Chicago.
content:
Show Caption
Tucked away in the Chicago suburb of Grayslake, the subdivision of Prairie Crossing has a community model to provide open land preservation, easy commuting by rail and responsible development.
That model has apparently been a successful one. Money magazine recently named the conservation community one of its 50 Best Places to Live in the U.S. of 2024, the only location in Illinois named to the list.
The subdivision occupies more than 650 acres that feature open prairies, wetlands, and an organic farm. Money noted that all homes in Prairie Crossing are built with U.S. Department of Energy approved green construction techniques. The community does not lack for suburban amenities or convenience. In addition to a charter school and a series of bike paths, the town offers commuters two rail stations with trains departing for Chicago every 40 minutes.
Money annually chooses its best places to live based on affordability, quality of education, and the local job market. The magazine also takes community spirit into account, looking for engaged citizens and receptive public servants. Money analyzes research from a variety of public policy and industry advocacy groups as well as statistics from various agencies including the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Labor.
The 50 Best Places to Live of 2024 were not ranked in any particular order.

title: 'More should be done': Sister of construction worker killed in accident upset by charges
author: Zach Roth
description: Chris Neff, 49, was struck and killed while clearing a roadway in Chillicothe in October 2023.
content:
When she heads into the polling booth on Nov. 5, Michelle Neff knows who exactly she isn't going to be voting for in the race for Peoria County state's attorney: the current Democratic incumbent, Jodi Hoos.
The reasoning is simple: She believes that Robert Anderson, accused of striking and killing her brother Chris Neff with a vehicle along Route 29 in Chillicothe last October, deserves to have more serious charges leveled against him. Neff, a construction worker, was clearing the roadway when he was hit.
Instead, Anderson faces a misdemeanor charge of illegally passing an emergency vehicle, leading to injury or death, leveled against him by the state's attorney's office.
"It would be different if it was a complete accident and somebody just walked out in front of him," Michelle Neff said. "It was not like that. My brother's wearing a high-visibility vest, a truck with lights on is right beside him — it was obvious he was in a construction zone."
A bench trial for Anderson is now set for Oct. 7 on the misdemeanor charges.
The Peoria County State's Attorney's Office did not respond to multiple Journal Star phone calls for this story.
Justice for Chris Neff, in his sister's mind, will most certainly come years after his death. A potential civil lawsuit is complicated by the number of children the 49-year-old East Peoria resident had — 14 in total — and grandchildren, many of whom are minors.
"It's tricky, because he had 14 adopted children and he's got grandchildren," Michelle Neff said. "(One of) his grandchildren is 7 and can't speak for himself at this point, so it would have to wait."
All that she has is the hope enough people will listen and take action for changes to be made at the highest level of Peoria County government.
Reckless driving or a 'tragic accident'?
Between Michelle Neff and Anderson's attorney, there isn't much in the way of agreement on how the accident occurred.
According to police in Chillicothe, in the morning hours of Oct. 23, 2023, Chris Neff was one of a group of construction workers who noticed an accident in the intersection of Route 29 and Hillcrest Drive south of the city. The workers walked over to the scene in order to help, and Neff was hit by another vehicle driving into the area.
First responders were unable to revive him, and he was pronounced dead at the scene by Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood.
In the version of events by Michelle Neff and her family, Chris Neff and his crew were helping clear the debris when Anderson's car hit him. Michelle Neff said witnesses at the scene told her Anderson was in a hurry that morning.
"He hit him (and) there was 20 witnesses," Michelle Neff said. "(The state's attorney's office) has to find a reason to charge him with something other than what he is going to get, which is a $250 fine."
She also said those witnesses said Anderson had road rage before he shifted lanes and struck Chris Neff.
"To me, there should be more charges," Michelle Neff said.
However, Anderson's attorney, Kevin Sullivan, told the Journal Star the ordeal was merely accidental.
That morning, Anderson, who lives in Marshall County, was driving to work in Peoria when he came across the accident. Sullivan said traffic was slowed down and funneled to one lane because one of the vehicles involved had been blocking much of the roadway on Route 29.
"As he approached this area, he was traveling below the posted speed limit of 45 mph," Sullivan said. "There were no emergency vehicles — police, fire, ambulance or anything — at the scene. We believe there was a white pickup truck with a white light that was parked adjacent to the roadway, but it was not your traditional red-blue type lights."
Sullivan said Anderson drove steadily past the initial collision before Chris Neff walked out into the lane too quickly for him to prevent a collision. He said it was completely unexpected that Chris Neff would go out into the roadway.
"My client cooperated fully with law enforcement," Sullivan said. "He stayed at the scene, underwent drug testing — he was clean of any substance whatsoever — provided his version of events. This was simply a tragic accident."
Ongoing frustrations over the charges
Michelle Neff says she has found the Peoria County State's Attorney's Office to be less than helpful.
She said one assistant state's attorney told her the office was not going to try to add charges against Anderson. She said they told her they didn't have enough evidence for felony charges, something that Michelle Neff doesn't believe.
"It's me fighting the system — I don't know what else to say," Michelle Neff said. "I feel like more should be done, but I've already been told nothing more's being done."
She criticizes Hoos and her office for not being aggressive enough and for not sending a message that killing a construction worker in a work zone means heavy consequences.
"I feel she is not trying to force more (charges)," Neff said. "I think the message they're sending to all those construction workers out on the road is the wrong one. They're saying it's OK for someone to hit and kill them and nobody's going to be held accountable."
A beloved father and brother is gone
All of this threatens to overshadow her brother and what he left behind. With 14 adopted children and eight grandchildren, many people grew to love Chris Neff and care about the legacy he left.
Michelle Neff said he was the sort of family man who would help their parents out when needed and made sure each of the 14 children were cared for and had the loving environment needed to succeed in life.
"He helped anyone who needed help," Michelle Neff said. "He had no problem (and) he wouldn't hesitate. My dog needed to be fixed (one time). I needed to take her to the vet, but I couldn't pick her up because she was 100 pounds. He rode with me just to take my dog to the vet. That's the kind of person that he was. He would just help, no matter what I needed for 48 years, and he was killed the day after my birthday."
That fact, the joy of celebrating a birthday juxtaposed with the horror of finding out a sibling died just one day later, still irks Neff to this day.
"He was a family man," Michelle Neff said of her brother. "He was at every family function he possibly could. He was at his step-daughter's volleyball games. He was there for his kids whenever he could."
In addition to family, Michelle Neff said co-workers at United Contractors Midwest loved Chris Neff, calling him a positive, upbeat man who got along well with everyone.
"(He was) very sociable (and) liked to joke around," Michelle Neff said.

title: 'Beautiful, bright, cheerful': Two-time cancer survivor mourned after dying in Pekin wreck
author: Mike Kramer
description: The 62-year-old Pekin woman was a cancer survivor and live music enthusiast.
content:
Christie Campbell's zest for life was apparent to everyone who knew her. Battling cancer on two occasions likely enhanced her appreciation for living.
Campbell died Sept. 19 in a two-vehicle collision in rural Pekin. She was 62. After her death, friends and family flocked to her Facebook page to post messages in tribute.
'Our hearts will forever be filled with love for Christie,' her friend Gina Kennedy told the Journal Star. 'I intend to celebrate her birthday (Nov. 19) every year with our friends, as she loved going out for it.'
In 2012, Campbell, of Pekin, was diagnosed with lung cancer that had spread to her lymph nodes. Her treatment went well, and her follow-up tests had encouraging results. Then, in November 2014, she suffered a seizure. Further tests revealed a small tumor in her brain and another in her lung. She underwent emergency surgery to remove the brain tumor and received extensive treatment.
'When I met Christie, her ongoing battle with cancer was the first thing we talked about as I lost my mother to cancer a few years before,' Kennedy said.
Among Campbell's passions were live music and dancing. Natalie Wilson, Campbell's longtime friend, recalled that she would dance with enthusiasm and seemingly without any self-consciousness.
'She could shake her butt,' Wilson said. 'If the mood struck her, she'd do a couple of butt bumps.'
Campbell's favorite local group was the jam band Brainchild. The group played for her when she was being treated for cancer. However, she could be found whenever and wherever there was live music in the Peoria area.
'She was a fixture at all the local shows, and she always had a smile on her face,' said Kindall Rueschel, the chief executive officer of Peoria Music Live.
In addition to live music, Campbell enjoyed playing the piano. She was also passionate about children, her friends, her family, her dog Cosmos, dining out, gardening and dressing up for special occasions. She worked for the State of Illinois Division of Rehabilitation as a rehabilitation case coordinator, and she helped to provide independent living for hundreds of people with disabilities.
'She didn't know a stranger and would make friends everywhere she went,' Kennedy said. 'She was always concerned about everyone else's well-being. Her spirit was beautiful, bright, and cheerful.'
Christie Jean Campbell was preceded in death by her parents, Gene and Verna Ratledge. Surviving are her sons, Dennis Campbell of Pekin and Joshua Campbell of Loveland, Colorado; adopted children Grant Freeman of Atlanta, Garrett Freeman of Oregon and Cirsten Freeman of Peoria; grandchildren Grayson Campbell of Loveland, Colorado, and Eli and Landon Hammond, both of East Peoria; siblings Karen Zimmerman of Pekin and Michelle Ratledge of Naperville; and foster mother Linda Townsend.

title: Iran is preparing 'imminent' missile attack on Israel: White House official
author: Tom Vanden Brook
description: A direct attack by Iran on Israel will carry \
content:
Show Caption
This story has been updated to add new information.
WASHINGTON — Iran is preparing to launch an "imminent" ballistic missile attack on Israel, according to a senior White House official.
The Pentagon is actively supporting Israel in its preparations to defend agains the attack, according to the official who was not authorized to speak publicly. A direct attack on Israel will carry "severe consequences for Iran," they said.
The imminent attack follows Israel's punishing airstrikes and covert attacks against the Iranian-backed Hezbollah militant group in Lebanon.
Earlier on Tuesday, Israeli troops crossed into Lebanon for the first time since 2006. The Israeli military said it was conducting a "localized and targeted" ground operation on Hezbollah command posts and weapons storage sites.
Israel hammers Hezbollah, 1,000 dead
Israel killed Hezbollah's longtime leader, Hassan Nasrallah in an airstrike on Sept. 27.
Israel has pummeled Lebanon with airstrikes in the last two weeks, killing more than 1,000 people, according to the country's health ministry. The escalation between Israel Hezbollah, the largest in nearly a year, was triggered by an Israeli operation that exploded thousands of pagers and walkie-talkies across the country.
In April, Iran launched a barrage of more than 300 missiles and drones at Israel. With U.S. and western allies, Israel shot down almost all of them.
Supreme Leader Khamenei moved to secure location
Iran's Supreme Leader Sayyed Ali Khamenei called for five days of mourning on Sept. 28 for his ally Nasrallah and was moved to a secure location, a second U.S. official said.
Tehran has in the past used mourning periods for operational planning , this person said.
Even as Israel, the U.S., and other allies prepared for a ballistic missile strike on Tuesday, an official noted Tehran could take longer to respond − opting to rebuild Hezbollah's leadership before striking back.
Hezbollah has been firing missiles and rockets into Israel since the Oct. 7 Hamas terror attacks in Israel that killed 1,200 Israelis.
Hezbollah is financially backed by Iran and is part of its "axis of resistance," a network of groups across the region that it funds and provides with weapons, including the Houthis in Yeman and Hamas in Gaza.

title: Could we see the northern lights in Illinois tonight? Here's what to know and how to watch
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: A powerful northern lights display is expected this week and should be visible in Illinois.
content:
The northern lights made a rare Illinois appearance on Monday, Oct. 7, and lit up social media. But the colorful, dancing, atmospheric light show's sequel could be even better.
Social media was abuzz with reports of the Monday light show. The Northern Lights Illinois Facebook page includes accounts and photos from Chicago, central Illinois and elsewhere.
The US National Weather Service Central Illinois Facebook page also posted pictures from Monday.
But Ed Shimon, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service branch in Lincoln, said the best may be yet to come.
"The big show will be Thursday night," he said. "Get your tickets now," he joked. Peak Illinois viewing could begin as early as 9 p.m. and continue until 3 a.m. Friday morning, he said.
Overnight on Thursday, Oct. 10, another "powerful" northern lights display is expected, Shimon said, possibly extending as far south as Alabama — a "highly unusual" occurrence. In Illinois, he predicted "brilliant colors," cloud cover permitting. "It looks pretty good" for a multicolored display, he said.
Friday into Saturday may offer a lesser display, he added.
What are the northern lights?
The northern lights are a type of aurora, a natural light display caused by disturbances in the Earth's upper atmosphere. In the Northern Hemisphere, these displays are called aurora borealis, aurora polaris, or northern lights.
Normally, these natural light shows are only visible at higher, more northern, latitudes. During geomagnetic storms, they can appear farther south, including Illinois. The northern lights can appear as green, pink, purple or blue rays, sometimes with a red border.
Can you see the northern lights tonight?
Shimon expects a lesser experience on Wednesday, Oct. 9. "A little bit of a break," he said, before Thursday. The northern lights are expected to be most visible in Illinois on Thursday, Oct. 10, into Friday, Oct. 11.
How to view the northern lights
The best time, of course, is after sundown. The best place is in dark spaces, away from city lights.
Camera tips for the northern lights
Don't be discouraged by what you see at first, Shimon says. Sometimes, your camera - even on your phone - will capture the beauty of the lights better than your eyes. "Your camera will almost always capture the image of the lights better than your eyes can see them."

title: Young boy killed in Peoria shooting remembered for his love of video games, singing
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Torres L. Johnson II was a 10-year-old fifth-grader whose life was cut short by gunfire.
content:
The 10-year-old boy killed during a botched drug deal last month is being remembered as a young man who enjoyed food and who was looking to become a YouTube influencer before his untimely death.
The family of Torres L. Johnson II posted their obituary of the boy this week, days before his funeral service at Sovereign Grace Missionary Baptist Church on Friday. Torres was described as a boy who loved to sing, eat snacks and play his favorite video games, Fortnite and Roblox.
A fifth-grade student at Elise Ford Allen Academy, Torres was looking forward to growing up and becoming an influencer on YouTube.
Torres was killed on Sept. 29 after he was caught up in what police and prosecutors say was botched drug deal between a group of teenagers and Maurice D. Sargent, 33, near his home in the 600 block of West Romeo B. Garrett Avenue. Torres was merely near the scene when Sargent and the teens got into a dispute that led to an attempted robbery, prosecutors allege.
A bullet intended for the teenagers ended up striking Torres in the chest. Sargent was arrested and has been charged with first-degree murder in the death.
Officers with the Peoria Police Department found Torres in the grass near his home around 7:30 p.m. that night and was transported to a local hospital, where he eventually died from his injuries.
Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood said that Torres likely died seconds after he was shot.
Torres was survived by his parents, Torres L. Johnson I and Kedeedra Coburn, both of Peoria; seven siblings, Jeremiah Sampson, Terrell Coburn, Torreon Johnson, Tamarreon Johnson, Latoria Johnson and Kenzie Coburn of Peoria and Che Blair of Springfield; his grandparents, Todd "Dino" Johnson I, Larnell Butler of Benton Harbor, Michigan and Felicia Shita; his great-grandmothers, Ethel Harris, Elnora Coburn and Jamie Bell-Hollins of Peoria; his great uncle Terrance "Brut" Harris and his great aunt Larnitra "Joy" Butler.

title: Skittles, PB&J and music: What is the gameday routine for high school football players?

description: Food. Music. Lock in. We asked Peoria-area high school football players what they do for a pregame routine. The answers will delight you.
content:

High school football players spend countless hours practicing, conditioning and hitting the weight room.

title: Springfield-area airport recognized as one of the best airports in the state
author: Claire Grant
description: A local airport has been named one of the best airports of the year in the state. Here's what you need to know.
content:
A local airport has been named one of the best airports of the year in the state.
The Illinois Department of Transportation announced the winners of the Airport of the Year award at the Illinois Public Airports Association fall conference in Galena last week.
The Jacksonville Municipal Airport ​won the Large General Aviation airport of the year category. A general aviation airport is a public-use airport that does not have scheduled service or has scheduled service with less than 2,500 passenger boardings each year, according to the FAA.
The awards reflect outstanding achievements of the state's aviation community in different aspects. The awards also celebrate the contribution of airports to the state's overall economy and transportation system. ​
What plays into Illinois' success as an airport hub? According to IDOT, Gov. JB Pritzker's bipartisan Rebuild Illinois capitol program could help strengthen airports outside of O'Hare.
The Rebuild Illinois capital program has been investing into the Illinois transportation through IDOT since 2021.
In that year, IDOT released the $20.7 billion six-year plan aiming to improve roads, bridges and help ensure Illinois remains a top transportation network in the U.S. Pritzker announced a $94 million commitment to airports throughout the state in the program, with an added $11.5 million in local contributions, the largest statewide capital investment for airports in the prairie state's history.
Currently, IDOT is investing a total of $150 million into the aviation industry.
Illinois Airports
Illinois is home to 100 public-use airports and heliports, with nearly 3,000 registered aircraft. The system of airports supports more than 492,000 jobs, with a combined payroll of $21.9 billion and a total economic impact of $95.5 billion according to Illinois.gov.

title: Illinois State Police trooper killed in crash with truck driver. Here's what we know
author: Steven Spearie
description: An Illinois State Police trooper who was part of a motorcycle patrol was struck and killed by a truck driver in Champaign County Friday afternoon.
content:
An Illinois State Police trooper who was part of a motorcycle patrol was struck and killed by a truck driver in Champaign County Friday afternoon.
Corey S. Thompsen, 28, was part of a Special Operations Group and had been with the state police for nearly five years, said ISP Director Brendan F. Kelly at a news conference in Pesotum Saturday.
Thompsen was on-duty finishing a traffic enforcement detail and traveling east on East Leverett Road Friday afternoon.
A truck, driven by Helen Torres, 32, of Thomasboro, was traveling south on County Road 1300 East and stopped at the intersection at Leverett Road when she pulled into the roadway, striking Thompsen's motorcycle.
A witness provided aid until first responders arrived and took Thompsen to an area hospital where he died of injuries around 4:30 p.m.
It is the first fatal crash involving a state police trooper this year.
The intersection is just east of Interstate 57 and northeast of Champaign.
Torres was cited for failure to yield right of way at a stop intersection and not having a valid driver's license (expired less than a year). Torres was treated at a local hospital for injuries.
'When we lose a public servant, a trooper like this, when we lose a noble knight like Corey Thompsen, I really have to ask you all for more than just your prayers and your thoughts," Kelly said Saturday. "Corey was a great trooper."
Gov. JB Pritzker tweeted that Thompsen "should have had a long life of service ahead of him. His family and loved ones will be in the thoughts of Illinoisans across our state."
Pritzker ordered all flags statewide to be lowered to half-staff in Thompsen's honor.
Thompsen, who attended St. Joseph-Ogden High School, is survived by his wife and parents.

title: Fire threatens Rockford apartment complex, damages garage
author: Jeff Kolkey
description: A fire on Sunday night threatened a Rockford apartment complex and badly damaged a detached six-unit garage.
content:
A fire about 7:40 p.m. Sunday in a detached garage complex behind 4520 Trevor Circle caused an estimated $100,000 in damage, according to information from the Rockford Fire Department.
When firefighters arrived, they found a rapidly spreading fire had engulfed the middle two garages of a six-unit garage complex. It was threatening to spread to a multifamily apartment complex, fire officials said.
It took firefighters about 25 minutes from the time of the original 911 call to bring the blaze under control. Damage was contained to the garage complex.
No injuries were reported and the cause of the fire is under investigation.

title: Think tank gives Pritzker average grade when it comes to taxes and spending
author: Tom Ackerman
description: A think tank site recently graded all 50 governors when it comes to taxes and spending. Here's what the report said about Gov. Pritzker.
content:
A think tank site promoting libertarian ideas in policy debates has given Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker an average grade when it comes to taxes and spending.
The Cato Institute recently graded all 50 governors in its Fiscal Policy Report Card on America's Governors report.
Governors receiving an A are those who have cut taxes and spending the most, whereas governors receiving an F have increased taxes and spending the most, according to the think tank.
The think tank gives governors a score from 0 to 100 with higher scores equaling a higher grade. Gov. Pritzker received a score of a 45 and a C grade.
'Governor Pritzker scored poorly on past Cato fiscal reports because of his huge tax increases but he was more restrained on tax and spending increases for the period of this report,' the report read.
The governor's report highlights his fiscal policies in recent years in a mostly chronological narrative.
'Pritzker seems unconcerned that Illinois is losing workers, entrepreneurs, and retirees, who are fleeing to warmer and lower-tax states,' the report reads. 'IRS data show that Illinois has the worst ratio of in-migration to out-migration of any state except New York. Illinois loses more than two households earning more than $200,000 per year for each one moving in. To reverse the migration outflow, the state needs to reduce taxes and embrace leaner government.'
Cato credits Gov. Pritzker for giving taxpayers a break in 2022 but said that 2023 and 2024 again saw tax increases.
'While Pritzker favors higher taxes on businesses in general, he hands out narrow breaks to big corporations. In 2023, for example, he awarded $213 million of incentives to a Chinese battery maker that is building a facility in Illinois. Because 'the company is making a minimum investment of at least $1.5 billion, it's also eligible for exemptions from state and local sales tax on building materials, utility tax, and telecommunication excise tax.' This sort of favoritism for large corporations is both unfair and distorts the economy,' the report read.
The report also criticizes Gov. Pritzker for touting the state's $2 billion Rainy Day Fund in his 2024 state of the state address.
'That figure is correct, but compared to state spending it is the second smallest rainy-day fund in the nation,' the report read, adding that Illinois also has the highest level of unfunded pension obligations of any state.
All six of the A grades given out by the institute were given to Republican governors.

title: What you need to know ahead of the IHSA football playoffs selections for 2024
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: On Saturday, the 256 high school football teams in the Illinois state playoffs will know who and where they play to open the 2024 postseason.
content:
On Saturday night, the 256 high school football teams in the 2024 Illinois state playoffs — 68 conference champions and 188 at-large teams — will know who and where they play to open the postseason.
But you have questions.
We have answers.
Here is a look at some of the frequently asked questions about the Illinois High School Association playoffs and how the eight-class field is set.
Looking for the brackets? They're coming soon. You can find them here on Saturday night
Who's already in the IHSA football playoffs?
Heading into Week 9, there are 221 eligible teams with five or more wins and another 58 with four wins. Officially, as of Friday morning, a total of 143 teams have earned berths via conference championships or by winning six or more games. The final 113 playoff teams will be those who win their sixth game this weekend and the remaining five-win teams with the highest playoff points. If there are still open spots after five-win teams are in, the four-win teams with the highest number of playoff points complete the field.
What are IHSA playoff points?
Add the number of victories by the nine teams on your schedule: those are your playoff points. The higher the number, the tougher the schedule and the more likely a team with fewer than six wins makes the field. For playoff teams with the same number of victories, playoff points also help determine seeding within a class.
How many IHSA playoff points does a team need?
Playoff points are becoming less important for qualification. The last two seasons, every eligible team with five wins has made the playoffs. In 2022, one four-win team made the field, and last season six four-win teams made the playoffs. Four-win teams need a very high playoff point total to qualify. The four-win teams to make the field in 2023 had between 49 and 56 playoff points.
Wait. Teams with losing records get in?
Yep. Last season, for just the second time since the IHSA expanded to eight classes in 2001, the field of 256 included at-large teams with four wins. This is mainly because fewer schools are playing 11-man football — either because of schools combining to join co-ops or programs shifting to 8-player football. Heading into Week 9, IHSA bracketologist Steve Soucie of Friday Night Drive projects five four-win teams to make the field of 256: Chicago Lane, Chicago Kenwood, Oswego East, Elmhurst Immaculate Conception Catholic and Glen Ellyn Glenbard West.
How do we know who is in each class?
First, forget everything about polls or playoff outlooks. A school's in-season classification is strictly a guideline and has no bearing on its postseason class. The IHSA will take the 256 teams that qualify and place them in order of football enrollment (including non-boundaried multipliers, teams playing up and success adjustments). The 32 qualifiers with the lowest enrollments will make up Class 1A, the 32 with the next highest will be 2A, and so on, through all eight classes.
What are ' playing up ' and ' success adjustment '?
Programs have the option to 'play up' into a larger class than their enrollment dictates, an option exercised this season by three schools: Glen Ellyn Glenbard South (6A), East St. Louis (6A) and Antioch (6A). Two teams are bumped up a class by the "success adjustment." Springfield Sacred Heart-Griffin will play in Class 5A, while Chicago St. Rita will play in 7A .
How are the playoff matchups determined?
For the six smallest classes (1A through 6A), the IHSA will divide each 32-team field into 16-team halves based on geography. Seeds within each half are based on: 1) wins, 2) wins by opponents, 3) wins of defeated opponents. After that, ties are broken based on: 1) head-to-head results and 2) random selection by computer. Teams will be paired 1 vs. 16, 2 vs. 15, and so on. The 32-team fields in Class 7A and 8A will be fully seeded (1 vs. 32, 2 vs. 31, etc.)
Who gets to host playoff games?
In the first round, the better seed is host. In subsequent rounds, the team that has hosted fewer times during the current playoffs series is host. If both have hosted an equal number of times, host site defers back to the better seed.
When are Illinois high school football playoff games?
First-round games are the weekend of Nov. 1-2. Playoff games must be played on Saturday unless both schools agree to play on Friday. Friday games must not be scheduled during school hours, and Saturday games must start between 1-7 p.m. The schools must agree on the starting time of the game; if not, the IHSA will set the kickoff time.
IHSA first round: Nov. 1-2
IHSA second round: Nov. 8-9
IHSA quarterfinals: Nov. 15-16
IHSA semifinals: Nov. 22-23
IHSA championships: Nov. 29-30
How can I watch the IHSA playoff pairings show?
In most statewide markets, the IHSA football pairings show will air live from 8-9 p.m. Saturday through the IHSA TV Network, on the NFHS Network and live on ihsa.org. In Peoria, the show will air live on WEEK's CW (channel 25.3). IHSA TV announcer Dave Bernhard will reveal the first-round matchups.
Where are 2024 Illinois state title football games?
At Hancock Stadium in Normal. The 1A through 4A title games will be on Friday, Nov. 29. The four largest class title games will be on Saturday, Nov. 30.

title: Perfection and the playoffs: What we learned about Peoria-area football in Week 9
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The IHSA scores and results are in for Week 9 of the 2024 Illinois high school football season. Here are a few takeaways from Peoria-area games.
content:
Peoria High lost the Big 12 Conference title game, Washington won the Mid-Illini, Dunlap bounced back — and the playoff field is all but set for Peoria-area high school football teams.
Here are some takeaways from Week 9 in Illinois high school football around the Peoria area:
Normal Community shuts down Peoria High
Peoria High ended its regular season 7-2 after a 40-18 road loss to Normal Community, missing out on a chance to share the Big 12 Conference title.Lions quarterback Breon Green finished 13-for-30 with 184 yards and a TD. Running back Detaurion Pollard had 131 yards and a TD on 26 carries.
The Lions could still get a home game in the Class 5A playoffs when pairings are announced Saturday night.
Washington wins outright Mid-Illini title
Washington won the outright Mid-Illini Conference title, beating Morton 54-24 at Babcook Field.
Hunter Reed had four touchdowns for the Panthers (7-2, 7-0), who won back-to-back undefeated M-I titles for the first time since Metamora had five undefeated league campaigns from 2004-2008. Washington has won 19 conference games in a row and has not lost a home M-I games since 2017.
Huge sack pushes Dunlap to the playoffs
Mack Sutter's defense helped Dunlap get back in the playoffs. The four-star recruit blitzed untouched from the edge and forced a key fumble late in the Eagles' 28-20 victory against Metamora.
Metamora (6-3, 4-3) trailed 21-20 and was driving with 2 minutes remaining when Sutter forced the ball loose after sacking Stephen Petri. Dunlap's Charlie Tiezzi returned it nearly 40 yards for a touchdown to give Dunlap a 28-20 lead.
Dunlap (6-3, 4-3) had gone ahead just moments before when Jackson Oldham scored his third touchdown of the game. Tyler Shane's extra point gave the Eagles a 21-20 lead.
Playoff-bound Peoria-area teams
Peoria-area teams will be well-represented in the 2024 playoff field when its announced around 8 p.m. Saturday.
The following 17 teams have officially secured a spot: Peoria High, Dunlap, Metamora, Pekin, Washington, Eureka, Farmington, Elmwood/Brimfield, Princeville, Stark County, Olympia, Annawan/Wethersfield, Illini West, Macomb, Princeton, Rushville-Industry and Monmouth-Roseville.
These 5-4 teams all became playoff eligible thanks to Week 9 victories and are all but assured a spot: Peoria Notre Dame, Deer Creek-Mackinaw and Kewanee.

title: New I-39/US 20 interchange in Rockford nearing completion. Here's what you need to know
author: Corina Curry
description: State and local leaders gathered in Rockford Friday to celebrate the nearly complete $98.8 million reconstruction of the I-39/U.S. 20 interchange.
content:
State and local officials gathered in Rockford Friday morning to celebrate the near completion of a nearly $100 million road project involve two of the city's main thoroughfares — Interstate 39 and U.S. Highway 20.
What does the project entail?
According to a news release from the Illinois Department of Transportation, the I-39/U.S. 20 interchange reconstruction project involved the construction of two new ramps to connect both directions of I-39 to and from U.S. 20 and five new or reconstructed bridges.
What was the goal of the project?
The project aims to improve safety, reduce congestion and enhance quality of life while creating jobs and long-term economic opportunity for the region.
What other physical improvements were made?
The ramps have been realigned with longer lanes and wider shoulders to increase capacity and improve the flow of traffic, resulting in better travel times and increased safety. ​
When did the project start?
The project began in the summer of 2023.
Driving tips
Traffic from I-39 already has been relocated to the new northbound and southbound ramps. Paving is wrapping up on U.S. 20, with all work expected to be complete by the end of November, weather permitting.
While the work zone remains in place, the public should continue to anticipate delays and allow extra time for trips through this area. Drivers are urged to pay close attention to flaggers and signs, obey the posted speed limits and remain alert for workers and equipment.
What other work has been done?
The interchange is part of a larger, $302 million multiyear project to improve I-39 between the U.S. 20/Harrison Avenue interchange and Blackhawk Road. The $44.3 million conversion of the Harrison Avenue/U.S. 20 and I-39 interchange from a traditional cloverleaf to a modern diverging diamond design started earlier this year.
Other elements include expanding I-39 from four to six lanes with an accessory lane between U.S. 20 and Harrison Avenue as well as replacing several bridges in the corridor. Also, U.S. 20 will be expanded from four to six lanes at the intersection of Mill Road, with the bridges crossing the Kishwaukee River replaced with wider structures.
When will the overall project be complete?
The majority of the project will be substantially complete by the end of 2025, with miscellaneous work to be completed in early 2026. All projects are anticipated to conclude by the end of 2027.
— Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker
— Congressman Eric Sorensen,
3,200 miles of highway by 2030
According to the news release, the Illinois Department of Transportation plans to improve more than 3,200 miles of highway and nearly 9 million square feet of bridge deck statewide in the next six years as part of Rebuild Illinois, which is investing $33.2 billion into all modes of transportation.
What they said
'Through Rebuild Illinois, my administration continues to deliver on its promise to modernize our state's infrastructure and enhance the quality of life for our communities. ... The new I-39 and U.S. 20 interchange will soon improve safety and ease traffic flow while driving economic growth for the Rockford area.' — Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker ​
'The rebuilt interchange, combined with other investments made to I-39 through Rebuild Illinois, greatly improves the movement of people, goods and commerce, while setting the stage for more jobs and economic development in the Rockford area.' — Illinois Transportation Secretary Omer Osman
'When my neighbors in northern Illinois get in their cars to go to work, see their families or pick up their kids from school, they deserve to drive on roads that are safe. This multimillion-dollar investment that made the reconstruction of the new I-39 and U.S. 20 interchange possible is an incredible achievement that will make Rockford and Northern Illinois sustainable for generations to come." — U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen, D-17.
'This project underscores the importance of Rebuild Illinois, which is improving our roadways for local travelers, supporting jobs and sparking further economic investment in this region. ... I appreciate the local and state support that went into making this vision a reality.' — State Rep. Dave Vella, D-Loves Park.
'From the upgrades on West State Street and East State Street to the revitalization of South Main, North Main and Alpine, IDOT has proven time and again that they are a true partner in helping Rockford thrive. ... This interchange is one of the most vital arteries in our region. Every day, more than 50,000 vehicles pass through here, connecting people to work, school, recreation and everything in between." — Rockford Mayor Tom McNamara

title: Nearly 5,000 designs submitted for new Illinois state flag. What happens next?
author: Tom Ackerman
description: Nearly 5,000 designs were submitted for a new Illinois state flag. What do you think should be on the new flag design?
content:
Nearly 5,000 new Illinois State Flag designs were entered by the Oct. 18 deadline that could lead to a new look since 1969.
Specifically, 4,844 residents sought to make their mark within the guidelines provided in late August.
For the next step, the Illinois Flag Commission will meet sometime before January to narrow those thousands down to the top 10 designs.
Beginning in January, the public will be able to vote for one of the 10 new designs, or for one of the three former flag designs including the current state flag, the 1918 Centennial Flag and the 1968 Sesquicentennial Flag.
The commission will then report these results to the Illinois General Assembly by April 1. Assembly members will vote on whether to adopt a new flag, return to a previous version of the flag or retain the current flag.
A constituent of Sen. Doris Turner, D-Springfield, introduced the idea, leading she and Rep. Kam Buckner, D-Chicago to move forward the legislation which created the commission later signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker.
"I have always said that history is living, breathing and ever evolving, and I think we need to ensure that government is also evolving so people are engaged," Turner previously said.
The original flag, designed by Rockford native Lucy Derwent in 1915, featured the state seal in front of a white background. It has remained the same since with exception for the addition of the word "Illinois" placed below the seal in 1969.

title: Illinois vs Minnesota score today: Live updates, highlights from Week 10 game
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: It's Illinois vs Minnesota in Week 10 of the 2024 college football season. Follow our live game and score updates as Luke Altmyer leads the Illini.
content:
Illinois football trails the Minnesota Gophers 13-10 early in the third quarter of a Week 10 college football game at Memorial Stadium in Champaign, Illinois.
The No. 24 Fighting Illini (6-2) are coming off a 38-9 loss to No. 1 Oregon, while Minnesota (5-3) has won three games in a row.
Illinois vs Minnesota score updates
Injury timeout for Illinois WR Zakhari Franklin
Illinois receiver Zakhari Franklin hits his head on the turf while leaping to attempt a reception. When they returned from the break, Franklin was ready to return. He was back on the field soon after.
After a short run and a sack, the Illini have to punt it away.
Good start to the half for Illini
The Illinois defense forces a three-and-out on Minnesota's first drive and gets the ball back trailing by three.
Illinois field goal record: Illini miss field goal at halftime buzzer
Illini kickoff specialist Ethan Moczulski tried another long field goal — this one from 55 yards — but it missed at the halftime buzzer as the Illini trail Minnesota 13-10 after two quarters. Moczulski earlier this season set an Illini school record with a 59-yard field goal in a victory against Central Michigan.
Illinois-Minnesota update: Minnesota leads before halftime
The Gophers grab a 13-10 lead just before halftime, with Dragan Kesich hitting a 45-yard field goal just 19 seconds before the break.
Illinois-Minnesota score update: Illini tie the game
And just like that, the Illini are back in it with their longest run play of the season. Josh McCray runs free from 42 yards out to tie the game with 3:28 remaining before halftime. The run capped a seven-play, 75-yard drive.
Illinois-Minnesota score update: Gophers grab the lead
The Gophers answer right back with a eight-play, 65-yard drive capped by a 29-yard TD run from back Darius Taylor, who was almost dragged down short of the goal line. Instead, Minnesota puts the first TD on the board.
Veteran broadcaster Tim Brando calls first game at Memorial Stadium
Veteran play-by-play guy Tim Brando said on the broadcast that this is first time calling a football game at Memorial Stadium in Champaign, Illinois. The Fox broadcaster said he has called basketball games nearby at the former Assembly Hall, now State Farm Center.
Brando, 68, is a former ESPN personality that has called myriad sports, including the NCAA Tournament, the NBA and the NFL.
Illinois-Minnesota score update: Fighting Illini tie the game
David Olano hits a 25-yard field goal to tie the game with 10:08 remaining in the second quarter. Nice drive for the Illini, who took 6 minutes, 25 seconds off the clock going 65 yards in 11 plays.
Pat Bryant catch: Illini receiver pulls in great grab
Pat Bryant is falling to the ground and grabs a throw from Luke Altmyer — an impressive grab for a 25-yard gain. This guy just makes some of these catches look so easy.
Illinois vs Minnesota score update: Gophers lead after one
Minnesota turned a fumble into three points — and after 12 minutes it's been all defense here in Champaign.
Illinois QB Luke Altmyer stays in the game
Despite hitting his head on the ground during the previous possession, Illini QB Luke Altmyer is back on the field with the offense. Backup QB Donovan Leary was shown warming up on the prior defensive possession, but did not come in.
Even with Altmyer, Illinois can't get much going against a very aggressive Gophers defense and punts again.
Illinois defense holds Minnesota to field goal
The Illini made a nice stand inside the 5 and force a 20-yard field goal Minnesota's Dragan Kesich, as the Gophers cash in on the fumble with three points.
Illinois football loses fumble on flip tackle
A tackle and drive by Minnesota's Justin Walley forced a fumble by Illini quarterback Luke Altmyer, who lost the ball while going head under heels on the tackle. Gophers take over.
Illinois Fighting Illini football and Minnesota off to slow start
Illinois and Minnesota trade punts to start the game, each able to gain just one first down before kicking the ball away.
Why does Illinois have stars on their helmets?
The Illinois football team is honoring military veterans with special helmets that have named etched into the stripe and blue stars around the Illinois logo.
The names of 189 students and alumni that died in World War I are etched into the stripe on Illinois' helmets, just like they are in the columns at Memorial Stadium. There are also 10 stars surrounding the Illinois logo on the helmet, which represents each of the 10 Illinois football players that died in battle, nine of which in World War II and one in the Vietnam War. There's also an American flag and a Prisoner of War/Missing in Action flag on the back of the helmet.

title: Playoff heroics in every sport: Vote now for Journal Star high school athlete of the week
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Nominees from Washington, Notre Dame and Limestone are among the postseason heroes up for vote as athlete of the week. Poll is open now.
content:
After plenty of solid fall sports performers over the last week, here are the Journal Star high school athlete of the week nominees for Oct. 28-Nov. 2.
Head to pjstar.com/sports to vote. The poll closes at noon Friday. Information about the nominees is below.
If you have a nominee for the honor, email us at sports@pjstar.com or tag us on Twitter @pjstarsports. Last week, Brogan Benassi of the Pekin football team was named JS athlete of the week.
Hunter Reed, Washington football
Reed put together one of more impressive ground games as the Panthers opened the Class 6A playoffs. The senior running back rushed for 209 yards and six touchdowns during a 52-21 first-round home playoff victory over Palos Heights Shepard on Friday. Reed ran for three first-quarter scores highlighted by a 53-yard TD with 30 seconds left in the frame. He rushed 23 times, averaging 9.1 yards per carry.
Lawson Alwan, Peoria Notre Dame football
The senior fullback/kicker put together one of the most memorable sequences in PND program history during Friday's 59-58 overtime Class 4A first-round victory win against reigning state champion Rochester. His game-tying field 30 yards with 1.8 seconds left forced overtime, then blocked the point-after kick in OT to give the Irish a chance. He scored the game-tying TD from inside the 1-yard line, and kicked a successful extra point for the win.
Bryn Williamson, Limestone volleyball
The sophomore setter came up in a huge spot for the Rockets in winning a Class 3A regional title. Williamson posted a double-double — 12 kills and 19 assists — in beating Metamora, 22-25, 25-17, 26-24 on Thursday night. Her classmate Mia Lamberti also chipped in a double-double with 16 kills and 17 digs. The Rockets (28-9) now play in the 7 p.m. Tuesday sectional semifinal in Ottawa against No. 7-seed Dixon (23-14).
Lauren Harbison, Henry volleyball
Harbison was key in helping the Mallards erasing a long regional championship drought on Tuesday. The setter dished out 18 assists and posted six digs as Henry beat St. Bede, 25-23, 25-19 for its first Class 1A regional title since 2010. Henry (29-7) heads to the Williamsfield Sectional and faces Brimfield (26-4-1) at 7 p.m. Tuesday.
Aiden Faulkner, Elmwood/Brimfield boys cross country
The junior turned in an impressive performance to help Elmwood/Brimfield claim its own sectional title on Saturday. Faulkner covered the 3-mile course at Maple Lane Country Club in 15:26.08 for a fourth-place individual finish. His time along with his four teammates (Reed Florey, Darwin Herman, Mika Nelson and Kai Nelson) gave the Trojans a 27-point win over runner-up Eureka, 53-80.

The sophomore goalkeeper quite literally saved the day for the Irish in Saturday's sectional final. His lone stop in penalty kicks helped Peoria Notre Dame win the Class 2A Dunlap Sectional over Washington. Schmidt saved the first shot he faced as the Irish head to the Elite Eight for a third consecutive season, facing Lemont at 6 p.m. Tuesday in the Kankakee Supersectional.
