title: College Football Playoff committee shows big crush on Big Ten while snubbing BYU, Big 12
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: The College Football Playoff selection committee harbors a November crush on the Big Ten's crème de la crème, with no love spared for the Big 12.
content:
The College Football Playoff selection committee harbors a November crush on the Big Ten's crème de la crème, with no love spared for the Big 12.
BYU is ranked No. 9 despite being undefeated and touting some quality victories.
Big Ten, SEC are well-positioned for four CFP bids apiece.
The College Football Playoff selection committee harbors a November crush on the Big Ten's crème de la crème.
The first CFP rankings paved a path for the Big Ten to snatch four spots in the 12-team playoff, including multiple teams seeded high enough to host first-round games.
The Big Ten's No. 1 Oregon, No. 2 Ohio State, No. 6 Penn State and No. 8 Indiana accounted for half the spots in the CFP's top eight.
Here are my five burning reactions after these initial rankings.
When in doubt, CFP committee values eye test
You can't make a compelling case for Texas to be ranked as high as No. 5 other than the Longhorns looked awesome throughout the season's first six games on the eye test – against a forgiving schedule, we should add. Texas stockpiled an impressive assembly of talent on each side of the ball, but the Longhorns showed vulnerabilities in their past two games against Georgia and Vanderbilt, and their strength of schedule trails Penn State and Tennessee, two other one-loss teams. The committee ranked Texas ahead of both, and also in front of undefeated Brigham Young, a nod to the Longhorns' early season ace-grade on the eye test.
Likewise, undefeated Indiana received some committee love despite having the softest strength of schedule among teams slotted into the current bracket. The Hoosiers look fabulous on the eye test on both sides of the ball. They're not just beating opponents, they're blowing them out.
The Hoosiers' ranking tells me they can afford a loss later this month at Ohio State and still make the playoff – assuming they don't get blown out.
BYU got snubbed, and that stings for the Big 12
The ACC and Big 12 each are vulnerable to becoming one-bid leagues, but the ACC retains an avenue to two qualifiers.
If No. 13 SMU wins out and claims the ACC's automatic bid, the committee positioned itself with these rankings to award an at-large bid to No. 4 Miami.
The Big 12 found no such luck.
No. 9 BYU became the Big 12's lone representative ranked inside the top 16.
If BYU wins the Big 12, the conference almost certainly will be a one-bid league. If the Cougars lose in the Big 12 championship game, they might slide to the wrong side of the bubble, thereby still limiting the Big 12 to one bid.
The committee really did BYU dirty. The Cougars play complementary football. They're among 11 teams that rank in the top 25 nationally in both scoring offense and scoring defense.
They're the only team to beat SMU – and they did so on the road.
They're one of two teams to beat Kansas State – and they routed the Wildcats.
BYU's schedule strength compares to that of Texas, which lost at home to Georgia, but the Cougars are ranked four spots behind the Longhorns. BYU also came in one spot behind Indiana, which has faced a squishier schedule.
'Indiana's strength of schedule is not at strong as BYU's, but what Indiana has done on the field when they're winning those games, they're winning by double digits,' CFP committee chairman Warde Manuel explained on ESPN.
Manuel specifically was asked about the gap between No. 4 Miami and BYU.
'It came down to more of an eye test,' Manuel said.
The upshot: Style points matter, and the committee just isn't smitten by BYU and the Big 12.
Big Ten, SEC set up nicely for CFP bracket
The Big Ten and SEC are positioned beautifully for four bids apiece.
Ohio State and Indiana are the Big Ten's only ranked teams scheduled to play each other, and the committee's early respect for each team gives cushion for either to absorb a loss in that clash and still make the playoff.
Seven SEC teams are ranked inside the top 16. The committee's tough choice on the SEC will come down to which teams to admit.
The committee's task will be more challenging if No. 16 Ole Miss upsets Georgia on Saturday. A win by the Rebels would carve out the possibility of as many as six SEC teams building playoff credentials, with with not much separation among team.
Boise State (almost) got the respect it deserves
Some would say the committee put respect on Boise State's name by awarding a No. 12 ranking to the Group of Five darling. I say the committee could have justified ranking the Broncos a couple of spots higher.
Boise State owns quality wins against No. 21 Washington State and UNLV, and the Broncos pushed Oregon to the brink in a 37-34 loss in September.
The Broncos enjoy the catbird positioning for the Group of Five's playoff bid, and if you combine a BYU loss with Boise State winning out, the Broncos could elevate their position into earning a first-round bye.
Byes are reserved for the top four conference champions. Based on these rankings, it's not automatic that the Big 12 will claim one of those byes.
The cutline for an at-large playoff bid
Based on résumé, future schedules and this peek into the committee's insight, I'm drawing the cutline at No. 16.
If you're a Power Four team ranked No. 16 or better, you retain a chance of earning an at-large bid. Those ranked 17th or lower probably need to win a conference championship to earn entry. That leaves out one-loss Pittsburgh and Iowa State and two-loss Kansas State and Clemson.

Who is historian Allan Lichtman's 2024 US presidential election prediction to win on Election Day − Donald Trump or Kamala Harris?
Distinguished American University, Washington, D.C. history professor Allan Lichtman has correctly predicted 9 out of the last 10 U.S. presidential elections. Lichtman earned his doctorate from Harvard, specializing in modern American history and quantitative methods.
This year, Lichtman has predicted Vice President Kamala Harris will win the 2024 U.S. presidential election. "I've been doing this for 42 years and every four years I have butterflies in my stomach," he told USA Today. "This year, I think I have a flock of crows in my stomach."

When will 2024 US presidential election results winner be announced for President of the United States?
Do not expect final results on Election Night.
Election workers have never completed ballot counting on Election Day at any point in the country's history. This year, local and state certification deadlines range from two days to more than a month after Nov. 5.
In recent decades, news outlets have typically called the presidential race late on election night or the morning after, with two notable exceptions. In 2000, a famously close race and legal challenges dragged out the process — things likely to affect this year's cycle. In 2020, a rise in mail-in ballots during the COVID pandemic delayed results.
This year, state laws still in place in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin prohibiting election workers from counting early votes until Election Day are expected to delay results again.

title: Federal judge strikes down Illinois assault weapons ban, setting up likely appeal
author: Peter Hancock
description: A federal judge struck down Illinois' assault weapons ban, however, the state will likely file an appeal to the ruling.
content:
A federal judge in East St. Louis on Friday struck down Illinois' assault weapons ban on the grounds that it violates the Second and 14 th amendments to the U.S. Constitution and issued an order barring the state from enforcing it.
That order, however, was stayed for 30 days, giving the state time to file an appeal before it takes effect.
In a 168-page opinion released Friday afternoon, Judge Stephen McGlynn sided with plaintiffs in the case who argued the assault-style weapons banned under the law are commonly used for legal purposes such as self-defense.
'What is particularly disturbing is that the prohibition of weapons that are commonly owned and used by citizens are now banned, depriving citizens of a principal means to defend themselves and their property in situations where a handgun or shotgun alone would not be the citizen's preferred arm,' McGlynn wrote.
In March, before the case went to trial, McGlynn issued a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of the law, saying the plaintiffs challenging the law were likely to prevail on the merits of the case.
But the 7 th Circuit Court of Appeals reversed that decision, and in July the U.S. Supreme declined to review it – along with several other cases challenging the law – and remanded all the cases back to district courts for full proceedings.
The case before McGlynn was the subject of a week-long trial in September. Two other cases, each with multiple sets of plaintiffs, are pending before district court judges in the Northern District of Illinois in Chicago.
Meanwhile, a three-judge panel of the 7 th Circuit is scheduled to hear oral arguments on Tuesday, Nov. 12, in a case challenging Cook County's local assault weapons ban.
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul did not immediately comment on McGlynn's ruling. Gov. JB Pritzker issued a statement saying he expects the attorney general will file "an immediate appeal" and for the law to be "upheld through this process."
'The Protect Illinois Communities Act was the result of hundreds of hours of deliberation between legal experts, legislators, and advocates, and it makes Illinois a safer place for everyone,' Pritzker said in a statement. 'Despite those who value weapons of war more than public safety, this law was enacted to and has protected Illinoisans from the constant fear of being gunned down in places where they ought to feel secure.'
Gun rights groups like the Firearms Policy Coalition, meanwhile, issued statements celebrating the ruling.
'We are gratified that the Court properly found that these bans violate the constitutionally protected rights of Illinois residents and visitors. As we clearly showed at trial, PICA fails even under the Seventh Circuit's misguided test that conflicts with binding Supreme Court precedent,' said FPC President Brandon Combs, noting the group was 'hopeful' the U.S. Supreme Court would strike down similar bans.

title: Your guide to 2024 Veterans Day activities around Peoria: Parades, ceremonies and more
author: Mike Kramer
description: November 11 is a day to recognize veterans living and dead for their service and patriotism. Here are a few Veterans Day events in the Peoria area.
content:
Unlike Memorial Day, which is a day to remember and honor military personnel who died in the service of their country, Veterans Day is a time to thank all veterans for their service, sacrifice and contributions to national security. The holiday always falls on November 11, the date World War I ended. Veterans Day was originally called Armistice Day.
Here are some Peoria-area events that will occur on or around Veterans Day, which falls on Monday this year.
Saturday's events
East Peoria: East Peoria VFW Post 2078 is hosting the city's 93rd annual Veterans Parade at 1:30 p.m. on Nov. 9. This year's parade will feature an air show by the Lima Lima Flight Team consisting of four Navy pilots.
Pekin: Pekin Community High School District 303 will place flags at Lakeview Cemetery on Nov. 9. The flags will fly at the cemetery until Nov. 16.
Monday's events
Marquette Heights: Georgetowne Middle at 51 Yates Road, Marquette Heights will host a Veterans Day celebration Nov. 11. The event will begin at 12:30 p.m. and will include a coffee and cake social, a Veterans Day program, and a roll call of veterans.
Chillicothe: St Edward's Catholic School at 1221 N. Fifth Street, Chillicothe will hold a Veterans Day celebration from 8 to 11 a.m. on Nov. 11. The program will include a veteran uniform display, Veterans Day cards and crafts, a flag-folding ceremony, and a fitness event. The City of Chillicothe will host a Veterans Day event at the Chillicothe Veterans Memorial, 1619 N. Santa Fe Avenue.
Peoria: Peoria's annual Veterans Day Parade kicks off at 10 a.m. Nov. 11 at William Kumpf Boulevard and Monroe Street in Downtown Peoria. The parade will continue on Adams Street, then will turn left towards Hamilton Boulevard. and conclude at the World War I and World War II monuments at the Peoria County Courthouse.

title: Illinois voters show support for creating a new 'millionaire tax.' Will it ever happen?
author: Ben Szalinski
description: Voters would have to approve a constitutional amendment to change the Illinois tax system.
content:
A week after ballots were cast, former Illinois Gov. Pat Quinn said the Nov. 5 election results show voters are willing to support a graduated income tax structure to provide property tax relief.
Quinn, who left office in early 2015, made a stop at the Illinois Capitol in Springfield on Tuesday to discuss the results of the election and how 60% of voters supported a question on the ballot to create an additional 3% income tax surcharge on people with taxable incomes exceeding $1 million per year to fund property tax relief.
The ballot question was advisory only, meaning any implementation of such a tax would require separate action from lawmakers – and, in this case, voters.
Illinois has a flat income tax system, however, meaning voters would have to approve a constitutional amendment to change the tax system in order to implement a surcharge on millionaires. A majority of voters rejected a proposed amendment in 2020, but Quinn said a question on the 2026 ballot could get more support if it clearly states a tax rate and income threshold and where the funds would go.
In Quinn's mind, money derived from such a surcharge should be deposited into an already-created property tax relief fund that has yet to receive state funding. Money in the fund would then be allocated to counties and distributed to taxpayers qualifying for a homestead exemption.
'We have a specific way that the voters have identified exactly how to put money into the property tax relief fund,' Quinn said. 'It's a fair way based on a principle that's as old as the Bible that income taxes, and all taxes, should be based on ability to pay.'
'We can win the referendum'
The results of the advisory question, Quinn said, show that voters would get behind a more specifically worded amendment.
'We can win the referendum no matter how much the big shots spend against it. I think we can take them on because our proposal, as exemplified here, is what the people want,' Quinn said.
Senate Republican Leader John Curran, R-Downers Grove, said Tuesday he believes voters would reject an amendment a second time, as they did in 2020 if there is a vigorous campaign opposing it like there was in 2020.
Quinn agreed there are other ways to reduce property tax burdens, but he said after a career of organizing ballot referendums and teaching a property tax law class he concluded that 'the only way to really get the ball rolling in the right direction for taxpayers is refunds, rebates, and that's what this law says.'

title: Comics, costumes and cash: The unique and creative way this Peoria mall keeps growing
author: Mike Kramer
description: As online commerce grows, brick-and-mortar locations like Northwoods Mall have adapted with events like Quad Con, a comic book and toy conventions.
content:
Show Caption
With the rise of online shopping and social media, indoor shopping malls seem to have become less popular shopping and gathering places. Peoria's Northwoods Mall, however, continues to see a steady traffic of visitors and vendors by hosting events like the Quad Con Comic and Toy Show.
'Quad Con has been coming to the mall for seven years and has quite a large following,' said Northwoods Mall general manager Julie Revallo. 'A lot of people call them 'nerds,' but they're fun people who collect vintage comics and toys, play games, and dress up as favorite characters.'
What is Quad Con?
The event comes to Peoria twice a year, and Revallo estimated that it has doubled in size in the past seven years. The most recent Quad Con attracted about 100 vendors and occupied two vacant storefronts as well as the mall's public areas.
'Over the years, it's definitely gotten bigger,' Revallo said. 'And I think it's going to keep growing.'
Even when the mall is not hosting Quad Con, the show seems to have helped bring in traffic and revenue for Northwoods. Revallo noted that The Zone II game store, which sells many items available from Quad Con vendors, has been able to expand and move into a larger space on the mall's upper level. Additionally, Northwoods has recently added new tenants, including the sports memorabilia store Hit List Collectibles.
'We're at 85% occupancy now,' Revallo said. 'We have our two anchor stores, and I believe we only have two empty spaces left. The events we do help because they bring in more people, and we've been kind of blessed with people wanting to open stores here.'
Creativity helps Northwoods Mall grow
A successful indoor mall in the age of online commerce must be nearly as much an events center as a shopping center, as Northwoods Mall is showing. In addition to Quad Con, Northwoods has hosted concerts, fashion shows, children's beauty pageants, and vendor events that focus on local businesses, said Revallo.
'Northwoods Mall is always up for any kind of events to draw traffic,' she said. 'Quad Con was something different we had never heard of, but we gave it a try. They came in and what they brought was just amazing. People came in and shopped and spent money. We always get a great group of people, and we've never had any problems.'
When is Quad Con coming back to Peoria?
Quad Con will return to Northwoods Mall in Peoria on Feb. 15-16, 2025. The show makes stops in Illinois, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, and Nebraska throughout the year. Other upcoming Quad Con stops in Illinois are the Market Place Shopping Center in Champaign, Feb. 1-2, 2025, and at Springfield's Crowne Plaza Convention Center on June 8, 2025.

title: What to know about East Peoria Parade of Lights: What's new for 2024, start time and more
author: Dean Muellerleile
description: Everything to know about attending or watching the 2024 East Peoria Parade of Lights.
content:
An enduring and expanding Parade of Lights will mark a four-decade milestone this year with two new floats.
With a theme of "40 Floats for 40 Years," the annual event begins at 6:30 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 23. The parade will kick off the East Peoria Festival of Lights.
What's new for the 2024 Parade of Lights?
The parade will feature two new floats suggested by the public in a survey. One is a replica of the festival's lighted wreath. The other is being kept a surprise.
Spectators can supplement the spectacle with free foam light sticks. The sticks will feature three functions and multicolored lights. They will be distributed along the route before the parade begins and will also be available at the Mix 106.9 tent in front of East Peoria Community High School.
The parade will feature an expanded soundtrack with Mix 106.9 as the official music provider. Speakers on floats will be tuned to the radio station, which will broadcast commercial-free holiday music throughout the approximately 40-minute parade.
What is the Festival of Lights Parade route?
The Parade of Lights will start at East Washington Street and Dolans Lane. It will continue along Washington Street, turning left at the intersection with Camp Street. The floats will turn right from Washington onto Taylor Street and continue along Taylor in front of Central Junior High School, ending at Taylor Street and Springfield Road at the U.S. Post Office.
A downloadable map of the parade route is available at folepi.org.
Where can I park?
Spectator parking will be available at East Peoria Community High School, 1401 E. Washington St.; the Fon du Lac Park District administration building at 201 Veterans Drive; and Central Junior High School at 601 Taylor St.
Those who park at the junior high school or anywhere along Taylor Street must remain parked until the Santa Claus float has passed by, indicating the end of the parade.
A limited number of designated handicapped parking spots will be available along Taylor Street.
What streets will be closed for the Festival of Lights?
Springfield Road will be closed from Taylor Street to North Main Street from 5:45 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 23, until 4 p.m. Monday, Nov. 25.
Taylor Street and the roads along the Washington Street route of the parade will begin closing at 6:15 p.m. Saturday and be fully closed at 6:30 p.m.
Can I watch from home?
The parade will be broadcast live on WMBD-TV and streamed live on ciproud.com as well as the East Peoria Festival of Lights Facebook page.
If I miss the parade, can I still see the floats?
The floats will be on display at the Folepi's Winter Wonderland drive-through attraction, which opens Friday, Nov. 29, and runs nightly through Jan. 5. Admission is $10 for cars, trucks and vans; $30 for small buses (party, shuttle, mini, school); and $150 for charter motor coaches. Hours are 5-9 p.m. Sunday-Thursday and 5-11 p.m. Friday and Saturday. Hours are 5-9 p.m. Dec. 24 to Jan. 5.
The display takes about 30 minutes to drive through. The Winter Wonderland entrance is off Springfield Road on Par 3 Lane.
History and holiday spirit
The Parade of Lights had humble origins. It was conceived as a singular affair.
'It's amazing to think that 40 years ago the original organizers envisioned this as a one-time event, and look at how it has grown and evolved over the past four decades," said Jill Peterson, public relations coordinator for the city of East Peoria.

title: Oregon is in Big Ten football championship game. Here's how Indiana makes it.
author: Scott Horner
description: The Big Ten released 10 potential scenarios for making the championship game. Here's how the Indiana Hoosiers fit in.
content:
Oregon has earned a spot in the Big Ten football championship game, the conference announced Tuesday. The Ducks have this weekend off and finish their regular season on Nov. 30 against Washington.
The Big Ten has determined even if Oregon loses, it wins tiebreakers involving Indiana, Ohio State and Penn State. It released a list of 10 potential scenarios involving these teams, and IU would make the title game in four of them, it is a "maybe" in one, and it's out in five.
How can Indiana football join Oregon at Lucas Oil Stadium on Dec. 7?
Indiana football scenarios for Big Ten championship game
∎ Indiana finishes 9-0 in conference play, and it's in. The Hoosiers would be the top seed if they're the only 9-0 team. If they and Oregon are both 9-0, the seeds would be based on highest cumulative conference winning percentage of all conference opponents. That's two of the outlined scenarios.
∎ IU gets the No. 2 seed if Oregon finishes 9-0 and the Hoosiers are 8-1, with the loss coming to Purdue. That means IU would have beaten Ohio State, which previously beat Penn State. IU has the best record among games involving those three.
∎ If all four teams finish 8-1, and IU's loss is against Purdue, Oregon and IU get the bids because of wins over common opponents with the highest rankings in the conference standings. In this scenario, IU and Oregon would both own wins over Ohio State, and the Hoosiers would get the No. 1 seed.
Indiana football is a 'maybe' for the Big Ten championship game
∎ In this scenario, Oregon is 9-0, IU and Penn State are both 8-1 (with losses to Ohio State), and OSU is 7-2. The Ducks are the top seed, and the other participant will be determined by the highest cumulative conference winning percentage of all conference opponents for IU and Penn State.
Indiana football misses Big Ten championship game
∎ If Oregon is 9-0, and IU loses to Ohio State, and OSU defeats Michigan the following week, the Buckeyes would get the berth based on beating IU and Penn State.
∎ If IU loses to Ohio State and Purdue, and Oregon, OSU and PSU all finish 8-1, IU is out.
∎ IU, OSU and Oregon are all 8-1, and PSU 7-2, an Indiana loss to Ohio State would knock it out of the title game.
∎ If all four teams are 8-1, and IU's loss is against Ohio State, the Buckeyes and Ducks get the berths.
∎ If Oregon and Penn State both finish 8-1 and IU and Ohio State both finish 7-2, the Hoosiers are out.

Some Big Ten women's basketball teams are using the early part of this season to secure quality victories that could boost NCAA Tournament stock down the road. Others are building confidence by piling up blowout victories over inferior foes.

title: More than 500 workers furloughed at Liberty Steel in Peoria, union says
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Uncertainty continues to surround the future of Liberty Steel as operations are idled at its Peoria facility.
content:
Liberty Steel is temporarily shuttering its Peoria wire mill as the company continues to struggle financially, facing deep debts around the globe amid a challenging steel market. The company has furloughed over 500 employees at its Peoria facility, according to the union representing workers.
In a statement to the Journal Star a spokesman for Liberty Steel said:
"After evaluating current steel market challenges, including the influx of low-priced imports, we have taken the difficult decision to idle the Peoria Wire Mill temporarily from December 6. Wire Mill staff will be retained on furlough during this period, and the organization plans to restart as the market improves, with a projected date of early February."
Liberty Steel declined to identify how many employees are impacted by the new round of furloughs.
Penny Wight, the president of the Independent Steel Workers Alliance in Peoria, said Tuesday in a statement to the Journal Star that the closure of the steel mill will impact 260 employees and the closure of the wire mill will affect another 280 workers.
"This is all due to the financial hardship the company is facing," Wight said.
The closure of the wire mill is yet another obstacle — and another round of furloughs — that Liberty Steel and its employees have faced since the company announced in September that it would be reducing production at its Peoria facility.
In September, Liberty Steel said operations at its wire mill would remain normal while the rod mill and melt shop closed.
Peoria isn't the only Liberty Steel location having troubles in the United States. A Liberty Steel plant in South Carolina is also sitting idle as hundreds of employees were laid off and the company began selling machinery from the plant, according to WPDE. Only six workers remained at that plant, down from 80, the report said in October.
Liberty Steel parent company in deep financial debt globally
Liberty Steel has blamed difficult economic conditions in the steel market as the reason for its struggles, but Liberty Steel and its parent company, the GFG Alliance, are also in deep economic trouble with creditors and tax authorities around the globe.
GFG Alliance owes roughly $870 million to creditors in the United Kingdom following the 2021 collapse of the bank and financing firm Greensill, according to Recycling Today. GFG Alliance is also being investigated by British Authorities from the Serious Fraud Office.
The Swiss Bank Credit Suisse had to recover over $10 billion in funds trapped within the disgraced Greensill firm, which collapsed after credit insurers raised concerns over the firm's massive ties to GFG Alliance owner and steel tycoon Sanjeev Gupta, according to The Guardian.
A London court recently found that Gupta was unlikely to pay more than $147 million in debts that the European branch of Liberty Steel owed after acquiring assets from ArcelorMittal in 2019, according to Reuters.

title: Here are the Peoria area's top 16 high school wrestlers for 2024-25
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: IHSA state champ and reigning wrestler of the year leads a talented list of Peoria-area high school wrestlers to watch for 2024-25.
content:
Here are the top 16 boys and girls wrestlers to watch heading into the 2024-25 season. Statistics and honors listed are from last season. Wrestlers are listed in alphabetical order.
Ian Akers, Peoria Notre Dame
Akers comes into his final prep season after a 113-pound second-place finish at the Class 1A Illinois High School Association state finals. The senior went 41-6 and was named to the Journal Star all-area team.
Jackson Carroll, Illini Bluffs
The senior is the reigning Class 1A 144-pound state champion. He went 51-2 last season and was a member of the Journal Star all-area team.
Ace Christiansen, Princeton
Christiansen was a third-place finisher in Class 1A at 138 pounds. The senior was 39-7 and one of three Princeton state medalists last season.
Peyton Cox, Washington
Cox will be searching for the elusive state title after back-to-back state runner-up finishes during his first two seasons. The junior went 26-2 in his run to the Class 2A 144-pound title bout.
Jose Del Toro, East Peoria
The senior made it to the 285-pound Class 2A third-place match and finished fourth. Del Toro posted a 30-9 record during his junior season.
Bowden Delaney, Tremont
Delaney wrestled for the Class 1A 165-pound state title, finishing second. He enters his senior season following a 45-2 campaign during his junior year.
Dylan Eimer, Olympia
Eimer was a Class 1A fourth-place finisher at 113 pounds last season. The senior went 33-5 last season.
Annalisa Gibbons, Galesburg
Gibbons was a sixth-place finisher at 140 pounds during her junior season. The senior went 22-7 last season.
Savannah Hamilton, El Paso-Gridley
Hamilton will go for another state medal after taking a fourth-place finish at 155 pounds. The senior was 14-4 last season.
Josh Hoffer, Washington
The junior, who is a Journal Star all-area football offensive lineman, took fourth place in Class 2A last season. He finished with a 35-12 mark at 190 pounds.
Katelyn Marvel, Canton
The senior was a fourth-place finisher at 145 pounds last season. She went 27-6 during a junior season.
Wyatt Medlin, Washington
Medlin was the 2024 Journal Star wrestler of the year, winning the Class 2A 138-pound state championship. He went 45-4 and 3-0 as the Panthers won back-to-back Class 2A dual-team state titles.
Cade Odell, Princeton
Odell took fourth place at 285 pounds in Class 1A. The senior went 32-4 during his junior season.
Kinnley Smith, Canton
Smith just missed out on winning a state championship, falling in the 125-pound title match. The senior went 27-4 last season.
Augustus Swanson, Princeton
The junior won the Class 1A 106-pound fifth-place match. He was 35-3 during his sophomore year.
Noah Woods, Washington
Woods is yet another Panther wrestler looking for the medal stand again this season. The senior took sixth place in the Class 2A 120-pound weight division. He finished 40-16 as a junior.

title: Oregon wins Big Ten title in its first season; 45-37 over Penn State
author: Charlotte Varnes
description: Oregon wins Big Ten title in its first season; 45-37 over Penn State; Dillon Gabriel 22-of-32 for 283 yards
content:
INDIANAPOLIS -- Oregon defensive back Nikko Reed stayed with Penn State wide receiver Harrison Wallace III, step by step from the 30 to the 20 and beyond. When quarterback Drew Allard sent a desperate shot to Reed, Wallace was ready.
He tugged the ball down, tumbled into the end zone and brought the Nittany Lions Big Ten Championship hopes down with him with two minutes to go.
Oregon won the Big Ten Championship 45-37, in its first year in the conference. It was a game the Ducks never trailed in, but it didn't feel that way at the time.
Its offense stunned from the get-go, when Oregon quarterback Dillon Gabriel found tight end Kenyon Sadiq frog-hopped his defender and made straight for the end zone. It was a feat of agility, and one emblematic of all that Oregon could do.
The unit looked just as it's been billed: fast, fun, furious, relentless. Route runners were steady on their feet, seemingly unfazed as Penn State defenders reached them. Gabriel was precise, going 22-for-32 as he threw for 283 yards.
Their efforts, plus a handful of detrimental Penn State penalties, pushed the Ducks to a 28-10 lead early in the second quarter. The Nittany Lion looked sluggish, Oregon's offense looked unstoppable and the result seemingly was decided.
Seemingly, but not certainly. Little gains turned into first down. An Oregon pass interference call helped the Nittany Lions to a first down . And what was an 18-point lead became four points at halftime.
But that fiery Oregon offense just didn't stop. Wide receiver Tez Johnson made a catch and juked his defender with ease at the start of the third quarter, sprinting straight into the end zone to make it 38-24. Penn State answered with a quick drive and touchdown (despite a punt pinning it to the third-yard line), but then came Oregon with another score.
Penn State brought the game within eight with a sharp touchdown pass from Drew Allard with less than four minutes to go, bringing a newfound anxiety to the game. But Reed's catch effectively ended their hops.

title: Why star receiver Pat Bryant opted out of Illinois upcoming bowl game
author: Dave Eminian
description: The Fighting Illini will play their bowl game without a star receiver, who has his sights set on the NFL.
content:
Illinois star receiver Patrick Bryant won't play football again for the Illini.
The senior star receiver will opt out of whatever postseason bowl game the Illini play in, coach Bret Bielema said Thursday. Bryant is turning his focus to preparing for the 2025 NFL Draft.
Bryant caught 54 passes for 984 yards and 10 touchdowns — the latter matching the Illini single-season all-time record. He had 137 catches for 2,095 receiving yards and 19 touchdowns in his career.
On Tuesday, Bryant earned all-Big Ten second-team honors and declared for the draft.
Illinois bowl game projections:Updated predictions highlighted by Citrus Bowl game
The No. 21-ranked Illini have won nine games and secured a bowl bid for the second time in three seasons with Bielema at the helm.
The Illini will find out on Sunday what bowl they will play in. Among the leading projections is a spot in the Citrus Bowl, which is a 2 p.m. Dec. 31 event at Camping World Stadium in Orlando.

title: Festive drinks and decor: Find Christmas cocktails at these four Peoria pop-up bars
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: Here are four Peoria pop-up bars to check out this holiday season.
content:
Show Caption
As festively adorned trees peek out of windows and seasonal set-ups sit outside of homes and buildings, it is clear that Christmas is drawing near.
If you are searching for a way to celebrate the season, here are four holiday-themed pop-up bars in Peoria to explore.
Jalapeños Metro Bar & Grill
Ornaments and Christmas lights are suspended from the ceiling at the bar inside of Jalapeños in the Metro Centre. The walls are adorned in a candy-cane like pattern, and a row of Santa hats sit on the backs of bar chairs.
Owner Nora Leon said they were inspired by the pop-up bars they saw while visiting Chicago last holiday season.
"And we thought, well, that's nice. We should start doing something like that in Peoria," she said.
Leon said the bar area was decked out with holiday décor the week of Thanksgiving. Since then, she said the restaurant has received a positive response from customers.
"They loved it," Leon said. "The drinks have been a hit and also, you know, like I said, when they walk in, they're like, 'Oh wow.'"
Jalapeños will host an ugly Christmas sweater day closer to the holiday. Along with this, Leon said visitors who post a photo of themselves at the business on social media will be entered into a raffle for a gift card.
How long will the pop-up last? Leon said the pop-up bar will continue until 'after the new year.'
What's on the menu? Customers can find five holiday cocktails at Jalapeños. The drinks cost $11 each and include:
Aperol cider mule with Aperol, cider and ginger beer.
Carajillo − which combines premium Anejo tequila with Owen's espresso mix and Licor 43.
Cranberry mule with cranberry juice, spiced rum, ginger beer and fresh lime.
Mistletoe margarita, which includes tequila, Gran Gala, agave, fresh lime juice and cranberry juice.
Pomegranate margarita, which features tequila, Gran Gala, agave, fresh lime juice and POM pomegranate juice.
Address: 4700 N. University St., Peoria
Kelleher's Irish Pub & Eatery
Oversized ornaments, strands of lights, large candy canes and colorful Christmas trees hang overhead at Kelleher's Irish Pub & Eatery. The Downtown Peoria restaurant has revived its Jingle & Sip pop-up bar for a second Christmas season.
Customers can attend the seasonal setup, situated in the back of Kelleher's, on Thursday, Friday and Saturday. The pop-up bar offers three seating times.
The first two time slots are from 5 p.m. to 6:45 p.m. and 7 p.m. to 8:45 p.m. Reservations can be made at https://tables.toasttab.com/restaurants/707b6e70-b261-4e3c-910a-b0d8bacd7c56/findTime. Reservations are not required for the final seating, which begins at 9 p.m., and the menu is limited to appetizers and drinks.
"9 o'clock is just kind of, hey, come on in. Enjoy the space," said manager Andy Sepich. "You certainly can still make reservations for it."
Along with the pop-up bar's regular hours, Kelleher's will host various holiday events in the space. This includes:
Paint & Sip on Dec. 11 from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m.
Wreath making on Dec. 18 from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m.
A family friendly Brunch with Santa on Dec. 21 from 11 a.m. until 2 p.m.
Kelleher's also hosted Brunch with Santa on Dec. 7. Sepich said the restaurant wanted to incorporate more family events after seeing a strong turnout at the Cauldrons & Kids Day during its Halloween pop-up.
"We could even do more and do it every weekend, but it's a matter of getting Santa Claus," Sepich said. "Santa Claus is a busy guy, so we were only able to get him for two of the Saturdays."
How long does it last? Jingle & Sip will continue through Dec. 28.
What's on the menu? The food menu features stocking stuffer starters, soups, under the tree entrees and elvish treats for dessert. Sepich said his goal was to create "feel good, 'I'm home,' kind of meals" for the pop up.
Dishes include:
Elven bites for $15. The starter includes baked brie, almonds, cranberries, strawberry fig jam and crostinis.
Reindeer food for $17. The starter includes ahi tuna tartare, avocado, cucumber, pomegranate seeds, scallion, ginger, soy and chips.
Lobster bisque for $9 a bowl and $6 a cup. Sepich said the soup has received lots of positive feedback from the community. He said, "What I heard from the staff is that it's – everybody loved it."
Mushroom Chicken for $25. The dish features chicken with a mushroom sauce and fried onions, green beans and mashed potatoes.
Customers will also find beers, wines and Christmas−themed cocktails and shots, which include:
Holly Jolly Shot, which is a green tea shot, for $7.
O' Christmas Tree for $13. The vodka pomegranate lemonade is served in a seasonal souvenir cup.
Rum Rum Rudolph for $11. The drink is a cranberry maple pina colada.
You Can't Catch Me, which is a gingerbread old fashioned which includes ginger molasses simple syrup and chocolate bitters for $14.
Address: 619 SW Water St., Peoria
Nightjar
Customers will find creative Christmas cocktails and cheerful holiday décor when they visit Nightjar's Snowflake Lane.
"It is fully decorated for Christmas," co-owner Jessie Yoskin said. "We have ornaments and snowflakes hanging from the ceiling. We have a decorated Christmas tree set up, Santa hats on back of the bar chairs, as well as some like, little bit of Christmas lighting. We're having a lot of fun with it."
During December, Nightjar will open at 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday − which is an hour earlier than normal. The business will operate from noon until 5 p.m. on Christmas Eve and will be closed Christmas and New Years Day.
Yoskin said online reservations are available and highly recommended for groups of six or more people.
How long will the pop-up last? Snowflake Lane runs through Dec. 30.
What's on the menu? Inspired by "The Twelve Days of Christmas," Yoskin concocted 12 festively named cocktails that incorporate elements of the song. She said customers who try all 12 during the pop-up will receive "a special little Nightjar Christmas gift." Along with eggnog, the menu features drinks such as:
Reindeer Games for $14. The drink combines cranberry and licorice root infused vodka, sweet vermouth, lemon and honey.
Santa Baby for $14. The drink includes pumpkin butter bourbon, Black Band coffee liqueur and pumpkin spice cream.
Silver Bells for $14. The drink melds pear cognac, sage honey, lemon and bubbles.
O. Tannenbaum! for $14. The drink combines fig leaf infused gin, fig liqueur, Tahitian vanilla syrup and lemon.
Die Hard is a Christmas Movie for $12. The drink features aged rum, rye whiskey, creme de menthe and Pedro Jimenez Sherry.
Oliver's in the Heights
This Peoria Heights pizza place is wishing guests a "Merry Grinchmas" with its Grinch-inspired décor and menu.
General manager Krystine Vos said Oliver's will host Breakfast with the Grinch on Dec. 14 and Dec. 21 from 8 a.m. until 11 a.m.
"We added an extra date because it's so popular and we have so many people interested," Vos said. "They can come on by and enjoy a great meal and get a picture with the Grinch."
The restaurant will also host a Grinch-themed trivia event on Dec. 10, as well as other Christmas events. Vos said customers can find the most recent information about events on the establishment's Facebook page.
How long will the pop-up last? The restaurant's Grinchy Wonderland will continue until mid-January, according to Vos.
What's on the menu? The pop-up menu is available all day alongside the establishment's regular menu. It features starters such as:
Grinchy garlic dough bites for $10. The green garlic dough bites are served with marinara.
Martha Mays Christmas Tree Bread with sausage and cheese for $12.
The Whos Sammys for $12. The dish includes ham, cheese, sautéed buttered onions and mustard served on sweet Hawaiian rolls.
Customers can also find a variety of seasonal drink specials, including:
Cindy Lou Who's Punch for $10. The drink features vodka with cranberry, orange and pineapple juice, along with an orange garnish.
Grinchtini for $12. This caramel apple martini is served in a glass with a green sugar rim.
Mayor Augustus Moonshine, which is a homemade caramel apple sangria, for $10.

title: Peoria takes first step to lure Par-A-Dice to its side of the river for new casino
author: JJ Bullock
description: The owners of Par-A-Dice Casino in East Peoria have indicated interest in building a new casino — but its location is up for debate.
content:
Show Caption
An effort to lure the Par-A-Dice Casino from East Peoria to Peoria was given a push forward Tuesday night when the Peoria City Council unanimously moved to hire an attorney and investment firm to help lead the relocation fight.
The move by Peoria is the first public action to take place in a battle between the two cities over the future of possible land-based casino gambling that has thus far occurred out of the public eye.
Peoria Mayor Rita Ali and East Peoria Mayor John Kahl exchanged a series of testy emails this summer over which city should be the future home of land-based casino gambling in the area.
Ali felt, according to emails, that East Peoria should honor a 1991 agreement signed between the two cities that dictated any land-based casino gaming would on Peoria's side of the Illinois River.
Peoria City Attorney Patrick Hayes said Tuesday night that the 1991 agreement was "straight forward" and "quite simple" in its dictation that any land-based casino must operate in Peoria — in yet another indication that the city has no plans to back down from its quest to bring the casino to its side of the river.
The council made clear Tuesday night it sits firmly behind Ali and her efforts to attract the casino.
In a unanimous decision with no debate, the council approved hiring Innovation Capital LLC and attorney John Elias to help Peoria craft a proposal to entice Boyd Gaming to build a land-based casino in the city. Hayes said their expertise was needed, and hiring them would show Boyd Gaming that Peoria was serious about a land-based casino.
City Councilman Tim Riggenbach gave Ali kudos for her "leadership" in working to bring a land-based casino to Peoria.
Hiring the firms will not be cheap, however.
Innovation Capital will be paid a minimum monthly retainer of $10,000 under the contract. Peoria will pay it another $250,000 if there is a development agreement that brings a land-based casino to Peoria.
The $10,000 monthly payment could be higher if the company's billed hours exceed $10,000 a month. Innovation Capital's managing directors command an hourly fee of $750. Its directors and vice presidents will be paid $500 per hour, and its analysts and associates will be paid $200 an hour for any casino-related work they do for Peoria.
Peoria will pay Elias, the attorney, $395 an hour.
The agreement with Innovation Capital has an initial expiration of six months, but Hayes said it could take a year or longer for the work to be completed, in which case, the deal could be extended.
Debate over future of gaming in the Peoria area
A debate surrounding the future of gambling in the Peoria area resurfaced early this year after Boyd Gaming signaled to the Illinois Gaming Board that it planned to build a new facility, offering a hint that it could be land-based.
That spurred officials from Peoria to go on the offensive and make sure that Boyd Gaming remembered the 1991 agreement that says any land-based casino must be built in Peoria.
Talks between Peoria and Boyd Gaming sparked a sharp response from Kahl, who felt that Peoria was overstepping its boundaries by attempting to lure Par-A-Dice to its side of the river.
Kahl said in an email to Ali this past summer that Peoria's efforts to land a new casino facility threatened to "strain" the relationship between the two cities.

title: 'Thank you for standing with us': Chillicothe business asks for help after fire
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The store's owners promised to rebuild the popular shop at another location.
content:
A Chillicothe resale store is looking to raise $10,000 on GoFundMe after a fire destroyed its building and left owners without a brick-and-mortar store for the time being.
The owners of Sweet Finds said that a fire destroyed their building at 3 a.m. Thursday morning. Ryan Caulfield, son of store owner Tina Lesauskas-Caulfield, said that her mother had been working late when the fire occurred, with her dog Coco being the one to alert her to the fire.
"Coco truly saved her life, and we will be forever grateful," Ryan Caulfield said in a video published to the store's Facebook page Thursday.
According to the Chillicothe Community Fire Protection District, they received a call around 3 a.m. Thursday about a fire in the corner of Chestnut and Fourth streets, where Sweet Finds is located on the corner. When fire crews arrived, they saw heavy smoke coming from the rear of the building and began to fight the blaze.
Crews felt that they had the fire under control quickly, but after opening up the site to heavy equipment, enough oxygen flowed back into the site where the fire re-ignited. It took three hours for firefighters to get everything under control, with crews working until 6 p.m. Thursday to address any hot spots.
Fire officials said the fire did not appear to be suspicious, although an investigation by the Office of the Illinois State Fire Marsha l is currently underway.
Lesauskas-Caufield and her sister, Laura Diazdeleon, are looking to raise $10,000 in funds to help support staff and continue to pay for operations. As of Friday morning, $5,205 had been raised, more than halfway to their goal.
The sisters opened their business in downtown Chillicothe in 2021 with a unique business plan. Each item at the store, from toys to clothing to appliances, sells for the same price, starting at $10 on Friday morning and going down until everything hits $2 on Wednesday. The store would be restocked on Thursday with new items before the cycle began again.
They opened in their current location on North Fourth Street in March. Ryan Caulfield said that he and the rest of their family were thankful for the continued support of the community and for the hard work of firefighters to fight the blaze Thursday morning.
"To everyone who reached out, your love and kindness is everything," Ryan Caulfield said. "To the firefighters who worked constantly from 3 a.m. to put out the flames, thank you. Your efforts kept a tragedy from being worse."
Ryan also said that the owners would keep their loyal customers abreast of any developments as they tried to rebuild, thanking them for supporting the business since 2021.
"Your love and support have carried us through so much already and we're grateful to have you in this community with us," Ryan said. "From the bottom of our hearts, thank you for standing with us."

title: Giving back during the holiday season: What you need to know to help out around Peoria
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: There are many ways to give back and help others this holiday season around Peoria, Illinois, including ways to volunteer and give to charity.
content:
As the holidays approach, it can be easy to get caught up in the twinkling lights, snowy fun and seasonal activities. However, with costs rising and snow falling comes hardship for some families and individuals who may not have access to a warm meal or home.
This year, 50% of Americans surveyed by online retail deal tracker RetailMeNot cited increasing prices as the main cause of holiday stress. Shoppers said they experienced uncertainty about their budget and concerns about fitting in the items they wanted to buy for loved ones.
If you have a little extra pocket change ― or time ― this holiday season, several Peoria organizations are seeking help with holiday shopping for families and children as well as extra hands for event planning. Here are a few ways you can help make the season magical for those in need.
EP!C
What: EP!C, which provides people with intellectual and developmental disabilities opportunities for work and community involvement, hosts holiday meals at its group homes.
When: Ongoing.
How to get involved: Volunteers will prepare a meal and festive table for EP!C residents. Contact Vanessa Estes for more information: epicdevelopment@epicci.org.
Sophia's Kitchen
What: The soup kitchen, formed by the Heart of Peoria Catholic Community, invites volunteers to help with preparing, serving and cleaning up after meals.
When: Sophia's Kitchen operates 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Monday through Friday. Volunteers must be at least 12 years old, have no peanut butter allergies and attend a two-hour training before serving.
The Salvation Army
What: Through the organization's Angel Tree program, The Salvation Army connects local donors to children in need, also known as "angels," to help them receive gifts tailored to their wants and needs. Donors can enter their ZIP code to search for their local Salvation Army unit and add gifts to their Walmart shopping cart. After shopping, Walmart can ship items directly to the Salvation Army or sponsors can drop them off directly. The Salvation Army is also looking for volunteers to assist with its Toy Shop and Food Box Distribution event. Volunteers can help parents and grandparents pick out toys, carry purchases to cars, keep tables stocked and help distribute food boxes.
When: Angel Tree Program through Dec. 18.; Toy Shop event Dec. 17-18 from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. and Dec. 19 from 8 a.m. to 12 p.m.
How to get involved: Visit https://www.salvationarmyusa.org/usn/walmart-angel-tree/ to find a Walmart Angel Tree Registry. For Toy Shop, contact Maddison Barnard at 309-252-9909 or maddison.barnard@usc.salvationarmy.org
Dream Center Peoria Christmas Experience
What: Dream Center Peoria, which offers the only 24/7 emergency shelter in the area for women, children and families, is hosting its Christmas event with games, crafts, stocking-stuffing, professional photos and more. This year's theme is Candy Land, inspired by the iconic board game. Families, individuals and students being served in DCP housing will be joining in on the fun.
When: Dec. 20 and 21
How to get involved: DCP is asking community members to consider donating gifts or money, becoming an event/station sponsor or volunteering. Prospective donors can shop the organization's Amazon Wishlist, and people or groups looking to give their time can sign up for shifts online. Contact volunteers@dreamcenterpeoria.org with questions.
Children's Home Association of Illinois
What: The Children's Home Association provides services to more than 1,800 at-risk youth in Peoria and the tri-county area. Each year the organization offers many ways to donate for the holidays, including both shopping and volunteering.
When: Continuous.
How to get involved: People looking to donate financial gifts can make contributions to A Light in Every Window, which accepts one-time and monthly donations, at https://giving.classy.org/campaign/631588/donate. The Children's Home also has a Target registry with toys, home decor, books and more available to purchase and donate. Those looking to volunteer in person can sign up online.
Is 'Die Hard' a Christmas movie? Peoria IT workers use the debate for a good cause
Neighborhood House
What: Neighborhood House is seeking volunteers to help pack food for its Meals on Wheels program. Tasks would include scooping food and packaging containers.
When: Dec. 22 from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. Prospective volunteers should register by Dec. 20.
Central Illinois Christmas Fund
What: For 112 years, the Central Illinois Christmas Fund — previously known as the Journal Star Christmas Fund — has helped provide food and gifts to families in need. This year, the Journal Star is partnering with WMBD/WYZZ and CIProud to strive toward its goal of raising $130,000 to provide four thousand food boxes, which include a holiday meal and gift card. Those who give a special message with their donation will see it published in the Journal Star and CIProud website.
When: Until the end of the year.

title: Homicide investigation launched after man missing for 5 years found dead in submerged truck
author: Galesburg Register-Mail
description: Human remains discovered in a vehicle found submerged in the Mississippi River in September have been identified of a missing East Moline man from 2019.
content:
Human remains discovered in a vehicle found submerged in the Mississippi River in September have been identified of a missing man from 2019.
A pick-up truck reported stolen out of East Moline in 2017 was found by a dive team on Sept. 15, 2024, submerged in the Mississippi River with human remains inside, according to a news release by East Moline Police Chief Jeff J. Ramsey.
The remains were identified on Dec. 9 as Daniel. L. Claeys by the Illinois State Police Crime Lab through DNA analysis.
Claeys was reported missing out of East Moline in 2019, according to the news release. Claeys would have been 31 years old at the time he was reported missing.
The East Moline Police Department was notified of a vehicle being found in the Mississippi River near the boat ramp at Empire Park in East Moline on Sept. 15, 2024. The vehicle appeared to have been in this location for a long time as it was buried deep in the mud, the news release said.
The vehicle was removed from the river and found to be a pick-up truck that was reported stolen out of East Moline in 2017.
Upon closer inspection of the vehicle, suspected human remains were observed inside. An Illinois State Police Crime Scene Investigator responded and processed the vehicle for evidence.
Examination and identification of the human remains were conducted through the Office of the Rock Island County Coroner Brian Gustafson along with the Illinois State Police Crime Lab.
East Moline Police continues to investigate this incident as a homicide.
Anyone with information related to this incident, can contact the East Moline Police Department at 309-752-1555, Crime Stoppers at 309-762-9500, or submit a tip through the P3 Tips App.

title: If college football coaches want transfer portal fix, how about ditching spring practice?
author: Blake Toppmeyer
description: As players enter transfer portal before postseason begins, coaches cry foul. Want a solution? Fine, then eliminate spring practice.
content:
Some problems feature no easy solution. Call them a sticky wicket, a wicked problem, or the Riemann hypothesis.
Or, college football's transfer portal windows.
Coaches from Steve Sarkisian of Texas to Lane Kiffin of Mississippi grumbled in recent days that the sport's winter transfer period disrupts the postseason, and they're not wrong.
The portal opened on Dec. 9. It will close to new entries after Dec. 28, giving players 20 days to decide whether to stay or go. Players on teams competing in the College Football Playoff have an additional five days to enter the portal after their team's season ends.
The timing of this transfer period means some players on playoff teams entered the portal and left their current team before the season ends.
Beyond the playoff, consider Duke, the Gator Bowl opponent of Ole Miss. Blue Devils starting quarterback Maalik Murphy entered the portal last week. He won't play in the bowl game as he seeks a new team, leaving Duke to play a backup quarterback while in pursuit of a 10th victory that would tie a program record for single-season wins.
'The season's not over yet, and there's a free-agency window open,' Kiffin said during a Gator Bowl news conference, while referring to this setup as 'a dumb system' and adding that you wouldn't see something like this in the NFL.
At Texas, multiple Longhorns entered the portal before their first-round playoff game Saturday against Clemson, including a couple of players who remained with the team for CFP preparation, even while they're in the portal.
'Imagine (NFL) players becoming free agents the day that they announce who's in the playoffs,' Sarkisian told reporters. 'That's what's happening in college football.'
The NFL, though, doesn't offer an apples-to-apples comparison point. For one, NFL players sign employment contracts, while the NCAA remains adamant about not making college athletes employees. More to the point, though, is the reality that this remains college football. The athletes are students, and the academic calendar affects the transfer windows.
Fixing winter transfer problem isn't so simple, but here's an idea
Shifting the transfer portal to after the season would better accommodate coaches pursuing a national championship, but transferring athletes need to get enrolled at their next school in time for the upcoming semester. And playoff expansion lengthened the season, stretching it into the third week of January.
Consider the Texas and Ole Miss academic calendars. The spring semester at Texas begins on Jan. 13, one week before the national championship game, while courses at Ole Miss begin on Jan. 21, one day after the national championship game.
Well then, what about eliminating the winter transfer window entirely and reducing to a single window in April? That would suit the playoff and academic calendars, but coaches would complain that not having transfers in place for spring practice would hamper their ability to prepare for the upcoming season.
Consider a school like Auburn, which must replace its starting quarterback. The Tigers on Saturday announced the addition of Oklahoma transfer Jackson Arnold. The December transfer period creates an avenue to get Arnold enrolled and installed for spring practice.
Think Auburn coach Hugh Freeze would prefer to navigate spring practice with a placeholder quarterback, while waiting until May to get his transfer quarterback in place? Nope.
OK, so here comes my bold idea for a potential solution to this transfer dilemma: Eliminate the December transfer window, but also eliminate spring practice. Dial back to one transfer portal period following the season, and begin preseason workouts in the summer.
Want to be like the NFL? Fine, but commit to that pro model. NFL teams don't play a spring game.
The NFL's organized team activities begin in May. In contrast, some college teams conduct spring practice as soon as February, making that December transfer period essential to coaches needing to reassemble their roster before spring practice.
Dumping the December transfer period merits consideration, as long as it's combined with an elimination of spring practice.
As players transfer before season ends, coaches leave, too
In the current setup, entering the portal allows other interested programs to contact a player, but it does not strictly prohibit an athlete from competing in postseason games with his current team.
A transferring player, though, might find it untenable to juggle preparing for a postseason game while considering transfer options for the following season.
Preston Stone, the backup quarterback for playoff qualifier SMU, entered the portal, but he's remained with the Mustangs as they prepare to face Penn State in the CFP's first round. Penn State backup quarterback Beau Pribula also entered the portal, but he's not sticking it out with the Nittany Lions.
'I feel so awful for our kids and kids around the country," SMU coach Rhett Lashlee told reporters. "There's no other sport at all that has free agency in the season. It's sad. It's terrible."
'(A player) shouldn't have to make that decision' while the season is ongoing, he added.
Maybe not, but what's the alternative? Starting the season at the beginning of August and concluding by Christmas? That opens other cans of worms.
Athletes aren't the only ones exiting before the season ends. Marshall won the Sun Belt championship, then opted out of its bowl game following a mass transfer exodus, amid Marshall's best season in a decade.
What spurred this? Marshall's coach, Charles Huff, flew the coop for Southern Mississippi coaching job one day after the Sun Belt championship game after failing to reach agreement with his now former school.
I'm not criticizing Huff. He's far from the only coach who left his team before the postseason concluded.
Most college football hires occur in November and December – weeks before the postseason begins. Would you be surprised if some coach of a playoff team changes jobs before the postseason concludes?
So, yeah, maybe it's a dumb system, and it's dumb for everyone – players and coaches alike – and the academic calendar puts some time constraints on the transfer period.
No simple fix would remedy every problem, and satisfying everyone seems about as likely as solving the Riemann hypothesis, but eliminating the December transfer window combined with dumping spring practice would be a step toward stability.

title: Our College Football Playoff bracket predictions. Who takes home the national championship?
author: Adam Duvall
description: The expanded College Football Playoff requires a long path for any team hoping to win a national title. Our prediction for the bracket will play out.
content:
The inaugural College Football Playoffs are here.
Twelve teams from across college football begin the march to the national championship beginning Friday night and Saturday on four campus sites across the nation.
With the pairings set for the opening round and the four top seeds locked into a bye before the quarterfinals, here's the Journal Star Sports reporters' predictions for the 12-team playoff:
College Football Playoff predictions: Journal Star picks CFP national champ
Each reporter picked every winner in the bracket and eventual national championship matchup, plus why each thinks the winning program will hoist the trophy on Jan. 20 at Mercedes Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia.
Adam Duvall: Oregon over Georgia
Why Oregon? Oregon continues to win in close games and this will be yet another one. The Ducks are 5-0 in games decided by 10 points or less including three victories over CFP teams in Boise State, Ohio State and Penn State. Georgia has shown its beatable with losses to Alabama and Ole Miss.

Why Oregon? I think the true national title game is the Oregon-Ohio State rematch in the quarterfinals, a coin-flip game won by the Ducks during the regular-season on a rules thing. Georgia likely without QB Carson Beck, so might get picked off by Notre Dame. Arizona State is the hottest team with six straight wins, making for an intriguing underdog. Oregon remains the deepest, most complete team of the dozen, though.

title: Three national chains lined up for Pekin's East Court Village shopping center
author: Mike Kramer
description: Three clothing and discount chains will be adding stores to Pekin's East Court Village in the fall of 2025. Here's what we know.
content:
Three new national retail chains are coming to Pekin next year.
Cullinan Properties announced Tuesday that Ross Dress for Less, Marshalls, and the previously announced Five Below, will join the tenant lineup at East Court Village in Pekin, with openings scheduled for Fall 2025.
'These retailers will help meet the real-world needs and interests of our neighbors here in Pekin and throughout the region, offering more choice and convenience," Cullinan Properties chairperson Diane Cullinan Oberhelman said in a release. "Our goal is to provide a functional, welcoming environment where people can find what they need — all in one place.'
East Court Village, located on Illinois Route 9, a high-traffic corridor that connects Pekin to Peoria and Bloomington, is anchored by such regional and national chains as Hobby Lobby, Tractor Supply Co. and Petco. The new stores are in the location of the former Bergner's.
Oberhelman said East Court Village is being upgraded, and these improvements aim to support the city's economic growth by creating jobs and encouraging further development.
'Pekin is pleased to see these well-known retailers choose East Court Village for their new locations,' Pekin Mayor Mary Burress said. 'Their arrival means more shopping options, more convenience, and more employment opportunities right here in our city."

title: 30 rebounds in one game? Nominees for Journal Star athlete of the week for Dec. 16-21
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Holiday hoops heroes, including one of the state's best all-time rebounding performances. Vote now for high school athlete of the week.
content:
After plenty of solid winter sports performers over the last week, here are the Journal Star high school athlete of the week nominees for Dec. 16-21.
Head to pjstar.com/sports to vote. The poll closes at noon Friday. Information about the nominees is below.
If you have a nominee for the honor, email us at sports@pjstar.com or tag us on Twitter @pjstarsports. Last week, Cole Dubois of the East Peoria boys basketball team was named JS athlete of the week.
Bo Windish, Elmwood boys basketball - Class 1A
Windish put together a trio of double-figure scoring efforts last week. The senior all-state football player capped his week with a 25-point, 11-rebound in Saturday's 65-50 victory over Galva. He scored 11 points to beat Havana, 51-36 on Friday. His week began last Tuesday with 10 points in a loss to Abingdon-Avon.
Jack Blunier, Eureka boys basketball - Class 2A
Blunier gave Eureka plenty of points and rebounds during three games last week. The sophomore's week ended on Saturday with 11 points and five rebounds in beating Havana, 74-30, at the Eureka College Shootout. On Friday, Blunier had 10 points and seven rebounds in a 44-39 defeat to Fieldcrest. His first game of the week last Tuesday resulted in 16 points and six rebounds in a 58-41 loss to Downs Tri-Valley.
Alex McKie, Morton boys basketball - Class 3A/4A
McKie made a living behind the 3-point line in three games last week for the Potters. He tallied 10 treys on the week highlighted by Friday's 14-point effort on four 3s. The junior scored 17 points in last Tuesday's victory over Pekin, hitting a trio of triples. His week ended on Saturday with another three 3-pointers for 10 points in beating Springfield Lanphier, 59-39, at the Eureka College Shootout.
Anna McGlasson, Midland girls basketball - Class 1A
McGlasson put herself in the state record books while posting a pair of double-doubles. The sophomore grabbed 30 rebounds to go with 28 points in last Tuesday's 66-37 victory over Flanagan-Cornell/Streator Woodland. That rebounding total ties McGlasson for 20th all-time statewide for rebounds in a game. Her week ended with 23 points and 13 rebounds to beat Stark County, 45-31 on Thursday. For the week, she had 57 points and 54 rebounds.
Savannah Jost, Tremont girls basketball - Class 2A
Jost stuffed the stat sheet in two games last week. On Thursday, Jost nearly posted a triple-double with 21 points, 13 rebounds and seven steals as Tremont beat Colfax Ridgeview, 53-32. Her week began last Monday with 18 points, four steals and three blocks in a 51-37 win over Lexington.
Keniya Todd, Dunlap girls basketball - Class 3A/4A
Todd continues to impress in her first varsity season. The freshman was named game MVP as the Eagles beat St. Louis University City, 53-50, in Saturday's Southern Illinois Classic Shootout Series. She went for 16 points and 14 rebounds in the victory. Todd also scored 17 points in last Tuesday's 47-41 loss to East Peoria.

Erwin recorded five pins en route to a 113-pound championship at the Clinton Holiday Tournament on Saturday. The freshman capped his undefeated tournament by pinning Clinton sophomore Briley Carter at the 5:26 mark. Erwin posted his first four victories in under two minutes including a semifinal win in just 61 seconds.

Johnson claimed the 170-pound title in Saturday's Metamora Holiday Classic. The junior improved to 11-1 with a pin in 2:48 over Manual sophomore Zanasisa Simmons in the championship bout. Johnson made the final match by winning her semifinal match in 1:49.
