title: Over 70 Boar's Head products recalled after listeria outbreak. Here's what to know
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The outbreak, 'linked to meats sliced at delis,' has included over 30 hospitalizations in more than a dozen states and two deaths.
content:
People who have weakened immune systems, are 65 and older or are pregnant are at higher risk.
So far, 34 infections have been reported, but the number is likely higher.
A Boar's Head liverwurst tested positive for listeria, leading to the recalls.
Roughly 7 million pounds of Boar's Head Provisions Co., Inc. products are being recalled in addition to the roughly 207,528 pounds of product recalled late last week. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service – or FSIS – shared the news on July 30.
Last Friday, the FSIS announced the initial recall after an unopened Boar's Head liverwurst tested positive for listeria. The Maryland Department of Health collected the sample 'as part of an outbreak investigation of L. monocytogenes infections,' which is being investigated by the FSIS, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and others.
The outbreak, ' linked to meats sliced at delis,' has included over 30 hospitalizations in more than a dozen states and two deaths, including a person in Illinois.
On July 30, the FSIS announced: 'Whole genome sequencing results show that a liverwurst sample collected by the Maryland Department of Health tested positive for the outbreak strain of Listeria monocytogenes.'
Which Boar's Head products are being recalled?
Initially, the recall included ready-to-eat liverwurst products which 'were produced between June 11, 2024, and July 17, 2024, and have a 44-day shelf life,' according to the FSIS.
That included 'Boar's Head Strassburger Brand Liverwurst MADE IN VIRGINIA' packages sliced at deli areas or sold in 3.5-pound loaves. Sell by dates on range from July 25 to Aug. 30.
Boar's Head also recalled other deli products produced on the same day and production line. Over 200,000 pounds of product were part of the initial recall.
After testing confirmed the liverwurst was linked to the outbreak, Boar's Head expanded its recall. The business's announcement said all products from its Jarratt, Virginia, facility are being recalled 'out of an abundance of caution,' and ready-to-eat operations are paused at the location.
The FSIS said 71 products sold 'under the Boar's Head and Old Country brand names' have been recalled. The recalled items have been distributed nationwide – with some also being shipped outside of the U.S. Affected items were produced between May 10 and July 29 and sell by dates range from July 29 to Oct. 17.
'The products shipped to retailers bear establishment number 'EST. 12612' or 'P-12612' inside the USDA mark of inspection on the product labels,' the FSIS wrote in its announcement.
A full list of recalled items can be found here.
The CDC said there are reports of 34 people from 13 states being infected from the listeria outbreak as of July 26. However, the CDC noted that the actual number of infections is most likely higher.
Information available to the CDC showed 33 individuals were hospitalized and two people died. One of the deaths was reported in Illinois. The other was in New Jersey.
A CDC Map highlights how many cases have been reported in each state so far. Affected states include:
New York: 12 sick
Maryland: 6 sick
Georgia: 2 sick
Massachusetts: 2 sick
Missouri: 2 sick
New Jersey: 2 sick
Virginia: 2 sick
Illinois: 1 sick
Indiana: 1 sick
Minnesota: 1 sick
North Carolina: 1 sick
Pennsylvania: 1 sick
Wisconsin: 1 sick
In its product recall, Boar's Head wrote: 'On behalf of all of us at Boar's Head Brand, we want to let our customers and consumers know that we deeply regret that our liverwurst products were found to be adulterated with Listeria monocytogenes. No words can fully express our sympathies and the sincere and deep hurt we feel for the families that have suffered losses and others who endured illness.'
What to know about listeria
According to the CDC, there are around 1,600 cases of listeriosis each year – which lead to roughly 260 deaths.
The CDC said people who are 65 and older, have weakened immune systems or are pregnant are at greatest risk. Listeria can lead to premature birth, pregnancy loss or life-threatening illness for newborns. Those who are not at higher risk can be infected but 'rarely become seriously ill.'
A CDC notice from July 26 notes: 'Symptoms usually start within 2 weeks after eating food contaminated with Listeria but may start as early as the same day or as late as 10 weeks after.'
Symptoms can include fever, tiredness and muscle aches for pregnant and non-pregnant individuals, according to the CDC. Those who are not pregnant may also experience symptoms such as:
Confusion
Headache
Loss of balance
Stiff neck
Seizures
For individuals at higher risk, the CDC recommends:
Throwing out or returning recalled meats
Avoiding meat 'sliced at deli counters, unless it is reheated to an internal temperature of 165°F or until steaming hot.'
Calling a doctor if symptoms develop

title: Former Journal Star columnist finds a new role in Peoria media
author: Mike Kramer
description: Former Journal Star columnist Phil Luciano will host a new afternoon radio show on WMBD, its parent company Midwest Communications announced Friday.
content:
A well-known longtime Peoria journalist has changed mediums.
Former Peoria Journal Star columnist Phil Luciano will join the 1470-AM and 100.3-FM WMBD radio team, both Luciano and Midwest Communications, Inc. announced Friday. Starting later this month, he will host the Phil Luciano Show from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m.
'For more than 30 years, I've been sharing intriguing stories and unique observations about central Illinois,' Luciano said. 'I look forward to doing that — again — at WMBD Radio.'
Luciano spent 33 years as a columnist for the Peoria Journal Star, from 1989 until 2022. He then shifted to WTVP-TV, Channel 47 where he did both writing and on-air work. He previously worked in radio, co-hosting a WMBD afternoon show with Jamie Markley.
In his new role, Luciano also will contribute columns and articles to wmbdradio.com.
'We are thrilled to have 'Looch' join our team,' Midwest Communications vice president Mike Wild said in a release. 'His extensive history and knowledge of the market makes him a perfect fit as we continue to WMBD Radio's reflection of our local communities.'
WMBD Radio brand manager Caleb Kelch said the goal of the new afternoon show is to help the station expand in both the broadcasting world and the digital world.
'Phil adds amazing dynamic to those content generation efforts across multiple platforms,' Kelch added. "We are ecstatic to have him as a part of the team.'

title: Looking for a job in the service industry? These Peoria-area restaurants are hiring

description: These Peoria restaurants are seeking servers, cooks, managers and others.
content:
From managers and dishwashers to servers and cooks, many restaurants depend on a strong staff to keep operations running smoothly.
If you are hunting for a restaurant job, here is a noncomprehensive list of local establishments which are hiring. The list only includes restaurants that included information about pay in their listings.
Avanti's
Avanti's is working to fill multiple positions at its various restaurant locations, according to a July 16 post.
On Indeed, the restaurant is hiring full-time carryout workers and full-time line cooks at all locations. The positions earn $15 an hour or more, according to the listings. Avanti's is also hiring an industrial kitchen cook and pay starts at $15 an hour or more.
The establishment is hiring multiple dining room managers. The position is described as full time, with the listing noting that 'an average work week will be 50+ hours.' The pay is listed as $45,000 to $50,000 a year.
In East Peoria, Avanti's is looking to hire a full-time general manager. title: Illinois Democrats pumping 'seven figure investments' into 2 key congressional races
author: Patrick M. Keck
description: Two congressional candidates facing competitive races this November will be getting campaign boosts from the Democratic Party of Illinois.
content:
Two congressional candidates facing competitive races in November will be getting a campaign boost from the Democratic Party of Illinois.
Through Organize Illinois 2024, Democrats will be looking to shore up efforts to keep U.S. Reps. Nikki Budzinski of Springfield and Eric Sorensen of Moline in office by pouring "seven figure investments" into down-ballot campaigns.
The party will be providing communications and organizing staff assistance to the congressional campaigns in addition to aiding Illinois House District 114 candidate LaToya Greenwood — knocked off by Rep. Kevin Schmidt, R-East St. Louis, in the Metro East district in 2022.
In addition to backing the presumptive presidential nominee and Vice President Kamala Harris, Illinois Democrats are hoping to add to their super-majorities in the General Assembly and maintain 14 of the state's 17 congressional seats.
All 118 seats in the Illinois House and 24 of the 59 Illinois Senate seats are up for grabs. Democrats have 78-seat foothold in the House and 40-seat majority in the Senate.
Budzinski and Sorensen are seen as the most sensitive to a potential flip, especially Sorensen where the National Republican Congressional Committee is putting resources to his challenger Joe McGraw. Both, however, have still significant fundraising advantages over their opponents.
"I'm not taking anything for granted in this race," Budzinski told The State Journal-Register during an unrelated press conference at Lincoln Land Community College. "Prior to just being elected in 2022, this was a seat that was flipped back and forth for a number of decades."
Budzinski won that 2022 election, the first one under newly drawn congressional maps, against Republican candidate Regan Deering by more than 13 points. The district was previously represented by former U.S. Rep. Rodney Davis, R-Taylorville, who was forced to run in a deep-red Illinois Congressional District 15 due to redistricting and ultimately lost to U.S. Rep. Mary Miller, R-Oakland, in the 2022 Republican primary.
In this election, Virden Republican Josh Loyd and Green Party candidate Chibu Asonye of Champaign are challenging Budzinski. Budzinski's campaign, as of the latest campaign finance data from the Federal Election Commission, holds more than $2 million in reserves compared to $2,883 for Loyd. There is no data available for Asonye and a challenge to her nomination papers filed with the Illinois State Board of Elections is still pending.
Sorensen, a former TV meteorologist in Rockford and the Quad Cities, similarly has the funding advantage over his Republican challenger. Federal Election Commission data shows Sorensen with $2.5 million on-hand as of June 30 with McGraw, a retired judge, holding just over $475,000.
McGraw, however, will get a helping hand from National Republicans after being named to the party's Young Guns program which provides mentoring and support to GOP candidates.
"Extreme House Democrat Eric Sorensen has fueled the border, crime and cost of living crises that are wreaking havoc on Illinoisans' safety and security," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella said in a news release. "Judge Joe McGraw is in a prime position to flip Illinois' Seventeenth District red and help grow our House majority in November."

title: What is Harvest Hosts? The travel website specializes in unique places to stay with an RV
author: Erich Murphy
description: Pontiac has two sites among the nearly 300 Harvest Hosts sites in Illinois.
content:
The City Hall parking lot in Pontiac, Illinois, is one of more than 5,250 Harvest Hosts sites across the country.
The city is planning a parking lot upgrade later this year, but intends on maintaining its relationship with Harvest Hosts, a travel site that connects recreational vehicle drivers with unique locations nationwide to visit and stay overnight for free.
Here's what Harvest Hosts is and how it works.
What is Harvest Hosts?
According to its website, harvesthosts.com, Harvest Hosts maintains a list of places where RV owners can sign up to "camp" overnight. Places include farms, orchards, wineries, breweries, downtown business districts and popular local attractions and businesses.
How much does Harvest Hosts cost?
Members pay an annual fee of $84.15 to $152.15. The basic membership includes unlimited stays at more than 5,250 sites across North America. Higher memberships include private properties and places like golf courses and country clubs.
The actual overnight stays are free but guests often will spend money in town the night before and the next morning, either stopping by a local restaurant or store or visiting a local attraction or buying gas.
Where does Harvest Hosts operate?
There are more than 300 Harvest Hosts locations in Illinois. They're located in all types of places — from the countryside to urban centers. For a full list of locations, visit harvesthosts.com.
Who can use Harvest Hosts?
Harvest Hosts is a membership program for owners of self-contained RVs. Self-contained RVs do not need to utilize hookups for electricity, sewer and water. There are some sites that offers some or all of these, but most do not.
How do you use Harvest Hosts?
Members make reservations online. If the spot is available, the member will receive a confirmation. Cancellations are made online, as well.
How many nights can you stay?
Harvest Hosts is designed to support travelers. Guests can only stay one night at a time.
What's it like using Harvest Hosts?
Dr. Larry Anthony of Dardenne Prairie, Missouri, recently stopped in Pontiac to use Harvest Hosts. He on his way back from an airshow in Wisconsin. He said he's a big fan of the site.
'I use Harvest Hosts a lot," he said. "It's a freebie.'

title: Meet the 20 principals at Morton and Pekin schools, including 3 new ones
author: Mike Kramer
description: Both Morton and Pekin high schools in Illinois will greet the 2024-25 academic year with new principals.
content:
As students in Morton and Pekin return to school for the 2024-25 academic year, there are three new principals among the 20 schools listed here.
Kirk Edwards takes over at Morton High School, while Shayla Ewing is in her first year as principal at Pekin Community High School. Both Edwards and Ewing have been assistant principals at their schools in the past. El Higus is also new to her role as principal at Morton's Ward Grundy Elementary School.
Morton Community Unit School District 709 students will return to school Aug. 13. Pekin's Rankin Community School District 98's first day of school will be Aug. 15. Pekin Community High School District 303 and Pekin Public School District 108 will begin classes Aug. 21.
Here are the principals for 20 schools in Morton and Pekin:
Morton Community Unit School District 709
El Higus, Ward Grundy Elementary School: Higus is entering her first year as a principal. She began her District 709 career in 2017 as a teacher at Lincoln Elementary School and has worked for the district as an instructional coach since 2022. An elementary school for kindergarten through sixth grade students, Ward Grundy is located at 1100 S. Fourth Avenue, Morton.
Kate Wyman, Jefferson Elementary School: Wyman has been Jefferson's principal since 2015 and was previously a teacher at Morton's Lincoln Elementary School and Lettie Brown Elementary School. Located at 200 N. Jefferson Street, Morton; Jefferson Elementary School teaches kindergarten through sixth grade students.
Faith Waterfield, Lettie Brown Elementary School: Lettie Brown's principal since 2012, Waterfield's prior roles three years as a social sciences teacher at Prairie Central High School in Fairbury, Illinois; and 13 years as a CUSD 709 social worker. Lettie Brown serves students from kindergarten through sixth grade. Its address is 2550 N. Morton Avenue, Morton.
Julie Horchem, Lincoln Elementary School: A Morton Community High School graduate, Horchem previously worked as an assistant principal at Thomas Metcalf School in Morton and as principal at Midland Elementary School in Lacon. Lincoln Elementary School is located at 100 S. Nebraska Avenue, Morton; and educates kindergarten through sixth grade students.
Chris Carter, Morton Junior High School: Before becoming principal in 2022, Carter was Morton Junior High School's assistant principal for 16 years. Morton Junior High School's curriculum is geared toward seventh and eighth grade students. Its address is 225 E. Jackson Street, Morton.
Kirk Edwards, Morton High School: The 2024-25 school year will be Edwards' first as Morton High School's principal. However, he spent five years as Morton High School's assistant principal and six years as Eureka High School's principal before returning to Morton. Morton High School is located at 350 N. Illinois Avenue, Morton.
Lindsay Franklin. Morton Academy: Franklin is also District 709's director of student support services. Located at 260 Queenwood Road, Morton; the school serves students from kindergarten through 12th grade.
Pekin Public Schools District 108
Traci Craig, Altman Primary School: Craig is entering her second school year as Altman's principal. Her earlier District 108 posts include terms as assistant principal at Willow Primary School and Wilson Intermediate School. Located at 1730 Highwood Avenue, Pekin; Altman Primary School serves kindergarten through third grade students.
Melissa Beckham, Dirksen Primary School: Beckham is entering her 22nd year as an educator and her 11th as Dirksen's principal. She was previously the assistant principal at Broadmoor Junior High School. Dirksen Primary School educates kindergarten through third grade students and is located at 100 Koch Street, Pekin
Luke Arnsman, Jefferson Primary School: The coming school year will be Arnsman's fifth as Jefferson's principal. Before becoming Jefferson's principal, he spent a total of seven years as assistant principal at Broadmoor Junior High School and Wilson Intermediate School. A primary school for kindergarten through third grade students, Jefferson is located at 900 S. Capitol Street, Pekin.
Annie Smith, C.B. Smith Primary School: Smith has 16 years of experience in education, including five years as an administrator. C.B. Smith Primary School serves kindergarten through third grade students and is located at 1314 Matilda Street, Pekin.
Matt Green, L.E. Starke Primary School: A District 108 veteran, Green is going to his 27th year working for the district. He previously served as principal at Wilson Intermediate School and is entering his 10th year as principal at L.E. Starke. The school educates kindergarten through third grade students. It is located at 1610 Holiday Drive, Pekin.
Amanda Rickenburg, Willow Primary School: A first-time principal, Rickenburg steeped into the role at the beginning of the 2023-2024 school year. Her prior experience includes 10 years as a teacher and five years as a special education coordinator and administrator. Located at 1110 Veerman Avenue, Pekin; Willow serves students from kindergarten through third grade.
Erin Johnson, Washington Intermediate School: Johnson is going into her second year as Washington's principal. Her previous experience includes four years as assistant principal at Central Primary School in Washington. Washington Intermediate School is at 501 Washington Street, Pekin; and provides learning for fourth through sixth grade students.
Josh Norman, Wilson Intermediate School: Norman has been working in District 108 for 25 years. The coming school year will be his ninth as Wilson's principal. Previous positions include four years as assistant principal at Washington Intermediate School and four years as principal at Altman Primary School, Wilson Intermediate School teaches fourth through sixth grade students and is located at 900 Koch Street, Pekin.
Ty Goss, Broadmoor Junior High School: Broadmoor is a learning institution for sixth through eighth grade students located at 501 Maywood Avenue, Pekin.
Bill Heisel, Edison Junior High School: Heisel became Edison's principal in 2008 after serving as the school's assistant principal for two years. Edison Junior High School educates sixth through eighth grade students. The school's address is 1400 Earl Street, Pekin.
Karla Kenny, Preschool Family Education Center: The Preschool Family Education Center offers pre-kindergarten programs and is located at 1000 Koch Street, Pekin.
Pekin Community High School District 303
Shayla Ewing, Pekin Community High School: Ewing is starting her first year as Pekin Community High School's principal. She was previously the school's assistant principal of curriculum. Pekin Community High School is located at 1903 Court Street, Pekin
Rankin Community School District 98
April McLaughlin, Rankin School: Rankin School serves rural Pekin and educates students from kindergarten through eighth grade. It is located at 15716 Fifth Street, Pekin.

title: Tazewell County home listings asked for more money in July – see the current median price here
author: USA TODAY Network
description: Here's a look at how monthly real estate listings changed in Tazewell County last month.
content:
The median home in Tazewell County listed for $248,650 in July, up 9.3% from the previous month's $227,450, an analysis of data from Realtor.com shows.
Compared to July 2023, the median home list price increased 25.6% from $198,000.
The statistics in this article only pertain to houses listed for sale in Tazewell County, not houses that were sold. Information on your local housing market, along with other useful community data, is available at data.pjstar.com.
Tazewell County's median home was 1,982 square feet, listed at $120 per square foot. The price per square foot of homes for sale is up 13.3% from July 2023.
Listings in Tazewell County moved briskly, at a median 28 days listed compared to the July national median of 50 days on the market. In the previous month, homes had a median of 25 days on the market. Around 154 homes were newly listed on the market in July, an 8.3% decrease from 168 new listings in July 2023.
The median home prices issued by Realtor.com may exclude many, or even most, of a market's homes. The price and volume represent only single-family homes, condominiums or townhomes. They include existing homes, but exclude most new construction as well as pending and contingent sales.
Across the Peoria metro area, median home prices rose to $179,450, slightly higher than a month earlier. The median home had 1,762 square feet, at a list price of $102 per square foot.
In Illinois, median home prices were $339,450, a slight decrease from June. The median Illinois home listed for sale had 1,793 square feet, with a price of $188 per square foot.
Throughout the United States, the median home price was $439,950, a slight decrease from the month prior. The median American home for sale was listed at 1,869 square feet, with a price of $231 per square foot.
The median home list price used in this report represents the midway point of all the houses or units listed over the given period of time. Experts say the median offers a more accurate view of what's happening in a market than the average list price, which would mean taking the sum of all listing prices then dividing by the number of homes sold. The average can be skewed by one particularly low or high price.

title: Buscher on CNN: Calls for sheriff to resign is a 'community-divided issue'
author: Steven Spearie
description: Springfield Mayor Misty Buscher appeared on CNN Friday and encouraged Sheriff Jack Campbell to share the department's hiring and training process.
content:
Mayor Misty Buscher, appearing on CNN Friday, said the call for Sangamon County Sheriff Jack Campbell 's resignation over the July 6 fatal shooting of Sonya Massey by a now-fired deputy is "a community-divided issue."
Earlier this week, Gov. JB Pritzker and Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton formally called on Campbell to step aside.
Buscher, interviewed by Jim Acosta, acknowledged the Republican sheriff does have his supporters. Within the last week or so, "Support Sheriff Jack Campbell" signs have popped up on public right of ways and in yards.
"If the sheriff were to call me," Buscher told CNN, "and ask me what I think he should do, I would say, 'What do you think is going to heal the community the best?' because that's what we're to do as leaders."
Buscher added she would encourage the sheriff's office to share its "hiring process and the training process so the community can learn about that."
Questions have centered around the hiring of Sean P. Grayson, who has been charged with Massey's murder. Grayson and another deputy responded to Massey's home in the 2800 block of Hoover Avenue after a 911 call was made about a possible prowler.
County deputies responded because the home is in an unincorporated area of Woodside Township.
Grayson shot Massey, a 36-year-old Black woman, in the face after a verbal exchange over a boiling pot of liquid quickly escalated.
In his written report three days after the shooting, Grayson admitted he was in "imminent fear of getting boiling liquid to my face or chest, which would have caused great bodily harm or death."
The scrutiny over Grayson's hiring included his employment at six different law enforcement agencies in a little over four years, though some of that work was on a part-time basis.
Grayson had two DUI convictions in Macoupin County, including one while he was still enlisted in the U.S. Army. Both occurred before he was employed as a police officer.
Grayson's separation from the Army noted a "serious misconduct" Campbell said he construed to be the first DUI charge.
Campbell said his stepping down would be "irresponsible."
"I was overwhelmingly elected to lead the Sheriff's Office through both good times and bad," Campbell said. "I am fully prepared to continue leading my office and serving the residents of Sangamon County through this difficult period, ensuring we learn from this tragedy and work toward a better future."
The Sangamon County Democratic Party called for the resignation of Campbell and senior leadership over a "tragically broken culture within (the department)."
Black Lives Matter SPI co-founder Sunshine Clemons said in a Facebook message that she was grateful to Pritzker for using his voice and platform "to support and elevate the Massey family's request for Sheriff Campbell to step down."
Three Sangamon County Board members also have asked Campbell to step aside. At its Tuesday meeting at the Bank of Springfield Center, the 29-member board will consider placing an advisory referendum on the Nov. 5 ballot that would allow voters to weigh in on recalling Campbell.
It is first county board meeting since the fatal shooting. Already, 17 people have scheduled to speak.

title: Despite new assault weapons ban, gun sales increased last year in Illinois
author: Zach Roth
description: Despite new laws designed to restrict gun use in Illinois, sales of firearms increased from 2022 to 2023.
content:
Gun sales in Illinois went up 5% in the past year despite a recently enacted ban on assault weapons, according to data compiled by a national home safety and security news site.
SafeHome, which deems itself as a "trusted authority on home and personal security," said that 504,452 firearms had been sold statewide in 2023, up 5% from similar numbers in 2022. SafeHome used data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation's NICS system, which tracks the number of background checks provided in each state across the country.
The data is then included in a formula that counts each check for handguns and long firearms as worth 1.1 purchases and each multiple-gun verification as worth two purchases. According to SafeHome, they looked to examine the impact of gun sales on American society as a whole.
"By analyzing this data, we aim to provide a clearer picture of gun sales trends and their broader implications for American society," the article said. "We hope that a deeper evaluation of this information can help policymakers and the public better understand this complex issue."
Illinois' 5% increase in projected gun sales was the second most in the United States in 2023, behind North Carolina, which saw a whopping 110% increase in sales.
SafeHome noted that the increase in gun purchases came despite the passage of the Protect Illinois Communities Act, which banned assault weapons from being sold and possessed across the state.
Indeed, the vast majority of background checks on firearms occurred in the early part of 2023, shortly after Gov. JB Pritzker signed the law banning assault weapons. During the first five months of 2023, Illinois had an average of 450,263 different background checks for firearms. In the final seven months, the number went down to 244,274.
Early projections for 2024 show that the new laws, which went into effect on Jan. 1 and survived a legal challenge from pro-gun groups last month, may be having some impact. According to SafeHome, Illinois had 173,562 gun sales during the first four months of the year, and the NICS data shows a lower level of background checks being conducted in that same period, with 241,389 different checks being conducted on average during this period.
Illinois was one of four states to see an increase in gun sales in 2023, with New Hampshire and Florida joining North Carolina as the others to see a jump. However, in per capita sales, Illinois is middle of the pack, with 538 guns sold per 10,000 adult residents. Montana, with 1,586 guns sold per 10,000 residents, topped that list, according to SafeHome.
How local gun shops are impacted
John Stoor, general manager of Pinnacle Gun and Ammo in Bartonville, said that sales of guns, in particular the sorts of assault weapons slated to be banned by Pritzker upon the signing of the bill, went up significantly in the first half of 2023.
"January of '23, sales were through the roof," Stoor said. "Once that ban was in place, they dipped off quite a bit, probably a 80-90% drop in sales until about August-September 2023 (when) sales started picking up again."
In total, sales have been lagging ever so slightly behind their pace at the beginning of last year and before the assault weapons ban, according to Stoor. He did note that customers and weapons companies have been trying to adapt to this new market in places like Illinois, with customers looking for higher-end – yet still legal – items for purchase.
"Where before we sold a lot of entry-level handguns, firearms and shotguns, now we get more people making deliberate purchases – higher-end handguns, hunting rifles, shotguns," Stoor said. "The customer count has decreased, but the sales have actually increased."
Stoor said that the companies themselves are looking back to nostalgia in some ways to maintain sales, with the return of classic models such as lever action rifles, innovating them for a new generation of firearm owners.
"We've seen some of the manufacturers – Sig Sauer, Glock, Smith & Wesson – innovating and bringing back the classic-type cowboy gun models, making those and just getting people interested in these different types of rifles," Stoor said.
For the most part, Stoor feels positive about the way that the firearms market is evolving for his business and for others, even as the landscape looks significantly different from what it was just a year ago.
"I've got a positive outlook," Stoor said. "I've seen the dip and the resurgence of sales. People are just looking for different things to stay in the sport."

title: How to view the Perseid meteor shower this weekend in Illinois
author: Dean Muellerleile
description: In central Illinois, the best chance at peak viewing of the Perseid meteor shower will be this weekend.
content:
Show Caption
The annual and beloved Perseid meteor shower will reach its peak on Monday, Aug. 12.
At that time, over 60 "shooting stars" — a misnomer — could ideally be seen per hour in the night sky, conditions permitting. Unfortunately, Peoria-area conditions might not permit.
The National Weather Service office in Lincoln predicts overcast skies overnight on Aug. 11-12, with 70% cloud cover.
"Conditions look unfavorable" for viewing the meteor shower, said Mike Albano, a meteorologist with the Lincoln office. "Before midnight, maybe there's a chance," he said. After midnight, clouds are expected to increase, with a 20% chance for light rain. Temperatures overnight should range from 55 to 60 degrees.
Meteors occur when small rocky or metallic bits of debris burn up in Earth's atmosphere, reports Adler Planetarium in Chicago. Meteor showers result when Earth passes through a trail of such debris, in this case from Comet Swift-Tuttle. (Though sometimes called 'shooting stars,' meteors do not come from stars.)
Perseid pronunciation and definition
The Perseid — pronounced PER-see-id — meteor shower is named for the constellation Perseus, where the meteors appear to originate. The constellation was named for a hero of Greek mythology.
How to view the Perseid meteor shower
The shower's peak is expected to occur from 12:01 a.m. to dawn on Aug. 12, the planetarium said. In central Illinois, the best chance at peak viewing may be late on Aug. 11, given the forecast.
When does the meteor shower start?
This year's Perseid meteor shower actually began July 14 and will continue until Sept. 1, according to EarthSky.org, which lists the peak as Aug. 11, 12 and 13.
Where to look for Perseid meteor shower
The Adler Planetarium offers the following suggestions for meteor viewing:
First, go outside and give your eyes about 20-30 minutes to adjust to the dark. (Avoid looking at your phone.)
Look all around the sky — in particular, to the northeast — for streaks of light.
You don't need any special equipment, such as binoculars or a telescope, to see meteors.
One rule of thumb for meteor viewing is to be under a dark sky, with no glare from artificial or natural light, such as the moon. This year's peak will occur with the moon near its first quarter phase. After it sets around midnight, the moon won't interfere with the Perseid meteors during their peak between midnight and dawn.

title: Illinois football uniforms: Fighting Illini unveil throwback sets for Michigan game
author: Austin Curtright
description: Illinois football unveiled new uniforms to wear against Michigan this season. See the full outfit here:
content:
This Illinois football season marks the 100th anniversary of Memorial Stadium. And to honor the Memorial Stadium Dedication Game from 1924 against Michigan, the Fighting Illini will don new, commemorative uniforms against the Wolverines this season.
Illinois, which faces the defending national champions Oct. 19., will sport throwback uniforms for the matchup, which are meant to resemble the past uniforms the team worn in 1924. That 1924 roster included Red Grange, a Pro Football and College Football Hall of Famer, who scored six touchdowns against the Wolverines that season.
'The program has done some throwbacks in the past, but it was really important to be more accurate to the time the stadium opened,' said Jake Rosch, director of football equipment operations. 'We kicked around some ideas, but we ultimately settled on recreating Red Grange's uniform from 1924."
The jerseys include a 100-year anniversary patch, with gold stripes that form at the bottom of the jersey. The helmets also are designed to resemble the old leather helmets that were worn during the early years of football. Each helmet was also hand-painted.
'The jerseys are pretty simplistic,' Rosch said. 'It was designed 100 years ago, so they were limited in their manufacturing capabilities at that time. We were able to match the jersey design, which is really cool because we wanted to be as historically accurate from 100 years ago as we could possibly make it.'

title: After contentious debate, Downtown Peoria restaurant denied liquor license for new space
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: Some council members questioned if race played a factor in the decision against the business.
content:
A liquor license saga that has played out for months in Peoria has finally reached a conclusion.
Highly Flavored restaurant will not be allowed to serve liquor at its new location in the Twin Towers Mall following a contentious 6-4 vote by the Peoria City Council on Tuesday night.
The vote came after nearly two months of deliberation over whether or not the business should be allowed to serve liquor from its new Downtown Peoria location.
Throughout the months-long debate surrounding Highly Flavored's liquor license application, opposition to the restaurant never seemed to anchor itself on any particular stance for too long, and on Tuesday night members of the city council — for the first time publicly — questioned if the opposition to the restaurant was based on race.
Some argued in front of the council that the matter had nothing to do with race, but when the council took its vote the four Black members of the Peoria City Council voted in favor of Highly Flavored receiving a liquor license while the rest of the council voted against it for myriad reasons.
Mayor Rita Ali, councilmember Andre Allen, councilmember Denise Jackson and councilmember Bernice Gordon-Young voted in favor of a Highly Flavored liquor license.
Councilmembers Denis Cyr, Zach Oyler, Tim Riggenbach, Chuck Grayeb, John Kelly and Kiran Velpula voted to deny the license, citing unpaid taxes by the restaurant's owner, a lack of faith the business would succeed, and opposition from residents and business owners at the Twin Towers Mall.
Councilmember Mike Vespa abstained from the vote because he owns property at the Twin Towers.
'At some point you have to call a thing a thing'
Gordon-Young, an at-large councilmember and one of the council's four Black members, questioned Tuesday night if Peoria was "redlining" its businesses by excluding a Black-owned operation like Highly Flavored from downtown.
Gordon-Young noted in her argument that the reasons for opposition to Highly Flavored changed as new facts came to light.
"At first we said, 'you had too many police calls.' Well, we dug through that and recognized there aren't any police calls — there was three, and of those three, there was nothing that was problematic," Gordon-Young said. "Then we said 'OK, it's taxes,' so we come up with a plan for that. Now we're saying, 'nobody wants to play with you.' At some point you have to call a thing a thing."
Gordon-Young, Andre Allen and Ali all also noted that other businesses operate out of the Twin Towers Mall with a liquor license. Kickback on Fulton is in the building and has a license, and the Creve Couer Club operated out of the spot Highly Flavored is moving into with a liquor license for two decades.
In his opposition to the site approval for Highly Flavored, Kelly said he did not feel the business should be rewarded when it has unpaid city taxes. Highly Flavored owes Peoria roughly $1,900 in unpaid fees and set up a payment plan to resolve the debt.
Allen retorted at this argument that there are six businesses in Peoria that have unpaid city fees and taxes that also have a standing liquor license.
"I am not looking to call anybody to the principal's office here, but we have to determine when do we want to be accountable and when do we choose to be accountable?" Allen said. "When I look at what happened in Downtown Peoria a couple of weeks ago — again I am not trying to call anybody to the principal's office — but we choose to determine when we want to wave the wand of accountability, and that's why I want to see Highly Flavored get approved for their site approval."
City councilmember Chuck Grayeb, whose 2nd District is home to the Twin Towers Mall, said his opposition to the site was based on feedback he got from residents and business owners at the complex.
"When you do not have buy-in from affected property owners in any neighborhood — you as councilmembers would be advised to answer one simple question, answer one super simple question ... 'who comes first?' The correct answer is the neighbors every single time, ahead of yet one more liquor license applicant," Grayeb said.
Gordon-Young still questioned exactly where the opposition to Highly Flavored stemmed from.
"The Creve Couer Club had been in operation for a long time with the exact thing that they are asking for, a liquor license," Gordon-Young said. "So what are we really questioning? What are we really questioning ... so I ask my colleagues to ask yourselves, what are you really questioning?"
Ali, too, made a point that the Creve Couer Club had a liquor license in that exact spot for many years and asked the council to "be fair" when making its decision about the liquor license. She said while it may be a Black-owned business it was not a business for just Black people.
"It would be a darn shame if there is a denial for this business and some other business comes a little bit later and gets site approval for a liquor license when we can approve site approval for this business," Ali said. "It was said before the liquor commission recommended approval, staff recommended approval, a plan of operation is pending. Those concerns about police calls at Landmark were resolved. So all that's left is somebody doesn't want them to be there, that's all that's left."
Councilmember Denis Cyr said his opposition to the site application was because he did not want to see the businesses' owner Jeremy Sargent lose any more money in this venture and he did not think it was a good idea to open the business downtown where others have been closing recently.
Riggenbach and Oyler did not offer reasoning for their opposition Tuesday night.
Highly Flavored's long road to council denial
When Highly Flavored first proposed moving downtown, the opposition to it was centered on allegations that it had caused an increase in crime and police calls at Landmark Recreation Center, where it had previously operated.
That argument was based on a letter written by Peoria Police Chief Eric Echevarria to the Peoria Liquor Commission in which he stated he had "significant concern" about Highly Flavored operating out of Landmark Recreation and cited that there was 119 calls for police service to Landmark while Highly Flavored was operating there.
Likewise, Landmark's management also wrote a letter in opposition to Highly Flavored, citing the police calls while also saying that Highly Flavored brought increased security concerns to their property.
As it turns out, there were actually fewer police calls to Landmark during the eight months Highly Flavored was there than over the same period of time the prior year, city attorney Patrick Hayes told the council.
Hayes told the council that he reviewed all 18 written police reports from Landmark during Highly Flavored's tenure there and noted that only three of the reports actually mentioned Highly Flavored. He said none of those reports indicated that Highly Flavored was at fault for the police presence.
"I am unable to indicate to the council that there is any verifiable proof of any increase in criminality or calls for service related to Highly Flavored's operational issues at Landmark," Hayes said. "Other people may have anecdotal issues, but I could not prove a case if I was before you seeking to sanction Highly Flavored for their business operations during that period of time."
Highly Flavored's owner Jeremy Sargent said the time it has taken the city council to make a decision about his business has impacted his family and his finances.
His business moved out of Landmark in May after an eight-month stint and soon after announced plans to open downtown. Since then, his business had been kept in limbo about whether it would be allowed to sell liquor.
On Tuesday night, Sargent got his long-awaited answer.

title: When is the DNC in Chicago? Pertinent information for the Democratic National Convention
author: Mike Kramer
description: The Democratic National Convention is Aug. 19-22 in Chicago, Illinois. Here's what to know about the 2024 DNC.
content:
The Democratic National Convention is happening soon in Chicago, and this one will be unique.
When Kamala Harris replaced President Joe Biden on the Democratic ticket last month, this prompted the Democratic party into action. The party used an online roll-call vote to officially nominate Harris and her vice presidential candidate Tim Walz. Political parties normally use the conventions to officially select the nominees.
Since that is already done, this DNC is more about "speeches and confirming the party platform," according to the New York Times. However, Harris has not yet formally accepted the nomination, which she will do at the DNC.
Here is what you need to know about the DNC, in Chicago for the first time since 1996.
Where will the Democratic National Convention be held?
The DNC is in Chicago, Illinois. The party is expecting an estimated 50,000 visitors to the Windy City.
When will the DNC be held?
DNC Chicago 2024 dates are Monday, Aug. 19 through Thursday, Aug. 22.
What time does the DNC start?
DNC 2024 starts with a delegates' breakfast at 7 a.m. Monday, Aug. 19 in Chicago.
Where is the DNC in Chicago?
DNC 2024 will have its morning and afternoon meetings, caucuses and briefings at McCormick Place, located at 2301 S. Martin Luther King Drive. Official proceedings and primetime speeches will be at the United Center, located at 1901 W. Madison Street, and home of the NBA's Chicago Bulls.
Where was the RNC?
The Republican National Convention was in Milwaukee last month — less than 100 miles north of the DNC — from July 15 to July 18.
How to get DNC 2024 convention tickets
The event is not open to the general public. Only credentialed delegates, media and guests can attend, according to the DNC. Viewers can watch the DNC on cable and network television channels and online streaming platforms. The official livestream will be available on the DNC website at chicago2024.com.
DNC 2024: Black women are in charge at this year's DNC. Expect a different kind of convention.
Who will speak at the DNC?
The DNC lineup includes at least three presidents, according to USA TODAY. The DNC speaker schedule is subject to change and a full list of speakers will be released at a later time. Among those expected to speak includes Jason Carter, the grandson of former President Jimmy Carter, according to USAT.
Monday, Aug. 19: President Joe Biden, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and former U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.
Tuesday, Aug. 20: Former President Barack Obama and Second Gentleman Doug Emhoff
Wednesday, Aug. 21: Former President Bill Clinton, Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg and vice presidential nominee Tim Walz, the governor of Minnesota.
Will there be protests at the DNC?
Likely, yes. Larger protests likely will take place on the first and last days of the Democratic National Convention, according to the New York Times, which said they will be focused mainly on opposing Israel's war in Gaza.

title: Peoria man was convicted of killing his wife. His defense was that she killed herself
author: Zach Roth
description: The Peoria man was accused of intentionally holding his wife's head under water until she drowned.
content:
A Peoria man accused of drowning his wife has been found guilty on first-degree murder charges in the third attempt by local prosecutors to convict him.
Michael Vorrath was found guilty this month following a two-day trial on charges of first-degree murder for his role in the drowning death of his wife Nancy Vorrath in November 2019 at their home in the 3300 block of West Lexington Court. The previous two attempts to convict him each ended in mistrials.
Vorrath was accused of intentionally holding Nancy's head under water in a utility basin until she drowned. At the time of her death, Peoria County Coroner Jamie Harwood said that she had suffered multiple blunt force injuries consistent with that of inflicted trauma.
Vorrath was arrested in December 2019 and the trial was continued for nearly four years before the Peoria County State's Attorney's Office began their first attempt to convict him in August 2023. That attempt ended in a mistrial, as did another attempt in April.
According to Vorrath's son, Ron Vorrath, both attempts ended up being thrown out as the result of a forensic pathologist brought on board by Vorrath's legal team to dispute the claims of the autopsy. The answers provided by the pathologist were enough to shut down each trial before it reached cross-examination by the state's attorney's office, but Ron feels that a different judge was able to ensure that every one got a fair shake in the third try.
"I don't know if he (Judge Paul Gilfillan) was able to instill in her what she is not allowed to say and finally get her to not (say) those things," Ron Vorrath said. "They were finally able to get through the defense's questions to her ‒ the prosecution had never gotten an opportunity to cross-examine her because they never made it that far. The judge must have had a better sense of how to keep her on-track to where she didn't do all that to cause a mistrial."
Ron Vorrath said that he and his fellow siblings felt a sense of vindication, having been suspicious of their father since the days after Nancy's death. He felt that his mother could get some justice for her death after being accused of killing herself by her husband and his legal team.
"I felt like it tainted her name, because she wouldn't do that," Ron Vorrath said. "Now she has justice. It felt like they understand what we all felt this whole time and what we all feel like we've known."
Ron Vorrath was frustrated that his father had managed to bond out and live a relatively normal life, all while facing first-degree murder charges. Meantime, Nancy Vorrath never got the chance to see her family grow.
"That's not fair," Ron said. "I can't hug her, call her (and) tell her about something my son did. I got a new girlfriend and step-daughter the last four years that she never got to meet. She would have spoiled them. I feel like we've missed so much from my mom not being here and she was loved by so many and loved us so much. It was like we got robbed of all of that."
Sentencing has been set for Oct. 16 at 1:15 p.m.

title: Worst-case scenario for Illinois football? One Big Ten win and a very hot seat
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The 2024 Illinois football season is near, so what can the Illini expect this year? Here is the worst-case scenario.
content:
We brightened up the 2024 college football preseason this week when we laid out the best-case scenario for the Illinois football season.
Let's get a little more bleak.
The Illini will kick off the 2024 season on Aug. 29 against in-state program Eastern Illinois at Memorial Stadium in Champaign. And no matter how pessimistic you are about the Illinois season, it's hard to imagine the Illini walk away without a win to begin the fourth year under Bret Bielema.
From there, the wheels could fall off pretty fast. Bielema began his Illini tenure with a 5-7 season in 2021; pushed the Illini to eight wins and a bowl in 2022; and last season fell back to 5-7. Prognosticators expect Illinois to finish around that same .500 mark.
But what's the worst-case scenario? Let's take a look.
What is Illinois football's worst-case scenario for the 2024 season?
Illinois' floor is 3-9 overall, with a 1-8 Big Ten record — and a very hot seat.
Illinois should win two of its three nonconference games. All of them are at home, with two against EIU and Central Michigan. The toughest noncon is a Sept. 7 game against Kansas, picked to finish near the top of the reworked Big 12 Conference. Easy to see the Illini dropping that one.
After that, Illinois could lose all four Big Ten games considered a coin flip: Purdue, Minnesota, Michigan State and Northwestern. But we'll give them at least one of those — most likely the Oct. 12 home game against the Boilermakers. Beyond that, Illinois also has a couple of tough Big Ten road games at Nebraska and Rutgers, both games the Illini could lose.
As for the rest of the schedule? Well, we're talking worst-case scenario here. The Illini are not beating Oregon, Michigan or Penn State.
A 3-9 season would leave Illinois out of the bowl season for the third time in four seasons under Bielema, hired in late 2020 to resurrect the Illini program. Bielema is on solid footing for now, but a disastrous showing like one laid out here likely would land him on the hot seat.
One month ago, Illinois athletics director Josh Whitman said the Illini being competitive in most games was "an important, necessary step," according to the Champaign News-Gazette.
'Now," he continued, "we need to start winning some more of those games."

title: Bowl or bust? What the experts think about Illinois football in 2024
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The Journal Star took a spin around the Internet to collect expert predictions for the Illinois Fighting Illini football season in 2024.
content:
The Illinois Fighting Illini are college football's version of a Rorschach test. Those who are optimistic see opportunity and a likely bowl game. The pessimists see danger lurking.
The truth is probably somewhere in between.
Such is predicting the outcome of the Fighting Illini season in the new-look Big Ten Conference for 2024. Nearly every expert prognosticator picks Illinois to finish between five and six wins, with betting sites laying out the ever-so-tempting 5.5 over/under line for Illini victories.
How will Illinois football do in 2024? Best-case scenario | Worst-case scenario
We took a spin around the Internet to find out what some of the top college football news sources had to say about the Illini in 2024:
Athlon Sports
The longtime college sports publication picked Illinois to finish 15th of 18 in the Big Ten Conference, which added four west coast teams in 2024 — Oregon, UCLA, USC and Washington.
"Both sides of the ball need attention after 2023," Athlon wrote of the Illini. "The defense gave up 12.8 points a game in 2022 but watched that total climb to 29.4 last fall."
Athlon pointed out defensive losses, but also that a few key transfers should stabilize. The offense, meanwhile, gets three offensive line starters back and Athlon says quarterback Luke Altmyer is "expected to take a step forward" while running back Kaden Feagin is a "rising star."
"More optimism surrounds the offense going into 2024," wrote Athlon.
Tom Fornelli, CBS Sports
The CBS Sports betting writer also picked the Illini at 5-7, but set an optimistic tone. He also set the over/under at 5.5 wins, expecting victories against Eastern Illinois, Central Michigan, Purdue, Minnesota and Michigan State.
"I've seen some articles written with extremely low expectations for the Illini, and while I understand the concerns about a defense that lost some key pieces, they won with their offense last season," Fornelli wrote. "They could have one of the best offensive lines in the league, which should help them continue to score points. The primary obstacle is the schedule."
Stewart Mandel, The Athletic
The New York Times college football writer picked the Illini to finish 5-7 overall and 3-6 in Big Ten, a pretty standard prediction for the Illini. They sit in that nebulous and muddy middle of the Big Ten. So much so that Mandel took space to write about 10 of the 18 teams in the Big Ten preview. Illinois didn't get an entry.
ESPN
ESPN also didn't have much to say about Illinois in its Big Ten preview, picking the Illini 13th of 18, pointing out that the program's minus-8 turnover margin ranked 123rd nationally in 2023.
Bob Asmussen, Champaign-News Gazette
Earlier this month, the longtime columnist from the Illini hometown News-Gazette assessed the Illini in a story headlined: "What's in store for Bielema in Year Four?" An excerpt:
"(Bret) Bielema is in his 16th year as a head coach. He has a system he believes in. But if it worked or not with the Illinois team at hand won't be known until the completion of the season. Finish 8-4 and it is a 'Yes.' Go 6-6 and it's a 'Maybe.' Finish under .500 and out of a bowl for the third time in four years and it's a 'No.' "
Pro Football Focus
The stats-driven football site says the numbers plant Illinois firmly in the middle, but on the high end. The Illini are 49th in the power ranks, 32nd in strength of schedule. PFF, however, projects Illinois with seven wins.
"After a very successful 2022 season in which the Fighting Illini finished 8-5, the team came crashing down with a 5-7 record in 2023. And that, unfortunately, now means that Illinois has finished with a losing record in 11 of the last 12 seasons. ... If Bret Bielema's squad is to bounce back, it'll likely be due to its defense. ... the Fighting Illini's front seven projects to be the team's strength."
Illinois football predictions: Game-by-game picks based on ESPN matchup predictor
College Football News
More optimism! The online college football site picks the Illini with six wins, which would make them bowl-eligible. The key to that? Get the defense working again.
"The 2022 Illinois defense was a brick wall to deal with," CFN wrote. "It allowed fewer than 100 yards six times and won five of them. In all six games the Illini allowed fewer than 3 yards per carry, and allowed more in the other seven. Last season? The D allowed fewer than 100 yards just three times — and won all three games. More disruption, more attitude, more consistency — Illinois needs to be feared again."

title: 'Brace yourself': Wet, snowy weather in forecast for central Illinois this winter
author: Dean Muellerleile
description: The Farmers' Almanac has released its latest weather predictions for fall and winter in Illinois.
content:
Warm sweaters and wool socks are in the forecast as a frosty, wet autumn and a cold, wet and white winter are expected for Illinois and environs.
The Farmers' Almanac has released its latest weather predictions, and they're heavy on alliteration.
The almanac's national outlooks include a "frosty fall forecast" followed by a "wet, winter, whirlwind."
What's the Illinois 2024 autumn forecast?
"Fall will be frosty and wet in the Great Lakes, Midwest region while the temperatures in the North Central region may be downright frigid, with lots of fall flakes and rain," writes the almanac.
Illinois is part of the almanac's Great Lakes, Ohio Valley & Midwest zone and borders on the North Central region.
One notable event predicted in the Farmers' Almanac Extended Fall Forecast 2024:
Nov. 8-11: An early-season heavy snowfall is expected across the North Central states. Presumably, this could cross into Illinois.
Fall officially begins on Sunday, Sept. 22.
What is the 2024 winter forecast for Illinois?
"Brace yourself for a Wet Winter Whirlwind!" the almanac rather breathlessly writes in its Winter 2025 Extended Weather Forecast.
The almanac expects an overall "season of rapid-fire storms that will bring both rain and snow, with little downtime in between." The Farmers' Almanac anticipates "the winter of 2024-25 will be wet and cold for most locations" in the United States.
For Illinois and the rest of the almanac's Great Lakes, Ohio Valley & Midwest zone, the forecast calls for the aforementioned cold, wet and white winter. The neighboring North Central region is expected to see a "cold, average snowfall" winter.
Indeed, the almanac writes, "The season's coldest temperatures will be found from the Northern Plains to the Great Lakes region." It adds, "The coldest outbreak of the season will come during the final week of January into the beginning of February, when frigid Arctic air brings a sharp plunge in temperatures almost nationwide, but especially across the Northern Plains." And, potentially, the bordering Illinois region.
Above-average precipitation is predicted for the eastern third of the country, especially the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley, and Midwest.
Winter officially begins on Saturday, Dec. 21.
When is the first snowfall in Peoria?
According to the National Weather Service, Peoria recorded the earliest measurable snowfall — defined as one-tenth of an inch or more — on Oct. 18, 1972. The average date of the first measurable snowfall is Nov. 22.
About the Farmers' Almanac
The Farmers' Almanac, which dates to 1818, says its long-range forecast is based on a "mathematical and astronomical" formula that incorporates "sunspot activity, tidal action of the Moon, positions of the planets" and more. It denies the use of computer satellite tracking equipment, weather lore or, rather defensively, groundhogs.
It adds, "Fans of the Almanac say our weather forecasts are accurate 80-85% of the time."

title: Hidden gem: Bosse Field in Evansville, Indiana, has hosted Hall of Famers and Hollywood
author: Ryan Reynolds
description: Long before \
content:
EVANSVILLE − Long before "retro" became popular in professional baseball, there was the "original" aesthetic at American ballparks.
Brick walls. Hand-painted signs. Iron gates. Seating that made fans feel like they were as close to the action as any player on the infield.
The original lives on at Bosse Field in Evansville, Indiana, a city of about 115,000 people along the Ohio River.
Bosse Field was built for $50,000 and opened in 1915. It is the third-oldest ballpark still in operation in the United States, trailing only Chicago's Wrigley Field and Boston's Fenway Park.
And over the past 109 years, it has seen its share of history.
The ballpark has been home to minor league teams of the Detroit Tigers, Boston (and Milwaukee) Braves, Chicago White Sox, Minnesota Twins and Milwaukee Brewers. Some of baseball's greatest players, including Warren Spahn, Hank Greenberg and Edd Roush, did time in the minor leagues at Bosse Field. Jim Leyland managed teams there in the late 1970s and early 80s.
In the early 1920s, the Evansville Crimson Giants played two NFL seasons at the stadium.
Its biggest (and most lasting) moment in the spotlight came in 1991, when Hollywood came to Evansville and used Bosse Field for scenes in the Tom Hanks/Geena Davis movie "A League of Their Own," which celebrated the World War II-era All-American Girls Professional Baseball League.
In the movie, Bosse Field is the home field of the Racine Belles. Visitors to the park can still see signs paying homage to the Belles along the top rows of fan seating.
The park is now home to the Evansville Otters, an unaffiliated baseball team that plays in the independent Frontier League. And while there have been upgrades to Bosse Field in recent years − there's a video board beyond the left field wall and state-of-the-art LED lights now illuminate the playing surface − taking in a game there still has an old-school feel.
On any given night from May through September, a general admission ticket at the front gate brings you past the iron gates, past the brick facade, up a concrete ramp and into another era in American history.
For nine innings, you can sit and watch would-be baseball pros make "gem" plays on the field, while sitting in an absolute "gem" of a stadium the entire time.

title: Blues fest, grape stomp and more: Here are 5 things to do near Peoria this weekend
author: Josh Jenke
description: Music, parties and an annual vineyard event are among the things to do this weekend in central Illinois.
content:
Labor Day weekend is full of activities. Here are five events you might want to check out in the Peoria area this weekend.
Blues & Heritage Music Festival
The 34th annual Peoria Blues & Heritage Music Festival will be held Aug. 30-31 at Peoria Riverfront Festival Park. This end-of-summer event will include a world-class lineup of artists from blues, roots, funk, soul and everything in between. For a full schedule of performances and to purchase tickets, visit www.PBHFest.com.
Pioneer Day at Wildlife Prairie Park
Pioneer Day will take place during regular park hours on Saturday, Aug. 31, at Wildlife Prairie Park, 3826 N. Taylor Road, Hanna City. Several vendors will be set up from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. and special performances, animal programs and other activities will take place throughout the day. All activities are included in regular park admission. For more information and a full schedule of events, visit www.wildlifeprairiepark.org.
Mt. Moon Fest in the Heights
Mt. Moon Fest 3 will be held Aug. 31-Sept. 1 in the parking lot/beer garden of The 33 Room, 4541 N. Prospect Road, Peoria Heights. The two-day music festival featuring over 20 local bands will also include vintage clothing vendors, artists and vegan food. Tickets are $20 for one day or $30 for both days and can be purchased at https://mtmoon.ticketleap.com/mt-moon-fest.
Grape Stomp and Harvest Festival
Mackinaw Valley Vineyard's annual Grape Stomp and Harvest Festival will be held from noon to 6 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 1, at the vineyard, 33633 Illinois Route 9, Mackinaw. There will be two large stomping bins and participants can stomp alone or with a partner. Wine flights will be available all day and live music will be presented by Shipwreck Kelly. Attendees can also come dressed as Lucille Ball and participate in a Lucy look-alike contest. Admission is $5 per person and free for children ages 12 and under.
Party in the Park at Shore Acres
A Party in the Park celebrating the grand opening of the "Play for All" inclusive playground will be held from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 1, at Shore Acres Park, 100 Park Blvd., Chillicothe. Activities include "Rumble on the River" featuring Homegrown Wrestling, a free concert from Mixtape Mayhem, a car cruise-in, M&K Parties inflatables, a KCBBQ rib burn competition, food trucks and more.

title: 'Amazing opportunity': Ex-NFL kicker makes Illinois high school coaching debut against Pekin
author: Dave Eminian
description: Ex-Chicago Bears kicker Robbie Gould launched his high school football coaching career on the Rolling Meadows sideline in a 28-14 loss in Pekin, Illinois.
content:
PEKIN — Robbie Gould had a reason for launching his high school football coaching career, and it wasn't just for kicks.
The former Chicago Bears and NFL kicker made his debut as a high school football head coach Friday, bringing his Rolling Meadows team to Memorial Stadium, where host Pekin beat them, 28-14, in the season opener for both teams.
"I was just taking it all in," Gould said after the game. "It's an amazing opportunity to show these kids how to play, and maybe change their lives. … (Joking) You sure don't coach high school football for the money."
Pekin built a 14-0 lead at halftime, and extended it to 21-0 when senior Landon Erxleben rambled 24 yards up the middle to the Rolling Meadows 8, then three plays later bulled across from the 2 for 21-0 with 5:52 left in the third quarter.
Rolling Meadows launched an inspiring comeback, shifting into a hurry-up tempo and getting on the board with a 9-yard run up the middle by wildcat receiver Shea Wells with 2:26 left in the third quarter.
The Mustangs stopped Pekin with an interception on a tipped ball at their 17 by defensive back Arman Lepuzanov.
They slugged out a 12-play, 64-yard scoring drive over the next 5:35 and closed to within 21-14 when Wells caught a 3-yard TD pass with 5:13 left.
"I'm proud of the way you guys played," Gould told his team afterward. "We didn't play bad football. We have a chance to be something special."
Pekin, meanwhile, held off Rolling Meadows on a late fourth-quarter drive kept alive by a gutty fourth-and-2 call.
The Dragons converted on a deep shot down the right sideline, a 29-yard pass from quarterback Brogan Benassi to senior Peyton Hess. Running back Ty Jackson finished off the game with a 5-yard TD run after that to cap a nine-play, 61-yard scoring drive.
Illinois high school football recap: Peoria-area highlights from IHSA Week 1
"Our guys were ready to battle four quarters," Pekin coach Doug Nutter said. "We have some things to clean up, and I'm sure Rolling Meadows would say the same thing.
"Robbie (Gould) did fine over there. His kids played hard and physical, they kept coming at us."
What advice would Nutter pass along to his rookie counterpart?
"He's a football guy, so he knows the game and knows what he's doing," Nutter said. "Coaching high school football is all a matter of patience. You're dealing with 16-, 17-year-old kids and you have to let them grow. That's always the case in high school."
This story will be updated.
Dave Eminian is the Journal Star sports columnist, and covers Bradley men's basketball, the Rivermen and Chiefs. He writes the Cleve In The Eve sports column for pjstar.com. He can be reached at 686-3206 or deminian@pjstar.com. Follow him on X.com @icetimecleve.

title: When does daylight saving time end in Illinois?
author: Mike Kramer
description: Some people want permanent daylight saving time in Illinois and beyond. Here are the facts about the controversial time change.
content:
The days are getting shorter.
You are probably noticing the decrease in sunlight as we transition from summer to fall. Soon, we will be due for a time change. Here's what to know
When does daylight saving time start?
Daylight saving time begins the second Sunday of March and ends the first Sunday of November. In 2024, clocks were set forward one hour at 2 a.m. March 10, according to the U.S. Naval Observatory.
When does daylight saving time end?
Daylight saving time will end 2 a.m. Nov. 3, when clocks will be set back one hour to standard time. U.S. clocks will 'spring ahead' for 2025 at 2 a.m. March 9.
What does daylight saving time mean?
The Oxford Dictionary defines daylight saving time as 'time as adjusted to achieve longer evening daylight in summer by setting the clocks an hour ahead of the standard time.'
Will we ever shift to permanent daylight saving time?
In the U.S., Congress has been kicking that one around since 2018 when U.S. Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Florida) introduced the Sunshine Protection Act. The measure would make daylight saving time permanent, meaning the time would no longer change twice a year. Congressional records show the U.S. Senate passed a 2021 iteration of the bill in 2022, but no iteration has passed in the U.S. House of Representatives.
European nations are also mulling over the idea of eliminating the biannual time change, according to the Council of the European Union (EU). In 2018, the European Commission (EC) tabled a proposal to end the seasonal clock changes in the EU. Six years later, the current system remains in place as the EC has taken no action on the proposal, and there is currently no defined timeline for a decision.
How did daylight saving time start?
According to timeanddate.com, Germany was the first country to apply daylight saving time on a national level, setting their clocks one hour forward on April 30, 1916. The town of Thunder Bay, Ontario was the first community in the world to use DST, implementing it as far back as 1908.
According to National Public Radio, the United States implemented daylight saving time with the passage of the Standard Time Act of 1918. The measure was a wartime effort to conserve energy resources by adding more daylight hours.
Benjamin Franklin often gets credit for the concept of daylight saving time because of a satirical 1784 letter he published in the Journal de Paris suggesting Parisians could economize on candles by rising an hour earlier.
When is the shortest day of the year in 2024?
The winter solstice marks the 24-hour period that will have the fewest hours of daylight. In Illinois, the 2024 winter solstice will occur at 2:21 a.m. Dec. 21, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich. The winter solstice was a time for pagan festivals in many cultures, and under the Julian Calendar, the event occurred Dec. 25.
