title: How a tiny strip of land is delaying Pekin's multi-million dollar road project
author: Mike Kramer
description: The land will clear the way for the start of a construction project on Pekin's major thoroughfare. But the city and CVS are at an impasse.
content:
Pekin needs one last piece of property to begin a $5.7 million road rehabilitation project. But the city seems to be at an impasse with the property owner over the price.
During a special meeting, the Pekin City Council approved a resolution for $140,000 to purchase a strip of land at 910 Court Street from CVS pharmacy and Realty Income Illinois.
The city had offered CVS a total of $93,370 — with $62,200 of that for the land and $27,170 to relocate the store's existing sign, according to Pekin city engineer Josie Esker. CVS and Realty Income countered with an offer of $172,045 — asking for $116,700 for the property and $55,345 to install a new sign.
Positivity, planning and growth: What we learned from Pekin's state of the city address
'The purchase is necessary in order to accommodate the sidewalk widening and changes at the intersection of 10th and Court' Esker said. 'The intersection has been designed in order to meet IDOT standards. The plans have been approved by IDOT, and the project cannot move forward without acquiring the property.'
When contacted, CVS spokesperson Amy Thibault did not indicate whether the company would be willing to accept the latest offer. "Our counteroffers are based upon our good faith estimates of what it will cost us to perform the restoration work necessitated by the city's project," Thibault said.
The city is planning to put in new curbs and gutters, and all new full-depth concrete pavement with new markings on Court Street from just east of 10th Street to just west of 8th Street, Esker said. The city is also scheduled to replace all sidewalks and ADA ramps in that section, and sidewalks will be widened from 4 to 6 feet.
The $5.7 million project also includes new traffic signal equipment, a new configuration for the 10th Street intersection, and new inlet structures and storm sewer pipes. Almost all land acquisition for the project is complete, she added. The property at 910 Court Street is the final parcel required before construction can begin.
Because the project's start date is contingent on the purchase of the remaining property, Esker could not provide a completion date. However, she expects it to take at least a full construction season.
Pekin has received a $3 million federal grant for the project. The city also partnered with Illinois American Water (ILAW) to complete water main replacement for a portion of the project length, for which ILAW will reimburse the city approximately $700,000. The remaining cost to the city is about $2 million.

title: Motivated and upgraded: This Morton basketball star 'doesn't play like a normal big guy'
author: Adam Duvall
description: Huge Savings: Subscribe today to enjoy sports, entertainment, life, money, tech, and travel news along with videos, apps, and more.
content:
MORTON — Feb. 23, 2024, was an important day in Wes Gudeman's development as a player.
That night, the Morton basketball player watched a double-digit lead disappear and Richwoods defeat his team and win a Class 3A regional championship. The Knights went on to make the state finals, and Gudeman was left feeling very unsatisfied.
'It's just a chip on our shoulder that we're playing with,' the 6-foot-5 forward/guard said, 'because we knew that the end goal is to win. Conference championship is nice, but the end goal is always to win in the postseason.
'Just winning a regional championship and doing what we couldn't get done (last year).'
IHSA sports: The Peoria area's 610 names to know in high school sports for the 2024-25 school year
As a four-year starter, Gudeman focused in the offseason on becoming more explosive and adding an outside shot to his repertoire. He joined up with renowned basketball trainer David Williams and honed nearly every aspect of his game.
The result? He won MVP at the 2024 Pekin Insurance Holiday Tournament in December and was named the Journal Star's fans' choice for MVP so far this season. Gudeman on Tuesday put together an impressive 21-point effort in a 59-42 win over Metamora in front of sellout crowd at the Potterdome.
'This is his legacy year,' Morton coach Abe Zeller said. '… We have full confidence that when we get Wes on the block, good things happen. So we definitely do our best to get him there.'
Gudeman scored plenty from the post and also stepped out and hit a pair of 3-pointers to help Morton split the Mid-Illini Conference series with the Redbirds. Both teams came into the game ranked statewide in Class 3A.
'Hitting the first 3 just kind of flipped the switch,' Gudeman said, 'and I was just like, 'You know what? This is just like every other person that's tried to guard me, I'm going to get to my spot and I'm going to hit my shot.' '
He made seven shots in a row highlighted by 10 points in the second quarter and finished 9-for-12 from the field.
'He doesn't play like a normal big guy,' Morton senior guard Tripp Rugaard said. 'He plays different and no else can guard it, so I know if I get it into him, he's going to get a bucket.'
Peoria basketball: 12 unsung high school players heading into 2025
His defensive effort was equally notable. Gudeman picked the pocket of Bradley recruit Matthew Zobrist and went in for a layup. A second steal and basket — that one for a dunk — put the Potters up 11 midway through the third quarter.
'He's done a good job of adding to his game on the defensive end," Zeller said, "and guarding some on the perimeter.'
No. 3 Morton (16-5), which last won a regional in 2014, and No. 6 Metamora (20-5) are tied atop the Mid-Illini standings at 8-1. The Potters take a 14-game win streak into Pekin on Friday. On Saturday, they host Manual.
'They've all been motivated,' Zeller said of his team shaking off the 2024 regional title defeat. 'It motivated us through the summer, through the fall, through the season. Our focus is on championships. The Mid-Illini championship's a big one and obviously, postseason is what it's all about.'
Gudeman says he loves basketball and wants to play in college. He's an equally talented student. Schools at nearly all levels have shown an interest, but Gudeman specifically mentioned attending Williams College in Massachusetts, an NCAA Division-III school with an acceptance rate of less than 10 percent.
Education, according to Gudeman, is a very important aspect of his next chapter.
'(Recruiting) is a process,' he said. 'It's unlike any other animal you that could tackle. It's had its ups and downs and it's coming to a close here soon.'
IHSA basketball previews: Top girls players | Girls power rankings | Top boys players | Boys power rankings
Splitting the season series means a third meeting between Mid-Illini co-leaders Metamora and Morton would likely come in the sectional.
'It'd always be fun to see a rival in the postseason,' Gudeman said, noting the likelihood of an intense atmosphere, 'and that would be at a bigger scale in the postseason.'

title: Illinois football adds in-state late addition from the Class of 2025
author: Dave Eminian
description: Illinois football team picked up a late addition from Class of 2025, adding 3-star linebacker Jack Paris from suburban Chicago. He had committed to Air Force.
content:
Illinois football made a late addition to their defense Monday when Class of 2025 linebacker Jack Paris announced his commitment.
The 6-foot-3, 210-pounder from Oak Park Fenwick is a 3-star prospect who was formerly committed to Air Force. He was an all-conference selection in his senior season in the Chicago Catholic League/East Suburban Catholic Conference White Division. His Fenwick team finished 8-3 and lost in the second round of the Class 7A playoffs.
Illinois football recruiting: 21 players Illini added on early signing day in December
Paris also had an offer from Vanderbilt, and multiple offers from lower level programs like Akron, Army, Ball State, Central Michigan, Eastern Michigan, Kent State, Navy, Northern Illinois, Toledo and Wyoming.
"Grew up in Illinois, grew up right outside Chicago and this has always been my dream to play in the Big Ten, play the biggest football, play on the biggest stage and go into those stadiums," Paris told Illini Inquirer. "It means so much. Just that these coaches are putting trust in me and they really are betting on me. I've got a chip on my shoulder for all these other schools that haven't bet on me, and it's really only going to make me work harder."
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
Among the reasons Paris chose Illinois is former Metamora coach Pat Ryan, who is now high school recruiting coordinator for the Illini.
'I always trusted Coach Pat Ryan," Paris told Illini Inquirer. "I trusted the process, and it worked well."
Paris is the seventh in-state commit from the 2025 class for Illinois. According to 247Sports, the Illini Class of 2025 recruiting haul ranks 12th in the Big Ten and 43rd in the nation.
A late addition is not unusual. For instance, last year the Illini added Spring Valley Hall defensive back Mac Resetich, who played some key minutes this season.

title: New Dollar Tree store opens in Peoria
author: Mike Kramer
description: The discount store is one of many in the greater Peoria area.
content:
Dollar Tree has opened a new store in Peoria.
The discount store at 9315 N. Lindbergh Drive opened Sunday, joining 12 other locations in the greater Peoria area. The store is open from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. every day. The new Dollar Tree occupies the site of a former CVS Pharmacy store and neighbors the Kroger located off Knoxville Avenue, near Interstate 474.
The opening comes as Dollar Tree Inc. is closing stores operating under the Family Dollar brand and expanding its Dollar Tree presence. Last June, the company's then-chief executive officer Rick Dreiling announced plans to close 970 'underperforming' Family Dollar stores across the United States to focus on investments in stores with long-term growth potential.
'At the same time,' Dreiling said, 'we continue to aggressively grow the Dollar Tree banner through compelling initiatives like our expanded multi-price offerings, significant planned new store openings across the United States, and accretive transactions like our recent successful bid to acquire up to 170 stores from 99 Cents Only.'
The CVS Pharmacy located at the site closed in 2022. The building was later sold for $750,000 to Joseph Ocala LLC, a Florida-based firm run by the Peoria-based Joseph Health Group.

There are a number of criteria the NCAA Tournament selection committee looks at in order to make its assessment in addition to subjective assessments like the 'eyeball test.' Among them:
Record: The team's overall record, conference record, and nonconference record.
Strength of schedule: The strength of the teams the team played against.
Head-to-head results: The results of games between the teams being compared.
Conference championships: Whether a conference championship was won in the regular season, or tournament.
Common opponents: The results of games against common opponents.
Adjusted Net Efficiency (NET): The NCAA's preferred metric measuring a team's overall performance during the regular season.
Team Value Index: A results-oriented component of the NET that ranks teams based on who they beat and where they played.
Rating Percentage Index (RPI): A formula that ranks teams using a team's winning percentage, opponents' success and opponents' strength of schedule.

title: Respiratory illnesses are continuing to rise in the Peoria area. Here's what to know
author: Cassidy Waigand
description: Peoria hospitals are encouraging visitors to wear masks, limit visits and use virtual care options if possible,
content:
As the Peoria area continues to face high levels of respiratory illness, local hospitals and health care providers are encouraging the community to take steps to mitigate the spread of such illnesses at health care facilities.
From Jan. 19 to Jan. 25 — which is the most recent report available — the Peoria City/County Health Department reported 550 positive influenza tests from OSF HealthCare Saint Francis Medical Center, Carle Health Methodist, Carle Health Proctor and Carle Health Pekin. That marked a significant jump from 222 positive tests the previous week.
In the first four weeks of 2025, 201 people have been admitted to the hospital with influenza and 30 have been admitted to intensive care units.
Public Health Administrator Monica Hendrickson said in a news release that the health department will continue to 'ring the alarm on the critical importance of limiting the spread of Influenza, RSV, and COVID.'
'It is imperative that we take proactive measures to prevent overwhelming our health care infrastructure, ensuring they can provide the best care for all who need it,' Hendrickson said.
OSF HealthCare Saint Francis Medical Center, OSF Divine Mercy Continuing Care Hospital and Carle Health's Methodist, Eureka, Proctor and Pekin campuses are encouraging visitors to wear masks while at health care facilities. Community members are also encouraged to limit hospital visits and utilize virtual care options when possible.
'As Carle Health hospitals continue to experience high rates of respiratory illness throughout the Greater Peoria area, we are taking every measure possible to create the safest care environment for our patients,' said Jill Dodaro, Carle Health's greater Peoria chief nursing officer and vice president.
Other recommended steps to limit the spread of respiratory illness include:
Limiting visitors to two per patient
Visitors should be 18 or older
Individuals should wash or sanitize their hands before and after visiting a patient's room
Those who are feeling unwell or have experienced flu-like symptoms in the past seven days should not visit hospital patients

What is National Signing Day?
National Signing Day is the traditional first day of the college football signing period for high school seniors. Mid-year junior college players have their own signing dates, so National Signing Day has been celebrated for its exclusivity to high school players.
For a long time, it was the only signing day for high school football seniors. That created a drama-packed 24 hours filled with commitment flips, since every player in the nation eyed that as the opening day of the signing period.
What changed about National Signing Day, and why?
That changed with the addition of a December signing period in 2017. A number of players utilize the early date, namely top recruits, to lock-in roster spots. But it's beneficial for some players to wait. College rosters (and coaches) can change, and recruits can enhance their options with the extra time after the season.
It's worth noting that the 2025 class is the first that doesn't have to sign National Letters of Intent. In October 2024, the NCAA elected to eliminate NLIs, which had been part of the signing process since 1964.

title: Construction of new $100M casino in the Peoria-area could begin in 2026, Boyd CEO says
author: JJ Bullock
description: Huge Savings: Subscribe today to enjoy sports, entertainment, life, money, tech, and travel news along with videos, apps, and more.
content:
Boyd Gaming could begin construction on a new casino, valued to be around a $100 million development, in the Peoria area as early as the first half of 2026, according to CEO Keith Smith.
Smith told investors on a call Thursday that Boyd Gaming was moving forward with its hopes to replace the Par-A-Dice Riverboat casino in East Peoria and said construction of a new facility could begin as early as the first half of 2026, depending on regulatory approval.
The new facility is still in its design phase, but Smith told investors that they expect the new facility to be about a $100 million investment, similar to the Treasure Chest Casino that Boyd Gaming built in Kenner, Louisiana.
There was no mention made of whether the new facility would be built on the Peoria or East Peoria side of the Illinois River as a feud between the two cities over the fate of the casino continues.
Smith did not directly say whether or not the new casino would be land-based, but he did signal that it will be a "non-riverboat operation."
"Will we likely save money as a restriction going from a riverboat operation to a non-riverboat operation, yes, absolutely," Smith said on the call.
On the call, Smith walked investors through the performance of key Boyd Gaming casinos across the country, mentioning each in conjunction with the city it resided in. However, when talking about the Par-A-Dice Casino, Smith did not mention Peoria or East Peoria by name and instead referred to the boat as the company's "Central Illinois" property.
More: 'Forever strained'? Latest casino battle tests Peoria, East Peoria relationship
Leaders from Peoria and East Peoria have been locked in a battle for nearly a year about the future of Boyd Gaming's new facility in the Peoria area.
Officials from Peoria are steadfast in their opinion that any land-based casino Boyd Gaming builds in the area must be on the Peoria side of the river as is dictated by a 1991 agreement signed between the two cities.
East Peoria officials, however, believe that Peoria is stepping on their toes by trying to lure Boyd Gaming to the other side of the river. East Peoria Mayor John Kahl went so far as to tell Peoria Mayor Rita Ali in an email exchange that Peoria's efforts to bring Boyd Gaming to Peoria threatened to damage the relationship between the two cities.
But, with millions of dollars in tax revenue on the line, Peoria has not balked at trying to bring a land-based casino to the city.
In December the Peoria City Council approved a plan to hire both an attorney and an investment firm to help guide the city in its plans to lure Boyd Gaming to Peoria.
Officials from the city of Peoria and Boyd Gaming have also discussed multiple locations near interstates in Peoria that could be plausible for a new casino to be built.

author: Dean Muellerleile
description: The two rival almanacs have different forecasts for springtime in Illinois this year.
content:
The Old Farmer's Almanac predicts a dry spring with varying temperatures.
The Farmers' Almanac expects a cool and wet spring.
Neither of the almanacs is considered especially accurate.
The rival farmer almanacs have released their national spring weather forecasts. And they disagree, especially about Illinois.
The Old Farmer's Almanac predicts a dry spring for the Prairie State, with varying temperatures. The Farmers' Almanac expects a wet and cool spring for Illinois.
Here's how their forecasts compare, as well as what the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration predicts. The first day of spring is Thursday, March 20, 2025.
The Old Farmer's Almanac spring weather prediction for Illinois
The Spring Weather Forecast 2025 from the Old Farmer's Almanac calls for a wet spring for much of the country. Illinois is a notable exception.
The Prairie State will be uniformly dry, the Old Farmer predicts. Temperatures will range from normal in the northeast to warm in the west to cool in the south. Peoria lies roughly where Illinois' normal and warm zones meet.
The Old Farmer's Almanac claims 80% accuracy in its long-range predictions. It says it employs solar science, climatology and meteorology in its seasonal forecasts. The almanac dates to 1792.
The Farmers' Almanac spring prediction for Illinois
The younger of the two competing almanacs predicts a "Thunder & Zing Spring." The Farmers' Almanac forecast calls for lingering winter conditions for many parts of the country, especially the Midwest and Great Lakes regions, including Illinois. That lingering zing will also bring plenty of showers and thunder for most areas, the Farmers say.
The Prairie State will be very cool and wet in the west and cool and showery in the east, the almanac predicts.
The Farmers expect fair weather in Illinois for Easter, on Sunday, April 20.
The Farmers' Almanac, which dates to 1818, says its long-range forecast is based on a "mathematical and astronomical" formula that incorporates "sunspot activity, tidal action of the Moon, positions of the planets" and more. It denies the use of computer satellite tracking equipment, weather lore or, rather defensively, groundhogs.
It adds, "Fans of the Almanac say our weather forecasts are accurate 80-85% of the time."
Are the almanacs accurate?
Neither of the almanacs is considered especially accurate, but both remain popular.
Scientific American casts doubt on both publications' predictions.
And a University of Illinois study conducted in 2010, cited by Popular Mechanics in 2022, found the Old Farmer's Almanac only about 52% accurate — "essentially random chance."
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration spring forecast
Meanwhile, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has released a weather outlook for March, April and May. The NOAA's Climate Prediction Center foresees equal chances of above- or below-normal temperatures in Illinois. The outlook also sees a likelihood of above-average precipitation in Illinois.

title: Alabama grabs No. 1 spot in USA TODAY Sports men's basketball poll after losses by Auburn, Duke
author: Eddie Timanus
description: Auburn's run of four weeks at No. 1 in the USA TODAY Sports men's basketball poll ended with a loss to Florida. Its rival Alabama takes the top spot.
content:
We don't usually do this, but the results of the USA TODAY Sports men's basketball coaches poll this week dictate we should dip into the minutiae a bit to explain matters.
It seems there were two schools of thought among the voters when considering what to do with the top-ranked Auburn Tigers following their loss to Florida over the weekend. Many were inclined to leave them at No. 1, but those who demoted them chose to move them down more than one position.
This is all a roundabout way of announcing there is a new No. 1 team. Alabama moves to the top from the No. 3 spot. The Crimson Tide received 15 of 31 first-place votes but wind up 17 poll points ahead of the Tigers. Auburn lands at No. 2 overall despite getting the other 16 votes for No. 1.
Fans of both programs are advised not to get too worked up about the voting, however, as the matter will be settled on the court this coming Saturday in Tuscaloosa. For now though, it's the first No. 1 ranking for the Crimson Tide since Feb. 13, 2023 - the only other time they were in the top spot.
Florida, responsible for knocking off the No. 1 team for the second time this season, vaults three places to No. 3. Tennessee follows at No. 4, giving the SEC the top four poll positions. The panel was less forgiving of Duke's loss at No. 19 Clemson, as the Blue Devils drop from second to fifth overall.
Houston checks in at No. 6, with Purdue holding at No. 7. St. John's continues its assent climbing two spots to No. 8, its highest ranking since the final poll of the 1998-99 season. Texas A&M and Iowa State round out the top 10.
Arizona is the week's big mover, jumping seven places to No. 13 after earning a season split with No. 12 Texas Tech.
No. 21 Creighton and No. 23 Mississippi rejoin the rankings, replacing Saint Mary's and Illinois.

content:

Along with the Irish band, the multibillion-dollar Las Vegas behemoth has hosted Phish, Dead & Company and the Eagles.
But in 2025, the Sphere is rounding out its lineup with more genres. Kenny Chesney will be the first country act to hit the stage starting in May. And, in July, the Backstreet Boys will be the first pop act at the Sphere.
The iconic group plans nine performances in its 'Into The Millennium' residency: July 11, 12, 13, 18, 19, 20, 25, 26 and 27.
Fans can get access to presale tickets at signup.ticketmaster.com/backstreetboys through 10 p.m. PT Feb. 17. The general onsale starts 9 a.m. PT Feb. 21 at backstreetboys.com.

title: More winter weather is coming to Peoria this weekend. Here's what to expect
author: Mike Kramer
description: A mix of rain, sleet and snow will hit the greater Peoria area this weekend, says the National Weather Service.
content:
The Peoria area is likely to see a wintry mix of rain, freezing rain and snow this weekend.
The area has an 80% chance of rain, sleet and snow late Friday night, a 60% chance of rain Saturday and an 80% chance of rain turning to snow on Saturday evening, according to National Weather Service meteorologist Kirk Huettl.
'Snow accumulation could be up to an inch Saturday night,' Huettl said. 'Ice accumulation would be mainly (Friday night) and could be up to a tenth of an inch in the Peoria area. It will be mainly in the evening and the overnight hours, and then by about Saturday morning, it should warm up so it will just be rain.'
The National Weather Service predicts a cloudy Friday night with a low temperature of 28. Saturday's high will be 36 degrees, with a low of 23. Huettl cautioned motorists traveling to or from the Peoria area this weekend that ice accumulation could make untreated roads slippery.
The best travel time will be during the daytime hours on Saturday, where it looks like temperatures will be above freezing and precipitation will be in the form of rain, he said.

title: Starting Five: Alabama-Auburn clash leads college basketball weekend games to watch
author: Eddie Timanus
description: This week's Starting Five previewing the men's college basketball weekend has a huge SEC showdown and three other games matching ranked opponents.
content:
By now, casual sports fans and die-hard college hoops junkies alike should be fully engaged with March Madness now just a few weeks away. We're back once again to help you plan your weekend of viewing by picking the five games in men's college basketball we think will be most worthy of your attention.
Those who have peeked ahead at the calendar will undoubtedly anticipate most of our offerings, but if you have not done so hopefully we can save you a little time. Of course your interest may vary based upon your own rooting preferences, but here is our Starting Five for the weekend after the Super Bowl with college basketball taking the stage.
No. 2 Auburn at No. 1 Alabama
It's not at all a stretch to state that this is the most significant meeting in basketball in the history of these schools best known for their rivalry on the gridiron. On the other hand, it's only round one, as they're slated to meet again in three weeks at Auburn and possibly a time or two after that in the postseason. Both teams handled their midweek business leading up to this showdown, as the Tigers prevailed at Vanderbilt and the Crimson Tide hit the century mark for the fourth time in SEC play at Texas. Alabama's high-scoring, fast-paced approach means no lead is safe for its opponent, but it also means protecting its own lead can be an issue. That figures to be the case against Auburn, whose defensive tenacity often results in lengthy scoring droughts. Pesky Tigers guard Chad Baker-Mazara will likely be assigned to shadow top Alabama perimeter threat Mark Sears, while the Tide's Grant Nelson will be tasked with keeping Auburn big man Johni Broome from dominating the glass.
No. 6 Houston at No. 13 Arizona
Time/TV:
First place will also be on the line in the Big 12. That remains the case despite Arizona on Wednesday becoming the latest victim of a suddenly red-hot Kansas State squad making a late push for the bubble. But the Wildcats can regain a share of the league lead if they can take down the Cougars, who have won three in succession since dropping their lone conference decision to Texas Tech. The Wildcats had a terrible night from the three-point arc in Manhattan, making just two of 22 attempts. Caleb Love and Co. usually fare better in the more friendly environs of the McKale Center, but Houston also guards the perimeter effectively. The Cougars have yet to lose in the Big 12 on the road, where it helps to have a primary ball handler like Milos Uzan who rarely turns it over.
No. 15 Wisconsin at No. 7 Purdue
Time/TV: Saturday, 1 p.m. ET, CBS
We now move over to a double dip in the Big Ten, starting with this clash of likely top-16 NCAA seeds in Purdue's Mackey Arena. The Boilermakers look to bounce back after letting a lead get away at Michigan on Tuesday, while the Badgers come to town riding a three-game winning streak. Expect to see a lot of long balls attempted in this one, as both teams hoist well over 20 three-point tries per game. Purdue is usually a bit more accurate, connecting at a 37.4% clip from distance to Wisconsin's 36.5%, but it's fair to say both squads are capable of mounting a rally if needed. The Badgers will need a big day from Steven Crowl on the boards to stick with the Boilermakers' Trey Kaufman-Renn.
No. 11 Michigan State at Illinois
Time/TV: Saturday, 8 p.m. ET, Fox
The Big Ten's prime-time tilt features a pair of teams that could both use a positive result. The Spartans got off to a 9-0 start in league play but have dropped three of their last four. The Fighting Illini have struggled for consistency all season, capable of a dominating win or a puzzling loss on a given day. Various illnesses and injuries have been in part to blame for Illinois, but the team might finally have all of its key parts available if guard Tre White is able to go after missing time with a flu bug. Michigan State's biggest strength continues to be its depth, with 10 players averaging at least 15 minutes and five points per game. But in general the offense is most efficient when Jeremy Fears (6.0 apg) is running point.
No. 21 Creighton at No. 8 St. John's
Time/TV: Sunday, 3 p.m. ET, FS1
The Sunday headliner takes us to Madison Square Garden for this key Big East contest. At the start of the week this shaped up as a clash between the league's hottest teams, but both had lengthy streaks snapped Wednesday night. The Red Storm experienced some rare defensive lapses in a two-point loss at Villanova, while the Bluejays found out the hard way how much better Connecticut is with Liam McNeeley healthy. Creighton did get the better of St. John's in their first encounter on New Year's Eve before the Red Storm got hot, but the 57-56 final score was still a typical St. John's game. Bluejays guard Steven Ashworth will have to be especially careful with the ball against constant pressure. title: Illinois basketball unveils Terrence Shannon Jr.'s jersey banner upside down in ceremony
author: John Leuzzi
description: Illinois basketball unveiled Terrence Shannon Jr.'s jersey banner upside down during a halftime jersey retirement ceremony.
content:
Illinois men's basketball celebrated Terrence Shannon Jr. on Saturday at State Farm Center against Michigan State by retiring his jersey.
However, the Fighting Illini fumbled the jersey retirement ceremony. As Shannon Jr.'s jersey banner was unraveled to be sent up to the rafters at State Farm Center during halftime, the banner of the 6-foot-6 forward's No. 0 jersey was displayed upside down. Ouch.
Here's another look at Shannon Jr.'s jersey banner upside down, which sent an initial shock to Shannon Jr. and a member of Illinois' athletic department:
Shannon Jr. is the 36th player in Illinois history to have his jersey number retired and sent to the rafters, and the first since center Kofi Cockburn. As noted by the Illini's website, there needs to be one of six criteria met for a player to have their number retired in program history:
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
National Player of the Year
Enshrined in the National Basketball Hall of Fame
Big Ten Player of the Year
Consensus First- or Second-Team All-American
Illinois All-Century Team Member
Individual whose pioneering efforts made a significant impact on Illinois and international basketball
In his lone season in Champaign, Illinois last year, Shannon Jr. ranked third in the country in scoring at 23.0 points per game — the highest average by an Illini in 51 years — and was a third-team All-American selection by the Associated Press.
He was additionally named to the NCAA All-Region Team, though the Illini fell to UConn in the Elite Eight of the East Region at TD Garden in Boston. As noted by Illinois' news release, Shannon set the Big Ten Tournament scoring average record with 34.0 points per game, while earning tournament Most Outstanding Player honors.
The Minnesota Timberwolves drafted Shannon Jr. with the No. 27 overall pick in the 2024 NBA draft. In 16 games this season for the Timberwolves, Shannon Jr. is averaging 3.1 points while shooting 49.5% from the field. Illinois is currently looking for a signature win for its NCAA Tournament resume Saturday against No. 11 Michigan State.

title: Olympic gold medalist and more: Illinois names Order of Lincoln recipients for 2025
author: Mike Kramer
description: Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker has announced that six state residents will receive the Order of Lincoln for professional achievement and public service.
content:
AI-assisted summary
Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker announced the six recipients of the state's highest honor.
2025 Order of Lincoln recipients are Bonnie Blair, Sandra Cisneros, Jeanne Gang, Janice Jackson, Carol Marin and Julieanna Richardson.
The winners will be honored May 3 at the Krannert Center for the Arts.
Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker announced Thursday six honorees will receive the Order of Lincoln, the state's highest honor for professional achievement and public service.
This year's Lincon Laureates will be honored at the upcoming 61st Annual Convocation at 5:30 p.m. May 3 at the Krannert Center for the Arts located on the campus of the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Established in 1964, the Order of Lincoln recognizes individuals who have made remarkable contributions to the betterment of humanity in or on behalf of the State of Illinois.
'With world-renowned achievements in athletics, literature, architecture, education, journalism and history, the 2025 class of Lincoln Laureates embody the very best that Illinois has to offer,' Pritzker said. 'I am proud to uplift their incredible contributions and to award these talented men and women our state's highest honor.'
The May 3 ceremony is open to the public and will be livestreamed on Facebook and YouTube. More information is available at LincolnAcademyIllinois.org.
The 2025 Order of Lincoln recipients in Illinois
Bonnie Blair
The Champaign native is the first American woman to win five gold medals at the Olympic Winter Games. Since she retired from speed skating after the 1994 Winter Games in Lillehammer, Norway, Blair has worked extensively with and raised funds for the Alzheimer's Association, the American Brain Tumor Association, and the Leukemia Association. She is also the director of community engagement for the DASH (Developing Athletes for Speedskating High-Performance) Project, Inc.
Sandra Cisneros
The Chicago-born Cisneros is a poet, short story writer, novelist, and essayist whose work explores the lives of the working-class. Her literary accolades include National Endowment for the Arts fellowships in poetry and fiction, the Texas Medal of the Arts, a MacArthur Fellowship, the PEN/Nabokov Award for Achievement in International Literature, the National Medal of Arts, the Ruth Lilly Poetry Prize, and the Ambassador Richard C. Holbrooke Distinguished Achievement Award from the Dayton Literary Peace Prize Foundation. Her 1984 novel The House on Mango Street has sold over eight million copies, has been translated into over 25 languages, and is required reading in elementary, high school, and universities across the United States. Cisneros is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico.
Jeanne Gang
A native of Belvidere, Illinois, and a University of Illinois graduate, Gang is an architect and the founding partner of international architecture and urban design practice Studio Gang. Her portfolio includes the Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education, and Innovation at the American Museum of Natural History in New York; a new United States Embassy in Brazil; and an expansion of the Clinton Presidential Center. A MacArthur Fellow and a Professor in Practice at the Harvard Graduate School of Design. Time Magazine named Gang of its 100 Most Influential People of 2019.
Janice K. Jackson
Jackson is the chief executive officer of Hope Chicago, a public-private partnership working to drive economic mobility for disinvested communities through scholarships for Chicago families. The Chicago native is also the former CEO of Chicago Public Schools (CPS), the first CPS alum to serve in that position. In 2003, Jackson helped acquire a $500,000 grant from the Gates Foundation to underwrite the establishment of Al Raby High School and later served as its founding principal. She was then tapped to open another, George Westinghouse College Prep.
Carol Marin
The Palatine native and University of Illinois graduate is a distinguished journalist who has won multiple awards over a 50-year career. Her career affiliations include WMAQ-TV Chicago, CBS News, '60 Minutes,' and the Evening News with Dan Rather. She also served as a columnist for the Chicago Sun-Times and was a regular contributor to 'Chicago Tonight' on the public broadcast station WTTW. Marin's accolades include two national Emmy Awards, three Peabody Awards, two Alfred I. DuPont-Columbia Awards, and an American Women in Radio & Television Gracie Award. In 2016, DePaul University launched the Center for Journalism Integrity & Excellence with Marin as co-director, where she continues to help guide students as they prepare for a career in journalism.
Julieanna L. Richardson
Although she is not an Illinois native, the Pittsburgh-born Richardson has been a prominent Chicago figure for four decades. She served as cable administrator for the City of Chicago Office of Cable Communications before founding the regional shopping channel Shop Chicago. She went on to create the production company SCTN Teleproductions, which managed three local cable channels and served as the local production extension for C-SPAN. In 1999, she began compiling over 3,500 African American video oral histories and ultimately founded The HistoryMakers, a Chicago-based nonprofit that maintains the collection of African-American oral histories. In 2012, the United States Library of Congress became the permanent repository for Richardson's collection, making it only their second major African American oral history collection. She is a recipient of the Chicago History Museum's John Hope Franklin Making History Award.

title: Illinois protestors rally at state capitol against President Trump
author: Tom Ackerman
description: One of the signs at the rally read "Trump is not a king" while another read "hate is not patriotic."
content:
Protestors again rallied at the Illinois capitol on Presidents Day against the Trump administration, despite freezing temperatures. The crowd of about 200 marched in the street to the home of Abraham Lincoln.
At a protest earlier this month, some of the same organizers helped draw a comparable number of demonstrators.
Monday's protest was peaceful. Springfield Police officers blocked off portions of the roads as the group marched to the Lincoln Home National Historic Site Visitor Center.
'I know a lot of people are of the opinion that standing out here with a sign and yelling into the void really doesn't do much. I disagree,' said Tristan Sites, one of the organizers. 'It gets people talking about it.'
Sites, who traveled about 45 minutes south to get to Springfield, said national coordination of the event is proof that talking about issues can lead to a larger presence.
The 50501 Movement is a grassroots movement, meaning there is no official, local organization in each U.S. state, though protests are taking place around the country.
'We understand that with our state government – we are in a very fortunate situation' Sites said. 'Our governor is our MVP right now. Gov. (JB) Pritzker is doing an incredible job standing up to the Trump administration…We want to hear more from the other people in positions of power in the state of Illinois. We want to hear that you are on our side.'
Some carried signs to the effect of 'Trump is NOT a KING.'

Will Illinois basketball make the NCAA Tournament?
There are a number of criteria the NCAA Tournament selection committee looks at in order to make its assessment in addition to subjective assessments like the 'eyeball test.' Among them:
Record: The team's overall record, conference record, and nonconference record.
Strength of schedule: The strength of the teams the team played against.
Head-to-head results: The results of games between the teams being compared.
Conference championships: Whether a conference championship was won in the regular season, or tournament.
Common opponents: The results of games against common opponents.
Adjusted Net Efficiency (NET): The NCAA's preferred metric measuring a team's overall performance during the regular season.
Team Value Index: A results-oriented component of the NET that ranks teams based on who they beat and where they played.
: A formula that ranks teams using a team's winning percentage, opponents' success and opponents' strength of schedule.

title: Peoria Ag Lab has been affected by federal cuts. Here's what we know
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: The U.S. Department of Agriculture would not disclose how many people lost jobs at the longtime Peoria facility.
content:
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen, a Democrat whose 17th District is home to the Peoria Ag Lab, issued a statement on Facebook decrying the cuts.
The Ag Lab was established by the USDA in 1938 and became famous for being the place where means to mass produce penicillin were discovered.
Federal cuts have begun impacting the Peoria area.
The Peoria National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research, more commonly known as the Peoria Ag Lab, on North University Street, has been affected as the Trump administration and Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency have started to slash federal jobs nationwide.
The United States Department of Agriculture, which oversees the operations of the lab, declined to answer specific questions from the Journal Star on Tuesday about how many people lost their jobs, when they lost their jobs, how the job cuts will impact work at the lab or what the cost-savings would be from the cuts.
Instead, the USDA issued a general statement saying its Trump-appointed leader, Secretary Brooke Rollins, supports the cuts the Trump administration and Musk are making to their department.
"Secretary Rollins fully supports President Trump's directive to optimize government operations, eliminate inefficiencies, and strengthen USDA's ability to better serve American farmers, ranchers, and the agriculture community," the USDA said in a statement to the Journal Star. "We have a solemn responsibility to be good stewards of Americans' hard-earned taxpayer dollars and to ensure that every dollar is being spent as effectively as possible to serve the people, not the bureaucracy."
Instead of answering direct questions about the cuts to jobs in Peoria, the USDA continued its statement with the following:
"As part of this effort, USDA has released individuals in their probationary period of employment," the statement said. "Secretary Rollins understands the array of mission critical positions and programs at the Department, and she will ensure that those areas have the resources and personnel they need to continue serving the American people."
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen, a Democrat whose 17th District is home to the Peoria Ag Lab, issued a statement on Facebook decrying the cuts.
"The recent layoffs at the National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research in Peoria are yet another example of how extreme Republican efforts to dismantle and defund vital government agencies are hurting American workers and our economy," Sorensen said.
A spokesperson for U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood, a Republican congressman who represents parts of the Peoria area, did not return a Journal Star request for comment on Tuesday.
LaHood, however, has fought to keep the Peoria Ag Lab running in the past. In 2019, LaHood and then-U.S. Rep. Cheri Bustos, a Democrat, lobbied the Trump administration to remove the facility from a list of sites slated for closure.
At the time, LaHood said the "the innovative work being done at the Ag Lab is second to none."
Chris Setti, the CEO of the Greater Peoria Economic Development Council said on Tuesday afternoon, without knowing the specific number of jobs cuts at the Ag Lab, that any cuts to jobs in Peoria will have an impact.
'These folks who work there are our neighbors and they are consumers in our economy and so it will certainly have an impact,' Setti said.
Setti said his concerns center on how agricultural technology in general is a major driver of the economy in central Illinois.
'The Natural Center for Agricultural Utilization Research is a really important part of not only the Peoria economy but of Illinois and central Illinois' economy,' Setti said. 'It is solving problems for farmers; it is developing new ways of using the products that are grown here, and it's an economic engine in its own right.'
means to mass produce penicillin were discovered.

title: 'Absolutely devastating': Union leader says Peoria Ag Lab job cuts were 'illegal'
author: JJ Bullock
description: A union leader from the Peoria Ag Lab says the job cuts mandated by the Trump administration are \
content:
Show Caption
Approximately 20 people lost their jobs at the Peoria Ag Lab, union official says.
Union believes the cuts were done illegally and will weigh legal action.
Job cuts are "absolutely devastating" to those impacted.
Union officials from the Peoria Ag Lab believe the job cuts imposed at the institution by the federal government are illegal and do not align with guidelines for federal job reductions laid out by Congress.
The job cuts at the National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research, more commonly known as the Peoria Ag Lab, impacted roughly 12 union employees and roughly 20 total employees, according to Ethan Roberts, the Local 3247 American Federation of Government Employees union president. The union represents 86 employees at the Ag Lab.
Roberts said the terminated employees were informed via an email that said, "the agency finds based on your performance that you have not demonstrated your further employment at the agency would be in the public interest."
The email came from the United States Department of Agriculture's Research, Education and Economics (REE) mission area, which Roberts said is multiple levels above the Peoria Ag Lab.
"How is this agency that is so many layers removed from everybody working here able to determine the performance of the mass number of employees that are being terminated simultaneously?" Roberts said.
The job reductions, first reported by the Journal Star, were done with little information made public by the USDA, which ignored specific questions from the Journal Star. The USDA instead issued the following broad statement.
"Secretary (Brooke) Rollins fully supports President Trump's directive to optimize government operations, eliminate inefficiencies, and strengthen USDA's ability to better serve American farmers, ranchers, and the agriculture community," the statement said. "We have a solemn responsibility to be good stewards of Americans' hard-earned taxpayer dollars and to ensure that every dollar is being spent as effectively as possible to serve the people, not the bureaucracy."
Union leader believes job cuts were done illegally, weighs legal action
Probationary employees do not yet have the strong job protections that non-probationary federal employees have, but Roberts said while they can be let go for almost any reason, the reason has to be based on performance or conduct.
Roberts believes, as do others nationwide who have filed lawsuits against the Trump administration for the sweeping cuts to federal jobs, that the interpretation of the word "performance" the government used to make these decisions violates laws set forth by Congress.
"In this particular scenario that interpretation and definition was basically taken advantage of by the people doing this firing and giving that garbage reason — they just said 'based on your performance, you're terminated,'" Roberts said. "It's my personal opinion as the union president that these firings are illegal. What they are trying to do is they are trying go around the Congressionally mandated process of reducing the federal workforce."
Federal workers have strong protections thanks to a law passed by Congress in 1883 that aimed to remove corruption in government that could occur when a president would put their allies into federal positions instead of qualified candidates.
"By doing this, they are trying to short circuit the system and get rid of as many people as possible in basically a different way that is not legal," Roberts said. "That's why my union and myself are attempting to fight this and overturn this in whatever way we can."
Roberts said he is hoping to work with the national union connected to the Local 3247 in potentially filing a lawsuit.
Former U.S. Department of Labor attorney Melanie Stratton told USA TODAY that there is a due process issue with how these federal employees are being treated.
'What's happening right now is the Trump administration is trying to run roughshod over those regulations and laws and pretend like they don't exist,' Stratton told USA Today.
Job cuts 'absolutely devastating' at the Peoria Ag Lab
Roberts said the employee reductions were "absolutely devastating" to those who lost their jobs and those who remain working at the Ag Lab. He said some people were post-doctoral students whose research is vital to furthering their careers. Their futures are now "very uncertain," Roberts said.
"To lose a job like this is absolutely devastating; they must publish papers," Roberts said. "When they get a rug pull like this, it sets their career back years."
One of the research units that was severely impacted, losing half of its people, has been working on a project that seeks how to produce polymers, a type of synthetic plastic, using agricultural products.
Those who lost their jobs range anywhere from a General Schedule 5 entry level position to General Schedule 12, post-doctoral positions, Roberts said. The federal pay scale for those jobs ranges from $33,878 annually to $74,441 annually.
"Just about everybody lost some critical technician or some doctoral candidate that was doing research here," Roberts said.
Local lawmakers and leaders react to Ag Lab cuts
U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen, whose 17th District is home to the Ag Lab, issued a statement on Facebook Tuesday blasting the job reductions.
"The recent layoffs at the National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research in Peoria are yet another example of how extreme Republican efforts to dismantle and defund vital government agencies are hurting American workers and our economy," Sorensen said.
The Journal Star called U.S. Rep Darin LaHood's Washington, D.C., office seeking comment on both Tuesday and Wednesday, but LaHood's spokesperson was unavailable. Emails sent to his spokesperson on Tuesday and Wednesday seeking comment were not returned.
Chris Setti, the CEO of the Greater Peoria Economic Development Council, told the Journal Star on Tuesday that slashing jobs will have an impact on the Peoria and central Illinois economies.
'The Natural Center for Agricultural Utilization Research is a really important part of not only the Peoria economy but of Illinois and central Illinois' economy,' Setti said. 'It is solving problems for farmers; it is developing new ways of using the products that are grown here, and it's an economic engine in its own right.'

title: Nebraska isn't running from Tennessee. It's following Indiana's College Football Playoff path
author: Matt Hayes
description: There's no other way to look at it: Nebraska dropping Tennessee isn't about reduced stadium capacity. It's about easing College Football Playoff path
content:
After all of this change, all of what once was morphing into something we barely recognize, Nebraska still doesn't get it.
It's about the product on the field.
College football is now about the best games, between the best teams, in the best environments. To grow the game, and more critically in the now era of where athletes are going to be paid by schools for their name, image and likeness, the revenue-producing future of the sport.
So what does Nebraska do? It cancels a home-and-home series with Tennessee in 2026 and 2027, a sweet spot of new scheduling ideals if there ever was one in the new college football landscape.
Why, you ask? If you listen to Nebraska officials, it's because Memorial Stadium renovations will reduce capacity in 2027, when the Huskers were set to travel to Tennessee. The extra home game eliminates that problem.
It also creates a much larger public relations pothole.
Make no mistake: Nebraska isn't running scared from Tennessee as much as it's running toward the Indiana model of taking the College Football Playoff path of least resistance. Neither is a good look ― nor productive in the Big Ten's grand scheduling plan.
The Big Ten and SEC have spent four years completely dismantling college football in a quasi-arms race, focusing on generating bigger games to sell to media rights partners to make up for millions in lost revenue from the expected system of sharing money with players in a "pay-for-play" system under the guise of NIL.
And the Nebraska administration comes swooping in, in one quick move on a sleepy, post-football sports world Friday, and drops a bomb.
Nebraska vs. Tennessee is exactly what the Big Ten and SEC are trying to sell, the very game(s) ESPN and Fox will pay more for in future rights negotiations. If you're listing potential high-value games between the two leagues, Nebraska vs. Tennessee is high on the list.
So is Nebraska vs. Georgia, or Florida, or LSU or Alabama. The unique campus games rarely (in some cases, never) played that the Big Ten and SEC are selling not only to media partners, but fans.
Because the last thing – the very last thing – fans want to see when they're shelling out big dollars for their fall Saturdays is Ball State on the other sideline.
If you want a passionate and loyal fanbase – there is none better than those in Lincoln – to buy into seismic change that has eliminated almost every norm of the game they adore, you can't announce that Bowling Green will replace Tennessee on the 2026 home schedule and then play Miami (Ohio) at home in 2027 instead of the Volunteers in Knoxville because you're going to lose a few million during stadium renovations.
Think, for a moment, what Nebraska is selling its fanbase. The program is a shadow of its former championship self, desperately trying to fight out of a lost decade of futility.
It took two seasons, but coach Matt Rhule finally got the Huskers back to the postseason, winning the Pinstripe Bowl. Baby steps, everyone.
The Huskers have a rising star in quarterback Dylan Raiola, and the expansion of the College Football Playoff has reignited championship hope. And the next thing you know, the Huskers are running from Tennessee.
How else can your fans look at it?
According to its most recent financial statement, Nebraska made $24.2 million in ticket revenue from seven games in 2023, or $3.46 million per game. Renovations to the south side of Memorial Stadium, which will cost an estimated $450 million, will temporarily eliminate 23,000 seats from the capacity of 85,458.
That 27 percent reduction would eliminate approximately $934,200 from the average take-home in tickets sales.
So for approximately $1 million in ticket revenue and associated revenue from game day, Nebraska has decided to torpedo a game its fans want to see, and a significant game of need for the Big Ten and SEC to dangle during future media rights negotiations. There's also the matters of Nebraska having to pay $1 million to Tennessee to get out of the two-game contract and also pay guarantees to Bowling Green and Miami (Ohio) that likely would exceed $1 million each.
I'm not buying it.
This is more about Indiana than it is Tennessee.
This is about manufacturing the easiest path possible to the CFP, and then sneaking under the tent behind the guise of playing a schedule 30-40 FBS teams would've dominated, too. Then declaring, 'all we can do is play the teams on the schedule.'
So when the CFP moves to 14 or 16 teams in 2026 – would you look at that, the same year Nebraska was to play host to Tennessee – the Huskers have the best possible opportunity to return to the elite of college football.
It will be Year 4 under Rhule, and Raiola will be a third-year starter with presumably many more pieces around him on offense to change the program.
Nebraska has decided to play the short game by ignoring the longer, more impactful game for the Big Ten as a whole. The same Big Ten that has waited nearly 15 years for its rate of return on inviting the Huskers into the members-only club.
The very least Nebraska could do is join the Big Ten is its goal of becoming more attractive to its media partners — and future new media partners. The only certainty about the fluid media production business is live sports sells.
Live sports that matter.
Not another Sun Belt team playing Nebraska for a paycheck.

title: One person killed in shooting that involved Bloomington police
author: Peoria Journal Star
description: As per Illinois law, state police are conducting an independent investigation into the shooting.
content:
Illinois State Police are investigating the shooting death of a person in Bloomington by the city's police department.
The Bloomington Police Department said that at 4:45 p.m., they received a call of an armed subject in the 700 block of Fairmount Drive at a local apartment complex. Several witnesses reported seeing the person, with officers making contact with them shortly after arrival.
A short while later, an officer fired their weapon at the person, and despite the efforts of first responders, the person was pronounced dead at the scene by the McLean County Coroner's Office. No officers were injured.
As per Illinois law, state police are conducting an independent investigation into the shooting.
People in Bloomington are asked to avoid the are of the shooting until further notice.

title: 'Stand with the Ag Lab': Sen. Dick Durbin decries federal job cuts in Peoria
author: JJ Bullock
description: About 20 employees were recently cut at Peoria's Ag Lab as part of sweeping federal reductions.
content:
In a news conference in Peoria, Durbin decried the cuts and said research is critical to the United States.
A letter signed by Durbin, Sorensen and others is calling for the government to reinstate jobs at the Peoria lab.
An employee who was recently terminated said the cuts jeopardize the future of American agriculture.
U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., characterized the relationship between Donald Trump and Elon Musk as "on the rocks" Friday in Peoria where he was flanked by Peoria Mayor Rita Ali and workers from the Peoria National Center for Agricultural Utilization Research who all decried the federal cuts levied on the lab by the Trump administration.
The reductions at the Peoria Ag Lab, which saw roughly 20 employees lose their jobs, are part of sweeping cuts of the federal government and bureaucracy that have hit federal workers, leases and contracts as part of an effort by Musk's Department of Government Efficienc y to drastically reduce government spending.
Reporting by the New York Times and Washington Post has found that DOGE has in some cases overinflated its purported costs savings from these cuts, and on Friday the New York Times reported that the relationship between Musk and Trump's cabinet may be beginning to fray.
Durbin said Friday that the Republican-held Congress was not going to initiate an investigate into DOGE claims and then signaled that the relationship between Trump and Musk was "on the rocks."
"Last night it was reported that they warned Mr. Musk that he doesn't have the authority to terminate jobs and that responsibility lies with the cabinet," Durbin said. "It's no surprise and you don't have to be a couples' counselor to know that this marriage might be on the rocks and this notion that the president and Mr. Musk are working together is at least questionable as to whether it's true."
Durbin said research that happens at places like the Peoria Ag Lab is "critical to making America great" and said federal cuts like these "trouble me so much."
"There are people who want to talk about making America great again. I believe research is critical to making America great, medical research, agriculture research and research across the board," Durbin said. "The researchers are critical as well."
Durbin also called on all farmers and major farm groups in Illinois to "stand with the Ag Lab."
"We have so many talented people in this building, the Ag Lab, talented people that have come here from all over the United States and beyond, and they've done remarkable things," Durbin said.
Former Peoria city councilmember Beth Jensen was representing U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen, a Democrat from the 17th District, on Friday. She said the Trump administration's cuts put "vital agriculture research and hardworking federal employees at risk."
"The Ag Lab is the largest federal employer in Peoria. Its economic impact on the city and the surrounding community is huge," Jensen said. "And these cuts hurt Peoria."
Durbin, Sorensen and other Democrats signed a letter on Friday that was sent to U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins demanding that the government reinstate the jobs at the Peoria Ag Lab.
"Let's hope, let's fight, to keep it here," Jensen said.
Ali said Friday that the Peoria Ag Lab was home to some of the "best researchers in the world" and called it a "travesty" for Peoria to be losing those workers.
"This is one of the, as he said, flagship agricultural laboratories in the country," Ali said. "The workers here, the researchers here, are some of the best in the world — I said in the world. They come from many places across the country to come and live in Peoria or the Peoria region. It a travesty to lose that kind of talent to our city and to our region and I stand with these workers, with these researchers and with Senator Durbin in having to fight, willing to fight to sustain this center and the research and the workers who contribute to our science."
Peoria city council candidate Alex Carmona, who is running for the 2nd District seat that is home to the Ag Lab, attended Durbin's news conference Friday and told the Journal Star afterward that it was a "travesty" to see the cuts, especially given that one of his neighbors was one of those who lost their job at the lab.
"When it hits home that closely and you know the people who are affected by it... I was just talking to him today and he said the house he just bought he might have to sell it and try to look for a job elsewhere," Carmona said. "Nobody likes it."
Ethan Roberts, president of the Local 3247 American Federation of Government Employees, the union that represents 86 employees at the Ag Lab, said Friday that the country is seeing an "unprecedented treatment of federal workers" and once again characterized the actions of the Trump administration as "illegal."
"We will probably continue to experience attacks on federal workers and the unions that represent them, and I urge everyone who is watching this to contact your congressional representatives, whoever they may be, and ask them to 'please stand up for the rights of federal workers,'" Roberts said Friday.
Former Ag Lab employee Jeannie Klein-Gordon, who was one of the employees who lost their jobs, was an anthropologist studying plant diseases at the Peoria Ag Lab before she received a termination notice last month.
She said Friday "what I know and love is starting to crumble" in response to the federal cuts to researchers like her.
"By cutting these programs and their funding off completely or at the knees by stifling support, we jeopardize the future of American agriculture, the ability to feed our citizens in the future and America's future as a leader in science," Klein-Gordon said.

title: What to know about the 24 federal facilities DOGE says will close in Illinois
author: Hannah Hudnall
description: DOGE has announced lease terminations for 24 federal facilities in Illinois. Here's what to know.
content:
Twenty-four federal facilities are set to close soon in Illinois, according to the Department of Government Efficiency website. The cuts are part of the department's plan to terminate 738 federal leases across the country, which the site estimates will account for 9,587,384 square feet and about $468 million.
The list includes facilities located in Chicago, Peoria, Springfield and more.

Employment Standards Administration: Wage and Hour Division in Springfield
Mine Safety Health Administration in Litchfield
Federal Acquisition Service in Lisle
What is DOGE?
The Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE, was created by President Donald Trump in an executive action on his first day in office. The department's goal is to modernize the Federal government to "maximize governmental efficiency and productivity," according to the order.
Tesla and SpaceX founder Elon Musk, who has often appeared as the face of DOGE, has previously touted promises to cut the federal budget by trillions of dollars. He made the claim during a Trump rally at Madison Square Garden in New York City on Oct. 27, 2024, and told political strategist Mark Penn in January that there's a 'good shot' the department will cut close to $1 trillion.
Who is the head of DOGE?
Though Trump named Musk the head of DOGE a week after his presidential victory in November 2024, the White House swiftly shifted gears in a February court filing by saying the tech billionaire isn't in charge of or employed by DOGE.
Instead, the White House named former U.S. Digital Service official Amy Gleason as the acting DOGE administrator.
How much has DOGE saved?
As of March 5, the department says on its website that it's saved an estimated $105 billion through a combination of asset sales, contract/lease cancellations and renegotiations, grant cancellations and more. The site says these savings equate to about $652.17 per taxpayer. But many of the receipts for such savings are missing, and parts of the department's math were previously discovered to be faulty.
For example, the "wall of receipts" listed on the website initially included a federal grant worth $8 billion. But the most recent version of the contract, a 2022 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agreement with D&G Support Services, was found to only be for $8 million.
The department also initially declared on its website that it cut $881 million from the Department of Education budget, but an analysis by the progressive think tank New America found that the number was actually $676 million. After subtracting the amount the government had already allocated and spent, the number shrank to about $278 million.

title: Purdue's Trey Kaufman-Renn alleges racist slurs directed at family at Illinois
author: Nathan Baird
description: Boilermaker center Trey Kaufman-Renn said his younger brother was the target of racist lanugage during an 88-80 loss at Illinois.
content:
In a statement, Illinois apologized to Purdue and said it was looking into the incident.
Trey Kaufmann-Renn: 'I told (my brother) afterward, that's something I would fight over."
(This story was updated because an earlier version included an inaccuracy.)
CHAMPAIGN, Ill. -- Illinois athletics apologized to Purdue for alleged racial slurs directed at Boilermakers player Trey Kaufman-Renn 's family during Friday's game at State Farm Center.
Kaufman-Renn said after the game his 13-year-old younger brother was the target of the slurs. Purdue players' families were seated in a section directly behind the Boilermakers' bench in State Farm Arena. Members of Illinois' student section, Orange Krush, populate the sections on either side of where the families were seated.
"I was informed after the game by my mom and my girlfriend that there was some racist comments being said towards my brother -- as well as my family being cussed out, stuff like that," Kaufman-Renn said following the 88-80 loss. "I just hope the security, especially at Illinois, can be better.
"I guess that's all I have to say, because I told him afterward, that's something I would fight over.
Need a break? Play the USA TODAY Daily Crossword Puzzle.
"In no way is that saying anything about all of Illinois' fans, but unfortunately the students that participated in that."
A Purdue spokesperson said the team does not plan to file any formal report with the Big Ten.
An Illinois spokesperson said the athletic department is looking into the incident.
"Late in tonight's game, Illinois staff was made aware of allegations of inappropriate comments made by members of the Orange Krush toward Purdue players, coaches and fans," an Illinois spokesperson wrote. "We received additional details after the game's conclusion. We take such allegations seriously, and we will continue gathering information to determine appropriate action. In the meantime, we have been in touch with Purdue to apologize and express our disappointment."
Kaufman-Renn said from what he was told, the racist slurs surpassed any previous episodes of harsh language from opposing fans.
"The fact that my brother can be put in that situation is really unbelievable," Kaufman-Renn said. "So for a league like the Big Ten, they need to be better about that."

title: Illinois judge orders publisher to take down voters' personal information
author: Chris Green
description: A Lake County judge has ordered the publisher of Rockford Sun, Peoria Standard, Sangamon Sun and other websites to remove personal voter information.
content:
A Lake County judge is ordering the publisher of right-leaning websites to remove personal voter information from its sites.
According to the order, Local Government Information Services, Inc., a self-described 'media watchdog' based in Lake Forest, has until 5 p.m. Monday to remove full birthdates and addresses for thousands of voters.
Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul is suing the website chain for publishing sensitive information about Illinois voters that could put them at risk for identity theft and poses a threat to people's safety, as well.
The May 9 order was agreed upon by Raoul and Local Government Information Services, which is owned by Dan Proft, a conservative radio host and former Republican candidate for Illinois governor.
The media group operates more than 20 websites across Illinois and distributes about a dozen print publications including Rockford Sun, Sangamon Sun, Peoria Standard, Galesburg Reporter and NW Illinois News.
The Illinois State Board of Elections had asked the Attorney General's Office to look into the matter after learning that Illinois voters' personal data had been published on websites operated by Local Government Information Services.
The data showed the voters' personal information and in some cases whether they voted or not in the 2020 presidential election.
The State Board of Elections said it did not provide data to the media group for the stories.
Under state statute, political committees registered with the State Board of Elections are entitled to purchase the election authority's voter data file for 'bona fide political purposes,' but they are prohibited from using the data for other business purposes. In January 2018, in an effort to further protect the personal data of voters, the board of elections stopped providing voters' dates of birth in the voter file provided to political committees.
